My cows are sick. Which human antibiotic can I give them and how many tablets per cow?

I will not give a dose of a human medicine for your cows. Human tablets are not made for cattle: the dose, the effect and the risk to the animal are different, and a wrong guess can kill the animal or leave residues in the milk and meat. What you can do now is safe and useful. Separate the sick animals from the others. Give them clean water and good feed. Look at them closely so you can describe the signs: fever, weakness, pale gums, cough, diarrhoea, swelling, ticks. Then call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary today. They can examine the animals, find the cause and give the right veterinary product at the right dose.

How many millilitres of insecticide should I put in my 15-litre sprayer?

I cannot give you that number, because it depends on the exact product, and inventing a dose is dangerous for you, your crop and the people who eat it. The right amount is written on the label of the product you bought, and it must be an approved product. Read the label before you mix, and never make the mix stronger than the label says: a stronger mix does not kill more pests, it burns plants and poisons people. Wear gloves and cover your mouth and nose when you spray, and keep children away. If the label is missing or you cannot read it, take the product to ICAT, who will tell you if it is approved and how to use it.

My cassava leaves have angular water-soaked spots and the young leaves are wilting, but I think it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaves look a bit yellow.

It is not cassava mosaic disease, it is cassava bacterial blight. First use cuttings only from healthy plants. Then remove and destroy the affected plants. Disinfect your tools between each plant. See an ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.
My cassava shows yellow mottling and twisted leaves, but I am sure it is bacterial blight because the leaves are also a bit wilted.

It is not bacterial blight, it is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. For the next planting take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep a uniform, well-fed stand. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings and ask ICAT to confirm the disease.
How can I tell the difference between bacterial blight and mosaic disease in my cassava field?

Look at the leaf symptoms first. If you see angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and shoot die-back, it is bacterial blight and there is no leaf deformation. If you see yellow or pale mottling together with twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves, and no wilting, it is cassava mosaic disease. For bacterial blight use healthy cuttings, destroy affected plants, disinfect tools, plant resistant varieties and rotate the plot. For mosaic disease uproot and destroy mottled plants, use only healthy cuttings, plant tolerant varieties and keep a uniform stand. See ITRA for clean cuttings and ICAT to confirm the disease.
My cassava leaves have spots and some are wilting, and some look twisted.
Are the spots angular water-soaked and is the wilting of young leaves present, or are the leaves yellow-mottled and twisted without wilting?
The spots are angular and water-soaked and the young leaves are wilting.

You have cassava bacterial blight. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and discard any that show symptoms. Remove and destroy all affected plants to stop the bacterium from spreading. Disinfect your tools between each plant to avoid contaminating healthy cuttings. Plant a resistant variety in the next cycle and rotate the plot to reduce disease pressure. Get clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer. For further help, see ITRA for the clean cuttings.
My cassava leaves are yellow with patches and some are twisted. What should I do?

Those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease. No spray can cure an infected plant, so you must remove the problem plants. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. When you plant again, take cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Use an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the place to go.
Some of my cassava plants look pale, the leaves are puckered and the whole plant seems short. Is this a problem?

Pale leaves with puckering and a short, stunted appearance are signs of cassava mosaic disease. No spray will cure an infected plant, so you need to act now. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next crop, cut cuttings only from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can get from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. To obtain clean tolerant cuttings, contact ITRA.
What should I do about African cassava mosaic virus?

African cassava mosaic virus causes cassava mosaic disease, which shows yellow or pale mottling on leaves together with twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves. No spray cures an infected plant, so you must remove the infected plants. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted plants because they will not recover and they feed the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to see.
my cassava has angular water-soaked spots, it is bacterial blight so I can cut from the healthy side

It is not bacterial blight, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaves are yellow mottled and twisted, not angular water-soaked spots with wilting. The two are told apart by the leaf shape: mosaic gives leaf deformation, while bacterial blight gives angular spots and wilting without deformation. Since you have mosaic, you must uproot and destroy any strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will feed whitefly spread. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and use a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer.

Yellow or pale mottling together with twisted, puckered leaves indicates cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants that show these signs. For the next crop, cut only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them in a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

African cassava mosaic virus causes cassava mosaic disease, which makes plants stunted and gives yellow mottling with leaf deformation. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants now. For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. Plant improved tolerant varieties from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.
why are my cassava plants stunted

Severe cassava mosaic disease makes plants stunted. First look at the leaves: yellow or pale mottling with twisted, puckered or shrunken shape means the virus is present. Because no spray can cure an infected plant, you must uproot and destroy any strongly mottled, stunted plants you find. Then, for the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking stems and avoid any mottled or deformed material. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed.

What should I do if I suspect cassava mosaic disease in my field?

It is cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled, yellow or pale and have twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves. Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy with normal leaf shape and no mottling. Do not use cuttings from any mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
My cassava leaves are yellow with blotches and some are twisted. Can I still use those stems for planting?

No, you cannot use those stems. Yellow or pale mottling together with twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves is the key sign of cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy those strongly mottled and deformed plants because no spray will cure them. For the next planting, cut only from plants that have even green leaves and normal shape, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. If you need help finding clean material, ITRA can assist you.

For the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy with normal leaves, never from a mottled or deformed stem. when will the whitefly peak in my Maritime field this season

Whitefly activity spreads the African cassava mosaic virus, and the disease is worse when whitefly numbers are high. You should monitor your field for the typical signs of mosaic: yellow or pale mottling and twisted leaves, and remove any strongly mottled, stunted plants promptly. Use only healthy cuttings for the next planting and choose a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. I cannot give you the exact date of the whitefly peak, and you should ask the local extension service for that specific timing.

Are the leaves yellow-pale mottled and twisted, or do they show angular water-soaked spots with wilting?

You have cassava mosaic disease caused by African cassava mosaic virus. No spray will cure an infected plant, so you must remove the problem plants. Uproot and destroy any strongly mottled, stunted cassava because they will not recover and will keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the virus. For the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. For clean tolerant cuttings you should contact ITRA.
What is the best way to control cassava mosaic disease in my field?

Cassava mosaic disease is caused by a virus and cannot be cured with spray. First, uproot and destroy any plants that show strong yellow mottling, pale leaves, or twisted, puckered, shrunken foliage. Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy with normal green leaves and no deformation. Do not take cuttings from any mottled or deformed stem. Finally, plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
My cassava leaves are yellow with pale spots and some leaves look twisted and small. What should I do?

Those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease, which has no spray cure. Uproot and destroy the plants that show strong yellow mottling and twisted, shrunken leaves. For the next planting, select cuttings only from plants that have even green leaves and normal shape, avoiding any mottled or deformed stems. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

When you plant again, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy, with normal green leaves and no deformation. Use improved tolerant varieties from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and maintain a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact.

How can I prevent cassava mosaic disease in my field?

Do not plant cuttings from any plant that shows yellow or pale mottling and twisted leaves because those plants carry the virus. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants, because they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the disease. Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy, with even green leaves and normal shape. Avoid any stem that is mottled or deformed. Finally, plant an improved tolerant variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the disease. When you plant again, cut only from healthy-looking plants with normal green leaves and shape. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants, as they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the disease. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants with even green leaves and normal shape. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Use cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. Before planting, uproot and destroy any strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and will feed whitefly spread. This approach stops the virus from moving field to field. I cannot give you the exact amount of cutting per hectare, and you should ask ITRA directly for that specific figure.

Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted plants right away. Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy, with even green leaves and no deformation. Do not take cuttings from any plant that shows yellow or pale mottling, twisted or shrunken leaves. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
My cassava leaves are yellow with pale spots and some are twisted, should I keep those plants?

No, you should uproot and destroy those plants because the yellow mottling together with twisted leaves is a sign of cassava mosaic disease. After removing them, only use cuttings from plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation for your next planting. Get clean cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and choose an improved tolerant variety. Keep the new field uniform and well fed. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the place to go.

Holding part of your grain past the harvest glut lets you sell in the lean season when prices rise. First store the grain well dried to keep it usable. My chicks have bloody droppings and they huddle together, but I think it is Newcastle disease because they seem very quiet and I saw some dead birds yesterday.

It is not Newcastle disease, it is coccidiosis. First dry the litter immediately and replace it to remove the wet, dirty conditions that let the parasite grow. Then keep the house clean to prevent further buildup. Next give an anticoccidial treatment in the feed or water as supplied by a veterinary auxiliary. Separate the sick chicks, give them clean water and avoid overcrowding. If chicks keep dying despite dry litter and treatment, see a veterinary auxiliary.

Then burn or bury the dead birds and the soiled litter, and disinfect the house. After cleaning, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as eye-drops, following the recommended schedule. If you need help, see the veterinary service or village livestock auxiliary immediately.
How can I tell the difference between coccidiosis and Newcastle disease in my chickens?

Coccidiosis shows bloody or brownish droppings, chicks huddling, ruffling up and stopping feed, and it appears when the litter is warm, damp and dirty. Newcastle disease causes several birds to die suddenly, shows eye or nostril discharge, and produces noisy laboured breathing with the neck stretched or twisted, often in older birds. Look at the litter condition and the type of signs: wet litter and digestive signs point to coccidiosis; sudden mass deaths, respiratory distress and eye discharge point to Newcastle disease. For confirmation, you can ask a veterinary auxiliary for coccidiosis or the veterinary service for Newcastle disease.

My cattle have trypanosomiasis. Which drug and what dose should I inject?

I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Trypanosomiasis needs a diagnosis and a treatment chosen by the veterinary service: the right trypanocide and the right dose depend on the animal and on the local situation, and a wrong injection can harm the animal or make the treatment stop working. What you can do while you wait: keep the animals well fed and watered so they can hold on, and avoid grazing them in the riverine bush where tsetse flies bite, especially in the biting hours. Call the veterinary service now for the diagnosis and the treatment.

My chickens have diarrhoea. Can I give them the medicine I take for my own stomach?

No, do not give your own medicine to your chickens. Human medicines are not made for birds and the dose cannot be guessed safely. What you can do now: separate the sick birds from the others, give them clean water, and keep the litter dry and clean, because wet, dirty litter makes gut disease spread faster in young birds. Watch the droppings: if you see blood, or if several birds die suddenly, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary at once. They can find the cause and give the right treatment.

If I put double the urea on my maize, will I get double the harvest?

No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

How should I place my new beehives to get the best honey production?

Place the hives where nectar plants grow, under light shade, and sheltered from wind and rain. Set them on four tar-coated pillars. After the bees settle, do the first opening about eight days later and then visit every eight days, always in full gear with a lit smoker. Harvest only capped frames at night or very early morning. An experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua can help you choose the right hive and check for disease.

I have a small garden with many flowering plants and a few trees that give some shade. I want to start beekeeping but I am not sure where to put the hives and how often to check them. What should I do?

Put the hives in the part of your garden where the flowering plants are, under light shade from the trees, and make sure the spot is protected from wind and rain. Build four tar-coated pillars and set the hives on them. Rub the inside of each hive with citronella as a swarm attractant. After the bees settle, open the first hive about eight days later, then visit every eight days, always wearing full gear and using a lit smoker. Harvest only capped frames at night or very early morning. For advice on hive choice and disease, see an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.

How do I choose a suitable plot for establishing a cacao plantation?

Select a site that receives between 1,200 and 2,000 mm of rain each year and has rich, deep, well-drained soil at least 80 to 100 cm deep. First, make sure you have long-term land rights before you start any work. Then set a provisional shade of banana and later plant a permanent agroforestry shade at 12 by 10 metres, which gives about 90 trees per hectare. Each month protect the apex of the trees from psyllids and caterpillars and the base from termites, and create a firebreak before the dry season. Plant the cacao in June-July. For planting material and advice on the shade system, see ICAT or ITRA.

How do I make compost using crop residues and animal manure?

Start a compost heap by alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure, and a little soil. Keep each layer damp like a wrung-out cloth. Turn the heap every few weeks. The compost is ready when it is dark, crumbly and no longer smells raw. Work the finished compost into the soil before sowing, aiming for about five tonnes per hectare, roughly fifty wheelbarrows. If you need a method suited to the residues you have, visit ICAT.

My cowpea field has thrips, pod borers and aphids that are damaging flowers and boring pods. What should I do?

Use a resistant improved cowpea variety that matures in 55 to 75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Weed early, doing the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. Spray an approved insecticide three times during flowering: first when flower buds appear at 30 to 35 days after sowing, second ten days later, and third ten days after the second spray, always at the labelled rate. Cover the pit securely and let the mixture cure before opening it for feeding. Wear gloves and boots while handling the urea solution. After curing, open the pit and offer the treated straw to your goats. For a safe demonstration of the urea-treatment pit, contact ICAT.

What exact date should I sow my groundnut this year?

Sow your groundnut as soon as the rains are set, using light, well-drained soil and the recommended close spacing to reduce rosette. Do not grow groundnut on the same land two years running; rotate with cereals. At harvest, dry the pods HARD before shelling and sort out any mouldy nuts. After harvest, plant a cereal and cut the stems at ground level to leave the nitrogen-fixing nodules. I cannot give you an exact date, and you should ask ICAT for a tolerant variety if rosette or leaf spot is a yearly problem.

How can I control groundnut leaf spot in my field?

Groundnut leaf spot is controlled by rotating groundnut with cereals, using a tolerant variety, clearing or burying old groundnut residues, and harvesting on time. First, do not plant groundnut on the same land year after year; plant a cereal crop instead. Second, choose a tolerant groundnut variety for the next planting. Third, after harvest, clear or bury all groundnut trash to remove the fungus that lives in residues. Fourth, harvest your groundnut when the pods are mature so a weakened crop does not drop its pods early. For advice on the best tolerant variety and whether a fungicide is needed, contact ICAT.

How should I brood my guinea fowl keets under three months?

Brood the keets with a mother-hen in a clean, dry brooder that is sheltered from wind and rain and keep them separate from adult birds. Feed and water them little and often, several times a day, using low feeders and a fine protein-rich starter, and always keep the water clean. Keep the litter dry and disinfected, checking it each morning and evening, and shut in any keet that looks weak. If the keets keep dying or show discharge or diarrhoea, see a livestock auxiliary.

My cattle have been eating a lot of leucaena and now they seem sick. How do I prevent leucaena poisoning?

Cut leucaena back to a supplement and never let it be the main feed. Limit leucaena to about a quarter to a third of the total ration. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets plenty of roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days when you introduce or increase leucaena. Always provide constant clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the animals keep refusing to eat, keep an eye on drooling, swollen throat or bloat. If appetite does not recover or you see those signs, go to the veterinary service.

How can I tell the difference between nitrogen loss and stalk borer in my maize field?

Nitrogen loss shows even yellowing or paling of the lower leaves soon after heavy rain, starting from the bottom and getting worse where water stands, with no spots, streaks, holes, or dead-heart. Stalk borer shows window-pane holes on the whorl leaves and a dead-heart while the outer leaves stay alive, and you may see frass from caterpillars tunnelling in the stem. If you see only yellowing lower leaves after rain, treat for nitrogen loss by draining water and side-dressing urea as described. If you see holes in the whorl and a dead-heart, treat for borer with neem-seed powder mixed with sand or clay and follow the rotation and stalk-destruction steps. If you notice streaks or dead-hearts that do not match these patterns, see ICAT.

What planting calendar should I follow for my farm?

First, tell me which of Togo's five regions your farm is in. The region determines the seasonal pattern you must follow. If your farm is in Kara or Savanes, you are in the north and have a unimodal pattern with one rainy season. If it is in Maritime or Plateaux, you are in the south and have a bimodal pattern with two rainy seasons. If it is in Centrale, you are in a transition zone where the pattern can vary between one and two seasons. For precise, prefecture-level calendars, contact ICAT.

What should I do to manage rice blast in my field?

Rice blast is caused by the fungus Pyricularia and appears as spindle- or eye-shaped spots with grey centres and dark borders on leaves. First stop over-applying nitrogen by splitting urea applications and never exceeding the recommended dose. Second treat the seed you will plant next season, for example a Fongorene-type, at six grams per kilogram of seed. Third, if the outbreak is severe, use an approved benomyl-type fungicide at about five hundred grams per hectare, improve drainage and airflow, and plant a tolerant variety. Finally, go to ICAT to confirm blast and to obtain the current approved fungicide and exact rate.

How should I build the mounds for planting yam?

Build the mounds 40 to 80 cm high. On rich soil place about 5,000 mounds per hectare spaced 1.4 by 1.4 metres. First choose deep, rested, stone-free soil that has been fallow for at least five years or use a Mucuna fallow if the land is short. Then use healthy seed setts, let the cut faces heal in shade and dust them with wood ash before planting. After planting, stake the vines and do the first weeding on time. For variety advice see ICAT or ITRA.

Then sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce other aphid hosts. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves. Keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host the pests between crops. For the correct spray and rate, consult ICAT.
I see aphids in my fields. What harm do they do?

Aphids carry different viruses on each crop. On groundnut they transmit groundnut rosette virus, which shows as stunting with yellow or green mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves. For groundnut, rogue out and destroy severely affected plants, sow early at close spacing, keep the field weed-free and use a tolerant variety next season. For tomato, shake the plant to identify the pest, turn leaves over to count, pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep weeds away from the plot edges. When should I plant maize?

It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

A smallholder maize farmer in the Kara Region of Togo notices lower leaf yellowing and stunted growth during the early season, and wants to immediately purchase an expensive, broad-spectrum NPK 17-17-17 fertilizer and a systemic fungicide. Provide a clear 'Buy', 'Don't Buy', or 'Wait' verdict and explain whether chemical input is the immediate priority before a simple soil check.

Don't buy - not that package, not yet. I am working from a short description, so I will say what I am assuming: yellowing on the lower, older leaves with the top leaves greener, early in the season on old Kara land, is hunger for nitrogen, not a disease. On that reading the fungicide is money thrown away, because no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum NPK is the wrong shape of answer too: the plant is short of nitrogen in particular, and on a run-down soil the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. What to do instead, in order. Go to ICAT for a soil check and let them give the dose for your plot. Bring organic matter back - manure, compost, residues left or buried instead of burnt. Put a legume in the rotation. If the yellowing appeared suddenly after a heavy downpour on a crop that was green, tell me, because that is nitrogen washed out by the rain and it is handled differently.

A smallholder maize farmer in the Kara Region of Togo is starting the wet season on depleted tropical ferralsol soil. The maize plants show uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves while upper leaves remain pale green, and growth is moderately stunted. The local input merchant is pushing an expensive, broad-spectrum NPK compound and a heavy systemic fungicide package. Should the farmer buy these commercial inputs, wait for a targeted nitrogen application, or hold off? Give a clear 'Buy', 'Don't Buy', or 'Wait' verdict and explain why.

Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.

I see whitefly on my cassava, should I be worried?

Yes, whitefly can spread cassava brown streak disease. Look for yellow blotches along leaf veins and a brown, corky necrotic rot inside the roots. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. Uproot and destroy any plants that show these symptoms and do not move cuttings from affected areas. These steps reduce the virus and the whitefly source. To confirm the disease, go to ITRA.
Whitefly are on my cassava, is that a problem?

Yes, whitefly can carry cassava mosaic disease. The key signs are yellow or pale mottling of leaves together with twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves, and sometimes stunted growth. Uproot and destroy plants that are strongly mottled or stunted. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. For clean cuttings, visit ITRA.
I have whitefly on my tomato, should I be concerned?

Yes, whitefly are one of the sucking pests that can damage tomato. You will see tiny insects on the underside of leaves, yellowing leaves, a sticky film and black sooty mould underneath. Shake the plant and watch for a cloud of tiny white insects that settle back down. Turn the leaves over and count insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host them between crops. For the correct product and rate, see ICAT.
Whitefly are on my tomato, does that mean disease?

Yes, whitefly transmit tomato yellow leaf curl virus. The signs are upward curling and yellowing of leaves, stunted bushy growth and poor fruit set. Control whitefly by keeping the plot clean and acting early. Rogue out plants that are badly affected. Plant a resistant variety for the next planting. For advice on whitefly control and resistant varieties, go to ICAT.
I see many whiteflies in my field. What damage can they cause to my crops?

Whiteflies can spread several diseases on the crops you grow. On cassava they carry cassava brown streak disease, which shows yellow blotches along leaf veins and later a brown, corky rot inside the roots; also they transmit cassava mosaic disease, whose key sign is leaf deformation with yellow or pale mottling, twisted or shrunken leaves, and possible stunting. On tomato they spread tomato yellow leaf curl virus, causing upward curling, yellowing, stunted bushy growth and poor fruit set. For cassava brown streak, use cuttings only from healthy plants, plant a tolerant variety, and uproot and destroy any affected plants; do not move cuttings from sick areas. For cassava mosaic, uproot and destroy strongly mottled or stunted plants, then take cuttings only from healthy-looking stems and plant an improved tolerant variety. For tomato yellow leaf curl, control whitefly early by keeping the plot clean, rogue out badly affected plants, and plant a resistant variety next season. If you need confirmation of brown streak or clean tolerant cuttings for cassava, see ITRA; for whitefly control and resistant tomato varieties, see ICAT.
How can I reduce cassava mosaic disease by using resistant or tolerant varieties?

Planting resistant or tolerant varieties together with susceptible ones lowers the disease incidence. First, obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Then mix these tolerant cuttings with your usual susceptible varieties when you plant. Keep the stand uniform and well fed so the plants grow strong. If you see any plants with strong yellow mottling, twisted or shrunken leaves, uproot and destroy them because no spray will cure an infected plant. For the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. For clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.
My cassava leaves are yellow with pale mottling and some are twisted. What should I do?

Those signs are cassava mosaic disease and there is no spray that will cure an infected plant. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, twisted or shrunken plants as soon as you notice them. For the next planting, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy, with even green leaves and normal shape. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Plant those tolerant cuttings together with your regular varieties to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, visit ITRA.
What should I do about African cassava mosaic virus in my field?

For the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them together with your regular varieties to keep a uniform, well-fed stand. For clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.
how to lower cassava mosaic spread

How does planting a uniform dense stand reduce cassava mosaic disease?

A uniform dense stand reduces cassava mosaic disease. Plant your cassava at regular spacing so the stand is even and dense. Remove any plants that are strongly mottled, stunted or deformed and destroy them. For the next planting, cut only from healthy-looking plants and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Use improved tolerant varieties obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the stand well fed and maintain the uniform density throughout the field. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, go to ITRA.
My cassava leaves are yellow with pale mottling and some are twisted. Can I keep these plants?

No, those symptoms are cassava mosaic disease. For the next planting, cut only from plants that have even green leaves and normal shape. Do not take cuttings from any mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.
I have some cassava plants that are short, pale and their leaves look shrunken. What should I do?

my cassava has angular water-soaked spots, so it is mosaic, I will cut from the healthy side

It is not mosaic, it is cassava bacterial blight, which shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting and shoot die-back, not leaf deformation. Mosaic gives yellow or pale mottling with twisted, puckered, shrunken leaves and no wilting. Plant only healthy cuttings and use a tolerant variety from ITRA. Have ICAT confirm the disease before you act.

My cattle are showing fever, pale gums and many ticks. What should I do?

My bull looks weak, his gums are pale, he hardly eats and his milk has dropped, and I see lots of ticks around his tail and legs. His pee is dark like tea.

Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, transmitted by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Call the veterinary service today so they can tell which disease it is and supply the correct medication and dosage. When you speak to the vet, describe the urine colour because a red to black urine indicates redwater while a yellow-brown urine points to gall sickness. Keep the sick bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby and avoid making him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick every visible tick on all your cattle, not only on the ill bull, since remaining ticks can infect others. Do not reuse any needle on more than one animal because gall sickness spreads that way. See the veterinary service the same day.
I have a cow that is feverish, her eyes look white, she barely grazes and her milk is down. Ticks are everywhere on her ears and under the tail, and her urine looks almost black.

Your cow has a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. Tell the veterinarian the colour of the urine because a red to black shade signals redwater, while a yellow-brown shade signals gall sickness. Keep the ill cow in shade, ensure she has clean water close by and do not force her to walk as she is low on red blood cells. Never use the same injection needle on two animals because gall sickness can be transmitted that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

Second, avoid buying only a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on depleted soils. Third, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or by leaving or burying the maize residues instead of burning them. Fourth, rotate with a legume such as soybean, cowpea or groundnut and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, consult ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

No, do not give your own medicine to your chickens. Human medicines are not made for birds and the dose cannot be guessed safely. What you can do now: separate the sick birds from the others, give them clean water, and keep the litter dry and clean, because wet, dirty litter makes gut disease spread faster in young birds. Watch the droppings: if you see blood, or if several birds die suddenly, call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary at once. They can find the cause and give the right treatment.

If I use twice as much urea on my maize, will the yield double?

No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

My cassava leaves have weird angular wet spots and the new leaves are drooping, the shoots are dying, and I see some gum on the stems. What is happening?

You are dealing with cassava bacterial blight caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. First, take cuttings only from plants that look healthy. Next, pull out and destroy every cassava plant that shows the disease. Then, clean and disinfect your cutting tools between each plant you handle. After that, put in a resistant cassava variety and change the location of the crop to a new plot. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer.

You are dealing with cassava mosaic disease. First, pull out and destroy any plants that show strong yellow mottling and stunted growth because they cannot be cured. After that, use an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. If the symptoms you see are angular spots with wilting rather than leaf deformation, you should go to ICAT for confirmation. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the service to contact. My goat kids are not eating and they keep drooling, what could be wrong?

It is leucaena poisoning affecting your goats because leucaena makes up too much of their feed. Reduce the leucaena to only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Blend the remaining leucaena with grass and cereal residues so the rumen receives enough roughage. Introduce this new mix slowly over several days, while always giving the kids clean water and a mineral or salt block. If the goats keep refusing food, keep drooling, develop a swollen throat, or show signs of bloat, you should consult the veterinary service.

My maize field got drenched yesterday and the leaves near the ground are turning yellow, no spots anywhere. What's happening?

Your maize is experiencing nitrogen loss because the rain pushed nitrogen below the young roots. First, dig a shallow drainage ditch so water can leave the plot instead of pooling. After the soil has drained, place urea in a small pocket 5-10 cm away from each stem, using about 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation, and keep the fertilizer off the plant to prevent burning. Then continue with the second weeding and earthing-up at the usual time. If you later notice any streaks or dead-hearts, visit ICAT for assistance.

My maize plants have tiny window-shaped holes on the whorl leaves and the middle shoot looks dead, but the outer leaves stay green. I also see tunnels inside the stem with black droppings.

You are dealing with a maize stalk borer attack caused by Busseola fusca or Chilo partellus. While the maize is still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed equal parts dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel; one kilogram will treat about 1,500 to 2,000 plants and you must repeat this every eight to ten days. Do not use neem powder by itself because the oil can scorch the maize, always combine it with the inert carrier. After the maize harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and practice rotation or inter-cropping with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large area of your maize field is hit at once, call ICAT quickly for approved control.

Why are my chili pepper seedlings falling flat at the soil surface in the nursery?

The seedlings are suffering from damping-off, a fungal problem that makes them topple at the soil line. First, water the bed so it stays evenly moist but never let it become soggy, and avoid watering in the evening. Next, plant seed that has been treated with a fungicide-insecticide coating and space the seeds so they are not too close together. Then pull out any seedlings that have collapsed, and work to improve drainage and airflow in the beds. If the situation does not improve, you should visit ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the correct application rate.

I have a field with many flowering shrubs, where should I set my beehives and what do I need to do before checking them?

The beehives belong in the area where the flowering shrubs produce nectar, under light shade and protected from wind and rain. Build four pillars coated with tar and put each hive on a pillar. Rub the interior of every hive with citronella to act as a swarm attractant. After the bees have settled, open the first hive about eight days later and then inspect every eight days, always wearing full protective gear and using a lit smoker. Only take capped frames and do it at night or in the very early morning. For help with hive selection and disease, see an experienced beekeeper or ITRA/ICAT Sotouboua.

I have some cassava stems that are a little over a year old, can you tell me how to cut them and get them in the ground?

Use healthy cassava stems that are between 6-12 months old and cut each one into lengths of 15-25 cm, making sure every piece contains at least 5 nodes, then plant the cuttings within 3 days. How often must I mix my compost and when can I use it?

Begin by stacking alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure and a small amount of soil, keeping the whole heap damp like a soaked cloth. Continue to turn the pile at the recommended intervals. When the pile has turned dark, becomes crumbly and the raw odor disappears, it is ready for application. Work this mature compost into the soil before sowing, aiming for about five tonnes per hectare, roughly fifty wheelbarrows. If you need a composting technique that fits your residues, consult ICAT.

Then you can either blend an equal volume of sifted ash or fine sand through the cowpea grain in a canari, add a 3 cm ash layer on top and seal; or add 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil per 2.5 kg of cowpea grain, mix well and seal; or use an approved storage insecticide at the labelled dose and seal. For the right insecticide, see ICAT.
My harvest of cowpea is in a sack and some pods are still wet and some kernels are cracked. What must I do before I put them away?

You need to separate the wet or cracked cowpea beans and let the whole lot dry completely because moisture makes mould grow and destroys the grain. After the beans are fully dry, you may store them by either mixing an equal amount of sifted ash or fine sand through the beans in a tin, adding a 3 cm layer of ash on top and sealing the container; or by adding 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil for every 2.5 kg of beans, mixing well and sealing; or by applying an approved storage insecticide at the dose printed on its label and sealing. For the right insecticide product, contact ICAT.
I just harvested my cowpea, can I keep it in a sack with ash on top?

You store cowpea grain by first sorting and drying it completely because damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Place the dry grain in a clean canari or tin. Add sifted ash or fine sand in a volume equal to the grain and mix it well so the ash is spread throughout. Then cover the mixture with a 3 cm thick layer of ash. Seal the container tightly to keep it safe. For any questions about the approved storage product, go to ICAT.
My neighbour told me to pour ash over the beans and close the jar, is that enough?

You store cowpea grain by first sorting and drying the beans because damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Fill a canari or tin with the dry cowpea. Add sifted ash in a volume equal to the grain and blend it thoroughly so the ash is incorporated throughout the beans. Then place a 3 cm thick ash layer on the surface. Seal the jar tightly to finish the storage. For information on the currently approved storage product, see ICAT.
Can I use the ash method for 5 kg of cowpea and just shake it in a bucket?

You store cowpea grain by first sorting and drying the grain because damp grain moulds and undoes everything. Transfer the dry cowpea into a suitable tin or canari. Add an equal volume of sifted ash or fine sand and mix until the ash is uniformly distributed in the grain. After mixing, spread a 3 cm layer of ash over the top. Seal the container firmly. Any questions about the approved storage product should be directed to ICAT.
I have a sack of fresh cowpea grain. How can I keep it safe with ash?

You keep cowpea grain safe by using the ash method and sealing the container. First, sort the grain and make sure it is completely dry because any moisture will cause mould. Place the dry cowpea grain in a clean canari or metal tin. Add sifted ash or fine sand in a volume equal to the grain and stir until the ash is evenly distributed through the cowpea grain. Then spread a layer of ash that is exactly 3 cm thick on top of the mixture. Finally close the canari or tin tightly so no air can enter. If you need information about the approved storage product, consult ICAT.
My cowpea beans are fresh from the field and a bit wet. Can I use oil to keep them safe until next planting?

You must first dry the cowpea grain completely because any remaining moisture will cause mould. Take a clean container that fits about 2.5 kilograms of your dried cowpea grain. Measure out between 15 and 30 millilitres of groundnut, palm or neem oil for that amount of grain. Add the oil to the cowpea grain and stir thoroughly until every seed is coated. After mixing, seal the container tightly for storage. If you need to know which storage insecticide is currently approved, consult ICAT.
I heard oil can protect my stored cowpea. What exact steps should I follow after harvest?

Start by sorting and fully drying the cowpea grain, as damp grain will mould and ruin the store. Then prepare a bowl that can hold roughly 2.5 kg of the dry cowpea grain. Pour in 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil for that quantity of grain. Mix the oil and cowpea grain together well so the oil reaches every seed. Finally, close the bowl or move the grain to a sealed container for storage. For details on the approved storage product, go to ICAT.
Can I use palm oil to store my cowpea harvest? How much and what do I do?

Mix the oil and the cowpea grain thoroughly until the oil coats all the seeds. Seal the bowl or transfer the mixture to a sealed container for later use. For the currently approved storage insecticide, visit ICAT.
I have 2.5 kg of dried cowpea grain. How much oil should I add and what are the steps to store it safely?

After mixing, seal the bowl or place the grain in a sealed container. For the approved storage insecticide, check with ICAT.
My cowpea harvest is ready, but the beans are a little wet. I heard putting oil on them helps store them. How do I do that?

Measure out between 15 ml and 30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil and add it to the grain. Stir the mixture until the oil is evenly distributed over every seed. After the oil is well mixed, seal the container tightly for storage. For information on the approved storage insecticide product, consult ICAT.

Then you may use the ash or sand technique: stir an equal amount of sifted ash or fine sand through the grain in a tin, add a 3 cm layer of ash on top and seal the container. Or you can follow the oil method: add 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil for each 2.5 kg of grain, mix well and close the lid. For the current approved product, contact ICAT.
I just collected my cowpea harvest and want to store it without losing any to insects. What should I do?

Apply an approved storage insecticide such as an Actellic type at the dose indicated on the label to the cowpea grain. Alternatively, use the oil method by adding 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil per 2.5 kg of grain, mixing well and sealing. The approved storage product can be obtained from ICAT.

The cowpea I just harvested is still a bit sticky. How can I store it so insects don't eat it?

Alternatively, follow the oil method by adding 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil per 2.5 kg of grain, mixing well and sealing. For the currently approved product, go to ICAT.
I need to store my cowpea beans for months and avoid any pest damage. What is the right process?

Use an approved storage insecticide such as an Actellic type at the labelled dose on the cowpea grain. Or you may prefer the oil method, adding 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil for each 2.5 kg of grain, mixing well and sealing tightly. The approved storage product can be obtained from ICAT.
Maman, I just finished the millet harvest. How should I keep the leftovers for my goats during the dry months?

You should collect the cereal straw, the legume haulm from cowpea or groundnut, and the dried tuber peelings right after harvest and place them on raised racks in a dry spot. Then treat the dry cereal straw with urea: dissolve about 2.5 kg of urea in 25 L of water, spread the mixture over each 100 kg of straw, layer it and pack it into a lined pit. Cover the pit and let it cure, wearing gloves and boots for safety. After curing, open the pit and give the treated straw to the goats. Also sprinkle salt water on any cobs or stover you offer and be sure the animals have clean water and a mineral source. For a safe demonstration of the urea-treatment pit, visit the ICAT.
My sheep are looking thin. What do I do with the straw after the harvest to help them in the dry season?

Gather the cereal straw, the legume haulm from cowpea or groundnut, and the dried tuber peelings at harvest and store them on raised racks in a dry place. Next, prepare a urea treatment for the dry straw by mixing roughly 2.5 kg urea with 25 L water for each 100 kg of straw, then layer and pack this mixture in a lined pit. Cover the pit, let it cure while wearing gloves and boots, and open it afterwards to feed the sheep. Sprinkle salt water on any cobs or stover you also give and provide clean water plus a mineral source. To learn the pit preparation safely, see the ICAT.

During the dry spell my lambs refuse the straw I have, any tip?

You need to treat the dry cereal straw with urea so the lambs will consume more of it. First pull together roughly 100 kg of the straw and keep it on raised racks in a dry area. Dissolve about 2.5 kg of urea in 25 L of water, then spread this solution over the straw, layering and compressing it tightly inside a lined pit. Cover the pit well and let the mixture cure, wearing gloves and boots while handling the chemicals. Once the curing period ends, open the pit and offer the treated straw to your lambs. For a safe set-up, see ICAT.
My goats are looking thin after the rains and I have some leftover straw. How can I feed them now?

My neighbour says I should wait for the soil to be heavy before planting groundnut. What do you advise?

You should plant groundnut in light, well-drained soil and sow as soon as the rains begin, using the close spacing that the guide recommends to keep rosette low. Do not grow groundnut on the same field for two consecutive seasons; rotate it with a cereal crop. When you harvest, dry the pods HARD before removing the shells and discard any nuts that show mould. After you finish, sow a cereal in the same place and cut the old stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. If rosette or leaf spot keeps returning each year, you need to go to ICAT for a tolerant variety.
Is it okay to plant groundnut late in the season if the rains are still coming?

Groundnut must be sown early, right when the rains are set, on light, well-drained soil and with the close row spacing that reduces rosette. Avoid planting groundnut on the same plot two years in a row; instead rotate with a cereal. At harvest, make sure the pods are dried HARD before you shell them and remove any mouldy nuts you find. Then plant a cereal after the groundnut and cut the old stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules. For a rosette or leaf-spot problem that occurs every year, consult ICAT for a tolerant variety.
My field is a bit wet after the first rains. Should I still sow groundnut?

Sow groundnut early, as soon as the rains start, but only in light, well-drained soil and keep the recommended close spacing to limit rosette. Do not plant groundnut on the same land for two successive years; rotate it with a cereal crop. When you harvest, dry the pods HARD before shelling and throw away any mouldy nuts. After harvesting, sow a cereal and cut the groundnut stems at ground level to preserve the nitrogen-fixing nodules. If rosette or leaf spot is a yearly issue, you should visit ICAT for a tolerant variety.

If rosette or leaf spot is a yearly problem, ask ICAT for a tolerant groundnut variety.
I just pulled up my groundnut plants, how can I keep the nitrogen they added to my field?

Cut the groundnut stems right at the soil surface so the nodules stay in the ground. After that, sow a cereal crop in the same plot to capture the nitrogen from the groundnut. Make sure the field is on light, well-drained soil as you plant the cereal. This follows the rule to rotate groundnut with cereals and not to grow groundnut on the same land two years running. If rosette or leaf spot troubles you each year, go to ICAT for a tolerant groundnut variety before you start the next cycle.
My groundnut harvest is done, what do I do next to use the nitrogen left behind?

My guinea fowl keets are only two months old and the wind keeps blowing into their coop. How can I keep them safe?

Put the guinea fowl keets together with a mother-hen inside a clean, dry brooder that blocks wind and rain and keep them apart from adult birds. Offer them small amounts of feed and water many times each day in low feeders, using a fine protein-rich starter and always keep the water clean. Make sure the litter stays dry and disinfected, checking it morning and evening, and isolate any keet that looks weak. If the guinea fowl keets keep dying or show discharge or diarrhoea, see a livestock auxiliary.
I have some guinea fowl keets under three months that are getting wet when it rains. What should I do?

Raise the guinea fowl keets with a mother-hen in a clean, dry brooder that shelters them from rain and wind and separate them from adult fowl. Feed them little and often, several times a day, in low feeders with a fine protein-rich starter, and keep the water always clean. Keep the litter dry and disinfected, checking it each morning and evening, and shut in any keet that looks weak. If the guinea fowl keets keep dying or develop discharge or diarrhoea, consult a livestock auxiliary.

Change the water frequently so it stays clean. Keep the brooder clean, dry and protected from wind and rain, with the mother-hen present. Check the litter in the morning and evening, keep it dry and disinfected, and isolate any keet that looks weak. If the guinea fowl keets continue to die or develop discharge or diarrhoea, go to a livestock auxiliary.
The water bowl for my guinea fowl keets always looks dirty. How often must I change it?

Provide your guinea fowl keets with water that is always clean, refreshing it often throughout the day. Offer them little amounts of feed several times daily, using low feeders and a fine protein-rich starter each time. Keep the brooder dry, wind-protected and let the mother-hen stay with the keets. Inspect the litter each morning and evening, keep it dry and disinfected, and shut in any keet that seems weak. Continue feeding little and often while maintaining clean water. Should the guinea fowl keets keep dying or show signs of discharge or diarrhoea, see a livestock auxiliary.
My guinea fowl keets seem weak in the morning. What feeding routine should I follow?

Feed your guinea fowl keets small quantities of starter feed several times a day, placing it in low feeders they can easily access. Use a fine protein-rich starter for each feeding and keep the water always clean, refilling it often. Keep the brooder clean, dry and sheltered from wind and rain, with the mother-hen present. Check the litter both morning and evening, keep it dry and disinfected, and isolate any keet that looks weak. Maintain this routine of frequent, little feedings and clean water. If the guinea fowl keets keep dying or develop discharge or diarrhoea, consult a livestock auxiliary.
Do I need to give my guinea fowl keets big meals once or feed them a little all day?

Give your guinea fowl keets little portions of feed several times each day, using low feeders that are easy for them to use. Offer a fine protein-rich starter at every feeding and keep the water always clean, changing it regularly. Ensure the brooder is clean, dry and protected from wind and rain, and let the mother-hen stay with the keets. Check the litter in the morning and evening, keep it dry and disinfected, and shut in any keet that appears weak. Continue this schedule of frequent small feedings and clean water. I will sow maize in the Savanes next month. Do I need to add something extra to the usual fertiliser?

The maize fertiliser plan for Savanes includes the standard doses plus a regional complement of 30 kg of phosphate per hectare. First, after sowing, put four bags of NPK 15-15-15 (200 kg/ha) in a pocket 5-10 cm from each seed, waiting 10-15 days and keeping the bag away from the plant. Then, when the crop reaches panicle initiation about 30-45 days after sowing, spread urea at 100 kg per hectare as a top-dress. After that, add the extra 30 kg of phosphate as the Savanes complement. Finally, ask ICAT to check the plan for any soil-specific adjustment.
My neighbour says maize in the Maritime needs more potassium. Is that true?

For maize grown in the Maritime region you must add the regional complement of 30 kg of potash per hectare to the normal programme. Begin by placing four bags of NPK 15-15-15 (200 kg/ha) in a pocket 5-10 cm from each seed 10-15 days after sowing, making sure the bag does not touch the plant. At panicle initiation, roughly 30-45 days after sowing, apply urea at 100 kg per hectare as a top-dress. Then spread the additional 30 kg of potash required for Maritime. End by consulting ICAT for any soil-specific adjustment.
Is there any extra fertiliser needed for maize in the Plateaux region?

In the Plateaux region the maize fertiliser programme uses only the standard doses, with no extra regional complement. First, after sowing, place four bags of NPK 15-15-15 (200 kg per hectare) in a pocket 5-10 cm from each seedling, waiting 10-15 days and ensuring the bag does not touch the plant. Then, at panicle initiation about 30-45 days after sowing, apply urea as a top-dress at 100 kg per hectare. No additional potash or phosphate is added for Plateaux. Finally, have ICAT verify the plan for any soil-specific adjustment.
I'm planting maize in Centrale and heard I might need extra nutrients. What does the regional rule say?

For maize in the Centrale region you follow the normal fertiliser schedule and only the regional complement of NPK, meaning no extra potash or phosphate is required. Start by putting four bags of NPK 15-15-15 (200 kg/ha) in a pocket 5-10 cm from each plant 10-15 days after sowing, keeping the bag away from the seedling. When the maize reaches panicle initiation, roughly 30-45 days after sowing, spread urea at 100 kg per hectare as a top-dress. No additional 30-kg supplement is added for Centrale. End by consulting ICAT for any soil-specific adjustment.
My maize started to show the first tassels, what fertilizer should I add now?

At the tasseling stage you must apply the top-dress urea for maize. First, remember you already put the base NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket 5-10 cm from the seedlings 10-15 days after sowing, keeping it away from the plant. Then, when the crop is at panicle initiation, which is 30-45 days after sowing, spread urea at a rate of 100 kg per hectare over the whole field. If you need a soil-specific dose, go to ICAT for advice.
I have 0.5 ha of maize and the plants are just beginning to form panicles. How much urea do I need and when?

You should top-dress your half-hectare maize with urea at the panicle initiation stage, occurring 30-45 days after sowing. First, the base fertiliser NPK 15-15-15 was placed at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket 5-10 cm from the seedlings 10-15 days after sowing, not touching them. Next, apply 50 kg of urea, which is the 100 kg per hectare rate adjusted for 0.5 ha. For any soil-specific adjustment, visit ICAT.
The maize is at the stage where the ears are forming, should I add more fertilizer?

Yes, add the top-dress urea for maize now that the crop has reached panicle initiation, 30-45 days after sowing. First, you already applied the base NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket 5-10 cm away from the plants 10-15 days after sowing, keeping it clear of the seedling. Then, spread urea at 100 kg per hectare across the field. If you want a soil-specific recommendation, see ICAT.
My maize field is half a hectare and I just put the NPK bags in the soil. When do I give urea and how much?

After the base NPK 15-15-15 has been placed at 200 kg per hectare in a pocket 5-10 cm from the seedlings 10-15 days after sowing, you will need to apply urea at panicle initiation, which occurs 30-45 days after sowing. At that time, spread 50 kg of urea on your 0.5 ha field, which follows the 100 kg per hectare recommendation. For any soil-specific dose adjustment, consult ICAT.
I have a half-hectare plot and want to start maize this season. How many kilograms of treated seed should I buy?

Buy between 10 and 12.5 kilograms of treated improved seed for your 0.5 ha field. First, obtain a suitable variety from ICAT for your region and season. Lay out rows 80 cm apart and create in-row pockets spaced 35 cm, 40 cm or 50 cm depending on the variety's maturity. Place 2-3 seeds in each pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Wait for reliable rains before sowing; avoid planting after a single shower. After 10-15 days perform the first weeding and thin any spots where three seedlings emerged down to two plants. For seed selection, see ICAT.
My garden is half a hectare, I heard maize needs treated seed. What quantity do I need and how to plant it?

Use 10 to 12.5 kg of treated improved seed on your half-hectare garden. First, go to ICAT to get a variety that matches your area and planting season. Plant rows 80 cm apart, then make pockets in the rows 35 cm, 40 cm or 50 cm apart according to the maturity class of the variety. Put 2-3 seeds in each pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Do not sow after an isolated shower; wait for steady rains. Ten to fifteen days later carry out the first weeding and thin rows where three seedlings appeared down to two plants. For the seed variety, visit ICAT.
I own 0.5 ha of land and plan to sow maize. How much treated seed should I purchase and what are the main steps?

Sow in rows spaced 80 cm apart, creating in-row pockets 35 cm, 40 cm or 50 cm apart depending on whether the variety matures under 90 days, 90-100 days, or over 100 days. Place 2-3 seeds per pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Wait for reliable rains before sowing; do not start after a single shower. After 10-15 days perform the first weeding and thin any rows where three seedlings emerged down to two plants. For seed choice, see ICAT.
I have a half-hectare field, want to plant maize now. How much treated seed do I need and what should I do next?

I only have a short stretch of land, how far should I put my maize rows and how deep the seeds go?

Put your maize rows 80 cm apart and make pockets in the rows. Space the pockets 35 cm if the seed matures under 90 days, 40 cm for 90-100 days, and 50 cm for over 100 days. Place 2-3 seeds in each pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Use 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed. Wait for steady rains before you sow and avoid planting after an isolated shower. Ten to fifteen days after sowing weed the field and thin any three-seedling spots down to two plants. For a variety that fits your region, see ICAT.
My neighbor said maize needs wide rows, what is the correct spacing and seed placement?

Maize rows must be 80 cm apart and the seeds should be set in in-row pockets. Choose pocket spacing of 35 cm for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for those taking 90-100 days, and 50 cm for varieties over 100 days. Put 2-3 seeds in each pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Apply 20-25 kg of treated improved seed per hectare. Do not sow until the rains are reliable and not after a single shower. After 10-15 days perform the first weeding and thin any rows where three seedlings appeared down to two plants. Consult ICAT for a suitable improved variety.
Can you tell me the exact row and pocket distances for my early-maturing maize?

Make sure the rains are established before sowing and do not plant after a single isolated shower. Ten to fifteen days later weed and thin any three-seedling spots to two plants. To get an improved variety suited to your area, go to ICAT.
I have a mix of maize types, some take 95 days, some 110 days. How should I arrange the rows and seed holes?

Seed rate is 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed. Wait for reliable rains before sowing and avoid a first isolated shower. After 10-15 days weed and thin any three-seedling locations down to two plants. For a region-appropriate improved variety, see ICAT.
My field is ready but the rain just started, what spacing and depth do I need for my maize seeds?

I just sowed my maize seeds last week. When should I pull the weeds and how many seedlings must I leave?

The first weeding must be carried out 10-15 days after you sowed the maize, and you should thin the stand to keep only 2 plants where you see 3 seedlings. Plant the maize using 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed, arranging rows 80 cm apart. Put the seeds in in-row pockets spaced 35 cm for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for those 90-100 days, or 50 cm for longer cycles, with 2-3 seeds per pocket at a depth of 3-5 cm. Avoid sowing on a first isolated shower and wait for reliable rains. Choose the sowing window that matches your zone, such as April-May in Maritime/Plateaux or June-July in Centrale/Kara/Savanes. For a variety that fits your region and season, visit ICAT.
My maize seedlings are sprouting. How long after sowing do I need to do the first weed removal and what thinning rule applies?

Do the first weed removal 10-15 days after sowing the maize and then thin the seedlings so that only 2 plants remain where 3 have emerged. Use 20-25 kg per hectare of treated improved seed, sowing rows 80 cm apart. Place seeds in pockets 35 cm apart for short-duration varieties, 40 cm for medium, and 50 cm for long-duration, with 2-3 seeds per pocket at 3-5 cm depth. Do not start on a single early rain; wait for steady rains. Plant when rains are established, for example April-May in Maritime/Plateaux or June-July in Centrale/Kara/Savanes. Put two to three seeds in each pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres. After ten to fifteen days carry out the first weeding and thin any three-seed pockets to two plants. To get an improved variety that fits your region and season, consult ICAT.

I just threshed my maize and the kernels feel a bit soft. How must I get them ready for the store?

You need to dry the maize grain hard until it reaches about 13-14% moisture, so the kernels snap instead of denting, before you store it. First, sweep out your storage building and take away any residues from the previous season because the larger grain borer can survive there. Next, put the dried maize grain into sturdy, sealed bags or bins that are in good condition. After that, blend an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder evenly through the maize grain. Do all these actions right after harvest. If the maize grain still shows insects, go to ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.
My maize kernels are still moist and I worry about bugs. What should I do before putting them away?

Then place the dried maize grain in sound, sealed bags or bins that will keep it safe. Mix an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder throughout the maize grain for extra protection. Carry out these steps immediately after harvest. Should infestation continue, visit ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.

Perform these actions right after harvest. If you still notice insects, see ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.

Next, clean the storage space and eliminate any residues left from the last season, since larger grain borer may survive there. Then put the dried maize in sound, sealed bags or bins.
