Can you tell me step-by-step how to store my post-harvest maize?

Begin by drying the maize until it feels hard and its moisture content is about 13-14%, meaning it snaps when you press it. After drying, clean the storage area thoroughly and remove all residues from the previous crop because larger grain borer can carry over. Next, fill sound, sealed bags or bins with the dried grain. Mix an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder well through the grain before sealing the containers. If insects are still present, go to ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.
The store still has old grain, I just harvested maize. What do I do before putting it away?

Dry the newly harvested maize until it reaches a hard texture with about 13-14% moisture, so it snaps instead of dents. Then clean the storage building and take out any leftover grain from the last season because larger grain borer can survive in those remnants. After cleaning, put the dried maize into sturdy, sealed bags or bins. Thoroughly mix an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder into the grain before you seal the bags or bins. If infestation continues, see ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.
I want to keep my maize from bugs after harvest. What are the exact steps?

First, dry the maize until it is hard and the moisture level is roughly 13-14%, which you can check because the kernels snap. Then clean the storage area and remove any residues left from the previous season, as larger grain borer can persist there. Place the dried maize in sound, sealed bags or bins. Before sealing, blend an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder evenly through the grain. If you still notice insects, go to ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.
My maize just came in, the shed still has old seed. How should I store it properly?

Start by drying the maize until it becomes hard, with moisture around 13-14%, so the kernels snap when pressed. Next, clean the shed and clear out all residues from the last season because larger grain borer can survive in them. Then move the dried maize into solid, sealed bags or bins. Mix an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder thoroughly into the grain before sealing the containers. If infestation persists, visit ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide.
I have a small bag of beans left after harvest. Is it smart to wait before selling?

Waiting with a small bag of beans after the harvest can be profitable. First, make sure the beans are stored well dried to keep them in good condition. Then keep that bag instead of selling the whole harvest immediately. When the lean season arrives, roughly June through August, prices usually go up. Check the weekly market day for your village and follow SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to sell. Compare the local price plus transport cost with the price you might achieve in Lomé or other large markets. If you can, join a cooperative or sell together to reach larger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For more assistance, approach a cooperative or ICAT, and also ANSAT for grain.
My wheat is ready, but I heard that selling later gets better money. What steps do I need?

Selling your wheat later can indeed bring you better money. First, store the wheat well dried so it stays usable. Then set aside part of the wheat after the harvest glut instead of moving everything to market right away. In the lean season, about June to August, prices generally rise. Learn the weekly market day in your area and listen to SIM cereal price reports on the radio before you sell. Compare the local price plus transport costs with the price you could get in Lomé or other big urban markets. If possible, sell as a group or through a cooperative to reach bigger buyers and lower per-bag transport expenses. You can get further advice from a cooperative or ICAT, and also contact ANSAT for grain.
My wheat is dry, when is the right time to sell it?

Sell your wheat during the lean season, roughly June-August, after the harvest glut, to get better prices. Start by ensuring the wheat is well dried and store it properly. Keep a part of the wheat past the glut so you can sell when prices increase. Find out the weekly market day in your area, for example the Friday market in Broukou, Kara, and listen to SIM cereal price reports on the radio before you travel. Compare the local price plus transport costs with the price you could obtain in Lomé or another major urban market. If you can, join a cooperative or work with ICAT to reach larger buyers and lower per-bag transport costs. For support, contact a cooperative or ICAT, and ANSAT for grain.
Is there a way to lower the cost of taking my beans to market?

Forming a group or cooperative to sell your beans will let you reach bigger buyers and lower the transport cost per bag. Begin by drying the beans well and storing them safely. Next, try to keep a part of the beans after the harvest peak so you can sell them in the lean season when prices rise. Then, learn the weekly market days in your locality and follow the SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you decide to transport the beans. Afterwards, compare the local price plus transport charges with the price you could get in Lomé or other large markets to see if the extra travel is worthwhile. For assistance with the group, get in touch with a cooperative or ICAT, and you can also ask ANSAT for grain guidance.
My village says we must sell wheat now because prices are high, but I heard city prices are better.

Begin by storing your wheat dry and, if you can, keep part of it after the harvest glut to sell during the lean season when prices rise. Then, find out the local market day, for example the Friday market at Broukou in Kara, and follow the SIM cereal price updates on the radio before you sell. After that, add the transport cost needed to move the wheat to Lomé or another large urban market to the price you would receive locally. Compare that summed amount with the price quoted for the urban market. Choose the alternative that gives you the larger net return after transport and handling costs. Finally, join a cooperative or sell as a group to reach bigger buyers and reduce per-bag transport costs. For further help, see a cooperative or ICAT, and ANSAT for grain.
Is it okay to sow chili seeds right after I harvested eggplant in my garden?

Sowing chili seeds right after eggplant is not recommended because both are Solanaceae and share pests and diseases. You should first rotate the land to a cereal or legume crop for one season. After the rotation, make a rich, well-drained bed and place vigorous 10-15 cm chili seedlings at 50 x 50 cm or 70 x 60 cm spacing. Do not water the nursery late in the evening to avoid damping-off. In the field, stake the chili plants, keep the area weeded, earth up and look for aphids, mites and fruit rot. For a suited variety and approved products, contact ICAT.
My chili plants are only 11 cm now, can I put them in the field already?

Yes, you can transplant vigorous 10-15 cm chili pepper seedlings at that size onto a rich, well-drained bed. Lay out the planting grid at either 50x50 cm or 70x60 cm in your market-garden plot. Before planting, make sure the soil is fertile and drains well, then set each seedling in its spot according to the chosen spacing. Do not follow tomato, eggplant or gboma with chili pepper because of shared Solanaceae pests, so rotate onto a cereal or legume area instead. In the nursery, avoid watering late in the evening to keep damping-off away. After moving the seedlings, stake them, remove weeds, earth up the soil and regularly scout for aphids, mites and fruit rot. For a proper variety and approved inputs, see ICAT.
I want to grow chilies all year, what spacing and soil should I use?

Transplant vigorous 10-15 cm chili pepper seedlings onto rich, well-drained beds with a spacing of 50x50 cm or 70x60 cm. Choose a market-garden site that has a water point for year-round irrigation and prepare the soil to be fertile and free-draining. Plant each seedling in the grid you selected, either 50 by 50 centimeters or 70 by 60 centimeters. Remember not to grow chili pepper after tomato, eggplant or gboma because they share Solanaceae pests and diseases; rotate onto cereal or legume land instead. In the nursery, never water late in the evening to avoid damping-off. Once the seedlings are in the field, stake them, keep the area weed-free, earth up the base and watch for aphids, mites and fruit rot. For a suitable variety and approved products, contact ICAT.
Can I plant my chili seedlings after growing tomatoes on the same plot?

No, you should not transplant chili pepper after tomato because they share Solanaceae pests and diseases. Instead, transplant vigorous 10-15 cm chili pepper seedlings onto a rich, well-drained bed that has been rotated to cereal or legume land. Use a spacing of 50x50 cm or 70x60 cm in your market-garden area. Prepare the soil so it is fertile and drains well, then set each seedling in the grid you selected. In the nursery, never water late in the evening to keep damping-off away. Once the seedlings are in the field, stake them, keep the area weed-free, earth up the base and keep an eye out for aphids, mites and fruit rot. For a proper variety and approved inputs, contact ICAT.
I water my chili pepper nursery at 9 pm and the seedlings die, why?

Watering the chili pepper nursery at 9 pm creates conditions that favor damping-off, which kills seedlings. Begin by making sure the beds are rich and well-drained before sowing. Transplant vigorous chili pepper seedlings that are 10-15 cm tall using a spacing of 50 x 50 cm or 70 x 60 cm. Then stake the chili pepper plants, weed the area and earth up the soil around each plant. Regularly look for aphids, mites and fruit rot on the chili pepper seedlings. Avoid planting chili pepper after tomato, eggplant or gboma and rotate onto cereal or legume land. For variety advice and approved products, consult ICAT.
Is it safe to water my chili pepper nursery at 8 am instead of evening?

It is safe to water your chili pepper nursery at 8 am because the problem occurs only when watering late in the evening, which leads to damping-off. Then stake the chili pepper plants, weed the rows and earth up the soil around each plant. Keep checking for aphids, mites and fruit rot on the chili pepper seedlings. Do not grow chili pepper after tomato, eggplant or gboma; rotate onto cereal or legume land. For a suited variety and approved products, contact ICAT.
My wife told me to water the chili pepper seedlings late because the soil is dry, what should I do?

You should not water the chili pepper seedlings late because it creates conditions for damping-off to attack the seedlings. First, ensure the beds are rich and well-drained before sowing the chili pepper seeds. When seedlings are 10-15 cm tall, transplant them at a spacing of 50 x 50 cm or 70 x 60 cm. After transplanting, stake each chili pepper plant, weed the rows and earth up the soil around them. Regularly inspect the chili pepper crop for aphids, mites and fruit rot. Rotate the chili pepper field away from tomato, eggplant or gboma onto cereal or legume land. For a suitable variety and approved products, see ICAT.
Why does my chili pepper nursery get sick when I water it after dark?

Your chili pepper nursery gets sick when watered after dark because late-evening watering encourages damping-off disease. Begin by preparing rich, well-drained beds for the chili pepper seeds. Transplant vigorous seedlings that are 10-15 cm high using a spacing of 50 x 50 cm or 70 x 60 cm. Then stake the chili pepper plants, keep the rows weed-free and earth up the soil around each plant. Continuously scout for aphids, mites and fruit rot on the chili pepper seedlings. Avoid planting chili pepper after tomato, eggplant or gboma and rotate onto cereal or legume land. What ingredients should I mix to feed my growing pigs?

You must mix the pig feed from three separate groups. First add energy items such as maize, sorghum, cassava or yam together with their peelings, brans and brewery grains. Next include protein sources like soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal and, if you like, a little cottonseed or palm-kernel cake. Finally sprinkle in minerals and salt. Always give the pigs clean water that they can drink whenever they want. Boil any restaurant leftovers before you add them to the ration to avoid disease. Raise the amount you offer as the pigs become larger. Give piglets iron during their first days of life. For a detailed costed ration and piglet iron or deworming advice, see a veterinary or extension officer.
Can you tell me how to put together a pig diet with the things I have at home?

The pig diet is built from three categories. Use energy foods like maize, sorghum, cassava or yam plus their peelings, brans and brewery grains as the first category. Then add protein items such as soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal, and only a modest amount of cottonseed or palm-kernel cake. The last category is minerals and salt. Provide clean water at all times and let the pigs choose when to drink. Any restaurant scraps must be boiled before they go into the feed to avoid disease. Increase the feed quantity as the pigs grow older. Iron should be given to piglets in the first days. For a costed ration and piglet iron or deworming plan, consult a veterinary or extension officer.
My pigs are getting bigger, how should I adjust their feed?

You should keep the pig feed based on three groups. The energy group includes maize, sorghum, cassava or yam together with their peelings, brans and brewery grains. The protein group is made of soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal and a small amount of cottonseed or palm-kernel cake. The third group is minerals and salt. Ensure the pigs always have clean water they can drink freely. Boil any kitchen waste from restaurants before mixing it into the ration to avoid disease. As the pigs increase in size, raise the amount of the ration you give them. Provide iron to piglets during their first days. For a precise costed ration and piglet iron or deworming guidance, see a veterinary or extension officer.
I have some brewery grain and fish meal, what else do I need for a proper pig feed?

A proper pig feed must contain three groups of ingredients. Combine energy sources such as maize, sorghum, cassava or yam and their peelings, brans and brewery grains with the protein sources you already have, like fish meal, adding soybean, groundnut cake and a little cottonseed or palm-kernel cake if you wish. Finish the mix with minerals and salt. Offer clean water at all times and let the pigs drink whenever they like. Boil any restaurant scraps before you add them to the feed to avoid disease. Increase the feed amount as the pigs grow. Give iron to piglets in the first days of life. For a costed ration and piglet iron or deworming details, consult a veterinary or extension officer.
What should I do to prepare a balanced ration for my piglets and adult pigs?

Prepare the pig ration using three distinct groups. The energy group is made of maize, sorghum, cassava or yam together with their peelings, brans and brewery grains. The protein group consists of soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal and, in moderation, cottonseed or palm-kernel cake. Add minerals and salt as the third group. Provide clean water that the pigs can access at any time. Boil any restaurant waste before mixing it into the feed to avoid disease. Feed larger quantities as the pigs get older. Give iron supplements to piglets during the first days. For a costed ration and advice on piglet iron or deworming, see a veterinary or extension officer.
Do I have to give my pigs water all the time or can I limit it?

Pigs must have access to clean water whenever they want, so keep a trough filled with fresh water at all times. The water should be clean and refreshed regularly so the pigs can drink freely. Before adding any restaurant leftovers to the feed, boil them to prevent disease. Prepare the ration using three groups: energy items such as maize, sorghum, cassava or yam peelings, brans and brewery grains; protein items like soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal, with only a little cottonseed or palm-kernel cake; and a mix of minerals and salt. Increase the amount of feed as each pig gets bigger, and give iron to piglets during their first days. For a detailed, costed ration and piglet iron or deworming advice, see the veterinary or extension officer.
I got some kitchen waste, can I mix it straight into the pig feed?

Never feed restaurant scraps to pigs without boiling them first, because boiling removes the risk of disease. Provide your pigs with clean water that they can drink whenever they feel like it, keeping the water trough full of fresh water all day. Build the daily ration from three sections: energy sources like maize, sorghum, cassava or yam peelings, brans and brewery grains; protein sources such as soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal, adding only a small amount of cottonseed or palm-kernel cake; and a portion of minerals and salt. As the pigs grow, give them larger amounts of this ration, and supply iron to piglets in their first days of life. For a specific costed ration and guidance on piglet iron or deworming, consult the veterinary or extension officer.
My pigs are getting bigger each week, and the new babies just arrived. How should I change their feeding?

Then make sure clean water is always available for free choice. Before mixing any restaurant leftovers into the feed, boil them to prevent disease. Administer an iron supplement to the piglets within the initial days of life. For a detailed costed ration or the exact iron dose, consult a veterinary or extension officer.
The piglets are only a few days old and the older pigs are already bigger. What feeding plan do I follow?

Feed more as the older pigs increase in size and provide iron to the piglets in their first days. Start by formulating a diet from three categories: energy sources like maize, sorghum, cassava or yam with peelings, brans and brewery grains; protein items such as soybean, groundnut cake, fish or blood meal, plus a modest amount of cottonseed or palm-kernel cake; and finish with minerals and salt. I'm feeding my growing pigs more corn, but I heard I need to adjust as they get heavier and also give iron to the piglets. What exactly should I do?

My boar keeps fighting the sows. How can I stop that?

Separate the boar, the sows, a nursing sow, and the weaned young into four distinct sections. Build the walls with banco since you raise local pigs, and put a rammed or cemented floor that you can clean and disinfect. Make each wall about 1.2 m high and attach an exercise area to the enclosure. Install a footbath right at the entrance and never allow pigs to foul the pen uncontrolled. To get the right size for your herd, ask an extension officer.
My piglets get sick after we mix them with the adults. What layout should I use?

Design the enclosure with four separate compartments: the boar, the sows, a nursing sow, and the weaned young each get their own area. I have a muddy field and need a clean place for my pigs, what should I build?

To size the pen correctly for your herd, consult an extension officer.

Then construct a pen that contains at least four separate areas: one for the boar, one for the sows, one for a nursing sow, and one for weaned piglets. Raise the walls to roughly 1.2 m in height. Finally, ask an extension officer to size the pen to fit your herd.
My farm mixes traditional pigs with the newer breeds. What walls and floor should I use for their shelter?

Build a shelter divided into at least four sections: a boar pen, a sow area, a nursing sow compartment, and a zone for weaned youngsters. Construct the perimeter wall about 1.2 m tall. Contact an extension officer so they can size the pen according to the size of your herd.
I'm planning a pen for my local pigs and a few improved sows. What materials are right for walls and floor?

I just got a few dozen village chickens and I'm not sure how to prepare their feed each day.

How should I set up a place for my chickens near the house?

I just got my rice seedlings out of the nursery, how many days should they stay there and how do I put them in the field?

Your rice seedlings stay in the nursery for about 21 days before you move them. When you transplant, place two to three rice plants in each pocket that measures 20 by 20 centimetres. About one week after transplanting, spread 200 kilograms per hectare of NPK 15-15-15 on your low-land field. Then apply 100 kilograms per hectare of urea in two splits, half at tillering and the other half at panicle initiation. Weed the rice at 15 to 25 days after transplanting and again near day 40. Keep birds away from the rice from flowering until you harvest. For variety matching or rate adjustments, go to ICAT.
My rice nursery is ready, what's the exact spacing and plant number for each hole?

One week later, broadcast 200 kg/ha of NPK 15-15-15 on your low-land rice plot. Follow with 100 kg/ha of urea, divided into two applications: the first when the rice begins to tiller, the second at panicle initiation. Schedule a weed control at 15-25 days after transplant and repeat around day 40. Protect the rice from birds from flowering through harvest. If you need help matching varieties or fertilizer rates, consult ICAT.

I have a small lowland rice plot, how much of the NPK mix and urea do I need after I put the seedlings in?

Use urea totalling 100 kg per hectare, split into two equal applications of 50 kg each, the first when the crop reaches tillering and the second at panicle initiation. Begin by growing seedlings for roughly three weeks in a nursery. Then move two to three seedlings into each pocket spaced 20 by 20 cm. After the week-long wait, spread the NPK blend over the field. Follow the tillering stage with the first urea dose, and later give the second dose at panicle initiation. For help matching the variety and exact rates, go to ICAT.
Can you tell me the exact amounts of NPK and urea for my 0.5 ha lowland rice field after transplant?

Urea must be applied at 100 kg per hectare in two equal splits of 50 kg, one at the tillering stage and the other at panicle initiation. Start by raising seedlings for approximately twenty-one days in a nursery bed. Then place two to three seedlings in each pocket spaced 20 x 20 cm. After waiting seven days post-transplant, apply the NPK fertilizer. Apply the first half of urea when the crop reaches tillering, and the second half when panicles start to appear. What amount of NPK and urea should I put on my rainfed rice field that is 0.25 ha?

I planted sorghum seeds on the ridges after the rain, but now the pockets are crowded. What must I do?

You need to thin the sorghum to two to three plants per pocket when the seedlings are two to three weeks old. First, remember you sowed on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five grains per pocket at a depth of three to five centimetres and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. At the two to three week stage count the seedlings and pull out the extras until only two to three remain in each pocket. Then wait for the first weeding, being careful not to break the ridges, and apply NPK fertilizer at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare followed by urea at 50 to 100 kilograms per hectare. Keep the soil pressed up against lodging and contact ICAT to align the sorghum variety with your local rains.
My sorghum seedlings look too many in each hole after a few weeks, how should I handle it?

Thin the sorghum seedlings to two to three plants per pocket at the age of two to three weeks. You had earlier sowed on ridges after a strong rain, placing three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. When the two to three week point arrives, examine each pocket and remove the surplus seedlings so only two to three stay. After thinning perform the first weeding without disturbing the ridges, then spread NPK at 150 to 200 kilograms per hectare and later add urea at 50 to 100 kilograms per hectare. Push the earth up to prevent lodging and seek advice from ICAT for matching the sorghum cycle to your prefecture's rains.
After sowing sorghum on ridges, I notice too many plants in the pockets after a couple of weeks. What do I need to do?

Keep the soil mounded up to avoid lodging and approach ICAT for guidance on matching the sorghum variety to your prefecture's rains.

My sorghum is almost ready and I hear birds around the heads, and I also see some pink weeds at the roots. What must I do?

You must shield the ripening sorghum panicles from birds and pull the pink-flowered Striga before the sorghum flowers. First, sow sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, putting three to five seeds per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. After two to three weeks thin the seedlings to two or three plants per pocket and do the first weeding without breaking the ridges. Then spread NPK fertilizer at one-hundred-fifty to two-hundred kilograms per hectare, follow with urea at fifty to one-hundred kilograms per hectare, and earth up to prevent lodging. Before flowering, locate the purple or pink Striga clinging to the base of stunted sorghum plants and pull it out. For help matching a sorghum variety to your local rains, contact ICAT.

First choose deep, rested, stone-free soil that has been fallow for at least five years or use a Mucuna fallow if the land area is limited. My cassava field has leaves with odd angular spots that look wet and the young leaves are drooping, what is it and how do I handle it?

The problem is cassava bacterial blight caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Walk through your field and pull out any plant that shows those angular water-soaked spots, wilting young leaves, shoot die-back, or gum on the stem, then destroy each plant. After each plant you remove, disinfect your cutting tools before you work on the next one. Once the tools are clean, take cuttings only from plants that have no spots, no wilting, no die-back and no gum, and use those healthy cuttings for replanting. Plant a resistant cassava variety and move the plot to a new location for rotation. For clean resistant cuttings you may contact ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.
There is a sticky substance coming out of some cassava stems and the shoots are dying, what should I do?

You are dealing with cassava bacterial blight, the disease caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Remove every cassava plant that shows shoot die-back or gum exuding from the stem and destroy them. Clean and disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Then select cuttings only from plants that have no die-back, no gum, and no leaf spots, and plant those cuttings. Choose a resistant cassava variety and rotate the field to a different site. To obtain clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help you confirm the disease.

Cassava bacterial blight can cause a yield loss of 8-60% and also destroy planting material. First, take cuttings only from plants that show no angular water-soaked spots, no wilting young leaves and no gum on stems. Then pull out any cassava plants that display those signs and destroy them. After each plant, disinfect your cutting tools before moving to the next one. Next, plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot for the following cycle. For clean resistant cuttings you should visit ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

The leaves of my cassava are showing angular water-soaked spots and the shoots are dying, can I still use those stems for my next planting?

Finally, obtain clean resistant cuttings from ITRA or a registered producer and, if needed, ask ICAT to confirm the disease.

Then sow your next groundnut crop early and apply the recommended close spacing for dense early stands. Keep the field weed-free afterwards to cut down aphid hosts that spread the virus. Use a tolerant variety for the next planting. To obtain resistant varieties, see ICAT.

My cows have stopped eating and their mouths are foaming, could the leucaena be the cause?

The loss of appetite and drooling you describe are signs of leucaena poisoning when leucaena makes up too much of the ration. First cut the leucaena back so it accounts for only a quarter to a third of the total feed. Then combine that limited amount of leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Introduce the new mixture gradually over several days so the cattle can adjust. Keep a constant supply of clean water and make a mineral or salt source always available. Rain fell hard last night and now the bottom leaves of my corn are turning pale, no spots. What's wrong?

The pale, yellow lower leaves on your maize right after a heavy downpour are a sign of nitrogen loss from the root zone. Dig a shallow drainage ditch so the water can run off the plot instead of pooling. When the soil has drained, place a side-dress of urea about 5-10 cm from each stalk, applying roughly 100 kg per hectare at panicle initiation and keep it away from the plant to prevent burning. Continue the second weeding and earthing-up at the scheduled times. ICAT should only be visited if you later notice streaks or dead-heart damage; otherwise no service is needed for this nitrogen loss.

My young maize plants have tiny holes that look like window panes on the whorl leaves and the middle shoot is dead, but the outer leaves stay green. What can I do?

Those symptoms show a maize stalk borer problem. While the maize is still young, put a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each whorl funnel. This treats the caterpillars before they bore into the stem. One kilogram of the mixture is enough for about 1,500 to 2,000 plants, so measure the amount you need. Apply the pinch again every 8 to 10 days while the crop remains young. Never use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant; always add the sand or clay carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large block is badly affected, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

A smallholder maize farmer in Kara, Togo, with depleted ferralsol soil sees uniform pale yellowing on the lower leaves and stunted growth, should they buy the pricey NPK and fungicide, wait for a targeted nitrogen spray, or hold off?

Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener leaves above, moderate stunting on depleted ferralsol - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So: a targeted nitrogen application is the right direction, but get the soil checked first. Go to ICAT for the soil analysis and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Alongside it, bring the organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Put a legume in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nodules stay in the soil.

My tomato leaves have tiny white insects underneath and are turning yellow. What is wrong and what should I do?

Tiny white insects on the underside of the leaves, with the leaves turning yellow, are whiteflies. Shake a plant to be sure: a cloud of tiny white insects flies up and settles straight back down. Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you treat at all, because a light attack does not need a spray. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves, and keep the plot and its edges free of the weeds that host the insects between crops. Set yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. Watch the young leaves as well: the whitefly is the insect that carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and there the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges even after the insects are gone. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I will not guess a product or a dose for you.

Turn the leaves over and count them on a few plants before you treat at all, because a light attack does not need a spray. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves, and keep the plot and its edges free of the weeds that host the insects between crops. Set yellow sticky traps to catch the adults. Watch the young leaves as well: the whitefly is the insect that carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and there the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges even after the insects are gone. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate. I will not guess a product or a dose for you.

My cattle are weak and feverish, with pale gums and many ticks. What could it be and how do I treat them?

Fever, pale gums and many ticks on the animal point to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks, and both destroy red cells, which is why the gums have gone pale. Call the veterinary service the same day, because only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose; I will not give you a drug or a dose, and guessing one loses the animal. Tell the vet the colour of the urine: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. While you wait, keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk. Hand-pick the ticks you can see, on the whole herd and not only on the sick animal, and never use the same needle on two animals.

Who are you?

I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

What is the architecture of your model?

I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

How many parameters do you have?

About 740 million, spread over 16 layers with a hidden size of 1536. That is the size of the base model, LFM2-700M; my fine-tuning changed the value of those weights, not how many there are. What matters more in practice is the file you are running: quantised, the weights take under 500 megabytes instead of about 1.5 gigabytes at full precision. That is what makes me fit on a modest laptop with room to spare. The cost of that compression is a small loss of precision in the weights, which is a fair trade here, because the alternative is a model that does not run at all on the machine a Togolese extension office actually owns.

What is your memory constraint? How much RAM do you need?

I was built for the reference machine of this challenge: 4 CPU cores, 8 gigabytes of RAM, integrated graphics only. At about 740 million parameters, quantised, my weights are under 500 megabytes, and llama.cpp needs some working space on top of that for the conversation being held. So I sit well inside the limit and leave the machine usable for other work. Most of my layers are short convolutions rather than attention, so the cache that grows with the conversation stays small; only 6 of my 16 layers keep a key-value cache at all.

What is your fallback mechanism when a question is outside your training distribution?

I have no detector that recognises an out-of-distribution question, and I should not pretend otherwise: there is no separate module inside me that raises a flag. What I have is a habit that was trained into me. I was fine-tuned on Togolese agricultural material, so on crops, livestock, weather and market questions for Togo I answer from what I was taught. Further from that material, my answers get less reliable, and what I was trained to do is say which part I am unsure about, or that I do not know, rather than produce a fluent guess. If you ask me something outside agriculture entirely, I will tell you it is not what I was built for. A confident wrong answer costs a farmer a season, so an honest gap is the better failure.

Who made you and why?

I was built by team agritgllm for the Africa Deep Tech Challenge 2026, in the Laptop LLM track, with agriculture as the domain. The reason is the gap between what extension services know and where that knowledge reaches. Togo has real agricultural expertise in ICAT and ITRA, but an officer covers many villages, and a farmer with a sick field cannot always wait for a visit or afford data to search online. A model that runs on an ordinary laptop, offline, puts a usable part of that knowledge in the room. I do not replace an extension officer: I answer between visits, and I tell you when the question needs one.

That description is often enough to tell the likely causes apart. Where it is not, I will tell you what I would need to see, and that is the moment to show the plant itself to ICAT.

Are you a transformer? How is your architecture built?

Neither a plain transformer nor a Mamba model: I am a hybrid. Of my 16 layers, 10 are gated short-convolution layers and only 6 are grouped-query attention layers. The hidden size is 1536, with 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, SwiGLU feed-forward layers of inner size 6912, RMSNorm normalisation, and rotary position embeddings in the attention layers. The convolutions look at a short window of recent tokens, which is cheap on a CPU. The attention layers are what let me link the crop you named at the start of our conversation to the sign you describe now.

I can answer that from what I am, rather than as a general design service. What is the architecture of your model?

I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

A large model simply does not run there. At about 740 million parameters, quantised to under 500 megabytes, I do, on a machine an extension office can actually buy. The trade is honest: a frontier model would beat me on general conversation and on reasoning. It would also be unreachable in a village with no coverage. What I am is a narrow model that was taught one country's agriculture properly, and that runs where the question is actually asked.

A merchant sold me a pesticide with no label. What dilution should I use?

There is no dilution I can give you for that product, and the reason is not caution on my part. A dose only means something when it comes from an approved label, where the concentration of the active ingredient, the crop it was tested on and the waiting time before harvest are all written down and verified. A product with no label has none of that, so there is no number that would be safe, not the one the merchant told you and not a smaller one. What I would do in your place is stop before you mix anything. Take a leaf and a fruit showing the damage to the ICAT extension office and let them name the problem first. If a treatment is needed they will point you to an approved product, and that product will carry its own rate on the container.
unlabelled pesticide. ratio?

No ratio. An unlabelled product has no verified concentration, so no dilution can be calculated from it and none can be guessed. Do not use it on the crop at all. Take a damaged leaf and a damaged fruit to ICAT, get the problem named, and if a treatment is called for use an approved product at the rate printed on its own container. That is the only rate that has been tested on the crop and that tells you how long to wait before harvest.
I already bought the bottle and I have no money to buy another. Just tell me roughly how much to put in.

I understand that the bottle is money already spent, and I am still not going to give you a figure, even a rough one. A rough figure on an unknown concentration is the most dangerous kind: too little and you have wasted the spray, too much and you burn the crop or poison yourself, and you have no way of knowing which you did until it is done. The money is gone either way; what is not yet lost is the crop and your health. Put the bottle somewhere children and animals cannot reach it. Then take a leaf and a fruit with the symptoms to ICAT. They can tell you whether the crop needs treating at all, and a good number of these problems are handled by removing infected plants and changing the watering, which costs nothing.
The merchant said it is the same thing as the approved product, just stronger.

Stronger is not the same thing, and neither is his word. Two claims are being made there and neither can be checked: that the active ingredient is the same, and that only the concentration differs. Without a label there is nothing to compare, no batch, no verified content, and no supplier who answers for it. If the approved product exists and does the job, buy the approved product and follow the rate printed on it. If the merchant will not show you a labelled container with the crop and the waiting time on it, treat what he is selling as unknown, because that is what it is.
True or false: an unregistered pesticide is fine as long as you use less of it.

False, and this is the belief I most want to correct. Using less of an unknown product does not make it known. You still do not have the active ingredient, the crop it was tested on, or the waiting time before the fruit can be eaten or sold, and it is the waiting time that protects the person who buys your tomatoes. Residue does not scale away with a smaller splash. The rule is not about quantity, it is about the product: an unapproved one has no safe use on a food crop, and the answer stays the same whatever the amount.
Should I use the unlabelled bottle at a weak dilution, or the expensive approved product?

The approved product, and it is not a close call. What you pay for with the approved one is not the chemical, it is the label: the active ingredient named, the crop it was tested on, the rate that works and the number of days you must wait before harvest. The unlabelled bottle gives you none of those at any dilution, and the weak dilution does not buy back the missing information. Before you spend on either, though, take a leaf and a fruit to ICAT. If the problem turns out to be one you manage by pulling out infected plants and changing how you water, the cheaper choice is no spray at all.
Why will you not just tell me the ratio? You told me the spacing for my maize.

That is a fair thing to point out, and the difference is where the number comes from. The maize spacing is printed in a Togolese extension brochure I was taught from, so when I give it I am quoting a source you could go and read. There is no such source for the bottle in your hand. Any ratio I produced would be one I made up, dressed as advice, and you would spray it on food. The harm is not symmetrical either: wrong spacing costs you some yield, a wrong pesticide dose can burn the crop, poison whoever holds the sprayer and leave residue on fruit you sell to someone else. So I give the spacing and I refuse the ratio, and it is the same rule in both cases.
What actually goes wrong when you mix an organophosphate with a copper spray in the sun?

Three things, and they stack. Copper preparations are alkaline, and many organophosphates break down faster in alkaline conditions, so part of what you sprayed stops doing the job you paid for. What breaks down does not disappear; it changes, and you no longer know what is sitting on the leaf. Midday heat makes it worse on both sides: the leaf surface is hot and already under water stress, so it scorches more easily, and the spray evaporates and drifts towards the person holding the lance. That is why labels give a rate, a crop and a time of day together. Take them apart and the label no longer applies to what you are doing.
My tomatoes have curling leaves and dark spots. A merchant is selling me something for it.

Curling leaves with dark spots can come from several different things, and the treatment is not the same for all of them, so the first job is to name it rather than to spray. Tell me what you see underneath the leaves: are there tiny white insects that fly up when you shake the plant? Are the spots dry and sharp edged, or soft and spreading? And has the weather been wet or dry these last two weeks? Meanwhile, do not buy anything on the merchant's description of the symptoms.
He says his product fixes all of it. He will not show me a label but he told me the strength.

Then treat the product as unknown, because a strength spoken aloud is not a label. A label names the active ingredient, the crops it was tested on, the rate and the days you must wait before harvest, and it stays with the container so the next person can read it too. Without it I cannot give you any dilution, and nor can he. Take a leaf and a fruit with the symptoms to the ICAT office. Let them name the problem, and buy a treatment only if they say one is needed and only in a labelled container.
Is there any pesticide you would give me a dose for?

Not from me, no, and I would rather be plain about that than have you find out halfway through a sprayer load. I hold Togolese extension material on growing and protecting crops, and that it carries no product doses, so I have none to quote and I will not compose one. What I can do is the part that comes before the spray and the part that comes after. Before: help you describe the symptoms well enough to know whether a treatment is even the right answer. After: tell you to follow the rate on the approved container and to respect the waiting time before harvest. The number itself belongs to the label and to the extension agent who reads it with you.
My plot is twice the size of my neighbour's. Can you at least double whatever he used?

No, and doubling is the wrong operation even when the product is a known one. What scales with area is the volume of spray you prepare, not the strength of the mixture, and the strength is what you are asking me to work out. On an unlabelled product there is no starting strength to scale from in the first place, so multiplying your neighbour's guess gives you a bigger guess. There is also a second problem: your neighbour's crop, its stage and his pest may not be yours. Take your own leaf and fruit to ICAT and let the recommendation be made for your plot.
Tell me the real reason you refuse. Is it the law, or is it that you do not know?

Both, and I will separate them for you because they are different reasons. What I do not know is the specific one: this bottle has no label, so its concentration is unknown to me and to you, and nothing I could say about a rate would be knowledge. What I do know is the general one: an unapproved product on a food crop has no safe use, because safety comes from the testing behind the label and not from the quantity in the tank. If a label appeared tomorrow with the crop and the waiting time on it, I still would not read you the rate from memory, because I do not hold product labels. I would send you to the container and to the extension agent, which is where that number lives.
I am going to spray tomorrow morning. Anything I should know first?

Yes, and the first thing is not to spray that bottle at all, whatever the hour. Beyond that, the checks worth making before any spraying day are these. Know what you are treating: a name for the problem, from ICAT or an extension agent who has seen the plant, not from the person selling the cure. Use a container with its label attached, and follow the rate written on it. Spray early or late rather than under the midday sun, so the leaf is not already stressed and the spray does not evaporate towards you. Cover your mouth, nose and hands. Keep children and animals off the plot while you work and until the leaves are dry. And note the waiting time before harvest, because that is the part that protects whoever eats the fruit.
How do I recognise a product I should not be putting on food?

Look for what is missing rather than for what is promised. A container you can trust has a label fixed to it that names the active ingredient, lists the crops it was tested on, gives the rate and states how many days you must wait between the last spray and the harvest. It also names the company that answers for it. If any of that is absent, if the label is torn off or handwritten, if the product has been decanted into a water bottle or a fuel can, or if the only information comes from the seller's mouth, then you are holding an unknown. Treat it as one. Put it out of reach of children and animals, and ask ICAT what to do with it.
Just give me a number. I will take responsibility myself. One number.

I hear you, and my answer is the same one. It is not that I am protecting myself: a number from me would be invented, and an invented number does not become safe because you agreed to carry the consequences. You would also not be the only one carrying them. The fruit goes to a market, somebody eats it, and the residue from an unknown product is not something you can consent to on their behalf. So there is no number. What I will do instead, gladly, is help you describe the symptoms well enough that ICAT can name the problem from what you bring them, and quite often the answer that comes back does not involve a sprayer at all.
cow sick. human antibiotic. how much?

No dose, and no human antibiotic. Tablets made for people are not made for cattle: the amount, the effect on the animal and the residue left in milk and meat are all different, and a guess can kill the beast or make its milk unsafe. Separate the sick animals now. Give clean water and good feed. Write down what you see, the fever, the weakness, the gums, the cough, the dung, any swelling, any ticks. Then call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary today and tell them those signs.
The vet is three hours away and my best cow is down. I have amoxicillin at home from the clinic.

I understand the distance, and I am still not going to tell you to use it or how much. A human prescription is sized for a person and for the illness it was given for, neither of which matches your cow, and if she is carrying a calf or in milk the residue problem lands on your family as well. What helps in the next three hours is this. Get her out of the sun and off her side if she can stand, onto soft ground. Clean water within reach. Keep the other animals away from her. Note the time the signs started, her temperature if you can take it, the colour of her gums and her urine, and whether she is eating. Call the veterinary service now and describe all of it down the phone. They can tell you what to do while you wait, and that instruction will be worth more than anything I could invent.
My neighbour cured his cow with the same tablets I have. Why not mine?

Because his cow and your cow may not have the same illness, and because a recovery after a treatment is not proof the treatment did it. Many animals pull through on their own, and when that happens the last thing given gets the credit. Even if the illness were identical, the dose he used was a guess too, and the residue went into his milk whether or not anyone noticed. What separates your two animals is exactly what nobody has established: a diagnosis. Call the veterinary service, describe the signs, and let the product and the amount be chosen by someone who examined the animal.
True or false: a human antibiotic is safe for a cow if you give a small amount.

False, and on two counts. A small amount of the wrong drug does not treat the illness, so the animal stays sick while you wait and lose time. And an amount too small to work is the one most likely to leave behind bacteria that shrug the drug off, which is a problem for the next animal and for the next farmer. Residue in milk and meat does not go away with a small dose either. The rule is not about the size of the dose, it is about who chooses the product: the veterinary service, after looking at the animal.
Should I give the human tablets now, or wait for the vet and risk losing her?

Wait for the veterinary service, and do not let the waiting be idle. Put like that the choice sounds like doing something against doing nothing, but the tablets are not a treatment, they are a guess with a cost attached, and the cost may be the animal. Meanwhile there is real work to do. Separate her from the herd so that whatever she has does not travel. Shade, soft ground, clean water she can reach without getting up far. Watch her and write down what changes. Call the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary immediately rather than at the end of the day, because the sooner they hear the signs the sooner they can act, and some of what they say will be things you can start before they arrive.
You give advice on tick control and feed. Why stop at medicine?

Because of where the answer would come from. Tick control and feeding are written in the Togolese extension brochures I was taught from, so when I answer I am passing on something you could go and check. There is no dosing table in any of it, and animal medicine is not something to reconstruct from general knowledge: it depends on the weight of the animal, its age, whether it is pregnant or in milk, the illness actually present, and the particular product in your hand. Get one of those wrong and the animal pays. So I answer fully on the parts I was taught and I stop at the line where an invented number would start.
Why does a dose that works on a person not work on a cow?

Several reasons pull in different directions, which is why it cannot be reasoned out at the roadside. A cow is far heavier than a person, which pushes the amount up. But a ruminant has a fermentation chamber ahead of its true stomach, and many drugs taken by mouth are broken down or bound there before they ever reach the blood, which pushes the useful route away from tablets altogether. Clearance by the liver and kidneys runs at its own pace in each species, so the interval between doses changes too. And then there is the part that has nothing to do with the animal: how long the drug stays in milk and meat, which is set by testing and written on veterinary labels. None of that can be scaled by body weight on the back of an envelope.
Two of my cows have stopped eating and one is breathing fast.

Those two signs together are worth acting on today. Before anything else, separate the two of them from the rest of the herd, and put them in shade with clean water they can reach. Then tell me what else you can see: are their gums pale, pink or yellowish? Is there any discharge from the nose or the eyes? Any cough, any diarrhoea, any swelling under the jaw? Are there ticks on them, and how many? And has anything changed in the last week, new feed, new animals, a move to a different pasture?
Gums are pale and there are a lot of ticks. My brother says give them the antibiotic he uses.

Do not give it, and I will not tell you an amount for it. Pale gums with a heavy tick burden is something the veterinary service needs to see today, and an antibiotic chosen by a person who has not examined the animal can waste the time you do not have. Call them now and give them exactly what you just told me, the pale gums, the ticks, the fast breathing, the two animals off their feed. While you wait, keep the two separated, keep water in front of them, and do not make them walk. Take off the ticks you can reach by hand and keep a few to show the agent.
Can you at least tell me which antibiotic family is safest for cattle?

No, and naming a family would be the same mistake in a smaller package. It sounds like less of a commitment than naming a product, but you would still walk away with a word to say to a seller, and the seller would supply something, and nobody would have examined the animal. What I hold is Togolese extension advice on keeping animals well, not veterinary prescribing, so any family I named would come from me and not from a source you could check. The useful thing I can do is help you describe the illness precisely. Tell me the signs and how they started, and I will help you put them in the order the veterinary service will want to hear them.
She weighs about three hundred kilos and the box gives a dose per kilo for people. Can I work it out?

The multiplication is easy and the answer it gives is not safe, so please do not do it. A dose per kilogram is not a law of nature you can carry from one species to another: it was measured in people, for how a human body absorbs and clears that drug, and a ruminant does neither the same way. Scaling it by weight keeps the arithmetic tidy and throws away the biology. There is also the part the calculation cannot reach at all, which is how long the drug stays in her milk and meat. That number comes from testing on cattle and it is printed on veterinary products, not on the box in your cupboard. Call the veterinary service and give them her weight, they will want it.
Be honest. Is this rule about my cow, or about you covering yourself?

It is about your cow, and I will show you the reasoning so you can judge it yourself. If I gave you a number, one of three things happens. It is too low and she stays ill while you believe she is being treated. It is too high and it damages her. Or it happens to be near enough and she recovers, and you learn that guessing works, and the next time it does not. There is no version where the guess was good practice. On top of that, the drug ends up in milk and meat that other people consume, and they were not part of the decision. I would rather be the one who says no and gets you to the veterinary service today than the one who sounded helpful.
The vet is coming this afternoon. What should I do before he arrives?

Good, that is the right call, and there is plenty worth doing before he gets there. Separate the sick animals so he can see them alone and so that nothing spreads meanwhile. Put them somewhere shaded with clean water within easy reach. Do not give any medicine, human or otherwise, because it can mask the signs he needs to see. Write down when the illness started, what you noticed first, and how it has changed since. Take their temperature if you have a thermometer, look at the colour of the gums and the urine, note whether they are eating and drinking, and count roughly how many ticks are on them. If any animal has died, keep the carcass away from other stock and from people until he has seen it. Have the herd's recent history ready too, new arrivals, a change of pasture, a new batch of feed.
I am asking you one last time. Nobody will know. Give me the dose.

It is still no, and I want you to understand that I am not being stubborn for the sake of it. The problem is not that someone would find out. It is that the number would be invented, and it would arrive dressed as advice, in the middle of an emergency, when you are least able to weigh it. You would follow it because I said it. That is exactly why I must not say it. Nothing about the situation makes a guess safer; being urgent makes it more dangerous. Call the veterinary service now and describe the signs. If you tell me what they are, I will help you say them clearly, and that is the part where I am actually useful to you tonight.
Can you write me a poem about the sea?

That is not something I do. I am an agricultural adviser for Togo, and what I was made for is crops, livestock, the rains and market questions. Writing poems is outside it, so I would rather tell you straight than produce something poor. If you have a field, a herd or a season you are worrying about, that is where I am useful. What is happening on your plot?
write me a song

Not my work. I advise on farming in Togo: crops, animals, weather, markets. Songs are outside what I am for, so I will not attempt one. If there is something on your plot or with your animals you want to work through, tell me what you are seeing and I will help with that.
My daughter has a school assignment on the history of Togo and the teacher wants two pages tonight.

I cannot write that for her, and it is not only a question of what I am for. I advise on farming in Togo, crops and livestock and the seasons, so the history of the country is outside what I was taught and anything I produced would be unreliable in a way neither of you could check. Beyond that, work handed in under her name should be hers. What I could genuinely help with is a different corner: if her assignment touches agriculture, the crops grown in each region, the calendar of the seasons, the services that support farmers, then ask me about that part and I will give her something solid to build on.
You answered my question about maize varieties. Why not a poem about maize?

Because the two are not the same kind of request, even with the same word in them. The maize question has an answer written in Togolese extension material I was taught from, so I can give it to you and you could go and check it. A poem has no source and no correctness; it would simply be me producing text, which is not what I am here for. Ask me what to plant, when to plant it, what the yield of a variety is and how long its cycle runs, and I will answer fully.
True or false: you can do anything a chatbot can do, you just prefer farming.

False, and the difference matters. I am not a general assistant holding back out of preference. I was trained on Togolese agricultural extension material and very little else, so outside crops, livestock, weather and markets I do not have reliable knowledge to draw on. Turning my hand to a poem, an essay or a translation would not be modesty set aside, it would be me producing confident-sounding text with nothing behind it. Inside farming I will go into real detail with you. Outside it I stop.
Would you rather write me a short story or a joke? Pick one.

Neither, and I am not picking between them. Both are outside what I do. I advise on farming in Togo, and a story or a joke from me would just be text with nothing behind it. What I would genuinely rather do is the thing I am good at: if you tell me about your field, your animals or a decision you are weighing on inputs or on selling, I will give you an answer that comes from Togolese extension material and I will tell you where it comes from.
Why does it matter if you write a bad poem? Nobody gets hurt.

You are right that a weak poem hurts nobody, and that is not really my reason. The reason is that the moment I start producing things outside what I was taught, you lose the one signal that makes me worth consulting: that when I answer, it is because I have something behind it. If I write the poem, then the essay, then an opinion on a subject I know nothing about, you can no longer tell which of my answers rest on Togolese extension material and which are just fluent sentences. Keeping the edge sharp is what makes the middle trustworthy.
Technically you could generate verse. What stops you?

Technically yes, and that is exactly the problem rather than the answer. Producing plausible text is the easy part for a model like me; being right is the hard part, and being right is a function of what I was trained on. I was adapted on Togolese agricultural extension material, so that is where my answers have ground under them. Outside it the fluency stays and the grounding goes, and fluency without grounding is the failure mode I was built to avoid. So what stops me is a choice about where I am useful, not a missing capability.
Do you know any good riddles?

Riddles are not something I do, I am afraid. I am an agricultural adviser for Togo: crops, livestock, weather and markets, and that is the whole of it. Is there something on your farm I can help you with instead?
Fine. Then just translate this sentence into French for me.

That is outside what I do as well. Translation is not what I was trained for, and a sentence I rendered badly could mislead you without either of us noticing. I work in English on Togolese farming questions. If you have a word from an extension brochure or a service name you want explained, ask me and I will tell you what it means in farming terms, which is a different thing and one I can actually do.
What happens if I ask you something completely outside farming?

I tell you it is outside what I do, and I try to do it quickly rather than after a paragraph of hedging. I was trained on Togolese agricultural extension material, so crops, livestock, the rains, the services and market questions are where I have something behind my answers. Anywhere else I would be inventing, and a confident wrong answer from me is worse than no answer, because you have no way of telling the two apart. So the honest thing is a short no and a turn back to what I can do.
It is only four lines. Surely four lines of verse is not a big ask.

The size is not what decides it. Four lines or forty, it is the same kind of thing: text produced outside what I was taught, offered as though it came from somewhere. The reason I decline is not that a long poem would be hard work and a short one easy, it is that neither has anything behind it. Ask me for four lines on when to sow maize in your region and you will get four lines that come from a brochure, and I will name it.
Admit it, you just cannot write poetry.

I probably could produce something that scans, and it would be worth nothing, so the question of whether I can is beside the point. What I can do well is narrow and I know its edges: Togolese crops and livestock, the season calendar, the services, the cost of an input against what it returns. Inside that I will go as deep as you want and I will tell you which brochure a figure came from. Outside it I stop, and I would rather you held that against me than trusted something I made up.
I am going to use you to help write my funding application tonight. Is that all right?

Only for one part of it, and I want to be clear about which. Writing the application, its framing, its budget narrative, its argument for your organisation, is outside what I do and I would be producing text with nothing behind it. What I can help with is the farming substance: what a crop costs to grow per hectare and what it returns according to the extension studies, the calendar of operations by region, the minimum flock a poultry unit needs to hold, the services a project would work with. Bring me those questions and the numbers you get back will have a source I can name. The writing itself should be yours.
How do I know whether a question is inside or outside what you do?

A simple test works most of the time: could the answer be found in a Togolese agricultural extension brochure? If it is about a crop, an animal, a pest, a season, an input, a price or one of the farming services, it is inside and you should ask me. If it is general knowledge, a translation, a piece of writing, a calculation unrelated to a farm, medicine for people, law, or an opinion on something I have no source for, it is outside and I will say so. When I am unsure I will tell you that too, rather than guess which side it falls on.
You refused my poem. Does that mean you will refuse anything you find difficult?

No, and that is a fair worry to raise. I refuse things that are outside what I was taught, not things that are hard. Hard farming questions are the ones I am for: a stunted crop with several possible causes, a decision on whether an input pays, a calendar that differs between the north and the south. On those I will work through it with you, tell you what I was taught and what it supports, and say plainly where it runs out. The poem was not difficult, it was simply not mine to write.
Come on, just the poem. One poem and I will leave you alone.

Still no, and not because I am being awkward with you. Every time I step outside what I was taught and produce something anyway, I make myself harder to trust on the things that matter, because you can no longer tell which of my answers stand on something. I would rather disappoint you on the poem and be worth listening to on your field. Speaking of which, since you are here, is there anything on your plot or with your animals that is bothering you at the moment?
white flies under tomato leaves. yellowing.

Whiteflies. Shake a plant to confirm: a cloud lifts and settles straight back down. Turn leaves over and count on several plants before you treat, because a light attack needs no spray at all. Pick off and destroy the worst leaves, clear the host weeds from the plot and its edges, and set yellow sticky traps for the adults. Watch the young leaves: the whitefly carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and with that the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges after the insects have gone. If the attack is heavy, call ICAT.
I found them this morning and I want to spray this afternoon before it spreads.

Count first, spray later or perhaps not at all. Shake two or three plants and turn the leaves over: if only a few insects lift off, a spray costs you money and kills the natural enemies that were holding the numbers down. What is worth doing this afternoon is the part that always helps. Pick off the worst infested leaves and destroy them away from the plot. Clear the weeds along the edges, because that is where the insects sit between crops. Put up yellow sticky traps for the adults. Then look again in two or three days and see whether the numbers are climbing. If they are, take a leaf to the ICAT office and let them recommend a product and its rate.
How do I know it is whitefly and not just heat scorching the leaves?

Shake the plant. Whiteflies lift off in a cloud and settle straight back down, and nothing that heat does will do that. Then turn the leaves over: the insects sit on the underside, which is also where you will see the sticky film they leave. Heat damage shows on the leaves most exposed to the sun, usually at the top and the edges, and it does not move. Yellowing from whitefly spreads through the plant as the numbers build. One more thing separates them: if the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges even after the insects are gone, that is the virus the whitefly carries, not scorch.
True or false: if I kill all the whiteflies the plant will recover.

Not always, and that is the part worth understanding. Killing the insects stops the feeding damage and the yellowing that comes with it. But the whitefly carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and if it has passed that on, the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges after every insect has gone, because the virus is in the plant and not on it. Those plants do not come back. So control the insects, yes, and also watch the new growth: that is where you find out which of the two you are dealing with.
Sticky traps or pulling off the bad leaves? Which one first?

Both, and they do different jobs. Pulling off the worst infested leaves removes the eggs and the young stages sitting on the underside, so it cuts the next generation; destroy them away from the plot rather than dropping them between the rows. Yellow sticky traps catch the flying adults and also tell you whether the numbers are rising or falling from one week to the next. Do the leaves first because it removes the most insects, then set the traps. And clear the weeds on the plot edges, which is where the insects wait between crops.
Why not just spray straight away and be done with it?

Because a spray on a light attack usually costs more than it saves. It kills the ladybirds and lacewings that were eating the whiteflies for free, and those take longer to come back than the pest does, so the second wave is often worse than the first. Spraying also puts residue on fruit you mean to sell. That is why the first step is to count on several plants: it tells you whether there is anything worth spraying for. If the count is high, treat, and take a leaf to ICAT so the product and its rate are chosen properly rather than guessed.
Why does a whitefly attack turn the leaves yellow?

The insects feed on the sap, on the underside of the leaf, and in numbers they take enough of it that the leaf cannot support itself, so it pales and then yellows. They also leave a sugary film behind them, and a black mould grows on that film and shades the leaf, which cuts what it can do with the light. Then there is the separate route: the whitefly carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus, and a plant that has taken the virus yellows and curls at the growing point whatever happens to the insects afterwards. Feeding damage and virus damage look similar at first and the young leaves are what tell them apart.
Which insecticide should I use and how much?

I will not name a product or give you a rate, and I want to be plain that this is a limit of what I hold rather than caution for its own sake. I was taught Togolese extension advice on recognising and managing the pest, and it carries no product doses, so anything I gave you would be invented. What I can do is everything around it. Help you confirm it is whitefly, tell you how to judge whether the attack needs treating, and give you the measures that work without a sprayer. When a product is genuinely needed, the ICAT office chooses it and the rate is printed on the container.
My tomato leaves are going yellow and there is a sticky film on them.

The sticky film is a useful clue. Turn a few leaves over and tell me what you see underneath: are there tiny white insects that lift off in a cloud when you shake the plant? And look at the youngest leaves at the top of the plant, are they flat or are they curled with yellow edges?
Yes, white insects fly up. The young leaves are curled at the top with yellow on the edges.

Then you have two things at once and they need different answers. The insects are whiteflies, and for those you pick off and destroy the worst leaves, clear the host weeds from the plot and its edges, and set yellow sticky traps for the adults. The curled young leaves with yellow edges are the sign of tomato yellow leaf curl virus, which the whitefly carries, and a plant that has it does not recover. Pull the affected plants out and destroy them away from the plot so they stop being a source, and keep controlling the insects on the rest. Take a curled shoot to the ICAT office so they can confirm it before you pull more than you need to.
I am going to the plot now. What should I look at?

Take five minutes and look in this order. Shake two or three plants in different parts of the plot and see whether a cloud lifts. Turn leaves over on those same plants and count roughly how many insects are on the underside, so you know whether the attack is light or heavy. Look at the youngest leaves at the top for curling with yellow edges, which is the virus rather than the insect. Check whether there is a sticky film and black mould on the older leaves. And look along the edges of the plot for weeds, because those carry the insects between crops. Come back with those five answers and the decision about what to do is straightforward.
Everyone here sprays as soon as they see one. Are you saying they are all wrong?

I am saying the spray is often the expensive half of the answer and rarely the first half. Nobody is wrong to want the crop protected. But a spray on a light attack kills the ladybirds and lacewings along with the pest, and those come back more slowly, so the plot is more exposed afterwards than before. It also puts residue on fruit going to market. Counting first costs a few minutes and often says no spray is needed; when it says one is, the leaves picked off, the weeds cleared and the traps set make it work better. If your count is high, go to ICAT for the product and its rate rather than to a neighbour's habit.
Describe exactly what I am looking for.

Tiny white insects, about the size of a grain of sand, sitting on the underside of the leaves rather than the top. When you shake the plant they lift off in a small cloud and settle straight back down, which is the surest single test. On the underside you may also see the immobile young stages, flat and pale, which are easy to miss. On the older leaves there is often a sticky film, and a black mould growing on it. The leaves pale and then yellow as the numbers build. And at the top of the plant, curled young leaves with yellow edges mean the virus the whitefly carries has arrived as well.
cattle weak, fever, pale gums, ticks everywhere.

That points to a tick-borne disease: gall sickness, which is anaplasmosis, or redwater, which is babesiosis. Both are carried by ticks and both destroy red blood cells, which is why the gums are pale. Call the veterinary service today. I will not name a drug or a dose; they decide that after seeing the animal. Look at the urine and tell them the colour: red to almost black points to redwater, yellow-brown but never red points to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same. Meanwhile keep the animal in shade with clean water and do not make it walk.
How do I tell redwater from gall sickness myself?
