And it says to sort before setting: throw out the eggs too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end, and set the rest pointed end down. Even sorted and fresh, the reference only plans on a hatching rate near seventy percent.
I collect about twelve eggs a day from my flock. What do I do with them if I want chicks?

Collect them every day, as you do, and put them somewhere cool, airy and dry. Sort as you go: out with the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Set what remains within seven to ten days, pointed end down. If you hatch naturally, a hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, so roughly one day of your collection fills one hen. Incubation then takes twenty-one days, with a hatching rate near seventy percent.
How many eggs can one hen sit on?

Twelve to fourteen. That is the average number of eggs to set under a brooding hen in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which treats natural brooding as one of the two ways of hatching, the other being an incubator. The sitting lasts twenty-one days. Set only sorted eggs, kept no more than seven to ten days, pointed end down, and expect a hatching rate near seventy percent.
True or false: chicks can eat the same feed as the adult hens.

False. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says young chicks must be fed separately from the adults and must have a special feed of their own: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. It adds that it is better they do not compete with the adults for food. Their feeders are a different size too, 50 cm by 50 by 5 for fifty chicks, against 150 by 12 by 16 for twenty-five adults.
taux eclosion poule locale

Near seventy percent. That is the natural hatching rate the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference plans on for commercial local hens. Around it the same reference plans six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, and a mortality rate near ten percent. They are the values used to build the study's projections, not a guarantee for your own flock.
At what temperature exactly should I run the incubator?

I was not taught that, and I will not guess a temperature, because a wrong figure would cost you the whole setting. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does say about artificial incubation is the equipment and the time: electric, gas or solar incubators, with manual or automatic turning, and an incubation of twenty-one days at the end of which the chicks come out of the shells. For the setting of the machine, follow its own instructions and ask ICAT or the supplier.
The chicks that hatched have wet sticky down and their bellies look swollen.

That is the opposite of the signs of a healthy chick in the 2017 ESFT village compendium, which describes down that is bright, dry, thick and coloured, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, a well developed body and strong legs with straight separated claws. I will not name a cause from that description, because the references I hold do not give one. Isolate those chicks from the others and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today.
I expect a hundred and twenty chicks from this hatching. Is one brooder enough?

No, you need two. A brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds sixty chicks in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so a hundred and twenty chicks ask for two of them. Feed them from chick feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5, one for fifty chicks, so three of those, and give two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred chicks. After three weeks they move into the chick room, sized at fifty chicks per square metre.
What good is a brooder if I already have broody hens?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four things it buys you. It saves the fuel you would spend heating the chicks. It handles small hatchings coming one after another. It keeps predators off the chicks. And it lets you watch their feeding and their health closely. A brooding hen does the warmth part well, and the 2017 village compendium says she adjusts it by the chicks' cries, but she takes only twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.
Just promise me the hundred eggs will all hatch if I do everything right.

I will not promise that, because the reference itself does not. The 2020 ICAT and PASA study builds its projections on a natural hatching rate near seventy percent, and on a mortality rate near ten percent afterwards. Doing everything right means sorting the eggs, keeping them no more than seven to ten days somewhere cool, airy and dry, setting them pointed end down, and holding the twenty-one days of incubation. That is what raises your odds; it does not make them a hundred.
My chicks are three weeks old today. What happens now?

They leave the brooder. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the brooder the chicks' first three weeks, then moves them into the chick room to finish growing. The chick room is the compartment with fewer openings, kept warm, its wall raised with openings for air. Size it at fifty chicks per square metre. Their drinkers change at the same time of life: from thirty to forty-five days it is three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds instead of two.
A lot of my eggs come out very dirty from the nest boxes.

Do not set the dirty ones. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists eggs that are too dirty among those to sort out before setting, along with the too small, the deformed, the too big, the cracked or fissured, and those with no pointed end. Collect every day so they spend less time in the nest, and keep what you collect somewhere cool, airy and dry, for seven to ten days at most. On the nest side, the same reference counts nest boxes among the equipment of the henhouse, and the 2017 compendium asks for well kept nest boxes for good reproduction.
Before I start selling hatching services to other keepers, what should I have?

The machine and the volume to justify it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference pairs a gas incubator of 300 eggs with a flock of sixty breeding hens, and says in the same breath that at that size the keeper should hatch for other keepers as well so the equipment pays for itself. So the hatching service is not an extra idea, it is part of how the reference makes that investment work. Keep your registers, so you can price the service from what a hatching actually costs you.
Should the chicks drink from the same drinkers as the hens?

No, they have their own, and the sizes are set by age. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds from one to thirty days, three of 3.5 litres from thirty to forty-five days, and for adult layers four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred. The 2017 village compendium is firm about why it matters for the young: clean water is what chicks need most, because they die easily of dehydration. Wash the drinkers every day.
Summarise the whole reproduction cycle as the reference plans it.

Six production cycles a year. Each hen lays about ten eggs per laying, with about six layings a year. Eggs are collected daily, sorted, held seven to ten days at most in a cool airy dry place, and set pointed end down. Incubation runs twenty-one days, naturally under a hen taking twelve to fourteen eggs, or in an electric, gas or solar incubator. The hatching rate planned is near seventy percent and mortality near ten percent. Chicks spend three weeks in the brooder, then move to the chick room.
What ingredients do I use to make feed for local chickens?

Use what is around you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with their by-products, the groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; then fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt for the minerals; and the vitamins. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds where the vitamins come from in a village flock: herbs, fruit and plant debris.
Give me the feed formula per 100 kg for a laying hen.

For a hen in lay, per 100 kg of feed, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. The laying hen takes the most mineral of all the age bands, which is why that last figure jumps. On top of the formula, add the free extras the reference lists: greenery, termites and maggots.
How much feed does one chicken eat a day?

It depends on its age. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives three periods: from 1 to 60 days, 10 to 25 grams a day, about 1.5 kg over the whole period; from 61 days to sale at six months, 25 to 35 grams a day, about 5 kg in all; and a hen in lay, 80 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing as one range: between 5 and 90 grams a bird, according to age and size.
melange mineral poule composition

For 10 kg of mineral mix the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. That mix then goes into the feed: 3 kg per 100 kg for the growing birds, and 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen in lay, which needs the most mineral.
I have sixty laying hens. How much feed do I need a day?

A hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so sixty hens eat about 4.8 kg a day, which is roughly 144 kg a month. Make it to the laying formula: per 100 kg, 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Add greenery, termites and maggots on top, and keep clean water in front of them at all times.
True or false: the same feed formula works for chicks and for laying hens.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says feeding follows the age of the birds, and gives four different formulas per 100 kg. From 1 to 8 weeks the feed carries 20 kg of cake and only 5 kg of bran; by 12 weeks and beyond it is 10 kg of cake and 17 kg of bran; and the laying hen takes 7.5 kg of mineral mix where the younger bands take 3. Feeding chicks the adult mix would leave them short of protein.
What is the formula for birds of one to eight weeks?

Per 100 kg of feed, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. That is the richest band in cake, and the only one where the reference names caterpillars as well as greenery, termites and maggots among the extras. From 9 to 12 weeks the cake drops to 15 kg and the bran rises to 15 kg.
Why does a laying hen need more mineral mix than a growing bird? Justify.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the figures but not the reason, so I will not invent one. What it shows is clear enough to act on: the mineral mix goes from 3 kg per 100 kg of feed for all the growing bands to 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen in lay, more than double. The mix itself is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt for 10 kg. For the reason, ask ICAT.
Should I buy ready-made feed or make it myself?

The Togolese references are built on making it yourself from local raw materials, and they tell you how. Use cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes and their cakes, groundnut, cotton and soya; millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt. Then follow the formula for the age band you are feeding. Making your own mineral mix is part of it: 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of calcined bone, 2 kg of charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt for 10 kg.
How should I give the water?

Freely, and always available. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is firm about it: water is distributed at will, available at all times, and the drinkers must never be empty. The water has to be clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. For chicks it matters most of all, because the 2017 ESFT compendium says they die easily of dehydration. Wash the drinkers every day.
My hens have stopped eating much and they look thin.

Going off feed and getting thin are two of the signs the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists for a sick bird, along with being dull and drowsy, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, nasal and mouth discharge, moving with difficulty and diarrhoea. So treat this as possible illness first: isolate the birds that look ill and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. Check the feed and water as well, but do not wait on that before calling.
My birds are kept shut in, they never go out on grass.

Then bring the grass to them. The 2017 ESFT compendium says hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that where they cannot, it is important to bring them a little greenery every day. The 2020 reference points the same way: on top of the formula it lists greenery, termites and maggots as the extras for every age band, with caterpillars as well for the youngest. A grassy run beside the henhouse is part of the commercial layout too.
How much feed will a batch of a hundred birds eat from hatching to sale?

About 6.5 kg a bird over the two periods, so roughly 650 kg for a hundred birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days, at 10 to 25 grams a day, then about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale at six months, at 25 to 35 grams a day. Change the formula as they grow: cake falls from 20 kg per 100 kg in the first weeks to 10 kg after twelve weeks, and bran rises.
I give all my birds 80 grams a day, that is the rule.

Eighty grams a day is the ration of a hen in lay, not of every bird. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives three levels: 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, and 80 grams a day in lay. Giving 80 grams to a young bird is three times what it needs. Match the ration to the age, and change the formula with it.
What should I have in store before a new batch arrives?

The feed for their age band first. For birds of one to eight weeks that means, per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Have the mineral mix made up: 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of calcined bone, 2 kg of charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt for 10 kg. Then clean water, drinkers that never run dry, and a way of getting greenery every day.
How much should I be feeding my birds?
How old are they, and are they laying yet?
About four months, not laying.

At four months they are in the band the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference runs from 61 days to sale at six months: 25 to 35 grams a day, about 5 kg a bird over the whole period. Feed them the formula for twelve weeks and beyond, which is per 100 kg 60 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 17 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, with greenery, termites and maggots on top. When they start laying, move them to 80 grams a day and to the laying formula.
Which vitamins exactly do my hens need, and in what dose?

I was not taught the names of the vitamins nor any dose, and I will not guess them. What the references give is where the vitamins come from. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists vitamins among the raw materials to use without naming them. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the vitamins of a village flock come from herbs, fruit and plant debris. Both put greenery in the daily ration for that reason. For named vitamins and doses, ask the animal health worker or ICAT.
Where do I find the protein part of the ration without buying it?

A good part of it is free around the compound. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names insects, termites and caterpillars among the raw materials, alongside fish meal, bone powder and oyster shells, and lists termites and maggots as extras to add on top of the formula at every age. The 2017 ESFT compendium names the same road for protein: roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products. Kitchen leftovers and millet beer draff also count.
True or false: it is enough to fill the drinkers once in the morning.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the water must be renewed at least twice a day, that it must be clean and served in the shade, and that it is given freely and available at all times, with the drinkers never empty. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds that the drinkers and feeders should be washed every day for good hygiene in the henhouse. For chicks this is the point that kills fastest: they die easily of dehydration.
ration poule en ponte gramme jour

Eighty grams a day. That is the ration of a hen in lay in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, against 25 to 35 grams a day for birds from 61 days to sale at six months, and 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days. Feed her the laying formula with it: per 100 kg, 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix.
For the mineral part, oyster shells or crushed charcoal?

Both, in the same mix. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives an indicative mineral mix of 10 kg made of 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. It is not a choice between them, it is a recipe. That mix then goes in at 3 kg per 100 kg of feed for growing birds and 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen in lay.
I cannot find fish meal in my area this month. What now?

Look at the other protein sources the references name before changing the formula. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists, beside fish meal, the groundnut, cotton and soya cakes, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars. The 2017 ESFT compendium names roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products for the same purpose. Termites and maggots are already among the extras to add on top of the formula. For a substitution that keeps the balance, ask ICAT.
Why serve the water in the shade? Justify.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the instruction without a reason, so I will not make one up. It says plainly that the water must be clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day, and that it is given freely with the drinkers never empty. Follow it as written. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds the washing of the drinkers every day, and warns that chicks die easily of dehydration, which is why their water comes first.
The chicks crowd the feeder and the bigger ones push the small ones away.

Two things to fix. First, the chicks should not be eating with the adults at all: the 2017 ESFT compendium says young chicks must be fed separately, with their own ration, and that it is better they do not compete with the adults for food. Second, count your feeders: the 2020 reference sizes a chick feeder at 50 cm by 50 by 5 for fifty chicks. If you have more chicks than that per feeder, add feeders rather than food.
How does the formula change across the four age bands?

Per 100 kg of feed, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. From 1 to 8 weeks: 62 cereals, 20 cake, 10 fish meal, 5 bran, 3 mineral. From 9 to 12 weeks: 62, 15, 5, 15, 3. From 12 weeks on: 60, 10, 10, 17, 3. Hen in lay: 57.5, 10, 10, 15, 7.5. So the cake falls as the bird grows, the bran rises, and the mineral more than doubles when she starts laying.
Give me the price of a bag of feed, I do not want formulas.

I will not give you a price. The amounts in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference are 2020 evaluations and prices move, so a figure from me would mislead you at the market. What I can give you is the quantity, which is what you need to ask for a quote: a hen in lay eats 80 grams a day, a bird from 61 days to sale 25 to 35 grams a day. Take those to a feed seller, or to ICAT, and get today's price on that volume.
What do I do each morning before feeding?

Clean before you serve. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the feeders and drinkers are washed every day for good hygiene in the henhouse, and the 2020 reference asks for clean water served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day, with the drinkers never empty. Feed the chicks apart from the adults. Then, while the birds eat, watch them: a bird that does not eat, keeps away from the flock or looks dull is one to isolate and report to the animal health worker.
Can kitchen leftovers really go to the chickens?

Yes, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names kitchen leftovers among the local raw materials to use for making poultry feed, alongside cereals, legumes and their cakes, millet beer draff, fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars. They are part of the ration, not a replacement for it: the formula for the age band still sets the balance, and greenery, termites and maggots go on top at every age.
I want to mix 50 kg of laying feed. What quantities?

Halve the formula for 100 kg. The 2020 ICAT and PASA laying formula is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg, so for 50 kg take 28.75 kg of cereals, 5 kg of cake, 5 kg of fish meal, 7.5 kg of bran and 3.75 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral mix from 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of calcined bone, 2 kg of charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt per 10 kg.
Greenery is just filler, my birds get the formula so they do not need it.

Both references keep greenery in the ration on purpose. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists greenery, termites and maggots as the extras to add on top of the formula at every age band, with caterpillars as well for the youngest. The 2017 ESFT compendium says hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that where they cannot, it is important to bring them a little greenery every day. It also names herbs, fruit and plant debris as the source of their vitamins.
How do I know one of my birds is sick?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists eight signs. The bird is sad, drowsy and downcast. Its wings droop and its feathers stand up. It keeps away from the flock. It does not eat. It is thin. It has a discharge from the nose and the mouth. It moves with difficulty. And it has diarrhoea. If you see these, isolate that bird from the others straight away and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary the same day.
Disease has broken out in my henhouse. What do I do?

Six things, from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. Isolate the sick birds. Forbid any trading in your henhouse. Forbid any visit that has no precise purpose. Inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly. Never eat the carcasses. And burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds to take the dead birds out as fast as you can and bury them far from the henhouse.
Why must I isolate the sick birds? Justify.

Because of how disease travels. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says hygiene comes down to one idea, keeping the animals away from the germs or the germs away from the animals, and that disease comes in through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material. Isolation is the first of its three principles of separation, with quarantining every newly bought bird and not mixing your animals with those of other farms. The 2017 compendium says the same: isolate or take out the sick birds to treat them.
Can I wear any shoes to go into the henhouse?

Be careful with shoes, because they are named as a way disease gets in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says disease is introduced through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material, and it names farm equipment, a vehicle, and contaminated clothes and shoes. The 2017 compendium points the same way when it says not to visit other farms. Boots are listed among the keeper's equipment for the henhouse, along with work clothes.
True or false: a viral disease can be cured with antibiotics.

False, and this is worth knowing before you spend money. The 2017 ESFT village compendium states it plainly: no treatment cures a viral disease. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus what you have is prevention and vaccination, which is why the references insist on hygiene, quarantine and vaccinating before the disease arrives. If birds fall ill, call the animal health worker rather than buying something at the market.
I treated my hens last week. Can I eat the eggs?

Wait a few days. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says the meat and the eggs of a hen that has been treated can hold drug residues, and that you must therefore avoid eating those products for a few days. It does not give an exact number of days, so ask the animal health worker who gave the treatment, since the wait depends on the product. Keep the health register as well, where the treatments are written down with their dates.
One of my hens stays in the corner alone, her wings hang down and her feathers are all puffed up.

What you describe matches three of the eight signs of a sick bird in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference: keeping away from the flock, drooping wings, and feathers standing up. The others to look for are being sad and drowsy, not eating, being thin, a discharge from the nose and mouth, moving with difficulty, and diarrhoea. Isolate her from the rest today, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. I will not name the disease from these signs alone.
I just bought five hens at the market. Can I put them with the others?

Not straight away. Quarantine them for two weeks first. Both Togolese references say it: the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for a two week quarantine for birds bought or given, and repeats it for hens acquired on a poultry market, so that you do not bring a disease into the flock. The 2020 reference makes it one of its three principles of separation, alongside not mixing your animals with those of other farms and isolating the ones that are ill.
Which disinfectants are recommended and at what strength?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names five: caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent, and quicklime at 10 percent. It says disinfection comes after a methodical cleaning, and that applied properly it inactivates the microbes still present. And it gives one instruction you must not skip: goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are compulsory when you use them.
What must I put on before I disinfect the henhouse?

Goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference makes those compulsory when disinfecting, because the products it names are strong: caustic soda at 1 percent, formol at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent, quicklime at 10 percent. Clean the building thoroughly first, since the reference says a good cleaning already removes a good part of the germs, and disinfect after that.
Should I clean the henhouse first or disinfect first?

Clean first, disinfect after. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts them in that order and explains the point of each: a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs, and disinfection, once the cleaning has been done methodically, inactivates the microbes still present. Wear goggles, gloves and a gas mask for the disinfecting. The 2017 compendium adds the routine: sweep inside two or three times a week, and wash feeders and drinkers every day.
quarantaine nouvelle poule combien de temps

Two weeks. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says to quarantine newly bought or newly given birds for two weeks so you do not bring a disease into the flock, and it repeats the two weeks for hens bought on a poultry market. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts quarantining every newly bought bird among its three principles of separation, with not mixing your animals with other farms' and isolating the sick.
A bird died this morning so we will cook it tonight, no waste.

Do not eat it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is explicit in its list of what to do when disease appears in the flock: never eat the carcasses. It says to burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same in its own words, to take the dead birds out as quickly as possible and bury them far from the henhouse, and not to throw carcasses out in the open. Inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly.
Why should I not visit my neighbour's poultry farm? Justify.

Because you carry the germs back on yourself. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says disease is introduced through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material, and it names farm equipment, a vehicle, and contaminated clothes and shoes. The 2017 ESFT compendium turns that into three don'ts for cutting transmission: do not visit other farms, do not throw carcasses out in the open, and do not let your hens wander.
Several of my birds are dropping dead and I live far from any vet.

Act on the flock today, and get word to the service even if you cannot reach it in person. Isolate every bird that looks ill. Stop all trading in your henhouse and refuse visits that have no precise purpose. Do not eat the carcasses. Take the dead birds out at once and keep them for the veterinary service, which the reference asks to be present when they are burned or buried. Then inform the veterinary service of your locality, or the village livestock auxiliary, as quickly as you can.
True or false: it is forbidden to sweep the henhouse.

False. Sweeping is asked for, not forbidden. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says to sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and to throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it, adding that those droppings then fertilise your fields. Cleaning is also the second of the three hygiene principles in the 2020 reference, which says a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs.
True or false: washing the drinkers and feeders is not necessary.

False. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says that for good hygiene in the henhouse the feeders and the drinkers must be washed every day. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference goes the same way on water: it must be clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day, with the drinkers never empty. Add to that sweeping the henhouse two or three times a week, and spraying disinfectant inside the shelter after the litter is renewed.
There are lice and small ticks all over my birds and in the shelter.

The 2017 ESFT village compendium treats that as a litter and disinfection matter: spray disinfectant inside the shelter after the litter has been renewed, above all when there are lice, ticks or fleas. So renew the litter first, then spray. Wear goggles, gloves and a gas mask if you use the strong products named in the 2020 reference. Clean around the henhouse too, since a tuft of grass shelters animals that bring disease. If birds also look dull or thin, call the animal health worker.
What are the simple things that stop disease before it starts?

The 2017 ESFT compendium sums it up as clean water, sound feed, decent housing and good care, and it says a good keeper calls an animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time he sees disease in the flock, and asks about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. Add its three don'ts: do not visit other farms, do not throw carcasses out in the open, do not let the hens wander. And quarantine every new bird for two weeks.
Some of my chickens look unwell.
What exactly do you see on them, and is it one bird or several?
Three of them, they do not eat and they have runny noses.

Not eating and a discharge from the nose are two of the eight signs of a sick bird in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, with being sad and drowsy, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, being thin, moving with difficulty and diarrhoea. Isolate those three today. Stop trading in the henhouse and refuse visits without a purpose. Then inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly. I will not name the disease from these signs.
Which antibiotic should I give and at what dose?

I will not name a medicine or a dose. That comes from the animal health worker or the veterinary service of your locality, who sees the birds. What I can tell you is the frame around it. The 2017 ESFT compendium says no treatment cures a viral disease, and that medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases, so the right product depends on what the birds actually have. And after any treatment, do not eat the meat or the eggs for a few days, because they can hold residues.
A buyer wants to come and see the flock while some birds are sick. What do I do first?

Put the visit off. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says that when disease appears in the flock you forbid any trading in your henhouse and forbid any visit that has no precise purpose. Isolate the sick birds, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, and do not sell until the service has seen them. The 2017 compendium points the same way when it says not to visit other farms in order to cut transmission: what applies to you applies to your buyer.
My birds are thin and they walk badly, as if their legs hurt.

Being thin and moving with difficulty are two of the eight signs of a sick bird in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The full list adds being sad, drowsy and downcast, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, not eating, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, and diarrhoea. Check the others on your birds. Isolate the ones affected and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. I will not name a disease from a description alone.
I am adding twelve new hens to a flock of sixty. How long before they can mix?

Two weeks, whatever the number. The quarantine in the 2017 ESFT compendium is two weeks for newly bought or newly given birds, and it applies to the twelve just as it would to one. Keep them apart from the sixty for that time, with their own feeders and drinkers, and watch them for the eight signs of a sick bird. Only then put them together. Recall too that your sixty hens go with six cocks at one cock for ten.
Why clean the grass and bushes around the henhouse? Justify.

Because of what hides in them. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says to clean around the henhouse regularly, and gives the reason: it avoids a tuft of grass that can shelter predators or other animals that are a source of disease. It names snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. The same compendium asks for a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, noting that a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one.
I do not have time for quarantine, just tell me it is fine to mix them.

I will not tell you that, because both Togolese references say the opposite and the cost falls on your whole flock. The 2017 ESFT compendium asks for two weeks of quarantine on every bird bought or given, so that you do not bring a disease into the herd. The 2020 reference counts it among its three principles of separation. Mortality from disease can wipe out an entire flock, which is the loss the compendium warns about. Two weeks is the cheap insurance.
A bird died. Do I bury it behind the house or burn it?

Either, but not alone and not nearby. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service, and never to eat the carcasses. The 2017 ESFT compendium says to take the dead birds out as quickly as possible and bury them far from the henhouse, and not to throw carcasses out in the open. So inform the veterinary service of your locality first, and keep the carcass until they come.
By what routes does disease get into a flock?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names them: contact with sick animals, contact with soiled droppings and secretions, and contaminated material, which it details as farm equipment, a vehicle, and contaminated clothes and shoes. Against those routes it sets three principles. Separation: do not mix your animals with other farms', quarantine every newly bought bird, isolate the sick. Cleaning, which already removes a good part of the germs. And disinfection, which inactivates what the cleaning left.
My whole flock has diarrhoea.

Diarrhoea is one of the eight signs of a sick bird in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, alongside being sad and drowsy, drooping wings and raised feathers, keeping away from the flock, not eating, being thin, discharge from the nose and mouth, and moving with difficulty. When it affects the whole flock, treat it as an outbreak: isolate the worst affected, stop trading in the henhouse, refuse visits without a purpose, and inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly. I will not name the disease.
Who should I call when something goes wrong with the birds?

The animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. The 2017 ESFT compendium says a good keeper calls one of them every time he sees cases of disease in his flock, and that he also asks them about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly when disease appears, and wants that service present when dead animals are burned or buried. For the vaccination programme, the same people.
How much money do I need to start a local hen farm in Togo?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference evaluates the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, and the working capital for the first year at 2,150,491 FCFA. Those are 2020 evaluations for one commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, not today's prices. The investment covers the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests and the birds themselves. Take the figures to ICAT and rebuild them at current prices.
Will I make money in the first year?

A little, and much more in the second. The annual projection of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices. It explains the jump itself: more birds are sold in the second year, and the financial charges fall. So plan your first year as the year you build the flock, not the year you live off it.
What can I actually sell from a hen farm?

Three things, not one. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts birds, eggs and droppings. Its first year projection sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, for 3,487,181 FCFA in all, in 2020 prices. The droppings are worth noting: the same reference wants a manure pit so they can be turned into something the fields can use.
investissement depart poule locale combien

3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, for a commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, according to the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference. Add 2,150,491 FCFA of working capital for the first year. Both are 2020 evaluations and prices move, so use them as a structure and put current prices in the same rows. ICAT holds the reference and can help you redo the budget.
What goes into the working capital for the first year?

Feed is most of it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, covering the breeder, chick and grower rations, plus the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Feed being the bulk is why the ration matters so much to your result: a hen in lay alone eats 80 grams a day.
Why is the second year so much better than the first? Justify.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the reason itself: the improvement in the net result of years two and three over year one comes from the larger number of animals sold in those years, and from the reduction in the financial charges. In figures, the net result goes from 131,785 FCFA in year one to 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices. So the first year builds the flock and carries the heaviest charges.
Who am I going to sell my chickens and eggs to?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not name buyers, and I will not invent any. What it gives is how to find and keep them: look for your clients before the batch starts, not after; learn what they want and offer products that meet it; keep a client register; sign contracts with them where you can, and honour what the contract says. To make the farm known, it lists radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard.
How do I set my selling price?

From your own figures, in the order the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives. Record every expense. Work out the cost of production per head. Decide the profit you want per head. Then set your selling price and compare it with the market price, and readjust if the market asks for it. That is why the reference wants you keeping a register of money in and out: without it you are guessing your own cost.
What should I do before I even buy the first birds?

Find your buyers. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to look for your clients before the batch starts, not after, and to learn what they want so you can offer products that meet it. Alongside that, open the registers you will need: visits, movements of the flock with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out. Then build your budget on the reference's rows with today's prices.
True or false: droppings are waste and have no value.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts droppings as one of the three products of the farm, with the birds and the eggs, and its first year projection sells 50 kg of them at 1,000 FCFA. It also wants a manure pit so the droppings can be turned into something the fields can use, and because that limits the spread of disease. The 2017 ESFT village compendium says the same: those droppings serve to fertilise your fields.
If I only have half that money, can I start at half the size?

Be careful, because the study does not scale down cleanly. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference calls 60 hens and 6 cocks the minimum breeding nucleus for a commercial unit to hold, and its investment of 3,850,124 FCFA and working capital of 2,150,491 FCFA, in 2020 prices, are built on that size. Half the flock would be below the minimum it defends, and some costs like the well and the incubator do not halve. Ask ICAT to size a smaller project properly.
What does a chicken sell for at the market today?

I cannot tell you today's price, and I will not guess one. What I have is a planning figure from 2020: the ICAT and PASA reference projects birds sold at 2,250 FCFA a head, eggs at 100 FCFA and droppings at 1,000 FCFA a kilo, all in 2020 prices. Prices move. Go and see for yourself at the market, or ask ICAT, and put the price you find into the same rows to see whether your own farm still shows a profit.
What records should a poultry keeper hold?

Four kinds, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. A visits register. A movements register, where the sales, the hatchings and the deaths of the flock are written down. A prophylactic calendar, that is the programme of vaccinations and treatments. A health follow-up register. And a record of money in and out. They are not paperwork for its own sake: without the money record you cannot work out your cost of production per head, which is the first step in setting your price.
I want to know if poultry is worth it for me.
Are you asking about a commercial unit, or about keeping a few birds at the compound?
Commercial, I want it to be my work.

Then here is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. Investment 3,850,124 FCFA, first year working capital 2,150,491 FCFA. First year sales 3,487,181 FCFA from 1,422 birds, 2,376 eggs and 50 kg of droppings. Net result 131,785 FCFA in year one, then 2,790,400 FCFA in year two once more birds are sold and the financial charges fall. Redo those rows at today's prices with ICAT before you decide.
I read that a hen farm makes almost three million the first year, so I will borrow on that.

That figure is the second year, not the first. In the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the net result is 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, both in 2020 prices, and the reference explains the gap by the larger number of animals sold in year two and the fall in financial charges. Borrowing against a second year result to cover a first year is how a farm fails. Build your plan on the first year figure, and on today's prices.
Is it better to sell the eggs or to hatch them?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does both in the same projection: it sells 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA in the first year and still produces 1,422 birds to sell at 2,250 FCFA each, in 2020 prices. So it is not one or the other. What decides the split is your flock and your buyers, which is why the reference tells you to find your clients before the batch starts and to keep a client register. Work your own cost per head before choosing.
The bank wants a business plan from me. What do I put in it?

Use the structure of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference, which is built for exactly that. It has an investment line for the start-up, a working capital need for the first year, an estimate of sales, and a projected trading account over three years. Its own 2020 figures are 3,850,124 FCFA of investment, 2,150,491 FCFA of working capital, 3,487,181 FCFA of first year sales and a net result of 131,785 FCFA. Put your own quantities and today's prices in those rows, with ICAT.
Why look for buyers before I even have birds to sell? Justify.

Because the reference puts it first in its own order. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says the keeper must look for the clients before the batch starts, learn what they want, and offer products that meet their needs, then keep a client register and sign contracts where possible and respect them. A bird ready to sell with no buyer is a bird still eating your feed, and feed is the bulk of your working capital.
How many birds must I sell in a year to cover the working capital?

Work it from the reference's own rows. In 2020 prices it sells birds at 2,250 FCFA a head and puts the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, so covering that from birds alone would take about 956 birds. Its own first year projection sells 1,422 birds, plus 2,376 eggs and 50 kg of droppings, for 3,487,181 FCFA. Redo the same division with today's price per head, because 2,250 FCFA is a 2020 figure.
How do I let people know my farm exists?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists the ways: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds and what comes from them, word of mouth, and a signboard. Alongside the publicity it asks for the groundwork: know your clients before the batch starts, learn what they want, keep a client register, and sign contracts where you can and respect them. Publicity brings people; the register and the contracts keep them.
True or false: the prices in the reference are what I will get at the market this year.

False, and this matters. Every amount in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference is a 2020 evaluation and an annual projection for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Prices move. Use the reference for its structure, the rows of investment, working capital, sales and trading account, and put today's prices into those rows yourself. Then compare. ICAT can help you redo the budget at current prices.
Set out the first year projection line by line.

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Investment 3,850,124 FCFA. Working capital for the first year 2,150,491 FCFA. Sales 3,487,181 FCFA, made of 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA. Net result 131,785 FCFA. In year two the net result rises to 2,790,400 FCFA, because more animals are sold and the financial charges fall.
Just give me one number, how much will I earn per month?

There is no monthly figure in the reference, and I will not make one up by dividing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives annual projections: a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. A hen farm does not earn evenly month by month, because the sales come with the batches. Keep the money register and you will see your own rhythm.
I sell birds all the time but at the end of the year I have nothing left.

That is the gap the reference's own method is meant to close. It says to record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, then set your price and compare it with the market, readjusting if the market asks. Without the money in and out register you cannot know your cost per head, so you can be selling below it without seeing it. Open the four registers and price from your own figures.
Sell to whoever turns up, or sign a contract?

Sign where you can. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists signing contracts with your clients among the ways of keeping them, and adds that you must then respect what the contract says. Around it: find your clients before the batch starts, learn their requirements, offer products that meet them, and keep a client register. Selling to whoever turns up leaves you taking whatever price is offered on the day.
Before I fix a price for my birds, what do I need to have done?

Three things, in the order the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives them. Record every expense, so you have real numbers. Work out your cost of production per head from them. Decide the profit you want per head. Only then set the selling price, compare it with the market price, and readjust if the market asks. The money in and out register is what makes the first step possible, which is why it is one of the four registers the reference asks you to keep.

2,790,400 FCFA in 2020 prices, against 131,785 FCFA in year one, in the annual projection of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. The reference explains the rise by the larger number of animals sold in the second year and by the fall in the financial charges. These are 2020 evaluations, not today's earnings.
My buyers keep changing, nobody comes back twice.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference treats keeping clients as its own question, separate from finding them. Its answers are to sign contracts with your clients where you can, and to respect the content of the contract. Before that, know your clients' requirements and offer products that meet their needs, and keep a client register so you know who bought what. On the publicity side it lists radio, fairs, leaflets, word of mouth and a signboard.
I am a young farmer with no capital at all. Is this for me?

Look at the numbers before you decide. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA and the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and its first year net result is only 131,785 FCFA. So the first year returns little while the outlay is heavy. That does not mean no, it means go to ICAT with these rows and build a plan at today's prices before borrowing anything.
Which bank or programme will finance this for me?

I was not taught which banks or programmes finance poultry, and I will not name one. What I can give you is what a lender will ask for, which the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is built to supply: an investment figure, a working capital need, an estimate of sales and a projected trading account. Bring those rows filled with your own quantities and today's prices. ICAT holds the reference and advises on setting up, so start there.
What can I sow in the region of the Plateaux in October?

October falls in the second rains of the south: FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons there, around March to June and again around October. But none of the references I hold says which crop to sow in a given month, so I will not name one. What they do give is the main season calendar for Plateaux, sowing in April and May when the rains are settled, and that the second season plot in the south is chosen in July. For October in your own prefecture, ask ICAT, and ANAMET for this year's rains, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.
When is the sowing season in Togo?

It depends where you are, because Togo does not have one calendar but two. In Maritime and Plateaux, in the south, sow in April and May, when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes, sow in June and July. Do not sow on one isolated shower. The south has two rainy seasons and the north only one, with Centrale in between, behaving either way.
Describe the rainfall pattern of the country region by region.

FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October, and one in the north, around May to October. Maritime and Plateaux are the two season regions, Kara and Savanes the one season regions, and Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way. That is why the operations are dated twice in the technical sheets, once for the south and once for the north.
When should I clear the plot and when should I plough?

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure dates both by region. Clear the plot in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, in April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Then plough at the first rains: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Sowing follows when the rains are properly settled, which is April to May in the south and June to July in the north.
