June to July, when the rains are properly settled. Kara is in the northern group with Centrale and Savanes, which has one rainy season, around May to October according to FAO GIEWS. Clear the plot in April and May there, plough at the first rains in June and July, and sow in the same window. Do not sow on one isolated shower: wait until it rains regularly.
Why should I not sow after the first rain? Justify.

Because a single shower is not the season. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and the maize brochure adds plainly not to sow on a first isolated shower. Behind that lies the reason the calendar fiche gives for calling ANAMET: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so the date on the calendar is a guide and the rain itself is the signal.
Give me a month by month table of what to sow all year in Togo.

I do not have that, and I will not build one from guesswork. None of the references I hold gives a month by month choice of crop for a region. What they give is the shape of the seasons, two rainy seasons in the south and one in the north, and the dated operations of the main season for maize: clearing, ploughing and sowing, once for Maritime and Plateaux and once for Centrale, Kara and Savanes. For a calendar for your own prefecture, ask ICAT, and ANAMET for this year's rains.
I am in the Plateaux and I want a second crop after my maize harvest.

The south does have a second season, and the Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot for it is chosen in July, against January for the main season. One warning goes with it: the maize brochure says maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and on late sowings in the north. So a second season maize needs an improved tolerant variety, and late sowing should be avoided. For what suits your prefecture and this year's rains, ask ICAT and ANAMET.
True or false: the whole of Togo sows at the same time.

False. The country has two calendars. Maritime and Plateaux sow in April and May; Centrale, Kara and Savanes sow in June and July. The clearing and the ploughing shift the same way: clearing in February and March in the south against April and May in the north, ploughing in April and May in the south against June and July in the north. The south also has a second rainy season, which the north does not.
Should I follow the calendar date or wait for the rain?

Wait for the rain, and use the date as the frame. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and gives the windows: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The calendar fiche explains why the rain wins: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. That is also why it sends you to ANAMET for this year's rains.
It rained hard once last week and everyone in the village is sowing.

One hard rain is not the settled rains. The maize brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and the sowing fiche says plainly not to sow on a first isolated shower. Check the window for where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, ask ANAMET what this season is doing before you follow your neighbours.
When is the plot chosen for each season?

The Togolese Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot is chosen in January for the main season and in July for the second, shorter season, in Maritime and Plateaux. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the plot is chosen in April. After that comes the clearing, February and March in the south and April and May in the north, then the ploughing at the first rains, then the sowing once the rains are settled.
I live in Kara and I will sow in April like they do in Lome.

April is the southern window, not yours. Kara belongs with Centrale and Savanes, where sowing is in June and July, once the rains are properly settled. April and May in Kara is the time for clearing the plot, and the ploughing comes in June and July with the first rains. The south and the north do not share a calendar: FAO GIEWS puts the northern rains around May to October against two seasons in the south.
How do I prepare for a season that starts late?

Choose the cycle against the season you have left rather than the calendar date. The maize brochure ties a cycle to timing in one place, the maize then cotton succession in the same year, where it says to sow an extra early variety of 75 to 85 days. Improved varieties of that length exist in the list of nine released in Togo. Avoid late sowing in any case, since maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and late sowings in the north. Ask ANAMET for this year's rains.
Is it too late to sow?
Which region are you in, and what month is it for you?
Savanes, and we are in August.

August is past the sowing window for your region, which is June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes once the rains are settled. FAO GIEWS puts the northern rains around May to October, so the season is running out rather than starting. Late sowing carries a known risk: the maize brochure says maize streak virus does its damage mainly on late sowings in the north. Ask ICAT for your prefecture and ANAMET for what is left of this year's rains before you commit seed.
Why does a second season crop need a tolerant variety? Justify.

Because of where the disease strikes. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says maize streak virus does its damage mainly on the second season sowings in the south and on the late sowings in the north. Its own answer is to use only improved varieties, which it says are all tolerant to the virus, and to avoid late sowing. So a second season crop is the exposed one, and the variety is the protection you choose before you sow.
What should I do before the rains come?

Choose and clear the plot. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot is chosen in January for the main season in Maritime and Plateaux and in April in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The maize brochure then puts the clearing in February and March in the south and April and May in the north, a little before the first rains. The ploughing comes with those first rains, and the sowing only once the rains are settled.
Will the rains be good this year in the Plateaux?

I cannot know that. I am offline, I do not forecast, and only ANAMET issues forecasts and warnings in Togo. What I can tell you is the pattern: FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October. And the reason the question matters, which the calendar fiche states: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why a sowing date is a guide and not a rule. Ask ANAMET for this season.
I have just moved from Lome to Dapaong and I do not know when to start.

You have moved from a two season region to a one season one, so your whole calendar shifts. In Maritime you sowed in April and May; where you are now, in the Savanes, sowing is in June and July, once the rains are settled. Choose your plot in April rather than January, clear it in April and May, and plough with the first rains in June and July. FAO GIEWS puts the northern rains around May to October. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your new prefecture.
True or false: Centrale follows the northern calendar.

Not exactly. Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way, which is why it is not simply northern. For the dated operations the maize brochure groups it with Kara and Savanes: clearing in April and May, ploughing in June and July, sowing in June and July. But the country's two patterns are two rainy seasons in the south and one in the north, and Centrale is the transition. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your prefecture rather than the region.
Just give me one date to sow, I do not want regions and seasons.

There is no single date, and giving you one would cost you the crop. The window depends on where you are: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And inside that window the signal is the rain, not the date, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Sow when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. ANAMET can tell you what this season is doing.
Explain the difference between the north and the south for farming.

The difference is the number of rainy seasons. FAO GIEWS describes two in the south, around March to June and again around October, and one in the north, around May to October. Maritime and Plateaux therefore have a main season and a second, shorter one, with the second season plot chosen in July. Kara and Savanes have a single season, with the plot chosen in April. Centrale sits between and can behave either way. Everything else follows: clearing, ploughing and sowing shift by about two months.
The rains stopped in the middle of my season last year and I lost everything.

I cannot tell you whether it will happen again, since only ANAMET forecasts. What the references let me say is where the choice lies. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why the sowing signal is regular rain and not a date. And the variety cycle is the lever you hold: the nine improved maize varieties released in Togo run from 75 to 85 days at the shortest up to 105 to 115 days, and one of them, Amen, is marked as drought tolerant. Ask ICAT which suits your prefecture.
Set out the full main season calendar for Maritime and Plateaux.

Plot chosen in January, according to the Ministry of Agriculture citing ITRA. Clearing in February and March, per the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure. Ploughing at the first rains, in April and May. Sowing in April to May, once the rains are settled and it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. The second, shorter season of the south starts from a plot chosen in July. Remember that the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so check with ANAMET.
For a short season, a 75 day variety or a 110 day one?

The brochure ties a short cycle to a tight window in one place: in the maize then cotton succession within the same year it says to sow an extra early variety of 75 to 85 days. So the two crops do not sit together for long. Among the nine improved varieties released in Togo, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM run 75 to 85 days, while Obatanpa runs 100 to 110 and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W 105 to 115. Ask ICAT which suits your region this season.
petite saison sud togo quand

FAO GIEWS places the second rains of the south around October, the main ones being around March to June. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA, says the plot for that second season is chosen in July in Maritime and Plateaux, against January for the main season. None of the references says which crop to sow in it, so ask ICAT for your prefecture, and remember that second season sowings in the south are the ones most hit by maize streak virus.
My neighbours say the seasons are not what they were when they were young.

The references I hold do not measure that change, so I will not put figures on it. What they do say points the same way in practice: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so a sowing date is a guide and the regular rain is the signal. That is why the calendar fiche sends you to ANAMET for this year's rains and to ICAT for your prefecture. Among the nine improved maize varieties, Amen is the one marked tolerant to drought.
What do I check before choosing my variety for the season?

Check the season you actually have. Your sowing window depends on region, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, and the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so ask ANAMET. Then match the cycle: the nine improved varieties released in Togo run from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115 days. And if you are sowing a second season crop in the south, take one tolerant to maize streak virus.
There are two seasons everywhere in Togo, so I can sow twice in Savanes.

Not in the Savanes. FAO GIEWS describes two rainy seasons in the south and only one in the north, around May to October. The two season regions are Maritime and Plateaux, where the second season plot is chosen in July; Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way. In the Savanes you have one window, sowing in June and July once the rains are settled. Ask ICAT for your prefecture before planning a second crop.
How much time do I have between clearing and sowing in the Plateaux?

About two months in the main season. In Maritime and Plateaux the maize brochure puts the clearing in February and March, a little before the first rains, then the ploughing at those first rains in April and May, and the sowing in April to May once the rains are settled. So clearing runs ahead of sowing by roughly two months. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes the same sequence sits two months later, clearing in April and May and sowing in June and July.
Which maize variety should I plant?

Choose on the cycle and on the yield, the two things the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure tells you to weigh. Nine improved varieties were released in Togo. The shortest, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, run 75 to 85 days for 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare on average. The longest, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, run 105 to 115 days for 3 to 4 tonnes. Obatanpa sits at 100 to 110 days for 3.5 to 4 tonnes. Buy the seed only from approved sellers, and ask ICAT which suits your region.
There is striga in my field. Which maize can I plant?

Two of the nine improved varieties are marked tolerant to striga: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days for 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare on average. And ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days for 3 to 4 tonnes. The variety alone is not the whole answer: the brochure says to use a striga tolerant maize together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and to pull the striga plants out before they flower.
The rains are short where I am. Which variety holds up?

Amen is the one the brochure marks as tolerant to drought, at 90 to 95 days for 2 to 3 tonnes a hectare on average, with a white grain. If your season is short as well as dry, the two extra early varieties are TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM at 75 to 85 days, which finish sooner, though they average only 1.5 to 2 tonnes. Ask ICAT which of them is available near you and suits your region this season.
Can I use grain from my own granary as seed?

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure warns against it. It says that farmers who take grain from their granaries to sow are using seed that is often of poor quality and that does not germinate well, and it counts that among the reasons national yields stay low. Its instruction is to use improved varieties and to buy the seed only from approved sellers, and it repeats the warning: avoid buying seed anywhere other than from approved sellers.
Give me the full list of released varieties with their figures.

Nine, from the ITRA and ICAT brochure, with cycle in days and average yield in tonnes a hectare. TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85, 1.5 to 2, white, striga tolerant. EV99 QPM, 75 to 85, 1.5 to 2, white. Pool 18 QPM SR, 90 to 95, 2 to 3, yellow. Amen, 90 to 95, 2 to 3, white, drought tolerant. AB11, 90 to 100, 2 to 3, white, streak tolerant. Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100, 2 to 3.5, white, very steady. Obatanpa, 100 to 110, 3.5 to 4, white. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115, 3 to 4, white, striga tolerant. Sotubaka, 105 to 115, 3 to 4, yellow.
Why does the brochure show two yield columns? Justify.

Because one is what the variety can do and the other is what you are likely to get. The brochure defines the potential yield as the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, and it names them: rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field. The average column stands beside it in the same table. Obatanpa shows the gap plainly: 6 tonnes a hectare potential against 3.5 to 4 on average. Read the average when you plan, and the potential as what good management could reach.
Obatanpa or Sotubaka?

They differ in cycle, grain colour and potential. Obatanpa runs 100 to 110 days, 6 tonnes a hectare potential and 3.5 to 4 on average, white grain, and is marked high in quality protein. Sotubaka runs 105 to 115 days, 7 tonnes potential and 3 to 4 on average, and is one of the two yellow grained varieties, marked for its yellow grain and high yield. So Obatanpa is a little shorter and averages a little more; Sotubaka has the higher ceiling. Ask ICAT which is available near you.
variete mais tolerante striure togo

AB11 is the one the table marks as tolerant to streak, at 90 to 100 days for 2 to 3 tonnes a hectare on average, white grain. But the brochure goes further: against maize streak virus it says to use only improved varieties, which it describes as all tolerant to the virus, and to avoid late sowing. So taking any of the nine released varieties is already the control against streak.
True or false: all the improved varieties have white grain.

False. Seven of the nine have white grain, and two are yellow: Pool 18 QPM SR, 90 to 95 days for 2 to 3 tonnes a hectare on average, and Sotubaka, 105 to 115 days for 3 to 4 tonnes. The brochure also notes in its section on seed that these varieties are for the most part resistant to streak and have white grain of tender texture, so the yellow ones are the exception in the list.
What do I check before buying maize seed?

Check the seller first. The ITRA and ICAT brochure says to buy the seed only from approved sellers, and repeats the warning against buying anywhere else. Then check the variety against your own case: the cycle and the yield are the two things it tells you to weigh, and the table gives both for the nine released varieties. If striga grows in your field, take one of the two striga tolerant ones. If your season is dry, take Amen. Ask the extension adviser of your locality if you are unsure.
A trader at the market sold me improved seed cheap, that is the same thing.

It is not the same thing, and the brochure is blunt about it. It says to buy seed only from approved sellers and adds a warning in its own words: avoid buying seed anywhere other than from approved sellers. The reason it gives elsewhere is what poor seed does: seed of bad quality does not germinate well, which is one of the causes it lists for low yields, alongside late weeding and fertiliser applied at low doses or not at all.
How much seed and what yield should I expect on half a hectare of Obatanpa?

For seed, the brochure counts 20 to 25 kg of grain to sow one hectare, so half a hectare takes 10 to 12.5 kg. For yield, Obatanpa averages 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare, which gives about 1.75 to 2 tonnes on half a hectare, with a potential of 6 tonnes a hectare when conditions are good. Those averages assume the rest is done: weeding on time and fertiliser at the right dose.
Which variety gives the most steady harvest year after year?

Ikenne 9449 SR is the one the table singles out for that, with the specific character of a very steady yield. It runs 90 to 100 days, with a potential of 5 tonnes a hectare and an average of 2 to 3.5. Steadiness matters because the average yield is what a field gives under ordinary conditions, while the potential is reached only when rain, fertilisation, pest pressure and upkeep are all good.
I need a maize variety for this season.
Two things decide it: how long your season is, and whether you have a particular problem in the field such as striga, streak or drought.
The season is short and there is striga.

Then TZEE W Pop STR QPM fits both: 75 to 85 days, the shortest cycle in the list, and marked tolerant to striga, with 3 tonnes a hectare potential and 1.5 to 2 on average, white grain and high in quality protein. Sow it together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. Buy the seed only from an approved seller.
Which is the newest maize variety available in Togo this year?

I cannot tell you that. The list I hold is the one released in the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure, and it is a 2008 list of nine varieties. New ones may well have been released since, and I would be guessing if I named one. ICAT holds the current list and knows what the approved sellers near you actually have in stock. What has not changed is the way to choose: on the cycle and on the yield, and on the tolerance you need.
My maize came up thin and patchy, many seeds never appeared.

Poor germination is one of the things the brochure links directly to the seed. It says that farmers who sow grain taken from their granaries use seed that is often of bad quality and germinates badly, and it counts that among the causes of low yields in the country. For the next sowing, take an improved variety from an approved seller, and treat the seed with a fungicide and insecticide product, asking the extension adviser of your locality which product to use. Sow 20 to 25 kg a hectare, two to three seeds a pocket at 3 to 5 cm.
Short cycle or long cycle, which gives more?

Long, on paper. In the table the two 75 to 85 day varieties average 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare, while the 105 to 115 day ones average 3 to 4, and Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days averages 3.5 to 4. But the brochure tells you to weigh the cycle as well as the yield, and a long cycle only pays if the season carries it. The one place the brochure ties a short cycle to timing is the maize then cotton succession, where it asks for an extra early variety of 75 to 85 days.
Which varieties are marked for protein quality?

Four of the nine carry high quality protein as their specific character: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, which is also striga tolerant, EV99 QPM, Pool 18 QPM SR, which is yellow grained, and Obatanpa. Their cycles run from 75 to 85 days for the first two, 90 to 95 for Pool 18, and 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, with average yields from 1.5 to 2 tonnes a hectare up to 3.5 to 4 for Obatanpa. Ask ICAT which are available near you.
Why is choosing an improved variety already a protection against streak? Justify.

Because of what the brochure says about the list itself. In its section on protecting the crop it states that to fight maize streak virus you must use only improved varieties, since they are all tolerant to the virus, and avoid late sowing. In its section on seed it puts it slightly more cautiously, that these varieties are for the most part resistant to streak. Either way, the variety is where the protection is chosen, before sowing, and no spray cures an infected plant.
I am sowing a second season crop in the Plateaux. Does the variety matter?

It matters more than in the main season. The brochure says maize streak virus does its damage mainly on the second season sowings in the south and on the late sowings in the north, and its answer is to use only improved varieties, all tolerant to the virus, and to avoid late sowing. AB11 is the one the table marks explicitly as streak tolerant, at 90 to 100 days. Ask ICAT what an approved seller near you has for the second season.
rendement obatanpa

Obatanpa averages 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare, with a potential of 6 tonnes, over a cycle of 100 to 110 days, white grain, marked high in quality protein. The potential is the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, which the brochure defines as rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field. It is also the variety the brochure uses for its costed hectare.
Just tell me the best variety, one name, no explanations.

There is no single best one, and naming one blind would cost you. The brochure asks you to weigh two things, the cycle and the yield, and the right answer changes with your field. Striga in the plot points to TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. A dry season points to Amen. A short season points to the 75 to 85 day varieties. A long season and good land points to Obatanpa or Sotubaka. Tell me your case, or ask ICAT.
What does the brochure say improved varieties change for a farmer?

It says they are very productive, and it sets a target: adopt the modern production techniques it proposes and you will get good harvests of 20 to 40 bags of 100 kg on one hectare. It contrasts that with the national average of the previous ten years, about 450,000 tonnes a year at around 1,100 kg a hectare, which it blames on traditional varieties, granary seed, late weeding and fertiliser applied at low doses or not at all.
I have my improved seed. Anything to do before it goes in the ground?

Treat it. The brochure says that for the seed to germinate well it must be treated with a fungicide and insecticide product, and tells you to ask the extension adviser of your locality which product is right. Count 20 to 25 kg of grain for a hectare of the variety you chose. Then sow in rows 80 cm apart, with the in row spacing set by the cycle: 35 cm under 90 days, 40 cm for 90 to 100 days, 50 cm over 100 days, two to three seeds a pocket at 3 to 5 cm deep.
I will plant Obatanpa at 35 cm between pockets like the short varieties.

Obatanpa does not take 35 cm. Its cycle is 100 to 110 days, and the brochure sets the in row spacing by cycle: 35 cm for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for 90 to 100 days, and 50 cm for varieties over 100 days. So Obatanpa goes at 50 cm between pockets, in rows 80 cm apart, two to three seeds a pocket at 3 to 5 cm. And widen it further if you are associating cowpea, groundnut or cassava with the maize.
True or false: a variety with 7 tonnes potential will give me 7 tonnes.

False. The brochure defines the potential yield as the one obtained when growing conditions are good, listing rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field, and it prints an average column beside it. The two varieties at 7 tonnes potential, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, average 3 to 4 tonnes a hectare. Plan on the average and treat the potential as what good management could reach.
Purple and pink flowers keep coming up between my maize plants.

That description matches striga, which the brochure describes as a parasitic plant with violet, red or pink flowers found in some maize and sorghum fields, in the east of the Maritime region around Vo prefecture and in Kara and Savanes. It warns that its presence in a maize field can cost the whole crop. The answer it gives is to use a striga tolerant maize, TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, with or in rotation with soya, cowpea or groundnut, and to pull the striga out before it flowers.
On two hectares of Sotubaka, what should I count on?

Sotubaka averages 3 to 4 tonnes a hectare, so on two hectares count on about 6 to 8 tonnes, with a potential of 7 tonnes a hectare when conditions are good. For seed, at 20 to 25 kg a hectare you need 40 to 50 kg. Its cycle is 105 to 115 days, so sow at 50 cm between pockets in rows 80 cm apart. Those averages hold only if the weeding is done on time and the fertiliser applied at the right dose.
White grain or yellow grain, does it matter?

The brochure records the colour for each variety without saying which to prefer, so I will not tell you one is better. Seven of the nine are white and two are yellow, Pool 18 QPM SR and Sotubaka. It does note in its seed section that these varieties are for the most part resistant to streak and have white grain of tender texture. If your buyers want a particular colour, that is your reason to choose; otherwise go on the cycle and the yield.
What does a kilo of improved maize seed cost and where exactly do I buy it?

I will not give you a price, because prices move and the figures I hold are old. On where to buy, the brochure says only to buy from approved sellers and to speak to the extension adviser of your locality if you need to. It does not list the sellers. ICAT keeps the list of approved seed producers for each zone and updates it, so ask them for the one nearest you, and ask them the current price at the same time.
What crops can I grow together with my maize?

In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops, and the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists the common combinations: maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices adds maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. If you associate, widen the spacing between the pockets.
What is a good crop rotation and why does it help?

The Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices defines a rotation as a succession of crops in time on the same plot, and says it improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops. Its worked four year example says what each crop does. Year one, legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that takes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes deeper for what is left, yam. Year four, an undemanding leafy plant such as okra. Then back to legumes.
What is the benefit of each crop in the rotation? Justify.

The Ministry and PASA catalogue gives a role to each year. The legumes of year one are the improving plants: they feed the soil with nitrogen, and it names beans, groundnut and cowpea. Maize in year two is the hungry plant that consumes a lot, and it can be planted because the soil is now rich in nitrogen. Year three takes a root or tuber crop such as yam, which goes down for the nutrients still left deeper. Year four takes an undemanding plant, a leafy one such as okra. Then the cycle starts again with legumes.
Which crop successions does ITRA recommend for maize?

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure gives five. Maize then cotton then sorghum then groundnut or cowpea then maize. Maize then cowpea or groundnut then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow. Maize then cassava then cowpea then maize. Fallow then yam then maize then fallow. And cotton then maize then cotton. The rule behind them all is that maize comes at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.
mais niebe ensemble ecartement

Widen the spacing between the pockets when you put cowpea in with the maize. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says to do it for cowpea, groundnut or cassava, and it does not give a reason. Take your normal spacing first: rows 80 cm apart, and in the row 35 cm for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for 90 to 100 days, 50 cm over 100 days. Then widen from there.
I am in the Plateaux with five acres. What can I grow and how?

In Maritime and Plateaux the usual way is association, and the ITRA and ICAT brochure lists maize with cassava, with cowpea, with groundnut, with cassava and cowpea, or with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue adds maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. Widen the pocket spacing when you associate. For a rotation, keep maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. Ask ICAT what suits your plot.
True or false: association and rotation are the same thing.

False. An association is growing two or more species on the same plot at the same time, to draw a better profit from the combination. A rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, which the Ministry and PASA catalogue says improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops. One works in space, the other in time. In Togo the ITRA and ICAT brochure notes that association is the more widespread practice in the south, while the north more often runs successions.
In Kara, should I associate or rotate?

Rotate. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure says that in Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize is more often grown pure, and it recommends running a succession rather than an association there. Association is the widespread practice in the south, in Maritime and Plateaux. Among the successions it gives for your part of the country: maize then cotton then sorghum then groundnut or cowpea then maize, or maize then cowpea or groundnut then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow.
What should I think about before setting a rotation plan?

Two things, says the Ministry and PASA catalogue: the fertility of the soil, and what grew on that plot last season. Then build the order so each crop takes over from the last: legumes that feed nitrogen. Then a hungry crop like maize, then a root or tuber crop that goes deeper, then an undemanding leafy crop. The ITRA and ICAT brochure puts the same idea as a rule: maize at the head of the rotation, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.
What rules govern which crops can be associated?

The Ministry and PASA catalogue lists them: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs, and the period over which the two crops share the plot. The association it recommends is cereals with legumes, that is maize, millet or sorghum grown with beans, cowpea or soya on the same plot. It also shows maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize.
How do I lay out maize and soya in the same field?

The Ministry and PASA catalogue says you can alternate a line of maize and a line of soya. Keep in mind what the spacings are when each is grown pure: maize at 80 cm by 40 cm, soya at 40 cm by 20 cm. And if you put the legume in among the maize pockets rather than in its own line, the ITRA and ICAT brochure says to widen the spacing between the pockets. Ask ICAT for the layout that suits your plot.
My soil is tired and I cannot afford fertiliser this year.

Put the rotation to work for you. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says a rotation improves soil fertility, and its four year plan starts with the improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Maize, which it calls a hungry plant that consumes a lot, comes the year after, on a soil now rich in nitrogen. Before you fix the plan, it says to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. Ask ICAT for the rotation that fits your plot.
I will plant maize on the same plot every year, it is my best field.

Maize is the crop both references put at the head of a rotation, not the one to repeat. The ITRA and ICAT brochure states the rule as maize at the head, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, and its five recommended successions all move maize on. The Ministry and PASA catalogue explains what you lose by staying put: a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops. And it calls maize a hungry plant that consumes a lot.
Why are legumes always in these rotations?

Because of what they leave behind. The Ministry and PASA catalogue calls the legumes the improving plants, the ones that feed the soil with nitrogen, and it names beans, groundnut and cowpea. That is why maize, which it calls a hungry plant, is planted the year after them. The ITRA and ICAT brochure builds the same order into its rule: maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. Against striga it also pairs a tolerant maize with soya, cowpea or groundnut.
I want to organise my field better.
Which region are you in, and do you want to grow crops side by side or one after another?
Maritime, and side by side if possible.

Association is the widespread practice in your part of the country, and the ITRA and ICAT brochure lists what is most often seen there: maize with cassava, with cowpea, with groundnut, with cassava and cowpea, or with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue adds maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. Widen the spacing between your maize pockets when you associate. ICAT can tell you which combination suits your plot.
Why widen the spacing when I associate crops? Justify.

I will be honest: the ITRA and ICAT brochure gives the instruction without giving a reason. It says to widen the distance between the pockets if you associate cowpea, groundnut or cassava with the maize, and stops there. The Ministry and PASA catalogue points in the same direction from another angle, saying an association must respect the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development and the light needs. For the reason in your own field, ask ICAT.
I grow cotton and maize. How do I fit them in the same year?

The ITRA and ICAT brochure covers exactly that. For a maize then cotton succession in the same year, sow an extra early maize variety of 75 to 85 days, so the two crops do not sit together for long and the field work stays simple. Then sow the cotton into the maize two to three weeks before the maize harvest. Among its five successions it also gives cotton then maize then cotton, and maize then cotton then sorghum then groundnut or cowpea then maize.
rotation 4 ans exemple

From the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, a hungry plant that consumes a lot, maize, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes for the nutrients left deeper, yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing it, take account of your soil's fertility and of last season's crop.
The same pests come back in that field every single year.

That is one of the two things a rotation is meant to address. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops, and it asks you to take account of the soil's fertility and of the preceding crop before fixing your plan. The ITRA and ICAT brochure gives five successions you can follow, all with maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. For what is attacking your field exactly, ask ICAT to confirm before you change anything.
After maize, cowpea or cassava?

Both appear in the ITRA and ICAT successions, but in different places. The rule it states is maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, which puts the legume first: cowpea or groundnut straight after the maize, and cassava or yam later. One of its five successions runs maize then cassava then cowpea then maize, so cassava directly after maize is also used. The Ministry and PASA catalogue backs the legume first order, because legumes feed the soil with nitrogen for the hungry crop.
How much extra yield will a rotation give me, in percent?

I was not taught a figure for that, and I will not invent one. Neither reference puts a number on what a rotation gains. The Ministry and PASA catalogue says only that a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops, and the ITRA and ICAT brochure gives the successions without a yield claim. What the brochure does chiffre is the variety: the nine released maize varieties average between 1.5 and 4 tonnes a hectare. For an estimate on your own plot, ask ICAT.
True or false: a fallow is wasted land.

False in the eyes of both references, which build it into the plan. The ITRA and ICAT brochure states the rule as maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, and two of its five successions end on a fallow: maize then cowpea or groundnut then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow, and fallow then yam then maize then fallow. The fallow is a stage of the rotation, not an interruption of it.
I have four plots. Can I run the four year rotation across them?

One way to use it is exactly that. The Ministry and PASA catalogue's plan has four stages: legumes that feed nitrogen, then maize the hungry plant, then a root or tuber crop such as yam, then an undemanding leafy crop such as okra, then back to legumes. With four plots you can hold one stage on each and move them round each year. Before fixing it, the catalogue says to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season, so check each plot, and ask ICAT for the plan that suits them.
Striga is spreading in the plot where I always grow maize.

The ITRA and ICAT brochure answers that with the variety and the rotation together: use a striga tolerant maize variety with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. The two varieties it marks striga tolerant are TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. Growing maize on the same plot every year is the opposite of what its rule asks, which is maize at the head, then a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow.
Give me the one best association, I do not want a list.

The references do not rank them, so I will not pretend one is best. What the Ministry and PASA catalogue does say is which family of association it recommends: cereals with legumes, that is maize, millet or sorghum grown with beans, cowpea or soya on the same plot. Inside that family, the ITRA and ICAT brochure records maize with cowpea and maize with groundnut among the most common in the south. Which one suits your plot depends on your soil and your market, so ask ICAT.
What has to be done before putting two crops in the same plot?

Choose the pair on the criteria the Ministry and PASA catalogue lists: the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs. And the period over which the two share the plot. Then prepare the soil according to the crops chosen, since it says the nature of that work depends on them. And when you set out the maize, widen the spacing between the pockets, as the ITRA and ICAT brochure asks for cowpea, groundnut or cassava.
Why is association more common in the south than in the north?

The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure records the difference without explaining it. It says that in all regions maize is grown either pure or in association with other crops, and that the practice of association is more widespread in the south of the country, in Maritime and Plateaux. It adds that in Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize is more often grown pure, and that under improved cultivation the crop successions are recommended there. For the reason behind the regional difference, ask ICAT.
What is crop association exactly?

It is a system that lets you grow two or more plant species on the same plot at the same time, the idea being to draw the best profit from the combination of the different species. That is how the Ministry and PASA catalogue defines it. The family it recommends is cereals with legumes, maize, millet or sorghum together with beans, cowpea or soya. In Togo the ITRA and ICAT brochure records association as the widespread practice in the south, with maize and cassava, cowpea or groundnut.
Name some associations that are not just maize and one legume.

The ITRA and ICAT brochure records three crop and four crop combinations from the south: maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. The Ministry and PASA catalogue shows others in its own examples: yam with okra and maize, and moringa with maize and cucumber. It also shows the simpler pairs, maize with pigeon pea and soya with maize. Whatever the mix, widen the spacing between the maize pockets, and check the criteria for choosing what goes with what.
Since maize feeds the soil, I will start my rotation with it.

Maize does not feed the soil, it draws on it. The Ministry and PASA catalogue calls maize a hungry plant that consumes a lot, and places it in year two, after the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, which are the legumes: beans, groundnut, cowpea. The ITRA and ICAT brochure states its own rule as maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume. Then a root crop, then a fallow, so maize is never the crop that stays on the plot.
What does it cost to grow one hectare of maize, and what do I get back?

In the costed hectare of Obatanpa published by ITRA and ICAT in their 2008 maize brochure, from a 2005 internal communication, the charges add up to 391,000 FCFA and the crop sells for 480,000 FCFA, leaving a profit of 89,000 FCFA on a yield of 3,500 kg a hectare. Those are 2005 evaluations for one hectare, not today's prices. Use the rows as a template, put your own quantities and current prices in them, and check with ICAT whether your own hectare still leaves a profit.
Break down the charges of that costed hectare.

In 2005 evaluations, from the ITRA and ICAT brochure. Inputs and machine work: 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for renting the plot, 10,000 for 25 kg of commercial seed. Then the small items: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 for jute bags, 20,000 for pallets, 2,000 for twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries. The rest is labour in man-days at 700 FCFA. Total charges 391,000 FCFA.
How much labour does a hectare of maize take?

The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare counts it in man-days at 700 FCFA each, in 2005 evaluations: 55 for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing, 25 for the second weeding, 20 for spreading NPK, 20 for treatment and bagging, 10 for sowing, 10 for the urea and 10 for drying. Harvest and transport is by far the heaviest single item, which is worth knowing when you plan who will help you.
Why does the study sell after six months instead of at harvest? Justify.

Because that is where the profit sits. The profit in the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, in 2005 evaluations. The brochure's own words are that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. It ties that to how you store: maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack. Follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before deciding when to sell.
Is growing maize profitable?

On the study's own figures, yes but thinly. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare of Obatanpa shows 391,000 FCFA of charges against 480,000 FCFA of product, so 89,000 FCFA of profit on 3,500 kg a hectare, in 2005 evaluations. That margin also depends on storing six months before selling. Since those are 2005 prices, the honest answer for you is to redo the same rows with your own quantities and today's prices, with ICAT, before you count on a margin.

89,000 FCFA in the costed hectare of the ITRA and ICAT 2008 maize brochure, which comes from a 2005 internal communication: 480,000 FCFA of product against 391,000 FCFA of charges, on a yield of 3,500 kg a hectare of Obatanpa. These are 2005 evaluations, not today's prices, and the margin assumes the crop is sold after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag.
What is a bag of maize worth right now?

I cannot tell you, and I will not guess. The only price I hold is 16,000 FCFA a bag, and it is a 2005 evaluation inside the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare, where 30 bags are sold after six months of storage. Prices move, and cereal prices move with the season in particular. Follow the SIM cereal prices broadcast on the radio, which is what the advice on selling points you to, or ask ICAT.
I have half a hectare. What does the study give for that?

Take the hectare figures and halve the ones that scale. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare, in 2005 evaluations, has 391,000 FCFA of charges, 480,000 FCFA of product and 89,000 FCFA of profit on 3,500 kg. On half a hectare that points to about 195,500 of charges, 240,000 of product, 44,500 of profit and 1,750 kg. Be careful though: some items do not halve neatly, such as renting the plot or a tractor pass. Redo the rows with ICAT at your own size and today's prices.
True or false: the seed is the biggest cost in a hectare of maize.

False. In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare, the 25 kg of commercial seed costs 10,000 FCFA in 2005 evaluations, which is one of the smaller lines. The heaviest single input is the fertiliser, 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, followed by tractor ploughing at 40,000 and the pulverising pass at 25,000. And labour as a whole is about half the budget, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA each.
What should I work out before I plant a hectare of maize?

Build the budget first, using the rows of the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare: plot rent, tractor ploughing, the pulverising pass, seed, fertiliser, the man-days for sowing, weeding, fertilising, harvest, drying, shelling and bagging, then the bags, the pallets, the grain protectant and the sundries. Put your own quantities in those rows with today's prices, not the 2005 evaluations, and see what is left against what you expect to sell. ICAT can help you do it.
The brochure says 89,000 profit, so that is what I will make this year.

Not as it stands. That 89,000 FCFA is a 2005 evaluation for one hectare of Obatanpa, built on charges of 391,000 and a product of 480,000, and it assumes 3,500 kg a hectare and a sale after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag. Every one of those numbers has moved since. Use the study as a template: same rows, your quantities, today's prices. Then you will have a figure that means something for your field.
Sell straight after harvest or store first?

The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare is built on storing. Its profit depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, in 2005 evaluations, and the brochure says plainly that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Storing well is what makes that possible: on treated pallets in an airy store the maize holds six months without weevil attack. Follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before you fix the moment.
Which small costs do farmers usually forget?

The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare counts them, and they add up. In 2005 evaluations: 14,000 FCFA of grain protectant, 21,000 for the jute bags, 20,000 for the pallets, 2,000 for twine and needle, and 20,000 of sundries. That is 77,000 FCFA out of 391,000 of total charges, on a profit of only 89,000. Leave them out of your own budget and the margin you think you have is not the margin you will get.
I want to know if I should put my land into maize.
How much land, and would you be able to store the harvest for a few months or would you need to sell straight away?
One hectare, and I would have to sell at harvest.

Then look carefully at the margin. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare shows 391,000 FCFA of charges against 480,000 FCFA of product for a profit of 89,000 FCFA, in 2005 evaluations, and that product assumes selling after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag. Selling at harvest changes the price side of that equation, and the brochure's whole point is that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer. Redo the rows with ICAT at today's prices for both cases.
I have no tractor, I work with a hoe. Does the budget still apply?

Two of its lines are machine work that you will not pay: 40,000 FCFA for tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations. But that work still has to be done, so it moves to the labour side, which the study counts in man-days at 700 FCFA each. So do not simply delete those lines: replace them with the man-days your own way of working costs. That is exactly what using the study as a template means. ICAT can help you cost it.
Why does the study insist on treated pallets in the store? Justify.

Because the storage is what protects the margin. The brochure says that maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack, and that this is what lets you sell dearer when the time comes. The costed hectare then builds its profit on exactly that: 30 bags sold at 16,000 FCFA after six months of storage, in 2005 evaluations. Lose the grain to weevils and you lose both the bags and the higher price.
I harvest well every year but there is never any money left.

Compare your own field against the rows of the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare, which shows how thin the margin is: 391,000 FCFA of charges for 480,000 of product, so 89,000 of profit, in 2005 evaluations. Two things in it decide the outcome. The small items, which are easy to forget: 14,000 FCFA of grain protectant, 21,000 for the jute bags, 20,000 for the pallets, 2,000 for twine and needle and 20,000 of sundries, which add up to 77,000 FCFA. And the moment of sale, since the study's profit assumes six months of storage. Write your own rows, and follow the SIM prices before selling.
How many bags should a hectare give me?

The costed hectare works on a yield of 3,500 kg a hectare of Obatanpa and sells 30 bags after six months of storage, in 2005 evaluations. The brochure also sets a wider target for its modern techniques: good harvests of 20 to 40 bags of 100 kg on one hectare. Obatanpa itself averages 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare in the variety table, with a potential of 6 tonnes when rain, fertilisation, pest pressure and upkeep are all good.
True or false: storage is a separate matter from the budget.

False. In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare the storage is inside the budget in two ways. It costs money: 20,000 FCFA of pallets, 21,000 of jute bags and 14,000 of grain protectant, in 2005 evaluations. And it makes the money: the profit depends on selling 30 bags at 16,000 FCFA after six months of storage, because maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack.
Where does this costed hectare come from exactly?

From the brochure Bien cultiver et conserver le mais, published by ITRA with ICAT in February 2008, in its section nine, a costed hectare of maize of the Obatanpa variety. The brochure gives its own source line for that table: a personal communication from Didjeira A. in 2005. So the amounts are 2005 evaluations for one hectare. That is why every figure from it should be given with its year, and why the table is a template rather than a price list.
Forget 2005, just tell me what I will earn per hectare today.

I will not, because I would be inventing it. The only costed hectare I hold is from 2005: 391,000 FCFA of charges, 480,000 of product, 89,000 of profit, on 3,500 kg. What I can do is tell you exactly which rows to fill so you get your own figure: plot rent, land preparation, seed, fertiliser, the man-days, the bags, pallets, protectant and sundries, then the bags sold and their price. Take that to ICAT, and check the SIM prices for the selling side.
Should I hire the tractor or save that money?

In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare the machine work is 40,000 FCFA for the tractor ploughing and 25,000 for the pulverising pass, in 2005 evaluations, out of 391,000 of total charges. If you drop it, the work still has to be done and moves to the labour side, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA. So the question is not whether to pay but in which form. Cost both versions in your own rows before deciding, and ask ICAT.
Weevils ate a good part of my stored grain last year.

That loss hits the budget twice, because in the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare the whole profit rests on selling after six months of storage. The brochure says maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack, and it counts the means in the budget: 20,000 FCFA of pallets, 21,000 of jute bags and 14,000 of grain protectant, in 2005 evaluations. Set the store up that way, and follow the SIM prices to choose when to sell.
Before I decide when to sell, what should I do?

Know your own cost and watch the price. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare shows a profit of 89,000 FCFA on charges of 391,000, in 2005 evaluations, and that profit exists only because the 30 bags are sold at 16,000 FCFA after six months of storage. So first make sure the grain will keep: treated pallets, airy store, six months without weevil attack. Then follow the SIM cereal prices broadcast on the radio, and sell when the price justifies the wait.
How do I use this table for a crop that is not maize?

Keep the shape and change the contents. The rows of the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare are the ones any field crop has: renting the plot, land preparation, seed, fertiliser, the man-days for sowing, weeding, fertilising, harvest, drying and processing, then bags, storage and sundries, then the quantity sold and its price. Its own figures are for one hectare of Obatanpa maize in 2005 evaluations, so they do not carry over. Ask ICAT for the quantities and prices of your crop.
I want to borrow to grow maize on two hectares.

Go to the lender with your own rows, not with the study's. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare gives 391,000 FCFA of charges and 89,000 of profit for one hectare in 2005 evaluations, so two hectares would point to roughly 782,000 of charges and 178,000 of profit at those old prices. The profit per hectare is thin and it assumes six months of storage before selling. Rebuild both hectares at today's prices with ICAT before borrowing anything.

It is the heaviest input line of that budget, ahead of tractor ploughing at 40,000 and the pulverising pass at 25,000. Spreading them also costs labour: 20 man-days at 700 FCFA for the NPK and 10 for the urea. Prices have moved since 2005, so ask ICAT or a supplier for the current cost of a bag.
Labour is free, my family works the field, so my charges are much lower.

The study counts family labour all the same, and that is deliberate. In the ITRA and ICAT costed hectare every operation is priced in man-days at 700 FCFA: 55 for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing, 25 for the second weeding, and so on, in 2005 evaluations. Counting it shows you what your own time is worth in the result. You may choose not to pay it out, but leave it out of the budget and you will not know whether the crop really pays.
Give me the same budget for a hectare of cassava.

I do not have one. The only costed hectare I hold is for maize of the Obatanpa variety, published by ITRA and ICAT in their 2008 maize brochure from a 2005 communication. I will not build a cassava budget by guessing quantities and prices. What I can give you is the structure, which is the same for any field crop, and ICAT can supply the quantities and current prices for cassava so that you fill it properly.
Which variety was the budget built on?

Obatanpa. The ITRA and ICAT costed hectare is for one hectare of Obatanpa maize, with a yield of 3,500 kg a hectare, in 2005 evaluations. In the variety table of the same brochure Obatanpa runs 100 to 110 days, averages 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare with a potential of 6 tonnes, has a white grain and is marked high in quality protein. If you grow a different variety, its yield and its cycle change, so the product line of the budget changes with it.
What is alley cropping?

It is growing your seasonal crops in the alleys formed by rows of fertiliser trees. The 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices, published by the Ministry of Agriculture with the PASA project and the World Bank, describes it that way: the land is worked in alleys made by fertilising trees, and the crop goes in between. In practice you set the tree rows first, 2 to 4 m between plants inside the row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one alley and the next. Then you sow maize or cowpea in the space between. One rule matters more than the spacing: lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. You can start the trees by direct sowing, by cutting, or with plants raised in a nursery.
Which trees do they call fertiliser trees?

The catalogue names three. Leucaena leucocephala. Senna siamea, the one called zanguerati here, which it describes as a fertilising plant and resistant to drought. And Faidherbia albida. Those are the three it puts forward for the alleys. I should tell you what it does not say: it does not say how much fertility each one brings back, and it does not compare them against each other. It names them and leaves it there. For which of the three is available as plants near you, and which suits your soil, ask ICAT.
The side of my field that faces the wind is 300 m long. How many plants do I need for a windbreak on a single line?

Between 198 and 300 plants. Here is the arithmetic so you can check it. The catalogue says that on a single line the plants are spaced 1 to 1.5 m apart, which it counts as 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. Your side is 300 m, so it is three times 100 m. Three times 66 is 198, and three times 100 is 300. The tighter you plant, at 1 m, the closer you are to 300; at 1.5 m you are closer to 198. Plant them during the rainy season, and orient the line opposite to the direction of the dominant wind.
If I plant Taungya trees at 2 m by 2 m, how many trees is that on one hectare?

About 2,500 trees, and here is how that comes out. The catalogue says you plant at a spacing of 2 m by 2 m and more depending on what you are after. A tree at 2 m by 2 m occupies 2 times 2, that is 4 square metres. A hectare is 10,000 square metres. Ten thousand divided by four gives 2,500. So 2,500 is the densest case, the one at exactly 2 m by 2 m. If you open the spacing, which the catalogue allows, you plant fewer. Remember what Taungya is for: replanting the trees is the first aim, and the crop is grown underneath for two or three years only, so the trees can grow.
Every year the wind comes through and flattens part of my maize before harvest. My field is open on that side, nothing stops it.

What you are describing is what a windbreak is for. The catalogue defines it as a barrier, most often a curtain of trees planted in lines, sometimes trees with a taproot, standing against the dominant winds. It has two sides, the windward side that takes the wind and the sheltered side behind it. So: orient your line opposite to the direction the dominant wind comes from, which is the open side you just described. On a single line, space the plants 1 to 1.5 m, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. If you want it stronger, plant a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m inside the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Plant at the rainy season, not now if the rains are finished. What I cannot tell you is how much of your maize it will save: the catalogue gives no figure for that, and I will not invent one.
The neighbours' goats and sheep keep getting into my plot and eating what I plant. I am tired of chasing them.

For that the catalogue points to a live hedge. Its definition is exactly your problem: a set of trees and shrubs planted so as to protect a space against animals wandering in, against the wind, or against the light. How to make it. Prepare the ground by digging a continuous trench, not separate holes: 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep if you plant a single line, or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep if you plant a double line with the plants staggered, that is in quincunx. Put the plants in by direct sowing, by cutting, or from plants raised in pots. Jatropha and thevetia are often used between the trees. Then, for the two seasons that follow, weed the hedge and replace the plants that died. Prune both sides and the top at the time of the first cut, which comes in the first year or from the second year on.
True or false: I should lay my alley rows down the slope so the water drains away quickly.

False, and it is the opposite. The catalogue says plainly: I put the alleys perpendicular to the slope. Perpendicular to the slope means across it, following the level, not running up and down the hill. That is the one instruction it gives about siting the alleys, before any question of spacing. The rest of the layout is 2 to 4 m between the plants in the row and 10, 20 or 30 m between the alleys, with maize or cowpea grown in between.
True or false: in the Taungya method the crop is the main aim and the trees are just there to help it.

False, and this one is worth getting right because it changes everything you do. The catalogue says the reverse: replanting the trees is the first aim in time, and the crops are practised secondarily, for a limited period of two to three years, so as to let the trees grow well. It is a technique for places where land pressure is strong. That is why the crop sequence is fixed and short: cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two following years. After those two or three years the cropping stops. The trees used are teak, gmelina, which is called Indian teak, cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna and neem.
For a windbreak, single line or a band of several lines? Which do I take?

The catalogue gives you both and lets you choose, so here is what separates them. Single line: plants spaced 1 to 1.5 m, which comes to 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. Band of two or three lines: 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m inside the line, which comes to 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. So the band costs you roughly twice the plants and takes more ground, and gives you a thicker barrier. In both cases you orient it opposite the dominant wind, and in both cases you plant at the rainy season. What the catalogue does not do is tell you which one protects better, or by how much. It gives no comparison and no figure. If your wind is strong and your plot is worth it, the band is the heavier answer; ICAT can look at your plot and say.
Between the three fertiliser trees, which one for a place where the rains are short?

Of the three, the one the catalogue itself marks for that is Senna siamea, the one called zanguerati. Its own words describe it as a fertilising plant and resistant to drought. The two others, Leucaena leucocephala and Faidherbia albida, are named as fertiliser trees but the catalogue says nothing about their behaviour in drought, so I will not rank them for you on something the catalogue does not treat. Take the note for what it is: it is a line in a catalogue, not a trial. ICAT will know which of the three is actually available as plants in your prefecture, which often decides the question before anything else.
Why do they tell me to cut at 2 m above the ground and not lower?

I have to be straight with you: the catalogue advises the high cut without saying why. What it does say is the rest. The first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, and by then the plants must be at least 1.50 m tall. It then advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that the prunings are regular, depending on the kind of tree planted, on how fast it grows, and on what you need, whether that is firewood or organic fertiliser. The reason for the height is not written there, so I will not supply one. If you want the reasoning behind it, an ICAT agent who works with these alleys can explain it, and that is a better answer than a guess from me.
Why go to the trouble of protecting the small trees that come up by themselves? They are just bush.

Because that is the whole point of assisted natural regeneration, and the catalogue states the reason in its own definition: it consists simply in selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that grow in the field, in such a way that the field is never left bare. Never left bare, that is the reason given. So instead of clearing everything, you look at what has come up on its own and keep the ones worth keeping. The method has four steps: know the area of your field, count the kinds of tree to protect, select the trees to protect, then protect and maintain the ones you kept. Protecting means weeding around them, making fire breaks, giving a stake to the ones that are not vigorous, removing the greedy branches, and keeping animals off them.
Give me the botanical names of the species used in these agroforestry practices.

Here are the ones the catalogue writes out. For the fertiliser trees in alley cropping: Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, which it also gives under the local name zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. For the Taungya method the list mixes common names and genus names as it stands: teak, gmelina which it also calls Indian teak, Anacardium which it also calls atchan and which is the cashew, Leucaena, Acacia, Senna which it also calls zanguerati, and neem. For live hedges it names jatropha and thevetia as plants often used between the trees. I am repeating that list as the catalogue writes it, with its local names beside it, rather than completing the Latin names myself where it stops short.
What exactly is meant by assisted natural regeneration, in technical terms?

The catalogue's own definition is short: it consists simply in selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that grow in the field, in such a way that the field is never left bare. So the trees are not planted, they are already there, and the work is selection and protection rather than establishment. The protocol has four steps: knowing the area of the field, counting the kinds of tree to protect, selecting the trees to protect, and protecting and maintaining the ones retained. Maintenance is listed as weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the trees that are not vigorous, removal of greedy branches, and protection against animals. For stocking, the catalogue gives an indication for the dry savanna zone only: about 25 to 30 adult stems per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. It gives no figure for the other zones.

For the dry savanna zone, the catalogue gives 25 to 30 adult stems per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. It gives that figure for the savanna zone only, as an example, so do not carry it to another zone as if it were the rule.
