What is the difference between a windbreak and a live hedge? They both sound like a line of trees to me.

They do look alike, and the catalogue treats them as two separate practices, so here is what separates them. The windbreak is defined as a barrier, most often a curtain of trees and sometimes trees with a taproot, planted in lines, which stands against the dominant winds. It has a windward side and a sheltered side, and you orient it opposite the direction of the dominant wind. That is its whole purpose: the wind. The live hedge is defined as a set of trees and shrubs planted so as to protect a space against animals wandering in, against the wind, or against the light. So the hedge covers three purposes, including animals, and the windbreak covers one. They are also built differently. The windbreak is set by spacing, 1 to 1.5 m on a single line, or 2 m between lines and 1.5 m in the line for a band. The hedge starts with a continuous trench, 50 cm wide by 60 cm deep on a single line, or 60 by 60 for a staggered double line.
Alley cropping and Taungya both mix trees and crops. How do I know which one I am doing?

By what you are aiming at, and by how long the crop stays. In alley cropping the crop is the point. You grow your seasonal crops in the alleys formed by fertiliser trees, the trees at 2 to 4 m in the row and the alleys 10, 20 or 30 m apart, and you grow maize or cowpea between them. In Taungya the tree is the point. The catalogue says replanting is the first aim in time and the crops are practised secondarily for a limited period of two to three years, in order to let the trees grow well, and it presents the method for places where land pressure is strong. The crop calendar shows it: cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two following years, and that is the end of the cropping. So if your crop has an end date, you are doing Taungya.
How much more will I harvest if I put in these agroforestry practices?

I cannot tell you, and I would rather say so than give you a number. The catalogue that carries these practices does not put a single yield figure against any of them. Its heading says let us durably increase yields by combining trees and animals with our crops, and it presents the practices as good practices in the era of climate change, but it measures no gain. It gives no cost either, and it does not say by how much these practices offset the effects of climate change. What it does give is the how: the spacings, the trench dimensions, the pruning ages, the stocking for the savanna zone. For what it would do on your land, take it to ICAT, who can look at your soil and your slope. A figure from me would be a figure I made up.
What does a windbreak cost to put in?

The catalogue gives no cost, for the windbreak or for any of these practices, so I have no price to give you. What I can give you is what drives the cost, which is the number of plants. On a single line the spacing is 1 to 1.5 m, which the catalogue counts as 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. On a band of two or three lines it is 2 m between lines and 1.5 m in the line, which it counts as 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Measure the side you want to protect, take the count per 100 m, and ask ICAT or a nursery near you what plants of the species you want are selling for. That is your cost, with today's prices in it, and not a figure invented on my side.
I was told jatropha is the tree you use to make a live hedge, so I will plant a line of jatropha.

Not quite, and the difference is small but worth correcting. The catalogue names jatropha and thevetia as plants often used between the trees of the hedge, not as the hedge itself. So they fill the gaps in the line rather than make the line. The hedge itself is described as a set of trees and shrubs planted so as to protect a space against animals wandering in, against the wind, or against the light, and the catalogue does not give a list of the main species for it. What it does give is the groundwork: a continuous trench 50 cm wide by 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 by 60 for a double line with the plants staggered, then planting by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, then weeding and replacing the dead plants for the two seasons that follow. For which species to put in the line itself in your area, ask ICAT.
Assisted natural regeneration means I buy seedlings and plant them out every year, right?

No, and that is the useful part of it: it costs you no seedlings. The catalogue defines it as selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that grow in the field, in such a way that the field is never left bare. The plants are already coming up on their own. Your work is to choose them and keep them alive. The four steps are: know the area of your field, count the kinds of tree to protect, select the trees to protect, then protect and maintain the ones you kept. Maintaining them means weeding, fire breaks, a stake for the ones that are not vigorous, taking off the greedy branches, and keeping animals away. In the dry savanna zone the catalogue suggests keeping about 25 to 30 adult stems per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare.
The rains have stopped here. I have my windbreak plants ready and I am going to put them in tomorrow.

Hold them. The catalogue is explicit on this one point: the planting of the trees and shrubs that make up the windbreak must take place at the time of the rainy season. If your rains are finished, you would be putting young plants into ground that is about to dry out, and the catalogue gives you no way to compensate for that. Keep the plants and set them at the next rains. Use the time in between for the part that does not need water: work out the direction of the dominant wind, because you orient the line opposite to it, and measure the side you want to protect so you know your count. On a single line that is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, and for a band of two or three lines 133 to 200 plants per 100 m.
My alley trees are eight months old and doing well. I am going out to give them their first cut this week.

Too early, wait. The catalogue puts the first pruning between 15 and 20 months, and it adds a condition on the plant itself: at that first cut the plants must have reached a height of at least 1.50 m. Yours are eight months, so they are short of both marks, the age and very probably the height. Let them run on. When you do cut, the catalogue advises going to 2 m above the ground, which it calls a high cut. After that first one, the prunings become regular, and their rhythm depends on the kind of tree you planted, on how it grows, and on what you want from it, firewood or organic fertiliser.
Describe a windbreak to me so I can picture it before I plant.

Picture a curtain of trees standing in a line across the way the wind comes. That is the catalogue's own image: a barrier made most often of a curtain of trees, sometimes trees with a taproot, planted in lines, which opposes itself to the dominant winds. It has two faces. The face that takes the wind is the windward side, the face behind it is the sheltered side, and everything you are protecting sits on that sheltered side. You place it by orienting it opposite to the direction of the dominant wind. Close up, on a single line, the plants stand 1 to 1.5 m from each other, which works out at 66 to 100 plants for every 100 m of line. If you want a thicker curtain you plant a band of two or three lines, 2 m from one line to the next and 1.5 m between plants inside a line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. And you put it all in during the rainy season.
I want to plant trees in my field but I do not know which of these methods is mine.

Two questions and I can point you. First, is the land yours to keep planting, or are you under pressure for space and expecting to hand the plot over to trees? Second, do you want to keep cropping between the trees year after year, or would you accept cropping for two or three years only?
The land is mine and I mean to keep it. I want to go on growing maize between the trees every year, not stop after three years.

Then it is alley cropping you want, not Taungya. Set your tree rows first, with 2 to 4 m between the plants inside a row, and leave 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next. Lay those rows across the slope, never up and down it. Then sow your maize in the space between, season after season, which is exactly what you asked for. The trees the catalogue names for this are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, the one called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. One date to hold: the first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, and a high cut at 2 m above the ground is advised. After that you prune regularly, and what you cut is either firewood or organic matter for the field. Ask ICAT which of the three species is available as plants near you.
Land is tight here. I have been given a plot on condition that trees go back on it, and I need to eat from it while they grow.

That is the situation the Taungya method was written for. The catalogue presents it as an agroforestry technique practised in zones where land pressure is strong, and it sets the order out plainly: replanting is the first aim in time, and the crops are practised secondarily over a limited period of two to three years, so as to allow the trees to grow well. So you plant the trees first. The spacing given is about 2 m by 2 m, and more depending on what you are after. Then you crop underneath on a fixed sequence: cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two years that follow. The trees the catalogue names for this are teak, gmelina, which it calls Indian teak, cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna and neem. Plan for two or three seasons of food from that plot, not more.
I hear you that there is no figure, but give me a rough percentage anyway, even approximate, just so I can decide.

I understand why you want one, and I am still not going to give it, because an approximate figure invented here would carry the same weight with you as a real one. The catalogue behind these practices gives no yield gain, no cost, and no measure of how much they offset climate change. There is nothing to round off. What I can put in front of you instead is what the catalogue does commit to, and you can decide on that. It says the combinations of trees, animals and crops are indispensable in the durable management of land and that they raise growers' incomes, and it lists the ways: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushroom growing, selling the wood that comes off the pruning, composting the animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding your stock on the leaves of the trees on your holding. Those are extra returns you can count yourself, at your own prices. And ICAT can put numbers from real plots in front of you, which I cannot.
Apart from the crop, what else can I get out of a field planted with trees?

The catalogue ends the agroforestry sheet on exactly that, and it lists six things a grower who practises agroforestry can also do. Add hives in the holding to produce honey, which is beekeeping. Rear snails, for money or for meat, which is snail farming. Grow mushrooms to sell, which is mushroom growing. Sell the wood that comes from pruning or from cutting the agroforestry trees, to raise the income. Use the animal droppings and the plant debris for composting. And feed the stock on the leaves of the trees and shrubs planted in the holding. The catalogue's own conclusion is that the combinations of trees, animals and crops are indispensable in the durable management of land and let growers raise their income. It puts no price on any of the six, so those are directions to look in, not a budget.
I have three hectares in the savanna. Under assisted natural regeneration, how many trees should I be keeping?

About 75 to 90 adult stems and 180 to 240 young shoots, and here is the working. The catalogue gives an indication for the dry savanna zone of 25 to 30 adult stems per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. You have three hectares. Three times 25 is 75 and three times 30 is 90, so 75 to 90 adults. Three times 60 is 180 and three times 80 is 240, so 180 to 240 young shoots. Take those as an order of size, because the catalogue itself gives them as an example for that zone and not as a rule. And remember it is a count of what you keep, not of what you plant: the method is selecting and protecting the valuable young plants that come up in the field, so the field is never left bare.
What is composting in a heap?

It is laying your plant and animal waste in a heap, in a shaded spot, so that it turns into an organic fertiliser called compost. That is how the 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices from the Ministry of Agriculture puts it, under its own heading: let us keep our soils fertile durably by using compost. The work has two parts. First the site and what goes into the heap: a shaded spot, easy to reach, sheltered from the weather, that is from the wind and the rain, and a water point nearby is an advantage. Then the heap itself, which is built in layers and watered as you go. It is not a pile of rubbish left to itself; the order of the layers is the method.
Give me the layers of the heap in order.

Five things go down, in this order, and you water each one as you lay it. First, a little wood ash spread on the topsoil. Second, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Third, a layer of manure 5 cm thick on top of that base. Fourth, a layer of plant residues about 30 cm high, trodden down well with your feet. Fifth, a layer of topsoil, or of well rotted compost, or of Mycotri, which serves as the activator. The watering is not a separate step: the catalogue says to water each layer as you put it down.
What is Mycotri?

The catalogue explains it in one line: Mycotri is a powder of fungi that encourages the rapid decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. It is one of the three things the catalogue offers you for the last layer, the activator layer. The other two are ordinary topsoil and well rotted compost of your own, so it is not compulsory: it is simply the one of the three the catalogue attaches a benefit to. What the catalogue does not give is how much shorter the time becomes, nor where to get hold of it. For that, ask ICAT.
ou mettre le tas

In a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, that is from the wind and the rain. The catalogue adds that having a water point nearby is an advantage, and that makes sense once you see the method: you water each layer as you lay it down, so the water has to be close to hand while you build. So the four things to look for when you choose the place are shade, easy access, shelter from wind and rain, and water nearby. Pick the spot before you start carrying residues, because moving a half built heap is work you do twice.
quoi eviter dans le compost

The catalogue puts a warning on the slow rotting harvest leftovers: avoid the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. What you want instead is the residues that break down quickly, and it names straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Those you chop up before they go in. Note that slow rotting material is not banned altogether: rice husks and ronier leaves are exactly what the catalogue asks for at the base of the heap, as the support layer, 10 to 20 cm thick.
I sweep my poultry house two or three times a week and the droppings are piling up behind it. What do I do with them?

You already have the habit the poultry sheet asks for. It says to sweep the inside of the house two or three times a week and to throw the droppings into a manure pit away from the house, and it adds that those droppings can serve to fertilise the fields. The 2020 catalogue picks the same thread up on the agroforestry side, where it lists using animal droppings and plant debris for composting among the ways a grower raises income. The compost sheet shows where they sit in the heap: after the base of slow rotting material comes a layer of manure 5 cm thick, then about 30 cm of plant residues on top, trodden down. One thing I should be exact about. Neither document tells you in so many words to empty your pit into your heap. Putting the three together is a step you can take, not a sentence I am quoting. Either way, keep the pit away from the house, and keep the heap in the shade, sheltered from wind and rain.
My land is tired and I have no money for fertiliser this year.

Then the compost heap is the one the catalogue was written for. Its heading is exactly that: let us keep our soils fertile durably by using compost. The catalogue puts no cost on it anywhere, and the materials it names are materials from the farm. Take a shaded spot, easy to reach, sheltered from the wind and the rain, with water nearby if you can. Chop the residues that rot fast, which the catalogue names as straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and keep out the slow ones, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. Then build in layers, watering each one: wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves as the base, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down, and a last layer of topsoil or well rotted compost as the activator. I have to be honest with you about one thing: the catalogue gives no figure for how much compost this replaces in fertiliser, so I cannot promise you it covers the whole need.
How do I know which residues rot fast and which rot slowly?

The catalogue does not give you a test, it gives you two lists, so use the lists. Fast: straw, and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Those are the ones it tells you to chop up before they go into the heap. Slow: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. Those it tells you to keep out of the body of the heap. And there is a third group it treats differently again: rice husks and ronier leaves, which are slow rotting, are asked for on purpose at the base as the support layer, 10 to 20 cm thick. So slow is not always bad, it depends where it goes. For a residue that is on none of the three lists, I have no answer from the source, and ICAT can tell you.
Manure and compost, is it not the same thing?

No, and the compost sheet makes the difference clear by using both. Manure is an ingredient. It goes into the heap as one layer, 5 cm thick, laid on the base of slow rotting material. Compost is what comes out at the end. The catalogue defines composting in a heap as laying plant and animal waste in a heap, in a shaded spot, to turn it into an organic fertiliser called compost. So you put manure in and you take compost out. There is one place where the two meet: the catalogue offers well rotted compost as one of the three choices for the activator layer, alongside topsoil and Mycotri, so an old finished heap can start a new one.
True or false: maize stalks are the best thing to put in a compost heap, they are what I have most of.

False, and the catalogue is explicit about it. Its note says to avoid the harvest leftovers that decompose slowly, and it names them: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. What it asks for instead, in the body of the heap, is the residues that decompose quickly, and it names straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, chopped up first. I understand the difficulty if maize stalks are what your farm produces most of. The catalogue does not offer a way to treat them so they can go in, so I will not invent one, and ICAT is the right place to ask what else your stalks can serve for.
True or false: you build the whole heap first and then water it at the end.

False. The catalogue puts the watering inside the building: water each layer as you lay it down, one after the other. That is why it lists a water point nearby as an advantage when you choose the site. The layers themselves are, in order, a little wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of slow rotting support such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues well trodden down, and a last layer of topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator.
Should I put the heap in the open where the sun can work on it, or in the shade?

In the shade, and the catalogue leaves no room on this one. Its first step says the site must be a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, meaning the wind and the rain, and it adds that a water point is an advantage. So all three conditions point the same way: you keep the heap out of the sun, out of the wind and out of the rain, and you bring the water to it yourself, layer by layer, as you build. The catalogue does not say what goes wrong in the open, so I will not tell you what would happen. I will only tell you that its instruction is shade.
For the last layer, topsoil, old compost or Mycotri? Which one?

The catalogue gives you the three and does not rank them, so the choice is yours on what you have. Topsoil, which is already on the spot. Well rotted compost, if you have a finished heap from last time. Or Mycotri, which the catalogue describes as a powder of fungi that encourages the rapid decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. That last line is the only difference the catalogue claims between them, and it claims it for Mycotri alone. It does not say how much time you save, and it says nothing about where to find Mycotri. If time matters to you and you can find it, Mycotri is the one the catalogue attaches a benefit to; otherwise topsoil does the job it is listed for.
Why should I bother chopping the residues up before putting them in?

I will be straight: the catalogue tells you to do it without saying why. Its instruction is to chop up the plant residues that decompose quickly, and it names them, straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. The reason is not written beside it, so I am not going to supply one. What the catalogue does explain is the other end of the same subject, the speed of decomposition: it keeps the slow rotting leftovers out of the heap body, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks, and it offers Mycotri as a powder of fungi that encourages rapid decomposition, for a mature compost in a shorter time. So the catalogue is clearly concerned with how fast things break down. That is the neighbourhood of the answer, not the answer. An ICAT agent can give you the reason properly.
Why would I add Mycotri when I already have good topsoil?

For this one the catalogue does give you the reason, in its own note: Mycotri is a powder of fungi that encourages the rapid decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. So the reason is time, and only time. That is the whole claim. Topsoil and well rotted compost are listed as the other two choices for the same layer, and the catalogue attaches no such note to them. Now read the limit with the reason: it says shorter time, it does not say how much shorter, and it does not say the compost is better in any other way. If your heap is not in a hurry, the topsoil you already have is one of the three the catalogue puts on the table.
Technically, what is the activator doing in the last layer?

The catalogue calls that last layer the activator and gives you three materials for it: topsoil, well rotted compost, or Mycotri. The only mechanism it describes is the one attached to Mycotri, which it defines as a powder of fungi that encourages the rapid decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. So the agent named is fungi and the effect named is faster decomposition. For topsoil and for well rotted compost the catalogue gives no mechanism at all: it lists them in the same position for the same purpose and stops there. I will not fill that in with reasoning of my own. If you want the biology behind it, ICAT is the right address, and they can put the question to a soil specialist.
What is the product of the process, exactly?

The catalogue names it: an organic fertiliser called compost. Its definition of composting in a heap is laying the plant and animal waste and debris in a heap, in a shaded spot, in order to transform them into an organic fertiliser called compost. The word it uses for the end state of a good heap is mature, which appears in the Mycotri note, a mature compost in a shorter time. Beyond that the catalogue does not characterise the product: it gives no analysis, no nutrient content, no rate to apply per hectare and no delay before the compost is mature. Those are all outside the catalogue, so I have none of them to give you.
I want to start a compost heap but I am not sure I have the right material.

Tell me two things and I can check it against the catalogue. What plant residues do you actually have on hand after this harvest, and in what quantity? And do you have animals on the holding, so that manure and droppings are available to you?
Mostly maize stalks, a lot of them, and some groundnut leaves. I keep a few chickens behind the house.

Then two of your three are usable and one is not. The groundnut leaves are exactly what is wanted: they are on the list of residues that rot fast, with straw and the leaves of soya and cowpea, and you chop them before they go in. Your chicken droppings give you the manure layer, 5 cm thick, laid on the base. The maize stalks are the problem: they are named among the leftovers that rot slowly, with sorghum and millet stalks and the husks, and the catalogue tells you to keep those out. So build with what you have: a little wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of slow rotting support such as rice husks or ronier leaves. Then 5 cm of your droppings, then about 30 cm of chopped groundnut leaves trodden down well, then a layer of topsoil as the activator, watering each layer as you lay it. For what to do with the maize stalks instead, ask ICAT, because the catalogue does not say.
How long before the compost is ready to use?

The catalogue does not say, and I am not going to guess a number of weeks for you. It uses the word mature only once, in the note on Mycotri, where it says the powder gives a mature compost in a shorter time, and it never says what the ordinary time is nor what the shortened one is. There is no delay written anywhere in the catalogue. What the catalogue does cover in full is the building: the site, the materials to take and to avoid, the five layers with their thicknesses, and the watering of each layer. For when your own heap will be ready, an ICAT agent who can look at it is worth more than a figure from me.
How much compost do I need to spread on a hectare?

The catalogue gives no rate, so I have no figure for you. It is a sheet about making the compost, not about applying it: it covers the site, the materials, the layers and the watering, and it stops when the heap is built. There is no dose per hectare, no dose per plant, and no timing for spreading it. I want to be clear that this is a gap in the catalogue and not a detail I am withholding. ICAT can give you a rate for your crop and your soil, and that is the right place for it.
How many times do I have to turn the heap over?

The catalogue does not mention turning the heap at all, so I have nothing to give you on it. What it does ask you to do to the residues is chop the fast rotting ones before they go in, tread the 30 cm layer of plant residues down well with your feet, and water each layer as you lay it. Those are the three handling instructions in the catalogue, and turning is not among them. That may mean the method does not call for it, or it may simply be outside what this sheet covers; I cannot tell you which, and I will not decide it for you. Ask ICAT.
If I follow the layers, how high does the heap come up?

I can give you part of it and not the whole, so here is the working. The catalogue gives a thickness for three of the layers: the base of slow rotting material is 10 to 20 cm, the manure on top of it is 5 cm, and the plant residues are about 30 cm. Add the low case: 10 plus 5 plus 30 makes 45 cm. Add the high case: 20 plus 5 plus 30 makes 55 cm. So those three layers give you roughly 45 to 55 cm. What I cannot add in is the wood ash at the bottom, which the catalogue says to spread lightly without a thickness, and the activator layer on top, whether topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, which has no thickness either. And note the order of the sentence: the catalogue gives the 30 cm and then tells you to tread that layer down well, so read the figure in that order. So take 45 to 55 cm as the part that is written down, not as the height of your finished heap.
My heap will sit on a base of 2 m by 2 m. How much manure is that 5 cm layer?

About 200 litres, and here is the calculation so you can check it. The catalogue puts the manure layer at 5 cm thick, laid over the whole base. Your base is 2 m by 2 m, so 2 times 2 gives 4 square metres. Five centimetres is 0.05 metres. Four square metres times 0.05 metres gives 0.2 cubic metres. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so 0.2 cubic metres is 200 litres. Two things to keep in mind. The catalogue gives no dimension for the base of the heap, so the 2 m by 2 m is yours, not the catalogue's. And it gives the thickness in centimetres of layer, not in weight, so 200 litres is a volume and not a number of kilos.
Compost is just waste left to rot. I do not see why I would go to the trouble of layers.

The layers are the method, so if you drop them you are not doing what the catalogue describes. The catalogue does define composting in a heap as laying plant and animal waste and debris in a heap in a shaded spot to turn them into an organic fertiliser, so you are right about the raw idea. But it then sets out an order, step by step: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure on that base, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well. And a layer of topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, with every layer watered as it goes down. It also sorts the residues for you, fast rotting in, slow rotting stalks and husks out. What the catalogue does not do is tell you what you lose by skipping the layers, and I will not invent a penalty to convince you.
I will build my heap out in the open so the rain waters it for me and I save the work.

That works against two of the catalogue's instructions at once, so I would not. On the site, its first step asks for a shaded spot, easy to reach, and sheltered from the weather, and it names the weather as the wind and the rain. So the rain is something the catalogue shelters the heap from, not something it uses. On the watering, the instruction is to water each layer as you lay it down, which is a thing you do during the building, layer by layer, not something that happens to the heap afterwards. That is also why the catalogue counts a water point nearby as an advantage when you pick the spot. What it does not say is what the rain would do to an unsheltered heap, so I am telling you the instruction, not the consequence.
I have everything gathered. I am going to tip it all on in one go and throw earth over the top.

Stop before you tip. The catalogue builds the heap in a set order and the order is the method, so tipping it in one go loses it. Lay it like this instead, watering each layer as you put it down. A little wood ash spread on the topsoil. Then the base, slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Then 5 cm of manure on that base. Then about 30 cm of plant residues, and tread that layer down well with your feet. Then your earth goes on last, as the activator layer, and the catalogue accepts topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri there. One more check before you start: sort your pile first, because the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are the ones the catalogue asks you to keep out.
The heap is going up dry today and I will water the whole thing tomorrow morning.

Water as you go instead, today. The catalogue's instruction is to water each layer as and when you lay it down, so the water goes in between the layers rather than on top of a finished heap. That is a small change in the order of your work and it costs you nothing extra. It is also the reason the catalogue tells you to choose a site where a water point nearby is an advantage. Keep the rest as planned: wood ash on the topsoil, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves as the base, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, then the activator layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri.
Describe the heap to me in cross section, as if I cut it with a knife.

Cut it down the middle and you would see five bands, bottom to top. At the very bottom, the topsoil of the site with a light dusting of wood ash on it. On that, a band of coarse slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick, which the catalogue calls the support. On the support, a thinner band of manure, 5 cm. Above that the thickest band, about 30 cm of plant residues, and that one is compacted because the catalogue asks you to tread it down well. On top, the activator: a band of topsoil, or of well rotted compost, or of Mycotri powder. Every one of those bands went in damp, because the catalogue has you water each layer as you lay it. And the whole thing stands in shade, sheltered from the wind and the rain.
The heap I made last season is still straw. Nothing has happened to it.

I cannot diagnose your heap, because the catalogue I have describes how to build one and carries no troubleshooting at all. What I can do is put its requirements beside what you have, and you can see which one is missing. It asks for a shaded spot, easy to reach, sheltered from the wind and the rain, with a water point nearby as an advantage. It asks you to chop the fast rotting residues, straw among them, before they go in. It asks you to keep out the slow rotting leftovers, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. It asks for the five layers in order, wood ash, then 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves, then 5 cm of manure, then about 30 cm of residues trodden down, then topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. And it asks you to water every layer as you lay it. If your straw went in whole, or dry, or with no manure layer under it, those are the places the catalogue would point. For an answer on the heap itself, show it to an ICAT agent.
Just tell me roughly, two months, three months? I need to plan my season.

I know that is an awkward answer to refuse, and I am still refusing it, because you would plan a season on it. The catalogue gives no delay. It says mature compost once, in the note where Mycotri is described as a powder of fungi that encourages rapid decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it never puts a number on either the ordinary time or the shortened one. If I said two months you would build your season on a figure I made up here. Two things you can do instead. Ask ICAT, who work with these heaps in your area and can tell you what they see. And in the meantime build the heap the way the catalogue sets out, because that is the part that is written down, and start it as early as your material allows rather than as late as your plan allows.
What is simple lowland development?

It is a way of getting the water to move properly over a rice lowland instead of sitting where it likes. The 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices from the Ministry of Agriculture puts it this way: it is a technique used to improve the use of water in rice lowlands, and the approach consists in building basins and drains to help the water circulate well over the whole cultivated plot. The basins you build let you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Its own heading is addressed to you directly: rice growers, carry out the simple development of your lowlands so as to manage the water under your crops better. The work on the ground is measuring the slope with a water level, clearing the site, and building the bunds that make the basins.
Give me the dimensions of the bunds.

There are two sizes, and the catalogue gives each one three measurements. The main bunds: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. The secondary bunds: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm. So a bund is wider at the bottom than at the top in both cases, and the secondary one is the smaller of the two on all three measurements. One instruction goes with the building: water them as you go, so that they compact well. And on the main bund, leave openings towards the ends, which are the spillways, to let the excess water out.
How do I make the water level they talk about?

The catalogue describes it as a farmer's tool you can build yourself, and it is what you use to work out the slopes so you can draw the plan that sets out the works of the development. On a small area, in a farmer's setting, a water level is enough. It is made of four things: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, a garden hose 5 m long running between the base of each stick, and a transparent tube that extends the hose. That is the whole description the catalogue gives. It does not explain how to read it or how to use it step by step, so ask an ICAT agent to show you once on your own ground rather than working it out from the list of parts.
