Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Water it as you build so it compacts well, and leave openings towards the ends, the spillways, to let the excess water out. For comparison the secondary bund is smaller on all three: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm.
piquets hectare bas-fond

Count 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. The catalogue gives that figure for marking the development plan out on the site, which means setting the layout on the ground before any earth is moved. It is the only quantity per hectare the lowland sheet gives, so take it as the one figure you can budget from. The pegs go in after you have determined the slopes with a water level and drawn the plan from them, not before: the plan decides where they stand. For two hectares that is two times 80 up to two times 100, so between 160 and 200 pegs.
In my lowland the water gathers in one corner and stands there, while the other end dries out. Every year it is the same.

That uneven water is what simple lowland development is meant to deal with. The catalogue calls it a technique to improve the use of water in rice lowlands: you build basins and drains so the water circulates over the whole cultivated plot, and the basins let you regulate the quantity of water on each parcel. The order of work it gives is this. First the slopes, which a water level is enough to find on a small holding, and from them you draw the plan that sets out the works. Then clearing, ridding the site of certain trees and shrubs with pickaxes and machetes. Then the bunds that make the basins: main ones 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary ones 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Water them as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund for the excess. Those stages are not the whole sequence, so do not read them as a complete list. Ask ICAT to walk the lowland with you before you start.
I like the idea but I am on my own here. I cannot move that much earth by myself.

The catalogue says the same thing and gives the same answer. Its practical advice is that to lift the constraint of the absence of labour, it is preferable to carry out the development as a group, through farmers' organisations. So the shortage of hands is treated in the catalogue as a normal obstacle, not as a reason to drop the work. What that means in practice is that the lowland is developed collectively rather than plot by plot. What the catalogue does not give is how many people a hectare needs, how many days it takes, or how such a group shares the work and the result afterwards. None of that is in the catalogue, so it is a question for ICAT and for the farmers' organisation in your area.
Main bund or secondary bund, how do I tell which one I am building?

By its dimensions, because that is how the catalogue separates them, and the main one is bigger on all three measurements. Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm. There is a second difference, and it is the useful one on the ground: the spillways belong to the main bund. The catalogue says that in building the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends so as to evacuate the excess water. It says nothing of the sort for the secondary bunds. So the main bund is the one that is bigger and the one that is pierced.
What is the difference between the basins and the drains?

The catalogue names them both in the same sentence and gives a purpose only to one of them, so I will be exact about what it says and what it does not. Its definition is that the approach consists in building basins and drains to help the water circulate well over the whole cultivated plot. Then it adds one line about the basins alone: the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. So the basins are what holds and regulates the water on a parcel. For the drains, the catalogue gives no separate definition, no dimension and no siting rule. It puts them in the technique and stops there. I am not going to describe a drain for you out of general knowledge. ICAT can tell you where the drains go on your own lowland, and that is a field question anyway because it follows your slopes.
True or false: I can build the bunds dry and the rains will settle them for me.

False. The catalogue's practical advice is the opposite: at the moment of making the bunds, you will have to water them as you go, in order to compact them well. So the watering happens during the building, by your hand, not afterwards by the rain. That is the one instruction it attaches to how the earth goes down. The rest of what it tells you about the bunds is their size: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the upper base, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30.
True or false: the main bund has to be solid all along, with no break in it.

False, and the break is deliberate. The catalogue says that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, which it calls spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the gaps are part of the design and they go towards the ends, not anywhere along the length. Everything else about the main bund stays as given: lower base 80 to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm, watered as you build it so that it compacts well.
Should I develop my own plot on my own, or wait and do it with the others?

On this one the catalogue expresses a preference, so I will pass it on as it stands. It says that to lift the constraint of the absence of labour, it is preferable to carry out the development as a group, through farmers' organisations. Preferable is its word. The reason it gives is labour and only labour: the work of moving that much earth. It does not claim the result is better done as a group, and it does not say what to do if there is no organisation near you or if the others are not ready. So the honest reading is this: if your difficulty is hands, the catalogue points you to the group. If your difficulty is something else, the catalogue does not answer it, and ICAT is the address.
The site has trees on it. Do I just clear them, or is there something else I am supposed to do?

Both, in that order. The clearing is in the method: the catalogue says the work consists in ridding the site of certain trees and shrubs, using pickaxes and machetes. Note the word certain, which is its word, not all. And then it puts a second instruction beside it in its practical advice: carry out a compensatory replanting, on another plot, of the trees cleared or grubbed out on the site. Its words are another plot, so the trees you take off the lowland are meant to go back on a plot other than this one. The catalogue does not say how many, or which species, or when, so I have no rule to give you there. If you want the replanting to earn something as well, the same catalogue's agroforestry sheet is where the tree practices sit.
Why water the bunds while I am building them?

For this one the catalogue gives you the reason in the same breath as the instruction: at the moment of making the bunds, it will be necessary to water them as you go, in order to compact them well. So the reason is compaction. That is the whole of it, and it is written down, which is why I can give it to you plainly. What the catalogue does not say is how much water, or how often during the work, or how you know the bund is compacted enough. Those are not in the catalogue. The dimensions are: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30.
Why would I deliberately leave holes in a bund I have just built?

Because the catalogue tells you why, and the reason is the excess water. Its words are that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water. So the openings are the way out for water the basin cannot hold, and they sit towards the ends rather than in the middle of the run. Read it alongside what the basins are for in the same sheet: the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. Holding the water and letting the surplus out are two halves of the same job, and the spillway is the second half.
What is a basin, in the technical sense used here?

The catalogue uses the term in its definition of the technique and gives it one function. The technique is described as improving the use of water in rice lowlands, and the approach consists in building basins and drains to facilitate a good circulation of the water over the whole cultivated plot. Then, of the basins specifically, it says that the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. So functionally a basin is a compartment of the lowland whose water level you can control. I should add that the catalogue never writes the sentence that says the bunds are what enclose the basins: it sets out the technique, then it gives the bund dimensions, main and secondary, and leaves you to see the link on the ground. What the catalogue does not give is the size of a basin, the number of basins per hectare, or the rule for setting them out, because that follows the slopes you measure on your own site. So I can give you the function and not the geometry.
How does the water level actually work?

I can give you what it is made of and not how it works, because the catalogue lists the parts and stops. Its description: a water level is made up of two sticks graduated every 5 cm, a garden hose 5 m long between the base of each stick, and a transparent tube that extends the previous one. That is the whole entry. It does not state the principle it works on, it does not tell you how to take a reading, and it does not tell you how to turn your readings into the plan. What it does say is why you reach for it: in a farmer's setting, on small areas, a water level will allow the slopes to be determined so as to draw the plan that materialises the works of the development. For the handling, ask an ICAT agent to show you on your own ground. That is one demonstration and you have it for life, which is better than a description from me.
I want to develop my lowland this year.

Two things first and I can be useful. Roughly what area is the lowland, in hectares or in the measure you use? And is there a farmers' organisation working near you, or would you be doing the earthwork with your own household only?
About two hectares, and there is a growers' group in the village that works together on other things.

Then the group is your answer for the work, and the catalogue says so itself: to lift the constraint of the absence of labour, it is preferable to carry out the development as a group, through farmers' organisations. For the pegs, the figure is 80 to 100 per hectare for marking the plan out on the site. You have two hectares, so two times 80 is 160 and two times 100 is 200: count between 160 and 200 pegs. Before any of that, determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the whole point is that the water should circulate well over the whole plot. Then the earthwork: main bunds at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30, watered as you build so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund. And plan a compensatory replanting elsewhere for the trees you clear.
Give me the full sequence of steps from start to finish.

I can give you three parts of it and I want to be clear that it is not the whole sequence. What I hold is this. Determine the slopes, for which a water level is enough on a small area, and draw the plan that sets out the works of the development. Rid the site of certain trees and shrubs, using pickaxes and machetes. Build the bunds, main ones at 80 to 100 cm lower base, 35 to 40 cm upper base and 30 to 35 cm high, secondary ones at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30, watering them as you go so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund. What sits between the clearing and the bunds I do not have, and I am not going to invent a stage to make the list look complete. Ask ICAT for the full sequence before you start, and take the three above as the parts you can already prepare for.
What will this cost me and what will it bring back?

Neither figure is in the catalogue, so I have neither to give you. It gives no cost for the development, no yield gain for the rice afterwards, and no measure of how much any of these practices offsets the climate. It presents them as good practices in the era of climate change and leaves the arithmetic out. I would rather tell you that than put a number in front of you that came from nowhere. What it does give you is quantities you can price yourself where you are: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking out the layout, the bund dimensions so you can judge the earth to be moved, and the advice to do the work as a group because of the labour. Take those to ICAT with your own area and they can help you build a real figure.
How big should each basin be, and how many on a hectare?

The catalogue does not say, and this is a real gap rather than something I am holding back. It gives you the dimensions of the bunds, both main and secondary, and it gives you 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking out the plan. It gives no basin size, no number of basins per hectare, and no spacing rule. And there is a reason that is visible in the catalogue itself: the first stage is to determine the slopes with a water level in order to draw the plan that materialises the works. So the layout comes out of your own ground, not out of a standard figure. That is precisely why ICAT should see the lowland before you set the pegs.
My lowland is two and a half hectares. How many pegs do I need?

Between 200 and 250 pegs, and here is the arithmetic so you can check it. The catalogue says to provide 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking out the development plan on the site. You have 2.5 hectares. Two and a half times 80 gives 200, and two and a half times 100 gives 250. So 200 at the low end of its range and 250 at the high end. Take that as what it is: a quantity for marking out the layout, not for the building itself. The number you actually drive in depends on the plan you draw after you have determined the slopes with a water level, and the catalogue gives no plan you can copy.
How much earth is in 100 m of main bund? I want to know what I am taking on.

The catalogue gives no volume, so I am building it from its own dimensions. Treat it as an order of size, not as its figure. The main bund is 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the upper base and 30 to 35 cm high, so its cross section is a trapezium. The small case: bases 80 and 35 cm average 57.5 cm, times a height of 30 cm gives 1,725 square centimetres, and since a square metre is 10,000 square centimetres that is 0.1725 square metres. Over 100 m: 17.25 cubic metres. The large case: bases 100 and 40 average 70 cm, times 35 cm gives 2,450 square centimetres, or 0.245 square metres, and over 100 m that is 24.5 cubic metres. So roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth for 100 m of main bund. Set that beside the catalogue's own advice, which is that it is preferable to carry out the development as a group through farmers' organisations, so as to lift the constraint of the absence of labour.
A bund is a bund. I will build them all to one size and save myself the measuring.

The catalogue does distinguish them, and it distinguishes them on every measurement, so I would not merge the two. Main bund: lower base 80 cm to 100 cm, upper base 35 to 40 cm, height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: lower base 70 to 80 cm, upper base 25 to 30 cm, height 25 to 30 cm. And there is a difference that is not about size at all: the spillways belong to the main bund, where the catalogue tells you to provide openings towards the ends to evacuate the excess water. And it gives no such instruction for the secondary bunds. What it does not do is explain what each size is for or what goes wrong if you swap them, so I am telling you that the catalogue holds them apart, not what the penalty is for joining them.
It is my plot. I will clear every tree off the lowland and that is the end of it.

Two things in the catalogue cut across that. First, its own instruction is narrower than yours: the work consists in ridding the site of certain trees and shrubs, with pickaxes and machetes. Certain, not all. Second, it does not treat the clearing as the end of it. Among its practical pieces of advice it says to carry out a compensatory replanting, on another plot, of the trees cleared or grubbed out on the site. So the catalogue expects the trees to come back somewhere, off the lowland. I cannot tell you which trees on your site fall under its certain and which do not, because it gives no criterion, and I will not decide that for you. That is a question to put to ICAT while they are looking at your slopes anyway.
I know my lowland well. I am going to lay the bunds out by eye and start tomorrow.

Measure the slopes first. The catalogue puts that before everything else: on small areas, in a farmer's setting, a water level will allow the slopes to be determined so as to draw the plan that materialises the works of the development. The whole point of the technique is that the water should circulate well over the whole cultivated plot, and where the water goes is decided by the slope, not by the eye. The level is something you can make: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, a garden hose 5 m long between the base of each stick, and a transparent tube extending it. Then mark the plan out on the ground with pegs, counting 80 to 100 per hectare. After that, the earthwork, with the main bunds at 80 to 100 cm lower base, 35 to 40 cm upper base and 30 to 35 cm high. Ask ICAT to check the plan before you move earth.
I am starting the main bund this morning. Straight run, right across, end to end.

Before the first load goes down, two things from the catalogue. Leave the openings. The catalogue says that in the construction of the main bund you should provide openings towards the ends, the spillways, in order to evacuate the excess water, so a straight unbroken run is not what it describes. And water the earth as you go, because its advice is that at the moment of making the bunds you will have to water them as you go in order to compact them well. Keep your section right as you build: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the upper base, 30 to 35 cm high. And if you have not yet set your pegs to the plan, at 80 to 100 per hectare, do that before the earth rather than after.
Describe a main bund to me as if I had cut through it.

Cut across it and you see a shape that is wide at the bottom and narrower at the top, with sloping sides. At ground level, the lower base measures 80 cm to 100 cm across. At the top, the upper base measures 35 to 40 cm, so it is roughly half the width of the foot, or less. Between the two, the height stands at 30 to 35 cm, so it comes up to about the middle of your shin. The earth in it is damp and packed, not loose, because the catalogue has you water it as you build it in order to compact it well. And along the run, towards each end, the wall is deliberately interrupted: those gaps are the spillways, provided to evacuate the excess water. A secondary bund is the same shape one size down: 70 to 80 cm at the foot, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high.
The bunds I put up last season have gone at the ends. The water took them.

I cannot tell you why yours went. The catalogue I have describes how to build a lowland and carries nothing on repairing or diagnosing one. What I can do is set its requirements beside what happened, and you can see which is in play. It asks you to water the bunds as you make them, in order to compact them well, so a bund built dry is one thing it warns against. It asks you to provide openings towards the ends of the main bund, the spillways, to evacuate the excess water, so if the surplus had no way out, the ends are exactly where it would be working. It asks for a main bund of 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, so an undersized section is a third thing to look at. And it asks you to determine the slopes with a water level first and draw the plan from them, so a bund placed against the slope is a fourth. Which it is, I cannot say from here. Show the ends to an ICAT agent before you rebuild.
Come on, just tell me how much more rice a developed lowland gives. Everybody knows it gives more.

I am not going to give you a figure, and I want to be clear it is not because I am being careful with you. There is no figure in the catalogue. The catalogue presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and puts no yield gain, no cost and no measure of impact against any of them, the lowland development included. If I answered your question I would be making the number up, and you would carry it to a decision. Here is what the catalogue does claim, in its own words, and it is a claim about water rather than about yield: the technique improves the use of water in rice lowlands, the basins and drains help the water circulate well over the whole cultivated plot, and the basins built allow the quantity of water on the parcels to be regulated. If somebody has told you a percentage, ask them where they read it. And ask ICAT, who see developed lowlands in your area and can tell you what they actually get, which is worth more than a figure from either of us.
I keep about a dozen hens behind the house for the family. Now I want to make it a business. What do I change first?

The flock size, before anything else. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference asks for a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, and a dozen birds is the family henhouse, not that. The ratio it works on is one cock for ten hens, so 60 hens call for 6 cocks and no more. Two things come with that number and you should know them before you start buying. The same reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, and it notes that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself. And it houses breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, so 66 birds need about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment. Go to ICAT for the reference itself and for help turning it into a business plan.
I have 15 hens and 2 cocks and I am calling it a commercial unit.

Your ratio is near enough, your flock is not. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets the minimum breeding nucleus of a commercial local hen unit at 60 hens and 6 cocks, and 15 hens is a quarter of that. On the cocks you are close to the mark: the ratio is one cock for ten hens, so 15 hens call for one or two. What the figure of 60 carries with it is the rest of the model, and none of it transfers down. The start-up of 3,850,124 FCFA, the first year working capital of 2,150,491 FCFA, the net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 in year two, all of it is evaluated on 60 hens and 6 cocks in 2020 prices. Fifteen hens is the improved village henhouse, which the 2017 ESFT compendium describes, and that is a different farm with its own figures. Ask ICAT whether you build up to 60 or keep what you have.
Give me the breeding nucleus and the zootechnical parameters the commercial reference works on.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, with a sex ratio of one cock for ten hens. Its zootechnical parameters are these: six production cycles a year; about ten eggs laid per hen per laying; about six layings a year; a natural hatching rate near 70 percent; and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Live weight at six months is about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock, and both hens and cocks are culled at 24 months. Those are 2020 evaluations and annual projections for one unit, not results you are promised. For the study itself, and for a plan built on your own flock, go to ICAT.
How many hens will fit in the henhouse I already have?

I cannot give you that number, because it depends on two things I do not have: the floor area of your building, and which model you are following. For a commercial unit the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference houses breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre. For the improved village henhouse the 2017 ESFT compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre. Those are different farms and the same floor gives a very different count. Measure the inside, tell me the length and the width and which of the two you are building, and the number follows. One thing I will not give you even then: neither reference says which way the building should face, so do not take an orientation from me. ICAT holds the plans.
I can only run 30 hens. Does the whole model just halve?

The birds halve, the equipment does not. At one cock for ten hens, 30 hens call for 3 cocks. But 30 is below the minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks that the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for a commercial unit, and that matters most at the incubator: the reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, and already warns that at 60 you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself. At 30 that problem is worse, not smaller. Housing does scale cleanly: at 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 33 birds need between 3.3 and 4.1 square metres. So run the 30 if that is what you can feed, but take the equipment list to ICAT before you buy an incubator sized for twice your flock.
I have decided to go into local hens commercially. What do I settle before I buy a single bird?

Settle the nucleus and everything it drags behind it. The number is 60 hens and 6 cocks, the minimum the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens. Before the birds arrive, build the henhouse: that reference wants at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, with the breeders at 8 to 10 per square metre. Dig the manure pit, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam. Put in the feeders, drinkers and nest boxes, and plan the grassy run and the store. Choose your breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. And look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after. ICAT holds the plans and the reference.
I bought 20 hens and 8 cocks last month and the cocks are always at each other.

You have four times the cocks that flock needs. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on one cock for ten hens, so 20 hens call for 2 cocks, and its minimum commercial nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks is the same ratio seen from the other end. Sell or cull down to two, keeping the vigorous and agile birds with a well developed bright red comb, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Managing the flock also means selling the cockerels born on the farm and culling the poor layers, so plan on doing this again. If any bird has been injured in the fighting, take it out or isolate it, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see illness in the flock.
My flock is 60 birds but I hardly get any chicks out of it.

Tell me how those 60 are split first, because the nucleus in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is 66 birds, at one cock for ten hens. If your 60 includes 20 cocks, or only one, that alone would explain what you are seeing. The parameters that reference works on are about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and six production cycles a year. If the split is right and the chicks still do not come, look at the eggs you set: keep them seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, set them pointed end down, and discard the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs.
Just tell me I can start with 20 hens and it will work out.

I will not tell you that, because the figure I hold says otherwise. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sets the minimum breeding nucleus for a commercial unit at 60 hens and 6 cocks, and calls it the minimum for the unit to hold. Twenty hens is a third of it, and every projection in that study rests on the 60: the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up, the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, the net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one. None of those numbers transfer to a third of the flock. You can certainly keep 20 hens and do it well, and the 2017 ESFT compendium describes exactly that improved village henhouse, but it is a different farm with different figures, and I would rather tell you which one you are running than agree with you. Ask ICAT which of the two fits your ground and your money.
How many cocks do I need for my hens?

One cock for about ten hens. That is the ratio the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference works on for commercial local hens, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium gives the same in its own words. It is why the minimum breeding nucleus in the commercial reference is 60 hens and 6 cocks. More cocks than that will not give you more chicks; it gives you fighting and worn hens. Where the care belongs is in which cock you keep: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, from a well followed farm or a research centre if you can, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.
True or false: more cocks means more chicks.

False. The ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference builds its minimum commercial nucleus on it: 60 hens and 6 cocks. What sets how many chicks you get is the laying and the hatching, not the number of cocks. In that reference it is about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and six production cycles a year. Extra cocks fight, tread the hens bare and eat feed for nothing. Cull back to the ratio and put the effort into choosing the cock you keep, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.
Sixty hens: do I keep six cocks or twelve?

Six. One cock for about ten hens is the ratio the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on, and 60 hens and 6 cocks is exactly the minimum breeding nucleus it gives for a commercial unit. Twelve is double, and it buys you nothing that makes chicks: the hatching figures in that reference are about ten eggs per hen per laying, about six layings a year and a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and a second cock per ten hens changes none of them. What twelve cocks do bring is fighting, hens with bare backs, and six extra birds on the feed bill. Sell or cull the extra six and keep the vigorous, agile ones with a well developed bright red comb.
Why one cock for ten hens and not one for five? Justify.

Because that is the ratio both Togolese references hold to, and the whole commercial model is built on it: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is that ratio exactly. Going to one for five doubles the cocks without touching anything that makes chicks. The parameters in that reference are about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year and a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and those belong to the hens and the eggs, not to how many cocks stand in the yard. The extra birds cost you feed, they fight, and they wear the hens. What the reference does ask you to be careful about is which cock, not how many: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.
State the sex ratio and how it sizes the nucleus.

The sex ratio is one cock for ten hens, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference and in the 2017 ESFT village compendium alike. Applied to the minimum commercial nucleus it gives 60 hens and 6 cocks, 66 birds in all. Housed at that reference's breeder density of 8 to 10 birds per square metre, those 66 birds call for about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment. The birds of the nucleus are culled at 24 months in the 2020 reference, hens and cocks alike, where the 2017 compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Those two figures describe two different farms and each should be given with the reference it comes from.
Which breed of cock gives the best chicks?

I cannot name a breed for you, because neither Togolese reference names one. What they give is the ratio, one cock for about ten hens, and what to look for in the bird rather than in its breed: breeders taken from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference adds the weights you should see at six months, about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. For a named breed, and for where to buy it near you, ask ICAT. That is not something I should answer from memory.
A neighbour is setting up a hen house and asks me how many cocks he should put in.

Tell him one cock for about ten hens. Both Togolese references work on that ratio, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference builds its minimum commercial nucleus on it: 60 hens and 6 cocks. Tell him two other things while he is listening. First, it is which cock that matters, not how many: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, taken from a well followed farm or a research centre, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Second, whatever bird he brings in, bought or given, it goes two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock, so he does not carry a disease home with it.
I am about to buy cocks tomorrow. What do I work out tonight?

Count your hens and divide by ten. That is how many cocks to buy, because the ratio both references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and it is the same ratio that gives the commercial nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Then decide what you will look at in the market: vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and if you can, bought from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from whoever is at the stall, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. And have the quarantine ready before you leave the house: every newly bought bird goes two weeks apart from the flock, bought or given, so you do not bring a disease in.
Several of my hens have bare backs and scratches on the shoulders.

That is what too many cocks does. Count them against your hens: the ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and above it the same birds get trodden over and over. Bring the number down, keeping the vigorous agile cocks with a well developed bright red comb and selling the rest; managing the flock also means selling the cockerels born on the farm and culling the poor layers. Watch the scratched hens while they heal, take out or isolate any bird that falls ill, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see disease in the flock. If you treat a bird, do not eat its meat or its eggs for a few days, because they can hold drug residues.
My hens are running away from the cocks and hiding in the corners.

Count the cocks first. The ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and hens that hide are usually hens being trodden too often. Bring the number down to the ratio, keeping the vigorous agile birds with a well developed bright red comb and selling the rest. While you are in there, look at the flock properly: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists eight signs of a sick bird, and they are worth knowing. The bird is sad, drowsy and downcast; its wings droop and its feathers stand up; it keeps away from the flock; it does not eat; it is thin; it has a discharge from the nose and the mouth; it moves with difficulty; and it has diarrhoea. If that is what you are seeing rather than simple wear, call the animal health worker.
Just tell me it is fine to keep one cock for every three hens.

I will not, because the figure I hold says one cock for about ten hens, and both Togolese references give it. One for three is more than three times what the model asks, and the whole commercial nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference rests on that ratio. It does not buy you chicks: the hatching in that study comes from about ten eggs per hen per laying, about six layings a year and a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and the cocks beyond the ratio touch none of it. What it buys is fighting, worn hens and a feed bill. If you have a reason of your own for wanting more cocks, take it to ICAT, but I am not going to confirm a figure the references contradict.
I want to fix my flock before the next season.

Tell me two things and I can be useful: how many hens you have, and how many cocks. The ratio both Togolese references work on is one cock for about ten hens, and that is where most flocks are out. If you know the floor area of the henhouse, say it too, because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference houses commercial breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre while the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre, and those are two different farms.
Forty hens, seven cocks, and the henhouse is four metres by three.

Then cut the cocks to four. At one cock for ten hens, 40 hens call for 4, and the three extra will fight and wear the hens for nothing. Keep the vigorous agile ones with a well developed bright red comb, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and sell the others. On the housing you have room either way: four by three is 12 square metres, which holds 96 to 120 birds at the commercial density of 8 to 10 per square metre, or 60 to 72 at the village density of 5 to 6, so your 44 birds are comfortable on either reading. One thing to know if you mean to go commercial: the minimum breeding nucleus that reference gives is 60 hens and 6 cocks, so at 40 hens you are still below it. Ask ICAT whether to build up and what it would cost you.
What should I look for when I pick a breeding cock?

Take him vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, and get him from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from wherever you happen to be. That is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks of a breeder, and the reason it insists is that the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. At six months he should be around 1.5 kg live weight in that reference, against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Keep one cock for about ten hens and no more. And whatever bird you bring home, bought or given, quarantine him two weeks before he joins the flock.
comment choisir coq reproducteur

Vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, and bought from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from the market if you can manage it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for exactly that in a breeder, and it gives the reason: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Keep one cock for about ten hens. At six months he should weigh around 1.5 kg. And two weeks of quarantine before he goes in with the others, whether you bought him or were given him.
I was given a cock by my uncle. Can I use him as my breeder?

Perhaps, but keep him apart for two weeks whatever you decide. Quarantine is the rule for every new bird, bought or given, so a disease does not come in with him. Then judge him on what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks of a breeder: vigorous and agile, a well developed bright red comb, around 1.5 kg at six months. That reference would rather you took breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, and the reason is not fussiness: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. If your uncle's bird is thin, drowsy, keeping away from the others or off his feed, he is not a poor breeder, he is a sick bird, and that is a matter for the animal health worker.
The cock only matters for fertilising the eggs, so any cock will do.

That is not what the references say the cock does for you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is plain that he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and that is why it tells you to take breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. Any cock will not do. What is true is that you do not need many: one for about ten hens, which is why the minimum commercial nucleus is 60 hens and 6 cocks. So the care belongs on which cock you keep, not on how many you run, and a cockerel born on your own well followed farm is often the better replacement.
True or false: a thin cock with a pale comb is still fine for breeding.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for breeders that are vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb, and around 1.5 kg at six months for a cock. Thin with a pale comb is the opposite of that description. Worse, thinness is on the list of signs of a sick bird in the same reference, along with being sad, drowsy and downcast, wings drooping and feathers standing up, keeping away from the flock, not eating, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, moving with difficulty and diarrhoea. Take him out of the breeding pen, isolate him, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Do not breed from him.
Should I keep my best cock for three years or change him at two?

The two Togolese references differ here and you should know which one you are following. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike. The 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. If you are running the commercial model, the one with the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, take the 24 months. If yours is the improved village henhouse, the three years is the figure written for that farm. Either way, renew from the cockerels born on your own farm where you can, and choose the replacement vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb.
What does the reference specify for the breeding cock?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the appearance, the weight, the ratio and the culling age. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Appearance: vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb. Live weight at six months: about 1.5 kg for a cock, against about 1.3 kg for a hen. Ratio: one cock for ten hens, which is what gives the minimum nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Culling: at 24 months, for cocks and hens alike, where the 2017 ESFT compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. The reason it gives for all that care is one sentence: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy.
If I go up to 120 hens, how many cocks and how do I pick them?

Twelve cocks, at one for about ten hens, which is twice the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks that the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives as the commercial minimum. The picking does not scale the same way: each one still has to be vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, and still better taken from a well followed farm or a research centre than from a market stall, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Two things do scale with the flock. Housing: at 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 132 birds call for between 13.2 and 16.5 square metres of breeder compartment. And hatching: that reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, so at 120 hens you are past what one such machine was sized for. Take the plan to ICAT before you buy.
My brother is choosing cocks at the market this week. What should I tell him?

Tell him three things. Look for a bird that is vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks of a breeder. Buy from a well followed farm or a research centre if he can rather than from the stall, because that reference says the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. And whatever he brings home, keep it two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock, bought or given, so he does not carry a disease in. Remind him of the count as well, since people always buy too many: one cock for about ten hens.
Before I put the new cock in with the hens, what do I do?

Two weeks of quarantine, apart from the flock, whether you bought him or were given him. That is the rule for every new bird and it is there so a disease does not come in with him. While he is apart, watch for the signs of a sick bird: sad, drowsy and downcast, wings drooping and feathers standing up, keeping away, not eating, thin, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, moving with difficulty, diarrhoea. Check he is what a breeder should be, vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, around 1.5 kg at six months. And count the cocks you already have, because at one for about ten hens you may be adding one too many. Wash the feeders and drinkers, and spray disinfectant inside the shelter if there have been lice, ticks or fleas.
My cock treads the hens but the eggs never hatch.

Look at the eggs and at how you set them before you blame the bird. Keep them seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. Discard the ones that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs; with an electric, gas or solar incubator the incubation lasts twenty-one days, after which the chicks come out of the shells. The natural hatching rate the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on is near 70 percent, so some failures are expected, but none hatching at all is not. Then the cock: he should be vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, at one cock for about ten hens. If he is thin, pale combed or keeping away from the flock, he is a sick bird before he is a poor breeder, and that is for the animal health worker.
Just tell me my cock is good enough, I do not want to buy another.

I cannot tell you that, because I have not seen the bird. But the reference hands you the test, so you can do it yourself tonight. Hold him and look: vigorous and agile, a well developed bright red comb, around 1.5 kg at six months. If he answers that description he is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for and you have no reason to buy anything. If he is thin, slow or pale combed, the same reference would have you replace him, and it says why: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Replacing him need not cost you money either, because you can keep back a cockerel born on your own farm and raise him for the job. If you are still unsure, put the bird in front of ICAT or the animal health worker rather than in front of me.
My chicks come out small and a lot of them die.

Several things do that, so let me narrow it down. Tell me where your cock came from and what he looks like, and tell me how you feed the chicks and what water they get. I start with the cock because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is plain that he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and I ask about the water because the 2017 ESFT compendium says chicks die easily of dehydration.
The cock is one I caught from the village flock. The chicks eat what the big hens eat and they drink from the same drinker.

Both of those need changing, and the feeding first because it kills faster. Take the chicks off the adults' feed and drinker: the 2017 compendium says to feed them apart so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, and to keep clean water in front of them at all times. The 2020 reference's own formula for 1 to 8 weeks, per 100 kg of feed, is 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Then the cock. A bird caught from the village flock is the opposite of what that reference asks for: it wants breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, with a well developed bright red comb. Replace him, and keep the mother hen with the chicks for the first weeks, because she adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. If the deaths carry on after all that, call the animal health worker.
parametres zootechniques poule locale commerciale

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference: six production cycles a year; about ten eggs laid per hen per laying; about six layings a year; a natural hatching rate near 70 percent; a mortality rate near 10 percent. Sex ratio one cock for ten hens. Live weight at six months about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Hens and cocks alike are culled at 24 months. Those are 2020 evaluations for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, not a promise about your flock.
My hens have been laying since February and I want to know whether what I am getting is normal.

Compare it against the parameters the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on, and count in layings rather than in months. That reference plans about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, and six production cycles a year on the unit as a whole. Of the eggs you set, it works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and it expects a mortality rate near 10 percent. So over a full year a hen in that model gives you roughly sixty eggs, not sixty chicks. If you are well under that, the first places to look are the feed, the water and the eggs you keep back for setting. Those figures are 2020 evaluations for a commercial unit, so treat them as a yardstick, not as what you are owed.
I read the hens lay ten eggs a year, so sixty hens give me six hundred eggs.

The ten is per laying, not per year. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on about ten eggs laid per hen per laying and about six layings a year, so it is closer to sixty eggs a hen over the year, and your sixty hens are nearer three thousand six hundred eggs than six hundred. Two other figures belong with it before you plan on that number: a natural hatching rate near 70 percent for the eggs you set, and a mortality rate near 10 percent. And not every egg is set; the same reference has you discard the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Those are 2020 evaluations for one commercial unit, so use them to plan, not to promise.
True or false: a good local hen weighs about two kilos at six months.

False. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives about 1.3 kg live weight at six months for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Two kilos is above both. If your birds are heavier than that at six months they are probably not the local hen this reference describes, and if they are well under it, look at the feed before anything else: from 61 days to sale at six months that reference counts about 5 kg of feed in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. The weights matter because they are also what you sell on, and the same study culls hens and cocks alike at 24 months.
Should I plan on six production cycles a year or on four to be safe?

Plan on six if you are following the commercial model, because that is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on, and every other figure in its projection is built on the same six. Change one and you have to change the rest: about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, a mortality rate near 10 percent, and the first year selling 1,422 birds, 2,376 eggs and 50 kg of droppings. If you want to be prudent, be prudent on the money rather than on the cycles: that reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two, so the first year is thin even at six cycles. Take your own version of the projection to ICAT.
Why does the reference bother giving a mortality rate at all? Justify.

Because a projection that assumes every bird lives is not a projection, it is a wish, and you would build your costs on it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a mortality rate near 10 percent, alongside a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, precisely so that the birds you plan to sell are the ones left after losses. It is what lets the study arrive at 1,422 birds sold in the first year rather than at the number hatched. It also tells you when to worry: if you are losing far more than one bird in ten, that is not the normal loss the model allows for, and you should be looking at the signs of a sick bird and calling the animal health worker rather than adjusting your spreadsheet.
How many eggs will my hens lay next month?

I cannot tell you that, and no reference can. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA study gives is an annual average for a commercial unit: about ten eggs laid per hen per laying and about six layings a year, with six production cycles a year for the unit. Those are evaluations across a year, not a forecast for a particular month, and laying is not spread evenly. What happens on your farm next month depends on the age of your hens, what they are fed, the water they get and whether the flock is healthy, none of which I can see. Keep the movement register the reference asks for, with sales, hatchings and deaths, and after a year you will have your own figure, which is worth more than mine. For help reading it, ask ICAT.
If I run 120 hens instead of 60, what do the parameters give me?

The rates do not change, the counts double. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on about ten eggs laid per hen per laying and about six layings a year, so 120 hens give you roughly twice the eggs of 60. The natural hatching rate stays near 70 percent and the mortality rate near 10 percent, because those are proportions. The sex ratio holds too, one cock for ten hens, so 120 hens call for 12 cocks. What does not simply double is the equipment: that reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, so at 120 you are past what one machine was sized for. And the money in the study, the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up and the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, is evaluated on the unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks in 2020 prices, so do not just multiply it by two without taking it to ICAT.
Someone at the cooperative asked me what a local hen unit actually produces in a year.

Give them the figures with the study they come from, because they are evaluations and not guarantees. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference works on six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, for a unit built on 60 hens and 6 cocks. On the selling side its first year projection is 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, which comes to 3,487,181 FCFA, all in 2020 prices. Tell them the prices are 2020 evaluations and that today's have to be checked on the market. ICAT holds the study itself.
Before I write my projection, which figures should I have in front of me?

Have the five zootechnical parameters of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, because everything else is built on them: six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Add the sex ratio of one cock for ten hens and the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks, the six month weights of about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, and the culling age of 24 months. Then the money, all 2020 evaluations: 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, and a first year projection of 3,487,181 FCFA of sales. Write your own prices beside theirs rather than over them, and take the whole projection to ICAT.
My hens sit well and hatch well but I still end up with far fewer birds than I counted on.

Then look at the losses rather than at the hatching. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, and if your hatching is good the gap is in the second figure. Losing far more than one bird in ten is not the normal loss that model allows for. Watch for the signs it lists: the bird is sad, drowsy and downcast, its wings droop and its feathers stand up, it keeps away from the flock, it does not eat, it is thin, it has a discharge from the nose and the mouth, it moves with difficulty, and it has diarrhoea. Isolate any bird like that, take dead birds out fast and bury them well away, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Keep the movement register with hatchings and deaths so you can see where in the cycle you are losing them.
My hens only come into lay two or three times in the year.

That is under what the commercial model works on. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans about six layings a year, with about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, and six production cycles a year on the unit. Two or three layings is half of it. The first things to check are feed and water, since a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in that reference and the water has to be clean, in the shade, freely available and renewed at least twice a day. Then look at the hens themselves: the same study culls at 24 months, and a flock kept past that will lay less. Managing the flock also means culling the poor layers rather than feeding them. If the birds are thin or off their feed, that is a health question and it belongs with the animal health worker.
reforme poule locale a quel age

At 24 months for hens and cocks alike in the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference. The 2017 ESFT village compendium gives a different figure for a different farm: breeding cocks culled after three years of keeping. Say which of the two you are following before you use either number. Renewal comes from your own flock: sell the cockerels born on the farm, keep back the ones you want as breeders, and cull the poor layers rather than feed them another year.
My first hens are coming up to two years old and they still look healthy.

Healthy is not the test the commercial model uses. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike, and it does that because the projection rests on birds in their productive stretch, not on birds that are merely alive. If you are running that model, this is the moment to renew. Take the replacements from your own flock: keep back cockerels born on the farm, choose them vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, and cull the poor layers at the same time. If yours is instead the improved village henhouse of the 2017 ESFT compendium, that source gives three years of keeping for the breeding cocks, which is a different farm and a different figure. The culled birds are not a loss, they are part of what the reference expects you to sell.
Both references say to cull at two years, so I will change everything at 24 months.

They do not both say that, and the difference is worth keeping straight. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike. The 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Those are two Togolese sources describing two different farms, the commercial unit and the improved village henhouse, and each figure is right for the one it was written about. So the answer depends on which farm you are running, and you should give the figure with the reference it comes from when you pass it on. What holds either way is the renewal itself: sell the cockerels born on the farm, keep back your replacements from among them, and cull the poor layers.
Cull the old hens and buy new ones, or keep back pullets from my own flock?

Keep back your own where you can. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference treats renewal as part of running the flock rather than as a purchase: managing the unit means selling the cockerels born on the farm and culling the poor layers, and your replacements come from the same hatchings. Buying in costs money and brings risk, because every bird that arrives, bought or given, has to spend two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock. Where buying is worth it is when you are refreshing the breeding cocks, and there the reference would rather you took them from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb. Cull at 24 months in that commercial model, and sell the culled birds rather than keeping them.
Why cull a hen that is still laying something? Justify.

Because she is eating against a projection built on birds that lay properly. A hen in lay takes 80 grams of feed a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and that cost falls the same whether she gives you ten eggs a laying or three. The same reference works on about six layings a year and culls at 24 months, and it names culling the poor layers as part of managing the flock, alongside selling the cockerels born on the farm. The culled hen is not wasted either: birds are one of the three things the study has you sell, with eggs and droppings, and its first year projection counts 1,422 birds sold at 2,250 FCFA in 2020 prices. So culling her turns a running cost into a sale and frees the place for a pullet you kept back yourself.
Set out what the references say on culling and renewal.

Two Togolese sources, two farms, and they differ on one figure. The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference, which describes the commercial unit, culls at 24 months for hens and cocks alike. The 2017 ESFT village compendium, which describes the improved traditional henhouse, culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Both agree on how renewal works: you sell the cockerels born on the farm, keep back replacements from among them, and cull the poor layers. The breeders you keep or buy should be vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, taken from a well followed farm or a research centre, and any bird brought in from outside spends two weeks in quarantine. Give each culling figure with the reference it comes from.
What will I get for a culled hen at the market?

I cannot give you a price, and I should not try. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does carry a figure, 2,250 FCFA a bird in its first year projection of 1,422 birds sold, but that is a 2020 evaluation used to build a projection, not the price on your market this week. Prices move, and the study names no buyer. What you can do is what the same reference tells you to do about price generally: record every expense, work out your cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that with the market price, and readjust. For the price today, ask at the market itself or through a cooperative, and ask ICAT for help building the calculation.
With 60 hens and 6 cocks, how many birds am I culling each year?

If you are following the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, the whole nucleus turns over on a 24 month clock, hens and cocks alike, so across two years you replace all 66 birds and in a steady year you are culling something like half of them. That is a rhythm, not a rule you should apply blindly: the same reference also has you cull the poor layers as you spot them, which does not wait for the calendar. Plan the replacements before the culls, keeping back cockerels and pullets born on the farm, so you are never short of breeders. And remember the culled birds count on the selling side: the first year projection in that study has 1,422 birds sold at 2,250 FCFA in 2020 prices, with eggs and droppings beside them.
I am about to cull a batch of old hens. What do I do first?

Have the replacements ready before the birds go. Keep back pullets and cockerels born on the farm, chosen vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, so the nucleus does not drop below the 60 hens and 6 cocks the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives as the commercial minimum. Check your register while you are at it: the same reference asks you to keep a movement register of sales, hatchings and deaths, and a cull is a movement. Line up the buyers before the batch is ready rather than after, which that study says plainly about selling in general. And if any of the birds has been treated recently, do not eat its meat or its eggs for a few days, because they can hold drug residues.
Half my flock is over three years old and I have never replaced anything.

Then you are well past the figure either reference gives. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls at 24 months, hens and cocks alike; the 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping. Do not empty the henhouse at once. Start with the poor layers and the oldest cocks, keep back cockerels and pullets born on the farm as replacements, chosen vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, and work down in batches so the nucleus stays near 60 hens and 6 cocks if you are running the commercial model. The birds you cull are stock to sell, not a loss. And write each movement down, because the reference asks for a register of sales, hatchings and deaths, and it is how you will avoid arriving here again.
Just say I can keep my best hen for five years, she is the best layer I have.

I will not say that, because neither Togolese reference goes anywhere near five years. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference culls hens and cocks alike at 24 months. The 2017 ESFT village compendium goes to three years for breeding cocks, and that is the longer of the two figures I hold. Five years is beyond both. What I would do instead of arguing about the one hen is take her chicks: keep back pullets she has hatched, chosen vigorous and agile, and you keep what you value about her without keeping a bird that is eating 80 grams a day against a falling lay. If you want a judgement on that particular hen rather than on the rule, that is a question for ICAT or the animal health worker, who can see her.
Where should I get my breeding birds from?

From a well followed farm or a research centre, not from wherever birds happen to be for sale. That is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for, and it tells you what to look at once you are there: birds that are vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. The weights it gives at six months are about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Whatever you bring home, bought or given, keep it two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock, so a disease does not come in with it. ICAT can tell you what is available near you.
