From a well followed farm or a research centre, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for. Look for birds that are vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, around 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. Buy the nucleus in the right proportion, 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens. Two weeks of quarantine for every bird before it joins the flock. Ask ICAT what is available near you; I cannot name a supplier or a price.
Birds are birds. I will buy the cheapest ones at the poultry market and save the difference.

The saving is real and so is what it buys you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks you to take breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and the reason is not appearance: the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy, and your whole first year rests on the chicks. The poultry market is also where disease travels, which is why every bird you bring in from anywhere, bought or given, spends two weeks in quarantine before it joins the flock. If money is the constraint, the honest answer is to start smaller with good birds rather than at full size with poor ones, and to take that decision to ICAT.
True or false: a bird bought from a known farm can go straight in with the others.

False. Quarantine is two weeks for every new bird, whether you bought it at a poultry market, bought it from a farm you know, or were given it. Where the bird comes from changes how good a breeder it is likely to be, not whether it can carry something in. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does want you buying from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and that is worth doing. But the separation rule stands on its own: do not mix your animals with those of other farms, quarantine every newly bought bird, and isolate the ones that fall ill.
Why go to a research centre for birds when the market is next door? Justify.

Because of what you are buying. You are not buying meat, you are buying the parents of every chick you will raise, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is plain that the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. That is why it names a well followed farm or a research centre as the source, and why it tells you what to look for: vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. The market is also the place where birds of unknown health meet, which is the reason every new bird, bought anywhere or given, spends two weeks in quarantine. You will make the trip once and live with the flock for two years. Ask ICAT what is reachable from you.
What does the reference specify about acquiring the breeding stock?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies the source, the selection and the size. Source: a well followed farm or a research centre. Selection: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb; at six months about 1.3 kg live weight for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Size: a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens, and those birds are among the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests. The separation rule applies to all of them: two weeks of quarantine before any new bird joins the flock.
I want to build up to 120 hens. Do I buy them all at once?

You do not have to, and there is a reason not to. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 60 hens and 6 cocks as the minimum commercial nucleus, and its own model grows from there: managing the flock means selling the cockerels born on the farm and keeping back your replacements, so a good part of your 120 can be birds you hatched yourself. Buying all 120 at once means 132 birds through quarantine, two weeks apart from the flock, and a much bigger bill in one go. If you do buy in, buy from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile birds, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, and keep the ratio at one cock for ten hens, so 120 hens and 12 cocks. Take the build-up plan to ICAT before you commit the money.
A women's group in my village wants to start keeping hens and they asked where to buy.

Point them at a well followed farm or a research centre rather than at the poultry market, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for, and tell them what to look at: birds vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. Tell them the numbers too, because groups usually buy badly: one cock for about ten hens, and 60 hens and 6 cocks if they mean to run it as a commercial unit. And tell them the quarantine, two weeks for every bird before it joins whatever they already keep, bought or given. ICAT is the one to ask about what is available near them; I cannot name a supplier or quote a price.
The birds I brought home last week are hiding in a corner and two of them will not eat.

Keep them where they are and do not let them near the rest of the flock. That is exactly what the two week quarantine is for, and it sounds as though it is earning its keep. What you are describing is on the list of signs of a sick bird: sad, drowsy and downcast, wings drooping and feathers standing up, keeping away from the flock, not eating, thin, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, moving with difficulty, diarrhoea. Isolate the two that are off their feed, call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, and do not visit other farms while this is going on. If a bird dies, take it out fast and bury it well away from the henhouse. Remember also that no treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones.
Ever since I added the new hens, the old ones have gone quiet and off their food.

Then the new birds most likely went in without a quarantine, and something came with them. The rule is two weeks apart from the flock for every bird that arrives, bought or given, and it exists for precisely this. Separate the new ones now even though it is late, isolate any bird that is off its feed, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary; disease in the flock is not something to wait out. Meanwhile stop the ways it spreads: do not visit other farms, do not throw carcasses out in the open, do not let the hens wander, and bury dead birds far from the henhouse. Clean the building well, because a good cleaning already removes a good part of the germs, then disinfect it.
I have the money together and I want to buy my breeding stock.

Good, but two questions before you spend it. How many birds are you buying, and where are you thinking of buying them? The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a minimum breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit, at one cock for ten hens, and it asks you to take breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre rather than from a market stall.
Sixty hens and six cocks, and there is a big poultry market in the next town on Fridays.

The count is right. The market I would use only as a last resort, and if you do use it, buy with the reference's own description in your head: birds that are vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, around 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. Ask ICAT first whether there is a followed farm or a research centre within reach of you, because the cock decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy and that is a two year decision. Whatever you buy and wherever, all 66 birds go two weeks in quarantine before they meet anything else you keep. And have the housing ready before they arrive: at 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 66 birds need about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment, with the manure pit dug and the feeders and drinkers in place.
Just tell me which farm to buy from, you must know one.

I do not, and I would be inventing it if I named one. What I hold is the description, not a directory: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for breeders from a well followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock at six months. Who near you answers to that changes from year to year and I have no way to know it. ICAT is the one to ask, and it is the same office that holds the technico-economic reference itself and can help you build the business plan around it. Take the description with you when you go, so the answer you get is a farm that matches it rather than whoever is selling.
I think my flock is getting old but I am not sure what to do about it.

Tell me two things and I can be concrete: how old the oldest birds are, and whether you are running the commercial unit or the improved village henhouse. The age matters because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference culls at 24 months for hens and cocks alike, while the 2017 ESFT village compendium culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping, and those are two different farms.
The first ones are close to three years. I keep about sixty hens and I sell birds and eggs.

Selling birds and eggs is the commercial model, so the figure that applies to you is 24 months, and your oldest are a year past it. Do not empty the henhouse at once. Start with the poor layers and the oldest cocks, and replace them from your own hatchings: keep back pullets and cockerels born on the farm, choosing them vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb. Work down in batches so the nucleus stays near the 60 hens and 6 cocks that reference gives as the minimum, at one cock for ten hens. The culled birds are stock to sell, not a loss, and birds are one of the three things the study has you sell alongside eggs and droppings. Write every cull into your movement register, with the sales, hatchings and deaths, so you can see the rhythm next time.
One of my hens went broody yesterday and I have about twenty eggs saved up.

Do not give her twenty. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and more than that means eggs at the edge go cold. Sort the twenty before you set any: discard the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, and check how long you have had them, because the keeping limit is seven to ten days at most. Set the chosen ones pointed end down. From there the incubation lasts twenty-one days, after which the chicks come out of the shells. That reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so from thirteen eggs expect around nine chicks, not thirteen.
I put my eggs under the hen three weeks ago and nothing came out, so the cock must be sterile.

Three weeks is about right for the timing, so hold on before blaming the cock. The incubation lasts twenty-one days in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, whether under a hen or in an electric, gas or solar incubator, so you are only just at the end of it. Before the cock, check the eggs and the setting: kept seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, and none of them too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end. Check the number too, because a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen and no more. If all of that was right and still nothing hatched, then look at the cock: vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, one for about ten hens.
True or false: an incubator hatches faster than a hen.

False, at least on the time. The incubation lasts twenty-one days in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it gives that figure for an electric, gas or solar incubator without making it shorter than what a hen does. What the machine changes is the scale and the timing of your work, not the biology. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens in that reference, and it adds a warning worth hearing: at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. A brooding hen, by contrast, sits on twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.
Should I hatch under the hens or buy an incubator?

It depends on how many chicks you need at once and whether the machine will be busy. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, and the incubation lasts twenty-one days either way, so the machine does not hatch faster, it hatches more at a time. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, and it says in the same breath that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the equipment does not pay for itself. So the question is really whether there is hatching work around you. The incubator is also one of the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices. Take that arithmetic to ICAT before you buy.
Why does the reference bother telling me the incubation is twenty-one days? Justify.

Because it is the one date in the whole cycle you can plan against. Knowing it is twenty-one days tells you when the chick room and the brooder have to be ready, when the mother hen will need to be left alone, and when to stop wondering whether anything is going to happen. It also tells you when a failure is a failure: at day twenty-five, with nothing out, the problem is behind you, in the eggs or the setting or the cock, not in front of you. And it lets you run the unit in a rhythm, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on with six production cycles a year. Without the date you are waiting rather than working.
Set out the hatching figures.

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference: a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs. With an electric, gas or solar incubator the incubation lasts twenty-one days, after which the chicks come out of the shells. The natural hatching rate the study works on is near 70 percent, and the mortality rate near 10 percent. On equipment, a gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, with the note that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself. Upstream of all of it, eggs are kept seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set pointed end down.
What temperature should I set the incubator to?

I do not have that figure and I will not guess at it, because a wrong temperature costs you the whole setting. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives on incubation is the duration, twenty-one days, for an electric, gas or solar machine, and the capacity, a gas incubator of 300 eggs for a flock of 60 breeding hens. The settings themselves are not in what I hold. Ask ICAT, and ask whoever sells or services the machine, because it will come with its own instructions. What I can tell you is what goes in: eggs kept seven to ten days at most, cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, none of them too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end.
My neighbour asks how long he has to wait once the eggs are under the hen.

Twenty-one days. That is the incubation in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it holds for an electric, gas or solar incubator as well as under a hen, after which the chicks come out of the shells. Tell him two things beside the date. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs and no more, so if he has piled twenty under her the outside ones will go cold. And the reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so he should not count on every egg: from thirteen he can reasonably hope for nine. If far fewer come out, the place to look is the eggs he chose and how long he kept them, which is seven to ten days at most.
The chicks are due out next week. What do I need ready?

The warm place and the feed, before the twenty-one days are up. The brooder is for the chicks' first three weeks, and a brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks; after that they move into the chick room to finish growing. The chick room has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in. Have their own feed and their own drinker ready, apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and clean water above all, because chicks die easily of dehydration. Keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks; she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries.
It is day twenty-four and only three chicks have come out of fifteen eggs.

The date has passed, so what was going to hatch has hatched. Twenty-one days is the incubation in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and three out of fifteen is far under the natural hatching rate near 70 percent that it works on. Look back at two things. The eggs: kept seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, and none too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end. And the number under the hen: twelve to fourteen is her limit, and fifteen is already at the edge, so the outer eggs may have gone cold. Then the cock, vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, at one for about ten hens. Look after the three you have: warmth, their own feed, and clean water at all times.
My hen keeps leaving the nest and the eggs go cold.

Count what is under her first. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and a hen given too many will shift about and leave some out in the cold whatever she does. Bring it down to that number, choosing the eggs properly: kept seven to ten days at most, cool, airy and dry, none too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or without a pointed end, and set pointed end down. Give her somewhere quiet and clean to sit, and keep the run and the henhouse swept, because a tuft of grass nearby shelters the rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards that will disturb her. The incubation is twenty-one days, so she has to settle for three weeks.
I want to get more chicks out of the eggs I collect.

Tell me how you hatch them, under hens or in a machine, and tell me how long the eggs sit before you set them. Those two decide most of it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so some loss is expected, but most of the losses I am asked about come from eggs kept too long or set in the wrong number.
Under the hens, and I gather eggs for two or three weeks until I have enough.

There is your answer. Seven to ten days at most is the keeping limit in that reference, and two or three weeks is well past it, so a good part of what you set was never going to hatch. Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, discard the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, and set them pointed end down. Give each broody hen twelve to fourteen and no more. Then wait the twenty-one days of incubation without disturbing her. If you want to set more at a time than your hens can cover, that is what an incubator is for, and the reference sizes a gas one of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, while warning that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself.

Seven to ten days at most. Collect them every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them pointed end down. Discard the eggs that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen. Those figures come from the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for commercial local hens, and the incubation that follows lasts twenty-one days.
The biggest eggs give the biggest chicks, so I always set those.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference puts eggs that are too big on the discard list, alongside those too small, too dirty, deformed, cracked or with no pointed end. It does not treat size as a sign of quality in either direction; it treats the extremes as reasons to leave an egg out. What it does care about is freshness and handling: collect the eggs every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, seven to ten days at most, and set them pointed end down. Choose within the ordinary ones rather than picking the outliers, give a brooding hen twelve to fourteen, and expect a natural hatching rate near 70 percent.
What are the selection and keeping rules for hatching eggs?

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference. Collection: every day. Storage: somewhere cool, airy and dry, for seven to ten days at most. Discard: eggs that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Setting: pointed end down. Number under a brooding hen: twelve to fourteen. Incubation: twenty-one days, under the hen or in an electric, gas or solar incubator, after which the chicks come out of the shells. Expected outcome: a natural hatching rate near 70 percent. Upstream of all this the flock runs at one cock for ten hens, on a nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks for a commercial unit.
How do I tell from the outside whether an egg is fertile?

I cannot tell you that, because the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not give a way to do it and I will not invent one. What it gives is a discard list you can apply by eye and hand: leave out the eggs that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. And it gives the handling that decides most of the outcome: collect them every day, keep them cool, airy and dry for seven to ten days at most, and set them pointed end down. With that done, it works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, which already tells you that some of what you set will not come out. If you want a technique for testing eggs, ask ICAT.
I collect about forty eggs a week. How many of those end up as chicks?

Fewer than you would like, and the reference lets you work it out. Start by taking off the ones you discard, those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, which you cannot know in advance but which are never none. Then only set what you can cover: a brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, so three hens broody at once is about your forty. On what you do set, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so from forty good eggs set you are looking at something near twenty-eight chicks, and then a mortality rate near 10 percent on the birds after that. Keep the eggs seven to ten days at most or none of this holds.
My sister keeps hens and asks which eggs she should save for hatching.

Tell her the discard list first, because it is the easy part: leave out any egg that is too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Then the handling, which is where most people lose their chicks: collect the eggs every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set them within seven to ten days at most. Set them pointed end down. Give a broody hen twelve to fourteen and no more. The incubation is twenty-one days and the hatching rate to expect is near 70 percent, so she should not be disappointed by a few that do not come out. Those figures are from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference for commercial local hens.
I am setting eggs tomorrow morning. What do I do tonight?

Sort them and count them. Go through what you have saved and put aside anything too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Check the dates: seven to ten days at most is the keeping limit in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so anything older than that goes out too. Keep the rest somewhere cool, airy and dry overnight. Count out twelve to fourteen for each broody hen and no more. Have the nest clean and quiet, and remember to set them pointed end down in the morning. Then leave her alone for the twenty-one days of incubation, and have the brooder or the chick room ready before the end of it.
The eggs in my nest boxes are always cracked by the time I collect them.

Cracked eggs are on the discard list for hatching, along with those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big or with no pointed end, so what you are describing is a loss every time. Two things in the routine bear on it. Collect every day rather than letting them pile up, which is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks and which is also how you keep to the seven to ten days of storage. And look at the nests themselves: the same reference counts nest boxes among the equipment to fit out, alongside egg trays for keeping the eggs to be hatched, so there should be enough of them and they should be bedded. Keep what you do collect somewhere cool, airy and dry, and set it pointed end down.
Just tell me I can keep eggs for three weeks if I store them well.

I will not, because the figure I hold is seven to ten days at most, and it is given as a limit rather than as a suggestion. Storing them well is part of it, not a way round it: cool, airy and dry, collected every day, set pointed end down. Three weeks is two to three times the limit, and the cost does not show until nothing hatches at day twenty-one, by which time you have tied up a broody hen for three weeks as well. If you need to collect over a longer stretch to fill a setting, the answer is more hens laying or an incubator you fill in batches, not older eggs. That figure is from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and ICAT is where to take it if you want it discussed.
Almost none of the eggs I set are hatching.

Let me narrow it before guessing. How long do the eggs sit before you set them, how many do you put under one hen, and do you sort them at all? Those three account for most of what I am asked about. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent, so almost none is well outside what it expects.
I keep them two weeks or so, I set whatever I have, sometimes eighteen under one hen, and I do not sort them.

All three are against you, and each one alone would hurt. The keeping limit is seven to ten days at most, so two weeks is already past it. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen, so eighteen leaves the outer ones cold whatever she does. And the sorting matters: discard the eggs too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Change all three at once. Collect every day, keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry, sort them, count out thirteen or so per hen, set them pointed end down, and leave her for the twenty-one days of incubation. If you then still hatch far under 70 percent, look at the cock: vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, one for about ten hens.
