Three things, not one: birds, eggs and droppings. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a first year selling 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, which comes to 3,487,181 FCFA in all. Those are 2020 evaluations and annual projections for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, not prices you will get today. Check a current price on the market or through a cooperative before you plan on any of it.
I sell birds when people come to the house and that is all. Is there more I could do?

There are two more products you already have. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts three, not one: birds, eggs and droppings. Its first year projection sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, 3,487,181 FCFA in all, in 2020 prices. The droppings are the one most keepers throw away, and they have a place to go: a manure pit, which turns them into something your fields can use and limits the spread of disease at the same time. Selling only to whoever turns up is the other thing to change. That reference says to look for your buyers before the batch starts, keep a client register, and sign contracts where you can.
Eggs are for hatching, so the only thing I can actually sell is chickens.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sells both, and droppings besides. Its first year projection has 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, 3,487,181 FCFA in all at 2020 prices. So eggs are two things at once, and the choice between setting an egg and selling it is a real decision you make each time rather than a rule. What decides it is the sorting: the ones too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end are not going under a hen anyway. Plan the split before the cycle rather than at the nest.
Why would anybody pay for chicken droppings? Justify.

Because they fertilise fields, and the reference treats them as a product rather than as waste. Its first year projection counts 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA among the three things the unit sells, alongside 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, for 3,487,181 FCFA in all in 2020 prices. The handling is what makes them saleable rather than a nuisance: sweep the henhouse two or three times a week and throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam. The reference gives two reasons for that pit, and the second is the one people forget: it limits the spread of disease.
Set out the three revenue streams with their first year figures.

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference, first year annual projection for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. Birds: 1,422 sold at 2,250 FCFA. Eggs: 2,376 sold at 100 FCFA. Droppings: 50 kg at 1,000 FCFA. Total sales 3,487,181 FCFA. Against that, the same study evaluates the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA and the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, and it gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, explaining the jump by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges. All of it is evaluation and projection, not a current price.
What is a tray of eggs worth in Lome right now?

I have no way to know that. I work offline and I do not see today's markets, and a number I made up would cost you money. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does carry an egg figure, 100 FCFA, but it is a 2020 evaluation used to build a projection of 2,376 eggs sold in the first year, not a price for this week and not a price for Lome in particular. For what eggs are fetching now, ask at the market itself, ask a cooperative, or follow the SIM price broadcasts on the radio for the pattern across markets. ICAT can help you turn whatever price you find into a calculation you can use.
A friend says poultry is only worth it if you sell live birds. What do I tell him?

Tell him the study counts three products and not one. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a first year selling 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, 3,487,181 FCFA in all in 2020 prices. Birds are the largest of the three, so he is not wrong about where the money is, but the other two come off the same flock at almost no extra cost, and the droppings would otherwise be a disposal problem. Tell him the prices are 2020 evaluations as well, so whatever he plans has to be checked against the market he actually sells in.
Before the first batch is ready, what should I have set up on the selling side?

Your buyers, before the batch starts rather than after: that is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says plainly. Keep a client register, sign contracts with them where you can, and honour what the contract says. Decide your price from your own figures rather than from the study: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that price with the market price, and readjust if the market asks for it. Plan for all three products, because the projection sells birds, eggs and droppings, and the droppings need the manure pit dug before they accumulate. And make the farm known: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard.
I have birds ready to sell and nobody is coming for them.

That is the problem the reference tries to prevent by order of operations: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after. Since the batch is already standing, do two things at once. Make the farm known now, by the means that study names: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard. And go through a cooperative or ICAT, which is where to turn for a larger outlet. For the next batch, start the client register, sign contracts where you can and honour them. Meanwhile the birds are eating: a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes about 5 kg of feed in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day, so the delay has a running cost you should put into your price.
The droppings are piling up behind the henhouse and it smells.

Dig the pit, and you turn the problem into one of your three products. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, and it gives two reasons for it: to turn the droppings into something your fields can use, and to limit the spread of disease. Sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throw the droppings in there, well away from the building. Keep the ground around the henhouse clear as well, because a tuft of grass shelters the rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards that bring disease. On the selling side, the first year projection counts 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, beside the birds and the eggs.
Just tell me how much I will make in my first year.

I can tell you what the study projects and not what you will make, and the difference matters here more than anywhere. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a first year of 3,487,181 FCFA in sales for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, from 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, and after costs it gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two. Those are 2020 evaluations and annual projections. Your first year depends on your prices, your losses and your buyers, none of which I can see, and the study itself names no buyer and gives no current price. Build your own version with ICAT rather than borrowing theirs.
I want to understand where the money actually comes from in a hen farm.

Three places, and most keepers only use one. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts birds, eggs and droppings. Tell me which of the three you already sell and I will show you what the projection does with the others. It may also help to say how many hens you keep, because the whole study is built on a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks.
Sixty hens roughly, and I only sell birds.

Then you are at the right size and using a third of it. The first year projection in that study sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, 3,487,181 FCFA in all at 2020 prices. The eggs you are not selling are partly a matter of sorting: the ones you would not set anyway, too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, are still eggs to sell. The droppings need a manure pit, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, which you want in any case because it limits the spread of disease. And two warnings from the same study. The net result it projects is thin in year one, 131,785 FCFA, against 2,790,400 in year two. And all those prices are 2020 evaluations, so check the market before you plan on them.
Nearly four million francs just for the birds. That is madness.

The birds are the smallest part of it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, and what that covers is the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests, and then the 60 hens and 6 cocks themselves. Most of the money is the buildings and the equipment, which you buy once and keep. And it is not the whole bill either: the same study evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA on top, mostly feed. Those are 2020 evaluations for one unit, so the numbers today will differ. Take the list to ICAT and price it locally before you decide it is madness or not.
True or false: the start-up figure in the reference includes the first year of feed.

False, and the distinction is the one that catches people out. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, covering the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks. The feed sits in a separate line: the first year working capital, evaluated at 2,150,491 FCFA, of which feed is most, with breeder, chick and grower rations, Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. So the money you need before the unit stands on its own is both figures, not the first alone.
If I have to cut something from the start-up list, what goes?

Not the manure pit and not the housing, and I would not cut the birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks, for 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices. The item most often worth a second look is the gas incubator, because that reference sizes one of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens and warns in the same place that you should hatch for other keepers as well or it does not pay for itself; hens will brood for you meanwhile, twelve to fourteen eggs each. Feeders you can have made by a local craftsman, which is often cheaper than buying them. The manure pit stays because it limits the spread of disease as well as feeding your fields. Work the cuts through with ICAT.
Why does a well appear in the start-up list? Justify.

Because water is the one input the flock cannot wait for. The rule in these references is that water is given freely, available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. You cannot do that on a long walk to a shared source. It matters most for the chicks, which die easily of dehydration. So the well is in the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the feeders, the drinkers, the nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks, and it is there for the same reason as the rest: it is what the unit needs before it can run rather than something you add later.
Set out the start-up investment and what it covers.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference evaluates the start-up investment for one commercial local hen unit at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices. The items it names are the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests, and the breeding stock itself, 60 hens and 6 cocks. Separately it evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, mostly feed, with breeder, chick and grower rations, Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Against those it projects first year sales of 3,487,181 FCFA and a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one, rising to 2,790,400 FCFA in year two. All figures are 2020 evaluations and annual projections, not current prices.
What would that same investment cost me today?

I cannot tell you, and I would rather say so than give you a number that looks precise and is not. The 3,850,124 FCFA in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is a 2020 evaluation, built on 2020 prices for the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers, the nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks. Cement, iron and gas have all moved since, and I have no way to see by how much. What you can do is take the item list, which is the durable part, and price each line locally: the craftsman for the feeders, the market for the birds, a dealer for the incubator. ICAT holds the reference itself and can help you rebuild the total on today's prices.
Someone at the cooperative wants to know what it costs to set up a hen unit.

Give them the two figures and say what each one is. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, covering the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks. On top of that it evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, mostly feed. Tell them both, because quoting the first alone makes the project look half its size. And tell them the prices are 2020 evaluations for one unit, so the cooperative should price the list locally rather than plan on the total. ICAT holds the study.
I put all my money into buying birds and now I have nothing left for the buildings.

That is the order reversed, and it is worth fixing fast because the birds are now living somewhere that was not built for them. In the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up goes mostly to what you have not bought: the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers and nests, with the 60 hens and 6 cocks as one line among them. What matters most immediately is the housing density and the water: breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, and water freely available, clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Dig the manure pit early even if it is rough, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, because it limits the spread of disease. And go to ICAT about a plan before you spend anything else.
Every month something else turns out to be missing and I have to buy it.

Then work from the list rather than from what goes wrong. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names what a unit needs before it starts: the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests and the 60 hens and 6 cocks, evaluated together at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices. Beside those it fits out the rest, nest boxes, egg trays for the eggs to be hatched, and for you a cool box, work clothes, a wheelbarrow, spades, rakes and boots. And it separates out the running money, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, mostly feed, with the rations, the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Price both lists with ICAT and you stop being surprised every month.
Just tell me I can start this with five hundred thousand francs.

I cannot tell you that, because the figures I hold are nowhere near it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up of a commercial unit at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, and the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA on top. Five hundred thousand is a fraction of either. What I will not do is pretend the commercial model scales down to that, because every projection in the study, including the net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one, rests on the unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks with its buildings and its equipment. What you can do with a smaller sum is the improved village henhouse the 2017 ESFT compendium describes, which is a real farm with its own methods, or build towards the commercial unit in stages. ICAT is the place to take that question, and it is also who to ask about financing.
I am trying to work out what I need to save before I start.

Two sums, not one, and people usually save for the first only. Tell me whether you mean the commercial unit or a family henhouse, because the figures I have are for the commercial one. If it is that, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up investment at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices and the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA separately.
The commercial one. So a bit under six million altogether?

That is the right way to add it, with two cautions. The first is that both figures are 2020 evaluations for one unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, so today's prices will differ and you should rebuild the total line by line: the houses, the store, the manure pit, the gas incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers, the nests and the birds on the investment side; the breeder, chick and grower rations, the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter on the running side, with feed as most of it. The second is what comes back. The same study projects first year sales of 3,487,181 FCFA and a net result of only 131,785 FCFA in year one, against 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, explaining the jump by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges. So plan to live through a thin first year. Take the whole thing to ICAT, which holds the study and helps build the business plan.
The birds are in and the buildings are done. How much do I need to keep in hand for the year?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks. Feed is most of it, with breeder, chick and grower rations, and beside the feed it counts Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. That is separate from the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up you have already spent. Plan it as money that goes out steadily rather than in one payment, because the feed does. And plan for a thin first year: the same study projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two. Those are 2020 evaluations, so price your own feed before you settle on the figure.
Once the henhouse is built and the birds are bought, the rest is just my labour.

Feed alone says otherwise. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, on top of the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up, and it says feed is most of that sum: breeder, chick and grower rations. The rest of the line is not labour either, it is Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Those are the things that keep the flock alive, and the mortality rate near 10 percent the study works on assumes you are buying them. So the running money is a real second budget, and a unit that has spent everything on buildings is a unit that will run out of feed in its first months.
True or false: vaccines are a minor line in the first year budget.

True as a share, but do not read that as meaning they are optional. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices and says feed is most of it, with breeder, chick and grower rations. The Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines sit alongside the vitamins, the dewormer, the disinfectant and the litter as the smaller lines. What makes them not optional is a rule from the same material: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. Ask the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary about the prophylaxis suited to your henhouse.
Should I buy ready-made feed or mix my own?

Mixing your own is what the reference expects, and it gives you the formulas. It builds the feed from local raw materials: cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with their cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins. For 100 kg from 1 to 8 weeks it gives 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, and it gives separate formulas for 9 to 12 weeks, for 12 weeks on and for a hen in lay. The mineral mix you make too: for 10 kg, 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, so this is where saving actually shows. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal.
What does a bag of feed cost now?

I cannot tell you, and a figure invented here would go straight into your budget. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a total, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in 2020 prices with feed as most of it, but it does not price a bag and those were 2020 evaluations in any case. What I can give you is the quantity, which is the part that does not move: from 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all at 10 to 25 grams a day, from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all at 25 to 35 grams a day, and a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day. Price those quantities at your own market, or ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal near you.
If I run 120 hens instead of 60, does the working capital double?

The feed roughly does, because it follows the birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, with feed as most of it, and feed is counted per bird: about 1.5 kg from 1 to 60 days, about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at six months, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. The vaccines, vitamins and dewormer scale with the birds as well. Litter and disinfectant follow the floor area rather than the head count, so they rise with the building, not with the flock. What does not double neatly is the investment side: the well, the store and the incubator are already there. Do the arithmetic line by line with ICAT rather than multiplying the total by two.
A friend has built his henhouse and asks me what he still needs money for.

For the year of running, which is a separate budget from the building. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and says feed is most of it, with breeder, chick and grower rations. Beside the feed it counts Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Tell him the other half of the picture too, because it is the part that hurts: the same study projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in the first year against 2,790,400 in the second. So he needs to be able to live through a year that returns very little, and that is the money people forget to save.
What do I buy in the first week, before the birds start laying?

Feed first, and enough of it to be ahead rather than catching up. Feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it is needed from day one: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and young birds from 61 days to sale about 5 kg in all at 25 to 35 grams a day. With it, buy the litter and the disinfectant, and arrange the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines with the animal health worker, since for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. Have the vitamins and dewormer to hand. And make sure the water is right before anything else: freely available, drinkers never empty, clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.
I am four months in and the feed money has run out.

That is the commonest way a first year fails, and the study anticipates it: the first year working capital is evaluated at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices, separate from the 3,850,124 FCFA of building and equipment, and feed is most of that running sum. Do not cut the feed to stretch it, because a hen in lay needs 80 grams a day and a bird from 61 days to sale about 25 to 35 grams a day, and underfeeding costs you the lay you were counting on. Cut elsewhere: mix your own ration from local materials rather than buying made-up feed, make the mineral mix yourself, and use the free extras the reference names, greenery, termites and maggots. Then go to ICAT with your figures, because that is who helps build the plan, and take a hard look at whether the flock is bigger than your money.
The birds are eating more than I budgeted for.

Check the quantities against the ration table before you conclude the budget was wrong. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts about 1.5 kg of feed per bird from 1 to 60 days, at 10 to 25 grams a day; about 5 kg per bird from 61 days to sale at six months, at 25 to 35 grams a day; and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. If you are well above that, look at waste rather than at appetite: feeders of the right size for the age, one for 50 birds for chicks, one for 20 for chickens, one for 25 for adults, and feed not spilled on the floor. Use the free extras the reference names as well, greenery, termites and maggots, and caterpillars for the youngest. Feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital, so this is exactly where the budget is won or lost.
Just tell me feed will not cost me more than five hundred thousand a year.

I cannot promise you that. What I hold is the study's total, 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in 2020 prices for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, with feed as most of it, which puts feed well above five hundred thousand at those prices. Your own figure depends on what you pay per kilo and how many birds you carry, and I cannot see either. What I can give you is the quantity, which does not move: about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days, about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale at six months, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. Multiply those by your flock and by your own prices, and you will have a number that is yours. If it comes out far under the study's, check the arithmetic before believing it, and take it to ICAT.
My accounts do not balance and I cannot see where the money goes.

Start by separating the two budgets, because most keepers mix them and then cannot read either. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference keeps the start-up investment, 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices, apart from the first year working capital, 2,150,491 FCFA, and the second is the one that leaks. Tell me what you are spending on month to month and I can point at the line.
Mostly feed, then medicines when birds get sick, and I bought a new drinker and some planks last month.

Then two of those three are running costs and one is not. Feed is most of the working capital in that study, which is as it should be, and the medicines belong there too, alongside the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. The drinker and the planks are investment: they belong with the houses, the store, the manure pit, the incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders and the nests, and putting them in the monthly column is why your accounts will not sit still. Two things to do. Keep the registers the reference asks for, visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out, with investment and running money in separate columns. And look at why you are buying medicines often: no treatment cures a viral disease, so if this keeps happening the answer is prevention and vaccination with the animal health worker, not a bigger medicine budget.
How much will a local hen unit earn in its first two years?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. It explains the jump itself: the larger number of birds sold, and the fall in financial charges. So the first year is thin and the second is the real one, and you should plan to live through the first rather than on it. Those are annual projections and 2020 evaluations, not a promise about your farm, and the study names no buyer and gives no current price. Build your own version of the figures with ICAT.
resultat net premiere annee poule locale

131,785 FCFA in year one, against 2,790,400 FCFA in year two. Those are the net results the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference projects for a commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. It explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold in year two and by the fall in financial charges. Treat both as evaluations for one unit, not as what you will earn, and check any price you plan on against your own market.
I have a salary and I want this to replace it within a year.

Within a year, the figures say no. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices. The first year is thin by design, and the study says why the second is different: more birds sold and lower financial charges. So the honest plan is to keep the salary through the first year and let the unit build. Use the time for the things that decide year two anyway: look for your buyers before the batch starts, keep a client register, sign contracts where you can, and set your price from your own recorded costs rather than from the study. Take the projection to ICAT and put your own prices into it.
True or false: the second year is better because the birds lay more as they age.

False on the reason. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does project a jump, from a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one to 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, but it explains it by two things and neither is older hens laying better: the larger number of birds sold, and the fall in financial charges. Ageing hens are in fact why the same study culls at 24 months. So the second year is better because the unit is finally selling at scale and paying less in charges, not because the flock improves with age. Those are 2020 evaluations and annual projections for one unit.
Should I take a loan for the start-up or build up slowly from my own money?

I cannot advise you on borrowing, and I am not the right place for that decision. What the figures tell you is what either choice has to survive: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the start-up at 3,850,124 FCFA and the first year working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA, both in 2020 prices, and it projects a net result of only 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two. It also names the fall in financial charges as one of the two reasons the second year is better, which tells you that charges weigh on the first. Whichever route you take, plan for a year that returns very little. Take the projection to ICAT, which helps build the business plan, and put the financing question to them rather than to me.
Set out the economic projection.

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference, for one commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, in 2020 prices. Investment: 3,850,124 FCFA. First year working capital: 2,150,491 FCFA, feed being most of it. First year sales: 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, 3,487,181 FCFA in all. Net result: 131,785 FCFA in year one, 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, the difference explained by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges. Underlying it, six production cycles a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. All of it is evaluation and annual projection, not current price.
At double the flock, do I get double the profit?

Not straightforwardly, and the study's own explanation tells you why. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, and attributes the jump to the larger number of birds sold and to the fall in financial charges. The sales side does scale roughly with the flock, since birds, eggs and droppings all follow the head count. The cost side does not: feed scales, but the well, the store and the incubator are already bought, while the financial charges depend on how you financed it and not on the number of hens. So doubling the flock changes several lines by different amounts. Rebuild the projection line by line with ICAT rather than multiplying the result.
A young man in the village is telling everyone he will be rich from chickens in a year.

Show him the first year figure rather than arguing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a commercial unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, against 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, and it explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges. Tell him what has to be spent first as well: 3,850,124 FCFA of investment and 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital. The trade is real and the second year is good, but the first year is thin and that is where people give up. And tell him those are 2020 evaluations for one unit, not a promise. ICAT holds the study and helps build the plan.
Before I commit to this, what should I be sure of?

Be sure you can live through a year that returns almost nothing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, in 2020 prices, and names the larger number of birds sold and the fall in financial charges as the reasons for the jump. Be sure of the two sums that go out first, 3,850,124 FCFA of investment and 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital. And be sure of your outlet before the birds are ready: look for your buyers before the batch starts, keep a client register, sign contracts where you can and honour them, and set your price from your own recorded costs. Take all of it to ICAT and rebuild the numbers on today's prices rather than on 2020 ones.
I have been running a year now and I have barely made anything.

That may be the projection working rather than the farm failing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one for a unit of 60 hens and 6 cocks, which is very little, and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two. It explains the difference by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges, so what you are living through is the thin part. Two things to check rather than despair. Are you selling all three products, birds, eggs and droppings, since the projection counts all three? And do you have buyers arranged before each batch, with a client register and contracts where you can get them? If both are yes, hold on through the second year. Take your own figures to ICAT and compare them against the study line by line.
The money comes in but it all goes straight back out again.

That is what the first year looks like in the projection, and it is also what poor records look like, so separate the two. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one against 2,790,400 in year two, so very little left over is expected at this stage. But you should be able to see it rather than feel it: keep the registers that study asks for, visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out. Then set your price properly, which is its own instruction there: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that with the market price and readjust. If after that the price you need is above what the market pays, that is a real answer and ICAT is where to take it.
What registers should I keep on the farm?

Five, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names them. A visits register. A movements register, with the sales, the hatchings and the deaths. A prophylactic calendar, for the vaccinations and the treatments. A health follow-up. And money in and out. Between them they answer the questions you will actually be asked: how many birds you have, what you lost and when, what each bird cost you to raise, and whether you are making anything. The money register is also what lets you set a price from your own figures rather than from someone else's, which that reference asks you to do.
registres elevage volaille lesquels

Visits; movements, meaning sales, hatchings and deaths; a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments; health follow-up; and money in and out. Those are the five the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference asks a keeper to hold. Keep them from the first day rather than starting when something goes wrong, because their value is in the comparison over time. The money register is what you build your selling price on: every expense recorded, the cost of production per head worked out, the profit you want per head decided, then compared with the market price.
I keep it all in my head. I know my birds better than any notebook.

You may know the birds, but the notebook answers questions memory does not. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for five registers: visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out. Two things you cannot do from memory. You cannot work out your cost of production per head, which is the first step in the pricing method that same reference gives, and without it you are taking whatever price is offered. And you cannot see a pattern in your losses, when the deaths cluster in the cycle, which is what tells the animal health worker something useful. A bank asking for a business plan will want the same figures.
True or false: the movements register is just for sales.

False. In the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the movements register holds sales, hatchings and deaths. The hatchings and the deaths are the half people leave out, and they are the half that tells you whether the unit is working: the study plans on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, and you cannot know whether you are near those figures without writing both down. It is also a register kept alongside four others: visits, a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out.
One notebook for everything or a separate one for each register?

Whichever you will actually keep up, but keep the five kinds of entry apart on the page. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out. What matters is that you can read one of them without the others in the way, because each answers a different question: the movements tell you whether your hatching and losses are near the study's 70 percent and 10 percent, the money tells you your cost of production per head, and the prophylactic calendar tells the animal health worker what has already been given. Money in and out is the one to keep separate whatever else you do, and inside it keep investment apart from running costs.
Why does the reference want a visits register? Justify.

Because visits are one of the ways disease arrives. The rule the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives is to keep the animals away from the germs or the germs away from the animals, and it names contaminated material as a route: farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes. When there is disease in the flock the instruction is to forbid any visit without a precise purpose. A register is what makes that enforceable and, afterwards, what lets you look back and see who was on the farm in the days before the birds fell ill. It sits with the other four the reference asks for: movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out.
Set out the record keeping the reference requires.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference asks for five records. Visits. Movements: sales, hatchings and deaths. A prophylactic calendar, covering vaccinations and treatments. Health follow-up. Money in and out. Alongside them it asks for a client register on the selling side, with contracts signed where possible and honoured. And it gives the use the money record is put to: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that price with the market price, and readjust if the market asks for it.
Is there an app or a form I can use for all this?

I do not know of one and I am not going to name something I cannot check. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says what to record, not what to record it in: visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out, plus a client register on the selling side. A ruled notebook with a page for each will do all of it. If there is a form or a tool in use locally, ICAT is who will know, and it is the same office that holds the reference and helps build a business plan. Start the notebook today rather than waiting for the tool.
With only sixty hens, is all this paperwork worth it?

Sixty hens and six cocks is exactly the unit the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is written about, so yes: the five registers it asks for are sized for that farm, not for a bigger one. Visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out. At this size the entries are a few lines a week. And the payoff is proportionally larger on a small unit, because a first year net result of 131,785 FCFA leaves no room for a cost you cannot see. Without the money record you cannot work out your cost of production per head, and without that you cannot set a price at all.
The birds arrive next week. What do I open the books with?

Open all five before the first bird is in, because the first entries are the ones people miss. Write the arriving stock into the movements register, with the date and the number, since that is your starting count against which every hatching and death will be read. Open the prophylactic calendar with whatever vaccination the animal health worker advises, since for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. Open money in and out with the investment already spent, kept separate from running costs. Start the visits register the day the birds come. And start the health follow-up empty, so that the first time you write in it you will notice. The client register can wait until you have something to sell, but not longer than that.
Just tell me the registers are optional if the farm is going well.

I will not, because it is when the farm is going well that they are cheap to keep and most useful later. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists them without conditions: visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out. Two things you lose by skipping them. You cannot set a price properly, because the method that reference gives starts with recording every expense and working out the cost of production per head. And when something does go wrong, you will have no history to show the animal health worker, at the moment you most need one. A few lines a week is the whole cost. If you want to argue the point with someone who can see your farm, ICAT is the place.
I want to start keeping proper records but I do not know where to begin.

Begin with two of the five and add the rest as you go, rather than opening six notebooks and abandoning them. Tell me whether you are already selling, because that changes which two. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for visits, movements with sales, hatchings and deaths, a prophylactic calendar, health follow-up, and money in and out.
Yes, I sell birds already, and I lose a few chicks every cycle.

Then start with movements and with money in and out. The movements register takes the sales you are already making, plus every hatching and every death, and it is the losses that will pay you back first: the study works on a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent, and once you have a few cycles written down you will see whether your chick losses sit near that or well above it, and where in the cycle they fall. That is the fact the animal health worker needs and cannot get from you otherwise. Money in and out is the second, kept with investment separate from running costs, because it is what lets you work out your cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head and compare it with the market price. Add the prophylactic calendar next time the birds are vaccinated, then health follow-up and visits. Within a year you will have the whole set without ever having done a big piece of work.
comment fixer prix poulet ferme

From your own figures, not from a study and not from what the neighbour charges. The method in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is: record every expense; work out the cost of production per head; decide the profit you want per head; compare that price with the market price; readjust if the market asks for it. That means keeping the money register from the start. And look for your buyers before the batch starts, keep a client register and sign contracts where you can. I cannot give you a current price for a bird; ask at the market or through a cooperative.
A trader came to the house and offered me a price for the whole batch. Should I take it?

I cannot tell you whether that price is good, because I do not know today's market and I do not know your costs. But you can tell, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives you the way: work out your cost of production per head from your recorded expenses, decide the profit you want per head, and compare the result with what he is offering. If his price is below your cost you know the answer without any market information at all. If it is above, then compare it with the market price before you agree. Two other things from that reference: it asks you to look for buyers before the batch is ready, which a trader at the door suggests you did not, and it asks you to sign contracts where you can and honour them. A cooperative or ICAT can help you reach a larger buyer next time.
The reference says 2,250 francs a bird, so that is my price.

That figure is not a price list, it is an input to a projection. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference uses 2,250 FCFA a bird in its first year projection of 1,422 birds sold, alongside eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, and all of it is in 2020 prices. Using it as your selling price makes two mistakes at once: it ignores what has happened to prices since, and it ignores your own costs, which are not the study's. The method that same reference gives is the opposite way round: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, then compare that price with the market price and readjust if the market asks. The number that comes out of that is yours.
Why start from my costs rather than from the market price? Justify.

Because the market price tells you what you can get and your cost tells you whether it is worth getting. Start from the market alone and you can sell a whole batch below what it cost you to raise, and only find out at the end of the year. That is why the method in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference runs in that order: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, and only then compare with the market price and readjust. The market still has the last word, because the final step is the comparison. What the cost gives you is the floor, and the knowledge of when to walk away from an offer. It matters most in a first year, which that study projects at a net result of only 131,785 FCFA.
Set out the pricing method and the market instructions.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference gives pricing as five steps: record every expense; work out the cost of production per head; decide the profit you want per head; compare that price with the market price; readjust if the market asks for it. On the market side it gives four instructions: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after; keep a client register; sign contracts with them where you can; and honour what the contract says. Beside those it lists how to make the farm known: radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard. The study names no buyer and gives no current price; its own figures, 2,250 FCFA a bird and 100 FCFA an egg, are 2020 evaluations used to build a projection.
Does my price change if I sell ten birds or two hundred?

Your cost per head may, and the reference has you price from the cost. Work out the cost of production per head from your recorded expenses; some of what goes into it is per bird, like feed at 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale, and some is spread over the whole flock, like the buildings and the equipment, so a bigger batch carries the fixed part more lightly. Then decide the profit you want per head and compare with the market price. On the selling side, size is also what a contract is for: the reference asks you to look for buyers before the batch starts, keep a client register and sign contracts where you can, and a large batch without a buyer arranged is the worst position to price from. A cooperative or ICAT is how you reach a buyer big enough for two hundred birds.
Someone in the group asked me how they should price their eggs.

Tell them the method rather than a number, because the number is theirs and changes. Record every expense; work out the cost of production per head; decide the profit you want per head; compare that price with the market price; readjust if the market asks for it. That is what the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives, and it applies to eggs as it does to birds. Tell them to look for buyers before the batch is ready, to keep a client register and to sign contracts where they can. And warn them off the study's own figure of 100 FCFA an egg as a selling price: it is a 2020 evaluation used inside a projection, not what eggs fetch today. For today's price, the market itself, or a cooperative.
I sell all my birds but at the end of the season there is nothing left over.

Then you are selling below what it costs you, or close enough that nothing survives. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the way out and it starts with paper: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that price with the market price and readjust. Until you have the cost per head you are guessing, and a batch sold fast at a bad price feels like success. Two other things to look at. Are you selling all three products, birds, eggs and droppings, or only the birds? And are you finding buyers before the batch is ready, with a client register and contracts where you can, rather than taking whoever turns up? A cooperative or ICAT can help on both.
Buyers always beat me down on price and I end up accepting.

You are negotiating without a floor. Work out your cost of production per head from your recorded expenses and decide the profit you want per head, which is the method the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives, and you will know the number below which the sale is not worth making. That changes the conversation. Two other things in the same reference put you in a better position. Look for your buyers before the batch starts rather than after, because a seller with birds ready and nobody coming has already lost. And keep a client register and sign contracts where you can, so the price is agreed before the birds are at the door. Selling through a cooperative reaches bigger buyers than a trader at the gate.
Just give me a price to ask for a six month cockerel.

I cannot, and this is one of the places where a made-up number would do real harm. I work offline and I do not see any market, so any figure I gave you would be invention. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does contain 2,250 FCFA a bird, but that is a 2020 evaluation used inside a projection of 1,422 birds sold, not a price to ask this week. What I can do is the part that does not need a market: work out your cost of production per head from your recorded expenses, decide the profit you want per head, and that gives you the number below which you should not sell. Then get the market side from the market itself, or through a cooperative, and readjust. ICAT can help you do the calculation.
I never know what to charge and I think I am losing money.

Then start from your side rather than from the market, which is the order the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives. Tell me whether you keep a record of what you spend, because the whole method rests on it: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare with the market price, readjust.
Not really. I know roughly what the feed costs and that is about it.

Feed is the biggest single line, so that is not nothing, but it will not give you a cost per head on its own. Start the money register now, with investment kept separate from running costs. On the running side put the feed, but also the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, the vitamins, the dewormer, the disinfectant and the litter, which are the other things the study counts in the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital. Then divide by the birds you actually sold, not by the birds you hatched, because the mortality near 10 percent is part of your cost too. That number is your cost of production per head. Add the profit you want, compare with what the market is paying, and readjust if you must. While you build that, do the other half: look for buyers before the next batch is ready, keep a client register, sign contracts where you can. ICAT can go through the first calculation with you.
How many birds per square metre in the henhouse?

It depends on their age, and the commercial reference of 2020 by ICAT and PASA gives three figures. Breeders: 8 to 10 birds per square metre. Chicks: 50 per square metre. Growers, the 3 to 6 month birds: 12 to 15 per square metre. Those are for the commercial model. If what you are building is the improved village henhouse instead, the 2017 ESFT compendium works on an average of 5 to 6 hens per square metre, which is a different farm and a different figure. Say which one you mean before you use either number, because the same floor gives very different counts.
True or false: chicks need more space per bird than adults.

False, and by a long way. In the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference the chicks go at 50 per square metre, the growers at 12 to 15, and the breeders at 8 to 10. So a chick takes about a fifth of the space a breeder does. What chicks need instead of space is warmth, which is why the chick room has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments, and why the brooder exists for their first three weeks: a brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks. They also need their own feed and their own clean water, apart from the adults.
Should I build one big room or separate compartments?

Separate compartments, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five: one with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. The reason is in the densities: breeders at 8 to 10 per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. One room cannot hold three densities, and the chick room in particular has fewer openings than the others so the warmth stays in. Plan two more things beside the henhouse, a grassy run and a store. For the plans themselves, ICAT.
Why does the reference give a range, 8 to 10, instead of one number? Justify.

Because it is sizing a building, not weighing out feed, and the right figure inside the range depends on how well the compartment is aired and how you run it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a henhouse well aired and roomy, and 10 birds per square metre in a stuffy corner is not the same as 10 in a well ventilated one. Its own worked layout uses the top of the range: a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre. The range also lets you round a real building to real dimensions. The same holds for the growers at 12 to 15 per square metre. The chick figure, 50 per square metre, is given as a single number.
My henhouse is round. How many birds does it hold?

Work out the floor area and the densities do the rest, but I cannot do the measuring for you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 per square metre for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers; the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse. Measure across the floor, tell me the distance and which model you are building, and I will give you the count. What I cannot tell you is anything about the shape itself: neither reference says which way a building should face or what a round plan changes, and I am not going to answer that from memory. ICAT holds the plans.
A friend is putting sixty birds in a room three metres by three. Is that all right?

Three by three is 9 square metres. If those sixty are breeders, the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 per square metre, which gives 72 to 90 birds for that floor, so sixty fits. If he is following the improved village henhouse of the 2017 ESFT compendium, that works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre, giving 45 to 54, and sixty would be over. So the answer depends on which farm he is running, and he should say which before he takes either number. Tell him the rest of the routine matters as much as the count: a fenced run around the henhouse, sweeping inside two or three times a week with the droppings into a manure pit well away, and the ground around kept clear of grass tufts that shelter rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards.
I am about to lay out the compartments. What do I work from?

From the densities and the worked layout, in that order. Breeders at 8 to 10 birds per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference then shows what that gives on the ground: a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre; and two grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds, one of 7 m by 4 m, 28 square metres for 420 birds, and one of 4 m by 3.5 m, 14 square metres for 210 birds, both at 15 per square metre. Build at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, with the chick room given fewer openings so the warmth stays in. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. Take the plan to ICAT before you start laying blocks.
The birds are crowded at one end and the other end stays empty.

Then the count against the floor may be fine and the compartment still wrong. Check the number first: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 growers and 50 chicks, so measure and divide before anything else. If you are inside the figure, look at why one end is unused. The reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind, so a cold or wet end will empty. Check the feeders and drinkers are spread rather than grouped: for adults, one feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, and four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred layers. And keep the compartments to their ages, since that is what the five compartment plan is for.
My birds are pecking each other and some have wounds.

Count them against the floor first, because crowding is the cheapest thing to rule out. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 12 to 15 for the growers and 50 for the chicks, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the family henhouse. If you are over, thin them or open another compartment. Then check the cocks, because at more than one for about ten hens they fight and wear the hens. Then the fittings: enough feeders and drinkers spread out, a grassy run outside, since a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk and lets the birds get out. Isolate the wounded birds while they heal and call the animal health worker if you see illness rather than injury.
Just tell me I can put a hundred birds in my ten square metre room.

That depends entirely on their age, so I will give you the arithmetic rather than a yes. At the commercial densities in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, ten square metres holds 80 to 100 breeders, 120 to 150 growers, or 500 chicks. So a hundred adult breeders is at the very top of the range and only if the room is well aired and roomy, which that reference asks for. If instead you are running the improved village henhouse of the 2017 ESFT compendium, its figure is 5 to 6 hens per square metre, so ten square metres holds 50 to 60 and a hundred would be double. Tell me which farm you are running and how old the birds are and you will have a real answer rather than a permission.
I want to know whether my building is big enough.

Give me two things: the inside measurements, and the ages of the birds you want to put in it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference works on 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for the growers, and the 2017 ESFT village compendium works on 5 to 6 hens per square metre for the improved family henhouse, so I also need to know which of the two you are building.
Seven metres by four, the commercial model, and I want breeders and growers both.

Seven by four is 28 square metres, which is exactly the grower compartment in that reference's own worked layout: 28 square metres for 420 birds at 15 per square metre. But you want two groups in it, so divide it rather than mixing them, because the densities differ and so does the management. If you split it in two halves of 14 square metres each, one half at 8 to 10 per square metre holds 112 to 140 breeders, and the other at 12 to 15 holds 168 to 210 growers. That breeder half matches the reference's own figure of a compartment 4 m by 3.5 m for 140 birds. Remember the plan asks for at least five compartments in all, so you will still need the brooding compartment, the chick room and a second grower space, plus a grassy run and a store outside. Take the division to ICAT before you build the partitions.
combien de compartiments poulailler commercial

At least five, well aired and roomy. One compartment with a shared yard for the breeders; one for brooding, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched; a chick room; and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Beside the henhouse, plan a grassy run for the birds and a store. That is the commercial model of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The improved traditional henhouse of the family compound is a different building and does not take these dimensions.
True or false: the chick room should be the airiest compartment.

False, and it is the other way round. The chick room, the poussiniere, is the compartment meant for keeping the chicks warm, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives it fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments precisely so the warmth stays in. The building as a whole is to be well aired and roomy, but that one room is the exception. On the walls, the low wall elsewhere is 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, while for the chick room you raise the whole wall and leave openings for air. Keep tarpaulins to close against rain and wind.
Why five compartments? Could I not manage with two? Justify.

Because the birds are in four different states at once and each needs something the others do not. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for one compartment with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding where the collected eggs are given back to the hens, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard. The densities alone force the separation: breeders at 8 to 10 per square metre, chicks at 50, growers at 12 to 15. The chick room needs fewer openings so the warmth stays in, which would make it a bad room for the adults. And keeping the ages apart is also how you stop chicks competing with adults at the feeder. Two rooms means running three managements in two spaces.
Set out the building the commercial reference describes.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a henhouse of at least five compartments, well aired and roomy: one with a shared yard for the breeders; one for brooding, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched; a chick room, with fewer openings so the warmth stays in; and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, with the chick room walled to full height but left with openings for air, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind. Beside the building, a grassy run and a store. Its worked layout: a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre; grower compartments of 7 m by 4 m, 28 square metres for 420 birds, and 4 m by 3.5 m, 14 square metres for 210 birds, both at 15 per square metre.
Which way should the henhouse face?

I do not know, and I will not guess at it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not say which way the building should face, and orientation is exactly the kind of thing that sounds harmless to invent and then costs you a hot or a wind-blown building for twenty years. What that reference does give is the rest of the shell: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, and tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. For orientation, ask ICAT, which holds the plans. The same goes for whether red wood shavings can be used as litter, which is also not in what I hold.
I want to build for half the flock. Do I still need five compartments?

You still need the five functions, even if the rooms are smaller. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a compartment with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard, and none of those disappears with a smaller flock: you still have breeders, still have eggs to hatch, still have chicks needing warmth and still have growers. What scales is the area, through the densities: 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks, 12 to 15 for growers. Its own worked breeder compartment is 4 m by 3.5 m for 140 birds; halve the birds and you halve the floor. The store and the grassy run stay in the plan either way. Take the reduced plan to ICAT.
I am starting the build next month. What do I need decided first?

Decide the five compartments and their sizes before a single block is laid, because you cannot add a chick room afterwards without cutting the building about. That is one compartment with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard. Size each from its density: breeders 8 to 10 per square metre, chicks 50, growers 12 to 15. Decide the low wall, 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, with the chick room taken higher and left with openings for air, and buy the tarpaulins for rain and wind. Site the grassy run and the store at the same time, and mark out the manure pit, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. Take the whole plan to ICAT before you start.
I built one long room and now I cannot keep the chicks warm.

That is the compartment you are missing. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five, and the chick room is the one with fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments, exactly so the warmth stays in. In a single long room the chicks are in the same draught as the adults. You can partition rather than rebuild: wall off one end, take that wall to full height instead of the 0.5 to 1 m low wall used elsewhere, and leave openings for air rather than sealing it. Hang tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. For the first three weeks the chicks should be in the brooder anyway, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks, and only then move into the chick room. Take the partition plan to ICAT.
When it rains the wind drives water right through the henhouse.

Tarpaulins, which are part of the design rather than an afterthought: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says to keep them to close against rain and wind. The building is meant to be well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, so it is open by design and the closing is done with what you hang. Check the chick room separately, since that one has its wall taken higher with openings left for air, and it is the compartment where driven rain does the most harm. While you are at it, look at the ground outside: keep it clear, because a tuft of grass shelters the rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards that bring disease, and standing water will make that worse.
I have a piece of ground and I want to put up a proper henhouse.

Tell me how many birds you are building for and whether you mean the commercial unit or the improved family henhouse, because they are two different buildings. If it is the commercial one, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, and it sizes each on a density: breeders 8 to 10 per square metre, chicks 50, growers 12 to 15.
The commercial one, starting with the minimum, sixty hens and six cocks.

Then work from the nucleus outwards. Your 66 breeders at 8 to 10 per square metre need about 7 to 8 square metres of breeder compartment, with a shared yard. Beside it you still need the other four rooms even at this size: the brooding compartment where the collected eggs are given back to the hens, the chick room with fewer openings so the warmth stays in, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard, sized at 12 to 15 birds per square metre once you know how many you will be raising. Build the low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most, take the chick room wall higher with openings left for air, and keep tarpaulins for rain and wind. Outside, plan the grassy run, the store, and the manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it. Take the drawing to ICAT before you buy materials, and note that neither reference tells you which way to face the building, so do not let me or anyone guess that for you.
How many feeders and drinkers do I need?

Both go by age, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts drinkers per hundred birds: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, and four of 10 litres for the adult layers. Feeders it counts per bird: for chicks, 50 cm long by 50 wide and 5 deep, one for 50 birds; for chickens, 125 cm by 10 by 12, one for 20 birds; for adults, 150 cm by 12 by 16, one for 25 birds. You can buy them in the shops, but a local craftsman can make the feeders, which is often cheaper.
