150 cm long by 12 wide by 16 deep, one for 25 adult birds. For chickens it is 125 cm by 10 by 12, one for 20 birds; for chicks, 50 cm by 50 by 5, one for 50 birds. Those are the 2020 ICAT and PASA figures for the commercial unit. On drinkers, per hundred birds: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, four of 10 litres for the adult layers. A local craftsman can make the feeders, often cheaper than buying them.
I have sixty laying hens and one long feeder. Is that enough?

Not by the reference's count. It gives one adult feeder of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, so sixty hens call for three of them, not one. On drinkers it counts four of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, so for sixty you want at least two or three. The reason to spread them rather than lengthen one is that the birds crowd: with a single point the weaker hens eat last and least, which shows up later as uneven weights. Wash the feeders and drinkers every day. And the water rule is its own: freely available, never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. A local craftsman can make the extra feeders more cheaply than a shop.
A feeder is a feeder. I use the same trough for the chicks and the big birds.

The reference gives three different sizes and a different ratio for each, and the chicks are the ones that suffer from sharing. It counts a chick feeder at 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for 50 birds; a chicken feeder at 125 cm by 10 by 12, one for 20; an adult feeder at 150 cm by 12 by 16, one for 25. A trough 16 cm deep is not something a chick eats out of comfortably. Beyond the size, there is the separation itself: chicks are to be fed apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on their own ration. Same for water, where chicks take siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres, two per hundred birds from 1 to 30 days.
Why does the reference count drinkers per hundred birds instead of just saying enough water? Justify.

Because enough is not something you can check at a glance, and water is the input where failure is fastest. The rule is that water is freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day, and a count is what lets you know before you run out rather than after. The figures are per hundred: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, four of 10 litres for the adult layers. It matters most for the youngest, because chicks die easily of dehydration. A number you can count against your flock is worth more than an instruction you can believe you are following.
What should the feeders be made of?

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the dimensions and the ratios but says nothing about what they are made of, so I will not name anything. What it says about supply is that you can buy feeders and drinkers in the shops, and that a local craftsman can make the feeders for you, which is often cheaper. The dimensions to give him: chicks 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for 50 birds; chickens 125 cm by 10 by 12, one for 20 birds; adults 150 cm by 12 by 16, one for 25 birds. Whatever they are made of, they have to be washable, because the feeders and drinkers are washed every day. Ask ICAT or the craftsman what is used locally.
The chicks hatch next week. What do I need in place for feeding them?

Chick feeders, 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 chicks, and siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres, two per hundred birds for the first 30 days. Put them in the brooder area, which is where the chicks spend their first three weeks: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks. Have their own feed ready, apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and clean water above all, renewed at least twice a day and served in the shade, because chicks die easily of dehydration. From 30 to 45 days you move to three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred. Wash everything daily from the first day.
There is always feed spilled on the floor under the trough.

Check the trough against the size for the age, because spillage is usually a depth problem. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 5 cm deep for a chick feeder of 50 by 50, 12 cm for a chicken feeder of 125 by 10, and 16 cm for an adult feeder of 150 by 12, and a shallow trough used by big birds throws feed out. Check the count too: one feeder for 50 chicks, for 20 chickens or for 25 adults, since crowding at one point pushes feed over the side. Feed on the floor is not only waste, it is also what draws rats and other visitors, and the ground around the henhouse should be kept clear for the same reason. Wash the feeders daily whatever you decide.
The drinkers are empty every time I look in the afternoon.

Then you are short of capacity or short of rounds, and both are countable. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts drinkers per hundred birds: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, four of 10 litres for the adult layers. Count yours against your flock. Then the routine: water is to be freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Twice a day is the minimum, not the target, and in the heat you will be filling more often. Put them in the shade if they are not already, and wash them every day.
Just tell me two drinkers is plenty for my hundred layers.

I cannot, because the figure I hold says four. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, and three of 10 litres per hundred for the chickens. Two would be half of it, and the consequence is not abstract: the rule is that water is freely available at all times and the drinkers are never empty, and with half the capacity you are relying on being there to refill at exactly the right moments. Water also has to be clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day, which is easier with more vessels, not fewer. If cost is the reason, note that the reference says a local craftsman can make the feeders more cheaply, and ask ICAT what is available for drinkers.
What do I do with the droppings?

Put them in a manure pit, and dig it before you need it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for one at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, and it gives two reasons: to turn the droppings into something your fields can use, and to limit the spread of disease. Sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throw the droppings in there, well away from the building. What comes out fertilises your fields. On the selling side, the same study's first year projection counts 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA among the three things the unit sells, with the birds and the eggs.
I have a small plot and the only flat spot is right beside the henhouse.

Then move something, because beside the henhouse is the one place the pit should not be. The instruction is to sweep the inside two or three times a week and throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it, and the reason is in the reference's own justification for the pit: it limits the spread of disease as well as turning the droppings into something your fields can use. Keeping a heap of droppings against the wall does the opposite. The pit itself needs at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, with an apatam over it. If the ground truly will not allow distance, that is a question for ICAT and the plans, not something to settle by putting it close anyway. Keep the ground around the henhouse clear in any case, since a tuft of grass shelters rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards.
The pit is just for tidiness. I could as well spread the droppings straight on the field.

The reference gives two reasons and tidiness is neither. It asks for a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, in order to turn the droppings into something your fields can use, and to limit the spread of disease. The second is the one your version loses: droppings are one of the routes disease travels, along with contact with sick animals and contaminated material such as farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes. Moving them straight out of the henhouse and onto the ground keeps them in circulation. The pit is also what makes the droppings a product rather than a problem: the first year projection counts 50 kg at 1,000 FCFA among the three things the unit sells.
True or false: the manure pit needs to be covered.

True. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for the pit to be roofed with an apatam, alongside its dimensions of at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. It sits with the two reasons the reference gives for having a pit at all: turning the droppings into something the fields can use, and limiting the spread of disease. The routine that goes with it is sweeping the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throwing the droppings into the pit, which should be well away from the building, and keeping the ground around the henhouse clear of the grass tufts that shelter rats, snakes, shrews, ants and lizards.
Should I sell the droppings or put them on my own maize?

Both are in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it depends on whether you have fields of your own. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the pit two purposes, and the first is to turn the droppings into something your fields can use; the droppings then fertilise those fields. On the other side, its first year projection counts 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA in 2020 prices among the three things the unit sells, with 1,422 birds and 2,376 eggs. So if you crop, using them is a saved cost rather than a lost sale; if you do not, they are a third product you would otherwise throw away. Either way the pit is the same: at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, well away from the henhouse.
Set out what the reference specifies for the manure pit.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies a manure pit of at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, sited well away from the henhouse. It gives two reasons for it: to turn the droppings into something the fields can use, and to limit the spread of disease. The routine attached to it is sweeping the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throwing the droppings into the pit, with the ground around the building kept clear because a tuft of grass shelters predators and the animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. On the economic side, the same study's first year projection sells 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, alongside 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, in 2020 prices.
How long do the droppings have to sit in the pit before I can use them?

I do not have that figure and I will not put a number on it. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives is the pit itself, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, the two purposes, to turn the droppings into something the fields can use and to limit the spread of disease, and the routine of sweeping the henhouse two or three times a week into it. A maturing time is not in what I hold. Ask ICAT, which holds the reference and the plans. If your question is really about making compost properly, that is a separate technique with its own layers and its own timing, and it is worth asking about by that name.
With a hundred and thirty birds, is the minimum pit big enough?

The 1.5 m by 2 m by 1 m is given as a minimum, so with roughly twice the nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks you should expect to build above it rather than at it. The reference does not give a pit size per bird, so I will not invent a conversion; what I can tell you is that the figure is a floor and yours is a larger flock. Two things that do not change with size: the apatam over it, and the siting well away from the henhouse, both of which serve the second reason the reference gives for the pit, limiting the spread of disease. Keep the sweeping to two or three times a week whatever the flock. For a pit sized to your own numbers, ask ICAT.
My neighbour keeps a heap of droppings behind his henhouse and it smells across the yard.

A heap is what the pit is meant to replace. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam and sited well away from the henhouse, and it gives two reasons: turning the droppings into something the fields can use, and limiting the spread of disease. Behind the henhouse fails the siting and the roof at once. Tell him the sweeping routine as well, two or three times a week inside, into the pit rather than onto the ground, and tell him to keep the ground around the building clear, because a tuft of grass shelters snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. And the droppings are worth something: the first year projection counts 50 kg at 1,000 FCFA.
There are rats coming into the henhouse at night.

Look at what is lying around outside before anything else. The instruction is to clean around the henhouse as well as inside it, because a tuft of grass shelters the predators and animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Droppings left in a heap are part of the same picture, which is why they belong in a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, well away from the building. Sweep the inside two or three times a week and take what you sweep to the pit. Check for spilled feed under the troughs too, and check the feeder sizes for the age, since a shallow trough used by big birds throws feed onto the floor.
Just say I can skip the pit, I will deal with the droppings later.

I will not, and of all the items on the list this is the one I would argue hardest about. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference asks for the pit as part of the start-up, alongside the houses, the store, the incubator, the brooder, the well, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests, and it is a hole in the ground rather than something you buy: at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam. The reason to have it before the birds is the second of the two the reference gives, limiting the spread of disease. Droppings accumulating against the building is one of the ways illness stays in a flock, and once you have birds you have droppings from the first week. Dig it now and you will never think about it again.
The henhouse smells and the birds have started coughing.

Two things at once there, and the second is the urgent one. Tell me whether the birds show any of the other signs of illness, and tell me what you do with the droppings at the moment. Coughing is not something to manage by cleaning alone, but poor handling of droppings is one of the ways disease stays in a flock.
A few are sitting apart from the others and not eating. The droppings I sweep into a corner outside the door.

Then call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today, because keeping away from the flock and not eating are two of the eight signs of a sick bird, along with being sad, drowsy and downcast, drooping wings, feathers standing up, thinness, discharge from the nose and the mouth, difficulty moving and diarrhoea. Isolate those birds now, do not visit other farms, and if any die take them out fast and bury them well away. Then fix the droppings, because the corner outside the door is working against you. Dig a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roof it with an apatam and site it well away from the henhouse; the reference gives limiting the spread of disease as one of its two reasons. Sweep the inside two or three times a week into that pit, wash the feeders and drinkers daily, and after the cleaning disinfect, because a good cleaning already removes a good part of the germs and disinfection inactivates what is left. Keep the ground outside clear of grass tufts as well.

A brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks. It is for the first three weeks; after that the chicks move into the chick room to finish growing. The chick room, the poussiniere, is the compartment meant for keeping them warm, and it has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in. Chicks go at 50 per square metre there. Those are the figures of the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference.
I have about thirty chicks coming out this week and no brooder.

Then build or borrow one before they are out, because the first three weeks are what the brooder is for. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks, so thirty chicks need about half that. What it buys you is in its own list: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets you watch feeding and health closely. If the chicks came from a broody hen, keep her with them for the first weeks as well, because she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. After three weeks they move into the chick room, which has fewer openings so the warmth stays in.
The brooder and the chick room are the same thing under two names.

They are two things used one after the other. The brooder is a box, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks, and it is for the chicks' first three weeks. The chick room, the poussiniere, is one of the five compartments of the henhouse, and it is where the chicks go after those three weeks to finish growing, at 50 birds per square metre. What they share is the purpose of warmth: the chick room has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the heat stays in. What the brooder adds, in the reference's own list, is that it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, handles small hatchings in series, keeps predators off, and lets you watch feeding and health closely.
Brooder or mother hen for the first weeks?

Both are in the two Togolese references, and they are not exclusive. The mother hen kept with the chicks for the first weeks protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries, which no box does. The brooder, 0.6 cubic metres at 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high for 60 chicks, is for the first three weeks and earns its place for four reasons the reference names: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets you watch feeding and health closely. If you hatch under hens in small numbers, the hens will do much of it. If you hatch in an incubator, there is no mother and the brooder is not optional. After three weeks, either way, they move into the chick room.
Why does the reference bother with a brooder at all? Justify.

It gives four reasons and they are worth taking one at a time. It saves the fuel of heating the chicks, because warming a small box is cheaper than warming a room. It handles small hatchings in series, so you are not obliged to wait for one big batch. It keeps predators off, which matters because the ground around a henhouse shelters rats, shrews, snakes, ants and lizards if it is not kept clear. And it lets you watch feeding and health closely, at the age when that matters most, since chicks die easily of dehydration and the first days are when you can still act. The size is 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, and it covers the first three weeks.
Set out the brooder and the chick room specifications.

Brooder: for the chicks' first three weeks; volume 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks. Its stated purposes: saving the fuel of heating the chicks, handling small hatchings in series, keeping predators off, and allowing close watch of feeding and health. Chick room, the poussiniere: one of the at least five compartments of the henhouse, meant for keeping the chicks warm, with fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in; its wall is raised to full height with openings left for air, where elsewhere the low wall is 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most. Density there: 50 chicks per square metre. All from the 2020 ICAT and PASA commercial reference.
What temperature should the brooder be kept at, and for how long each day?

I do not have that and I will not put a figure on it, because a wrong brooding temperature kills chicks quickly. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives is the box and the period: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, covering the first three weeks, after which they move into the chick room. It gives the purposes too, including that the brooder saves the fuel of heating the chicks. The settings are not in what I hold. Ask ICAT, and ask whoever supplies the brooder. One thing the 2017 ESFT compendium does give you: if the chicks came from a broody hen, keep her with them for the first weeks, because she adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries better than a thermometer will.
I am hatching about two hundred chicks at a time. What does that mean for the brooder?

More than three of them, since the reference sizes one brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, at 60 chicks. Two hundred needs four. That is one of the things the same reference says the brooder is good at: handling small hatchings in series, so running several is the expected pattern rather than a workaround. Plan the chick room to match, because at 50 chicks per square metre two hundred birds need four square metres once they leave the brooder at three weeks. And plan the equipment: chick feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 birds, so four of them, and siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres, two per hundred birds from 1 to 30 days, so four again. Take the numbers to ICAT before you buy.
A friend is hatching for the first time and asks what he needs for the chicks.

A brooder for the first three weeks, then a chick room. The brooder is 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, and holds 60 chicks. Tell him why it is worth the trouble, in the reference's own terms: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets him watch feeding and health closely. After three weeks the chicks go into the chick room, which is the compartment with fewer openings so the warmth stays in, at 50 birds per square metre. And tell him the two things that kill chicks fastest: they must be fed apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and they must have clean water in front of them always, because they die easily of dehydration.
The incubator is on day nineteen. What do I set up now?

The brooder, ready and warm before they come out, because there is no mother hen to do it for you. It is 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, and it covers the first three weeks. Put their feed and water in it: chick feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 chicks, and siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres, two per hundred birds for the first 30 days, kept clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Have the chick ration ready, apart from what the adults eat: for 100 kg from 1 to 8 weeks, 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Then prepare the chick room for the move at three weeks, at 50 chicks per square metre. Incubation is twenty-one days, so you have two.
Just tell me I can put a hundred chicks in one brooder if I am careful.

I will not, because the figure is 60 and a hundred is two thirds again as many. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, and one of the four things it says the brooder is for is letting you watch feeding and health closely, which is precisely what you lose when it is crowded. Build or borrow a second one; the same reference says the brooder handles small hatchings in series, so running more than one is the normal way to work. If it is a question of cost, the brooder is a simple box and the reference notes elsewhere that a local craftsman can often make equipment more cheaply than a shop. Ask ICAT.
My chicks keep dying in the first two weeks.

That is the stretch the brooder covers, so let me start there. Tell me where the chicks spend their first three weeks, what they drink from and what they eat. Those three account for most early losses, and the water most of all, because chicks die easily of dehydration.
They are in the corner of the big room with the adults, and they drink and eat from the same things the hens use.

Then change all three. The first three weeks belong in a brooder, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holding 60 chicks; among the reasons the reference gives for it are that it keeps predators off and lets you watch feeding and health closely, neither of which you can do in a corner. After three weeks they go into the chick room, the compartment with fewer openings so the warmth stays in, at 50 chicks per square metre, not in with the adults. Second, feed them apart so they do not have to compete, on their own ration: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Third, give them their own water, in chick drinkers, two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds for the first 30 days, clean, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day and never empty. If you hatched under a hen, leave her with them for the first weeks, because she adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. If the deaths carry on after that, call the animal health worker.
Which direction should I orient the building, and can I use red wood shavings for litter?

Neither of those is in what I hold, and I am not going to answer them from memory. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference describes the henhouse in some detail, at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, tarpaulins for rain and wind, and the densities for each age. It does not say which way the building should face, and it does not say whether red wood shavings can be used as litter. Both questions go to ICAT, which holds the plans and the reference itself. I would rather tell you the gap than fill it.
