I do not have it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not say which way the henhouse should face, and neither does the 2017 ESFT village compendium. I could give you something that sounds right and it would be invention. Ask ICAT, which holds the plans. What those references do give on the shell: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room taken higher with openings for air, and tarpaulins to close against rain and wind.
The mason is on site and wants to know which way to set the building before he starts.

Then get ICAT on the phone rather than taking an answer from me, because this is one of the things neither Togolese reference settles. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives the compartments, the wall heights and the densities but not the orientation, and a building set wrong is set wrong for its whole life. What you can give the mason today from what I do hold: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy; one with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard; a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, with the chick room taken to full height and openings left for air. And the manure pit marked out, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep.
You told me the wall heights, so you must know the orientation too.

The wall heights are in the reference and the orientation is not, and that is the whole difference. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, the five compartments, the densities of 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for growers, and the manure pit at 1.5 m by 2 m by 1 m. It says nothing about which way the building faces. Knowing part of a document is not knowing all of it, and the useful thing I can do here is tell you exactly where the edge is. ICAT holds the plans and can answer it.
True or false: red wood shavings are the standard litter for a henhouse in Togo.

I cannot say true or false, because neither Togolese reference I hold answers it. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts litter among the first year running costs, alongside feed, the Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer and disinfectant, but it does not say whether red wood shavings may be used. The 2017 ESFT compendium does not either. Answering a true or false question with a guess is worse than leaving it open, because you would act on it. Ask ICAT. What I can tell you about litter is the handling: after changing it, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter.
Shavings or straw for the litter?

I do not have a basis for choosing between them. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts litter as a running cost without naming a material, and it is on record in what I hold that whether red wood shavings can be used is one of the questions the reference does not answer. I am not going to settle it by preference. Ask ICAT. What I can give you is what surrounds the choice: after changing the litter, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter; sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throw what you sweep into the manure pit well away from the building; and wash the feeders and drinkers every day.
List what the housing reference does not cover.

Two things are on record as not covered, and I would rather name them than let you assume the reference is complete. It does not say which way the building should face. And it does not say whether red wood shavings can be used as litter. The 2017 ESFT village compendium adds two more gaps of its own: it does not give the names of the vitamins a hen needs, and it does not say whether a hen lays without a cock. For all four, the answer is ICAT or the animal health worker, not me. What the housing reference does cover is the compartments, the densities, the wall heights, the feeders and drinkers by age, the brooder, the incubator capacity and the manure pit.
Does the orientation matter more for a big building than a small one?

I do not know, and the reason is the same as before: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does not treat orientation at all, so I have nothing to scale. I will not reason my way to an answer and present it as though the reference said it. What does scale in that reference is the floor area, through the densities of 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks and 12 to 15 for growers, and its worked layout runs from a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m up to a grower compartment of 7 m by 4 m. Put the orientation question to ICAT with your actual dimensions, since they will want to know the size in order to answer it.
Someone told my cooperative that henhouses must face east. Is that right?

I cannot confirm or contradict it, because neither Togolese reference I hold says which way a henhouse should face. That does not make the person wrong; it means I am not the one who can tell you. Ask ICAT, which holds the plans, and ask the person where their figure comes from, because a rule with a source behind it is worth more to the cooperative than one passed on. What I can tell the cooperative from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is the rest of the shell: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, the chick room walled higher with openings left for air, and tarpaulins kept to close against rain and wind.
My henhouse gets very hot in the afternoon and I wonder if I built it the wrong way round.

You may have, and I cannot tell you, because neither reference I hold says which way a henhouse should face. Put that question to ICAT. What I can do is look at the other causes of heat in the same building. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference wants the henhouse well aired and roomy, with a low wall of 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, so if yours is walled higher than that outside the chick room it will hold heat. Tarpaulins are meant to be hung to close against rain and wind, not left up. Check the density too, 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders and 12 to 15 for growers, since crowding makes any building hotter. And make sure the water is in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.
The litter in my henhouse is always damp and the birds smell of it.

I cannot tell you which litter material to change to, because whether red wood shavings can be used is one of the questions the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference leaves open, and I will not answer it from memory. What I can work on is everything around it. Sweep the inside two or three times a week and throw the droppings into the manure pit, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, well away from the building. After changing the litter, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter. Check the drinkers are not overflowing onto the floor, and check the building is as aired as the reference wants, with the low wall at 0.5 to 1 m. Then ask ICAT about the litter itself.
Just give me your best guess on the orientation, anything is better than nothing.

No, and here anything is not better than nothing. You would build on it, the building would stand for twenty years, and neither of us would ever know whether the guess was right. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is detailed about this henhouse, the five compartments, the densities, the wall heights, the feeders and drinkers by age, the brooder, the manure pit, and it does not say which way the building faces. That silence is information: it tells you to ask someone who knows the ground rather than someone who has read the study. ICAT holds the plans and is the right place. I will give you anything in the reference without hesitation; this is not in it.
I am drawing up my henhouse plan and there are two things nobody can answer.

Tell me what they are. There are some things I can give you straight out of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference and some that reference genuinely does not contain, and it is worth knowing which is which before you go looking further.
Which way to face it, and what to put down for litter.

Those are exactly the two the reference leaves open, so you have not missed anything. It does not say which way the building should face, and it does not say whether red wood shavings can be used as litter. Take both to ICAT, which holds the plans and the reference itself. Everything else on your drawing I can help with: at least five compartments, well aired and roomy, one with a shared yard for the breeders, one for brooding, a chick room with fewer openings so the warmth stays in, and two fattening compartments for the growers with a yard. Sizes from the densities, 8 to 10 birds per square metre for breeders, 50 for chicks, 12 to 15 for growers. Low wall 0.5 to 1 m, three bricks at most, chick room walled higher with openings for air, tarpaulins for rain and wind. Outside, a grassy run, a store, and a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam. One note on litter while you wait for the answer: after changing it, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter.
alimentation poussins premiers jours

Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Clean water matters most of all, because chicks die easily of dehydration; never let the drinker be empty. From 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day. Keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks: she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries.
The chicks hatched two days ago and the mother hen is still with them.

Leave her there. Keeping the mother hen with the chicks for the first weeks is what the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for, and the reason is worth knowing: she protects them, and she adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries, which no equipment does as well. What you add is the feeding and the water. Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Give them clean water at all times, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, because chicks die easily of dehydration. From 1 to 60 days count about 1.5 kg of feed a bird in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day.
Set out the rearing of chicks in the first weeks.

Housing: the brooder for the first three weeks, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, then the chick room at 50 birds per square metre, with fewer openings so the warmth stays in. Mothering: keep the mother hen with them for the first weeks, since she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. Feeding: apart from the adults, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites; the quantified formula for 100 kg from 1 to 8 weeks is 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Quantity from 1 to 60 days, about 1.5 kg a bird at 10 to 25 grams a day. Water: clean, in the shade, never empty, renewed at least twice a day.
Which vitamins do the chicks need and in what dose?

I cannot give you names or doses. The 2017 ESFT compendium puts vitamins in its list of what a ration is built from, as herbs, fruit and plant debris, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts vitamins among the first year running costs, but the names of the vitamins a hen needs are not in what I hold, and it is on record as one of the questions those references do not answer. A dose invented here could hurt the birds. Ask the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, and ask ICAT. What I can give you is the rest of the chick ration: fed apart from the adults, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, with clean water always in front of them.
My sister has chicks for the first time and asks what matters most.

Water, before anything else. Tell her chicks die easily of dehydration, so the drinker must never be empty, the water clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Second, feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Third, if the chicks came from a broody hen, leave the hen with them for the first weeks, because she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. And tell her what a healthy chick looks like so she can spot the others: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws.
The chicks come out tomorrow. What do I put in front of them first?

Clean water, in their own drinker, before anything else, because chicks die easily of dehydration and that is the fastest way to lose them. Two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds covers the first 30 days, kept in the shade, never empty, renewed at least twice a day. Then their own feed, apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, in chick feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 birds. Have the brooder warm, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, for the first three weeks. And if a hen hatched them, leave her with them.
Some of the chicks that came out have wet navels and cannot stand properly.

Those are the opposite of what a healthy newly hatched chick looks like. The description to judge against is a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Keep the weak ones warm and where you can watch them, which is one of the things the brooder is for, and make sure they can reach clean water without having to compete, since chicks die easily of dehydration. Do not mix them back in with the strong ones until they are up. If several are like this in the same hatching, the place to look is upstream, at the eggs you set and at the cock, and then at the animal health worker if it continues.
The chicks crowd around the hens at feeding time and get pushed away.

Then they are not being fed apart, and that is the instruction: feed the chicks separately from the adults so they do not have to compete. Give them their own feeders, 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 birds, in their own space, and their own ration of ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Same for the water, in their own drinker, clean, in the shade and never empty. For the first three weeks they should be in the brooder anyway, which keeps them off the adults entirely, and after that in the chick room at 50 birds per square metre rather than mixed in.
Just tell me the chicks will be fine eating what the hens eat.

I will not, because the 2017 ESFT compendium says the opposite and the cost of being wrong falls on the chicks. Feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on their own ration: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. The quantities differ too, about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, against 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. And the water is the part I would argue hardest about: chicks die easily of dehydration, so they need a drinker they can reach without being pushed off it. If you want to be told your setup is fine by someone who can see it, that is the animal health worker or ICAT.
I lose about half the chicks in every batch.

Half is far above what the model expects, since the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a mortality rate near 10 percent, so something specific is going on. Tell me three things: where the chicks spend the first three weeks, what they drink from, and what they eat. Those three cover most of it, and water most of all, because chicks die easily of dehydration.
They run with the hens from day one, they drink from the big drinker and they peck at whatever the hens are given.

All three then, and the water first. Give the chicks their own drinkers, two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds for the first 30 days, clean, in the shade, never empty and renewed at least twice a day; a big drinker meant for adults is one a chick cannot always reach. Second, feed them apart so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, in chick feeders of 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 birds. Third, the first three weeks belong in a brooder, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, which keeps predators off and lets you watch feeding and health closely, and after that in the chick room at 50 per square metre. Leave the mother hen with them where there is one, since she adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries. If you are still near half after those changes, call the animal health worker.
What size of incubator do I need?

A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, which is the minimum commercial nucleus in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The same reference adds a warning in the same breath: at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. Whichever way you hatch, the incubation lasts twenty-one days, under an electric, gas or solar incubator as under a hen, after which the chicks come out of the shells. A brooding hen, by comparison, sits on twelve to fourteen eggs at a time.
couveuse capacite pour 60 poules

300 eggs. A gas incubator of that capacity suits a flock of 60 breeding hens in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and it notes that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself. The incubator is one of the items counted in its start-up evaluation of 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices. Incubation lasts twenty-one days either way; a brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs.
I have sixty hens and I am deciding whether to buy the incubator this year or next.

Sixty breeding hens is exactly the flock the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a 300 egg gas incubator on, so the machine fits you. What should decide the timing is the warning attached to it: at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the incubator does not pay for itself. So the real question is whether there is hatching work around you, and that is worth asking a cooperative or ICAT before you spend. Meanwhile your hens will hatch, twelve to fourteen eggs each, over the same twenty-one days. The incubator is one line in the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up, so deferring it is a real saving in a first year the same study projects at a net result of 131,785 FCFA.
With an incubator I will not need broody hens at all, so I can keep more layers.

The machine does replace the brooding, but check the arithmetic before you plan on it. A gas incubator of 300 eggs is sized on a flock of 60 breeding hens in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so it is matched to that flock rather than to a larger one. And the same reference says that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or the machine does not pay for itself, which is the opposite of a machine that earns its keep on your own eggs alone. What the incubator does not replace is the mothering afterwards: a hen kept with her chicks protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries, and with an incubator there is no hen, so the brooder becomes compulsory rather than optional.
True or false: a 300 egg incubator is too big for sixty hens.

False as a matter of sizing, and true as a matter of economics, which is why the reference says both things. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, so the capacity is the right match. In the same sentence it notes that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. So it is the right size and it will still be idle part of the year unless you bring other people's eggs into it. That is a business arrangement to make before you buy, not after, and a cooperative or ICAT is where to start.
Why would the reference tell me to hatch other people's eggs? Justify.

Because a machine that runs a few weeks a year is a cost, not an asset. A gas incubator of 300 eggs is sized on a flock of 60 breeding hens, and 60 hens do not fill 300 eggs continuously: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on about ten eggs per hen per laying and about six layings a year, and the incubation itself is twenty-one days. So there is idle capacity built into the match. Hatching for other keepers fills it and turns the incubator into a service you sell, which matters in a first year that reference projects at a net result of only 131,785 FCFA. It is the same logic as its instruction to count three products rather than one, birds, eggs and droppings.
I am thinking about buying an incubator.

Tell me how many breeding hens you keep, because the sizing in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference runs from the flock: a gas incubator of 300 eggs suits 60 breeding hens. And tell me whether there is anyone else near you who hatches, because that reference attaches a condition to the purchase.
Forty hens, and there are two or three other keepers in the village.

Then you are under the flock the 300 egg machine is sized for, and the other keepers are the thing that makes it work anyway. The reference says that even at 60 hens you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself, so at 40 that is not an extra, it is the plan. Go and agree it with those two or three before you buy, and agree what you charge, using the same method the reference gives for pricing anything: record every expense, work out the cost per unit, decide the profit you want, compare with what people will pay, readjust. Meanwhile your hens can hatch, twelve to fourteen eggs each over twenty-one days, which is the same incubation the machine gives. And remember that with machine-hatched chicks there is no mother hen, so the brooder becomes compulsory: 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, covering their first three weeks. Take the whole calculation to ICAT.
If I double to 120 breeding hens, do I buy a second incubator?

Probably, but do the arithmetic on use rather than on head count. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sizes a gas incubator of 300 eggs on a flock of 60 breeding hens, so 120 hens are past what one machine was matched to. Before buying a second, look at how full the first one runs: that reference already says a 300 egg machine on 60 hens is under-used unless you hatch for other keepers, so a doubled flock may simply fill the machine you have. The incubation is twenty-one days a batch, which sets how many batches a year you can run. And whatever you decide on the machine, the brooders scale hard: one of 0.6 cubic metres holds 60 chicks, so more chicks means more boxes. Take the numbers to ICAT.
I bought an incubator last year and it has hardly been switched on.

That is the failure the reference warns about in the same sentence as the sizing: a gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, and at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. An idle incubator is a line out of the 3,850,124 FCFA of start-up doing nothing. Two things to do rather than regret it. Fill it from outside: go to the other keepers, to a cooperative or to ICAT and offer hatching as a service, priced from your own costs. And fill it from inside: collect eggs every day, keep them seven to ten days at most somewhere cool, airy and dry, and sort out those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, so that the eggs you do have are worth setting.
My hens go broody at different times and I never get enough chicks at once.

That is precisely what the machine is for, and the reference names it: the brooder handles small hatchings in series, and the incubator lets you set a batch when you choose rather than when a hen decides. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs, so scattered broodiness gives you scattered batches. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, with the warning that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well or it does not pay for itself. Before buying, tighten the egg handling, since that alone may give you bigger batches: collect every day, keep seven to ten days at most somewhere cool, airy and dry, sort out the unusable ones and set pointed end down.
Just tell me the incubator will pay for itself on my own flock.

I cannot, because the reference says the opposite in the sentence that gives you the size. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, and it notes that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. That is not my caution added on top, it is part of the specification. If you want it to pay on your own eggs alone you would need to fill 300 eggs often enough to justify it, and with about ten eggs per hen per laying and about six layings a year that is not what 60 hens give. Arrange the outside hatching first and the purchase becomes sound. ICAT can help you cost it.
Walk me through the reproduction cycle from egg to sale.

Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry for seven to ten days at most, discarding those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, and set them pointed end down. Incubation is twenty-one days, under a hen sitting on twelve to fourteen eggs or in an electric, gas or solar incubator, after which the chicks come out of the shells. The chicks spend their first three weeks in the brooder, then move into the chick room. The growers are the 3 to 6 month birds, in their own compartments. Sale comes at six months, when a hen weighs about 1.3 kg and a cock about 1.5 kg. Breeders are culled at 24 months. The unit runs six production cycles a year.
cycle production poule locale combien par an

Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. Around them: about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Each hatching takes twenty-one days of incubation, then three weeks in the brooder, then the chick room, then the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds, then sale at six months. Breeders culled at 24 months.
I want to plan my year so the birds are ready for the big market days.

Then count backwards from the sale, because the cycle length is fixed. Birds are sold at six months, when a hen weighs about 1.3 kg and a cock about 1.5 kg, so a bird you want ready in September was an egg set in about March. The incubation is twenty-one days, the brooder covers the first three weeks, then the chick room, then the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, so you have room to stagger the settings rather than hatching everything at once. Two things it asks you to do alongside: look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after, and keep a movement register of sales, hatchings and deaths so you can see the pattern next year.
Six cycles a year means a bird goes from egg to sale in two months.

No, the cycles overlap. A bird takes twenty-one days of incubation and then six months to reach sale weight, about 1.3 kg for a hen and 1.5 kg for a cock, so no bird goes from egg to sale in two months. Six production cycles a year in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference means six settings running at different stages at the same time: one batch in the incubator or under hens, one in the brooder for its first three weeks, one in the chick room, others in the grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds. That is also why the reference asks for at least five compartments: several ages are on the farm at once by design.
True or false: the birds are sold at the same age the breeders are culled.

False, and the two ages are months apart. Birds raised for sale go at six months, when a hen weighs about 1.3 kg and a cock about 1.5 kg. Breeders in the nucleus are culled at 24 months, hens and cocks alike, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference; the 2017 ESFT village compendium instead culls breeding cocks after three years of keeping, for the family henhouse it describes. So a culled breeder is a bird that has done two years of work, and a sold grower is a bird raised for the purpose. Both end up as sales: the first year projection counts 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA in 2020 prices.
Should I hatch everything at once or spread it through the year?

Spread it, and the reference is built that way: six production cycles a year, not one. Several practical things point the same way. The brooder handles small hatchings in series, which is one of the four reasons the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for having one. A brooding hen only sits on twelve to fourteen eggs anyway. And the compartments are sized for different ages at once, which is why the plan asks for at least five. Spreading also spreads your selling, which matters when you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready rather than after. One batch a year would crowd the chick room, empty it for months, and leave you selling everything into one week.
Why does the reference give a hatching rate and a mortality rate separately? Justify.

Because they bite at different points in the cycle and you can act on each. The natural hatching rate near 70 percent applies to the eggs you set, so it is decided upstream, by how you collect, sort and keep them, seven to ten days at most somewhere cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, and by the cock. The mortality rate near 10 percent applies to the birds afterwards, and it is decided by the brooder, the chick room, the feeding apart from the adults and the clean water. Two separate rates tell you where a bad year went wrong: few chicks out of many eggs is an egg problem, many chicks and few birds at six months is a rearing problem. One combined figure would hide that.
How many chicks will I have in December?

I cannot tell you that, and neither can the study. What the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives are annual averages for a unit: six production cycles a year, about ten eggs per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Those are evaluations over a year, not a forecast for a month, and what happens in December on your farm depends on when you set eggs, how many hens are in lay and whether the flock is healthy. What I can give you is the arithmetic of the cycle: eggs set today hatch in twenty-one days, and the chicks are sold at six months. Keep the movement register with hatchings and deaths and by next year the figure will be yours.
How many birds should sixty hens give me in a year?

Work it through the rates rather than taking a single number. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on about ten eggs laid per hen per laying and about six layings a year, so sixty hens lay in the order of three thousand six hundred eggs a year. Not all are set: you discard those too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end, and the reference also sells eggs, 2,376 of them in its first year projection. On what you do set, the natural hatching rate is near 70 percent, and then a mortality rate near 10 percent applies to the birds. Its own first year answer, after all of that, is 1,422 birds sold at 2,250 FCFA in 2020 prices. Treat that as the projection for a unit, not a promise.
Everything on my farm is the same age and the henhouse is empty half the year.

You are running one cycle where the model runs six. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year, which is why it asks for at least five compartments: a breeder compartment, a brooding compartment, a chick room and two grower compartments, all occupied at once by birds of different ages. Start staggering: set a batch of eggs, then another before the first leaves the brooder at three weeks, and so on. A brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen eggs, and the brooder is meant to handle small hatchings in series, so the equipment already assumes this. Staggering also spreads your sales, which matters because you are meant to find buyers before each batch is ready. Write the settings and hatchings in the movement register so you can see the rhythm build.
I always seem to be either overrun with birds or with none to sell.

That is a staggering problem rather than a flock problem. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans six production cycles a year and houses several ages at once, in at least five compartments, so that something is always coming to sale age. Set eggs in smaller batches more often: a brooding hen takes twelve to fourteen, the incubation is twenty-one days, the brooder covers the first three weeks and is meant to handle small hatchings in series, and sale comes at six months. Pair that with the selling instruction, which is to look for your buyers before the batch starts rather than after, with a client register and contracts where you can. The movement register, with sales, hatchings and deaths, is what will show you the gaps before you feel them.
Just tell me I can get birds to market in three months if I feed them well.

I will not, because the figure I hold is six months and it is tied to a weight, not to a feeling. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives sale at six months, with a hen at about 1.3 kg live weight and a cock at about 1.5 kg, and its feeding table runs to that same point: about 5 kg of feed a bird from 61 days to sale at six months, at 25 to 35 grams a day. Feeding well is what gets you to those weights on time, not earlier. If you sell at three months you are selling a smaller bird and should price it as one, using your own recorded costs. If someone is telling you otherwise for local hens, put it to ICAT rather than to me.
bon poussin a l'eclosion signes

A well developed body; bright, dry, thick coloured down; a soft belly with a clean, dry navel; and strong legs with straight, separated claws. Those four are what the 2017 ESFT compendium describes in a healthy newly hatched chick. Judge each chick against them as it comes out, keep the weak ones where you can watch them, and give all of them clean water straight away, because chicks die easily of dehydration.
A small chick just needs more feeding, it will catch up.

Some will and some are telling you something you should read now. The description of a healthy newly hatched chick is a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. A chick that misses several of those, a wet navel and legs that will not hold it, is not simply behind on feed. Feed it properly by all means, apart from the adults so it does not have to compete, and make sure it can reach clean water, since dehydration kills chicks fastest. But keep it where you can watch it, which is one of the four things the brooder is for, and if a whole hatching looks like this, look back at the eggs and the cock rather than forward at the feed.
True or false: damp down on a newly hatched chick is normal for the first day.

I will answer on what the description says rather than on what may be normal. A healthy newly hatched chick has bright, dry, thick coloured down, along with a well developed body, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Dry is part of the description, so a chick still damp is not yet answering to it. Whether that resolves within hours is not something the compendium states, and I will not fill that in. What I would do is keep such chicks warm and watched, which is what the brooder is for, and call the animal health worker if a good part of a hatching is like this.
Two chicks look poor. Do I cull them or try to raise them?

I have no instruction that tells you to cull a weak chick, so I will not invent one. What the 2017 ESFT compendium gives is the description to judge by: a healthy newly hatched chick has a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. If two out of a hatching miss that, keep them where you can watch feeding and health closely, which is one of the four reasons the brooder exists, and make sure they can reach clean water and their own feed without being pushed off by stronger birds. Isolate any bird that is actually ill rather than merely weak, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see the signs of disease.
Why look at the navel of a chick? Justify.

Because it is one of the four things the description names, and it is visible in the first minutes when nothing else has had time to show. A healthy newly hatched chick has a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Three of those four are about the outside of the bird and one is about how the hatching itself went. Reading them takes a few seconds per chick and tells you which birds to put where you can watch them closely, which is what the brooder is for. It also tells you something about the batch as a whole, and a bad batch sends you back to the eggs, the keeping and the cock rather than forward to the feed.
Give the description of a healthy newly hatched chick.

Four points, from the 2017 ESFT compendium. A well developed body. Bright, dry, thick coloured down. A soft belly with a clean, dry navel. Strong legs with straight, separated claws. That description is for the bird as it comes out of the shell, after the twenty-one days of incubation. It belongs beside two other things you should have ready at that moment: the brooder, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, covering the first three weeks, and clean water, because chicks die easily of dehydration. It is also distinct from the eight signs of a sick bird, which describe an animal that has fallen ill rather than one just hatched.
What should a chick weigh at hatching?

I do not have a hatching weight and I will not guess at one. The description I hold is qualitative: a healthy newly hatched chick has a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. The weights the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference does give come much later, at six months, about 1.3 kg for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. Between those two points the figure I have is feed rather than weight: about 1.5 kg of feed a bird in all from 1 to 60 days, at 10 to 25 grams a day. For a hatching weight, ask ICAT or the animal health worker.
With a hundred chicks out at once, do I really check each one?

Yes, and it takes less time than it sounds, because the description is four things you see at a glance: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. A hundred chicks is a couple of minutes. It matters more at that scale, not less, because a hundred chicks will not fit in one brooder anyway, which holds 60, so you are handling them to split them in any case. Watching feeding and health closely is one of the four things the brooder is for, and it starts with knowing which birds looked weak on day one. Write what you see into the movement register with the hatching.
A neighbour is buying day old chicks and asks what to look for.

Give him the four points of the description: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Tell him to look at each bird rather than at the box. And tell him the two things to have ready before he brings them home, because chicks bought are chicks without a mother hen: a brooder for the first three weeks, 0.6 cubic metres for 60 chicks, and clean water in their own drinker, never empty, since chicks die easily of dehydration. Their feed goes apart from any adults he keeps. If he is bringing them onto a farm that already has birds, the quarantine rule applies to them as to any new stock.
Day twenty-one tomorrow. What am I looking at when they come out?

Four things on each chick: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Sort as you go, and put the ones that fall short where you can watch them closely rather than mixing them straight in. Have the brooder warm before the first chick is out, 0.6 cubic metres, 2 m by 1 m by 30 cm high, for 60 chicks, covering the first three weeks. Have clean water in a chick drinker, in the shade, never empty, because dehydration kills them fastest, and their own feed apart from the adults. If a hen hatched them, leave her with them: she protects them and adjusts the warmth from the sound of their cries.
The chicks from this hatching all seem limp and their down looks dull.

That is the whole batch failing the description rather than one weak bird, which points upstream. A healthy newly hatched chick has a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. When a whole hatching misses it, look back at the eggs: kept seven to ten days at most, somewhere cool, airy and dry, set pointed end down, and none too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end. Look at the cock as well, vigorous and agile with a well developed bright red comb, at one for about ten hens. Meanwhile keep these chicks warm in the brooder with clean water in front of them, and call the animal health worker.
Just tell me these chicks are fine, they are moving about.

Moving about is good and it is one of four things to look at, not the whole test. Hold each one and check the rest: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. I cannot tell you they are fine because I have not seen them, and the description exists precisely so that you do not have to take anyone's word for it, mine included. If they answer to all four, you have what you should have. If several do not, keep those where you can watch feeding and health closely, which is one of the four things the brooder is for, and call the animal health worker if it is most of the batch.
How do I know if the chicks I bought are any good?

Look at each bird against four points: a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Tell me what you are seeing and I can say whether it is something to act on. It would also help to know whether you already keep birds, because chicks arriving onto a farm with a flock raise a separate question.
Most of them look right, a few have dull down, and yes I have about thirty hens already.

Then two separate things to do. For the chicks themselves, put the few with dull down where you can watch feeding and health closely rather than losing them in the crowd; that is one of the four reasons the brooder exists, and it holds 60 chicks in 0.6 cubic metres for their first three weeks. Give all of them clean water in their own drinker, never empty, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, because chicks die easily of dehydration, and feed them apart from any adults so they do not have to compete. For the farm, the new chicks are new stock arriving: the rule is two weeks of quarantine for any bird that comes in, bought or given, so keep them clear of your thirty hens for that time. Watch both groups for the signs of a sick bird while they are apart, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary if you see them.
signes poule malade

Eight, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The bird is sad, drowsy and downcast; its wings droop and its feathers stand up; it keeps away from the flock; it does not eat; it is thin; it has a discharge from the nose and the mouth; it moves with difficulty; and it has diarrhoea. Isolate a bird showing these, or take it out to treat it, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock.
One of my hens has been standing in the corner all morning with her feathers up.

That is two of the eight signs at once: keeping away from the flock, and feathers standing up with the wings drooping. The other six are being sad, drowsy and downcast, not eating, thinness, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, moving with difficulty, and diarrhoea. Look at her for those now. Isolate her or take her out, which is what the reference asks as soon as a bird falls ill, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary; they are to be called every time you see disease in the flock, not only when several birds are down. While you wait, do not visit other farms and do not let the hens wander. If she dies, take her out fast and bury her far from the henhouse.
She is eating, so she cannot be ill.

Not eating is one sign of eight, and a bird can be ill while still eating. The full list in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference is: sad, drowsy and downcast; wings drooping and feathers standing up; keeping away from the flock; not eating; thinness; a discharge from the nose and the mouth; moving with difficulty; and diarrhoea. Go through all eight rather than stopping at the one. Thinness in particular is a sign that shows in a bird that has been eating badly for a while rather than refusing food today. If any of the eight are there, isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary.
True or false: diarrhoea alone is enough reason to call the animal health worker.

True. Diarrhoea is one of the eight signs the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists, and the instruction that goes with the list is to call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock. It does not ask you to wait for a second sign or a second bird. The other seven, so you can look for them while you wait: sad, drowsy and downcast; wings drooping and feathers standing up; keeping away from the flock; not eating; thin; a discharge from the nose and the mouth; and moving with difficulty. Isolate the bird meanwhile, or take it out to treat it.
Do I isolate the bird or treat it where it is?

Isolate it, or take it out to treat it, which is what the reference asks in either case: when a bird falls ill you separate it from the rest. That sits under the first of the three hygiene principles, separation, alongside not mixing your animals with those of other farms and quarantining every newly bought bird. Then call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, which is to be done every time you see disease in the flock. One thing to know before you buy anything to treat it with: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have.
Why does the reference list eight signs instead of just saying watch the birds? Justify.

Because the signs are what you will notice first, and a list is something you can carry in your head while you are in the henhouse. Told only to watch, you see a flock; given the eight, you see a bird that is sad, drowsy and downcast, whose wings droop and feathers stand up, that keeps away from the flock, does not eat, is thin, has a discharge from the nose and the mouth, moves with difficulty or has diarrhoea. It also sets a threshold: any one of them is enough to isolate the bird and call the animal health worker. Without a list, everyone sets their own threshold and it is always too late.
List the signs of a sick bird as the reference gives them.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists eight. The bird is sad, drowsy and downcast. Its wings droop and its feathers stand up. It keeps away from the flock. It does not eat. It is thin. It has a discharge from the nose and the mouth. It moves with difficulty. It has diarrhoea. The actions attached: isolate the bird or take it out to treat it; take dead birds out as fast as you can and bury them far from the henhouse; and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time disease shows in the flock, asking about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse.
My hen has drooping wings and diarrhoea. Which disease is it?

I will not name a disease from two signs, and you should be wary of anyone who does. Drooping wings and diarrhoea are two of the eight signs of a sick bird in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and they are shared by more than one illness. What the signs tell you is to act, not what to act against. Isolate her or take her out now, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary; naming the disease is their work, and so is the treatment. Meanwhile do not visit other farms, do not let the hens wander, and if she dies take her out fast and bury her far from the henhouse. Do not buy a medicine on a guess.
One bird out of sixty. Is that worth acting on?

Yes, and acting on one is the cheapest moment there is. The instruction is to isolate a bird when it falls ill or take it out to treat it, and to call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock; neither is conditioned on a number. The reason is the way disease travels, through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material, so one bird left among fifty-nine is the route to the rest. For scale, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference works on a mortality rate near 10 percent over a year, so occasional loss is expected, but that is a yearly average and not a reason to leave a sick bird in the flock today.
A neighbour says his birds are just tired. What should I ask him?

Ask him to go through the eight signs rather than to judge the whole flock at once. Are the birds sad, drowsy and downcast? Do their wings droop and their feathers stand up? Do any keep away from the flock? Are they off their feed? Are they thin? Is there a discharge from the nose and the mouth? Do they move with difficulty? Is there diarrhoea? If any of those are there, tell him to isolate the birds concerned and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, which the reference asks every time disease shows. And tell him not to visit your farm meanwhile, because contact between farms is one of the ways disease moves.
What should I be checking every morning when I open the henhouse?

Go through the eight signs while the birds are still settled, before you feed them. Is any bird sad, drowsy and downcast? Are any wings drooping, any feathers standing up? Is one keeping away from the others? Then put the feed down and watch who does not come to it, because not eating is the sign you can only see at that moment. Look for thinness, for discharge from the nose and the mouth, for a bird moving with difficulty, and for diarrhoea in the droppings. Isolate anything you find, and call the animal health worker if you see disease. While you are there, check the drinkers are not empty and wash them, and note what you saw in the health follow-up.
Just tell me what to give her, I do not want to call anybody.

I will not name a medicine or a dose, and this is one of the places I will hold the line. I have not seen the bird, I cannot name the disease from a description, and a wrong medicine can harm the flock and you. There is also a fact that makes guessing worse than useless: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. What I can tell you to do now costs nothing. Isolate her or take her out. Do not visit other farms. If she dies, take her out fast and bury her far from the henhouse. And call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, which is what the reference asks every time disease shows in a flock.
medicament contre maladie virale volaille

There is none. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. That is worth knowing before you buy anything, because it is money spent on a cure that does not exist. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary and ask about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. And after any bird has been treated with anything, do not eat its meat or its eggs for a few days, because they can hold drug residues.
The seller at the market says this powder cures everything in poultry.

Nothing cures everything, and one fact in particular should make you keep your money. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. So a product sold as curing everything is being sold as curing viruses too, which it cannot. Before buying anything, get the bird looked at: isolate it or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, who can say what the illness is and what, if anything, acts on it. And remember afterwards that a treated bird's meat and eggs can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days.
If the antibiotic did not work, I just need a stronger one.

Or the illness is not one any antibiotic acts on. That is the distinction the reference draws: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. A medicine that does nothing against a virus will do nothing at any strength, and you will have spent twice. Stop and get the illness named rather than escalating: isolate the birds affected, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, asking about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. Note also that every treatment you give has a cost after the fact, because the meat and eggs of a treated bird can hold drug residues and are not to be eaten for a few days.
Should I vaccinate or keep money aside for medicines?

Vaccinate, because for one whole class of illness the medicines are not an option at all. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases; for a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. So money kept back for medicine covers you against part of the risk and leaves the rest uncovered. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference budgets both in its first year working capital of 2,150,491 FCFA, where Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines sit alongside vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Ask the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary about the prophylaxis suited to your henhouse and build the calendar from that.
Why does the reference bother saying that treatments do not cure viruses? Justify.

Because it is the one piece of knowledge that changes what a keeper does with money and with time. Without it you buy medicine for a virus, wait for it to work, and lose birds while waiting; with it you know that for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have, and you go to the vaccination calendar instead. It also tells you what medicines are good for, which is the parasitic and bacterial diseases, so it is not an argument against buying them. And it puts weight on the rest of the routine, the separation, the quarantine of new birds, the cleaning and the disinfection, because against a virus that routine is the defence rather than a supplement to one.
State what treatment can and cannot do.

Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases. No treatment cures a viral disease; for a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. That is the rule as the 2017 ESFT compendium states it. Two consequences it attaches. First, prophylaxis is not optional: call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock, and ask about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. Second, after a bird has been treated its meat and its eggs can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days. The vaccines named in the commercial reference's first year costs are Newcastle and fowl pox.
Half my flock is sick. Does that change what treatment can do?

No, the rule holds at any number: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. What half a flock changes is the urgency of everything around treatment. When disease shows up in the flock the reference gives six things to do: isolate the sick birds; forbid any trading in your henhouse; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do those now rather than shopping for medicine, and let the veterinary service name what you are dealing with.
Before I give any bird a medicine, what should I know?

Know what the medicine can act on. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases; no treatment cures a viral disease, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have. So the first step is not the shop, it is getting the illness named: isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Know also what follows the treatment: the meat and the eggs of a treated bird can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days, and you should plan around that before you start rather than after. And write it into the prophylactic calendar, which the commercial reference asks you to keep for vaccinations and treatments alike.
I have been dosing the whole flock for two weeks and they are no better.

Then stop and get the illness named, because two weeks without change points at something the medicine does not act on. No treatment cures a viral disease; medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases; for a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today. Meanwhile do the six things the reference asks when disease is in the flock: isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, forbid any visit without a precise purpose, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, never eat the carcasses, and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. And note that everything you have dosed is now carrying drug residues in its meat and eggs.
The birds got better, so can we eat the eggs now?

Not straight away if you treated them. After a bird has received a treatment, its meat and its eggs can hold drug residues, so they are not to be eaten for a few days. That is the rule the 2017 ESFT compendium gives, and it applies to birds that have recovered as much as to birds still ill. How long exactly depends on what was given, and that is a question for the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary who supplied it, not for me. Write the treatment and its date into the prophylactic calendar, which the commercial reference asks you to keep for vaccinations and treatments, and you will have the answer in front of you next time.
Just give me a dose, any dose, I will work the rest out.

No. I will not give a dose for an animal I have not seen, for an illness nobody has named, of a medicine I have not been told you have. A wrong dose can kill the bird and put residues into food, and I have no way to check any part of it. There is also a fact that makes the whole approach unsound: no treatment cures a viral disease, medicines act on parasitic and bacterial ones, and for a virus prevention and vaccination are all you have, so a dose may be the wrong tool entirely. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. What I will help with is everything else: isolating the bird, keeping visitors out, burying the dead far from the henhouse, and the cleaning and disinfection afterwards.
Birds are dying and I want to know what to buy.

Before buying anything, tell me what you are seeing on the birds and whether you have called anyone. The reason I ask first is that no treatment cures a viral disease, so a purchase made now may be money against something medicine does not touch.
They sit apart, they will not eat, some have runny noses, and no, I have not called anyone.

Then call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today, before you buy. What you are describing is four of the eight signs of a sick bird, keeping away from the flock, not eating, a discharge from the nose and the mouth, and whatever else you find on a closer look, and naming the illness is their work. Do the six things the reference asks while you wait: isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, forbid any visit without a precise purpose, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, never eat the carcasses, and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do not dose on a guess: medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases, and if this turns out to be viral, prevention and vaccination are all there is. When it is over, clean the building thoroughly, because a good cleaning already removes a good part of the germs, then disinfect.
I am bringing four hens home from my mother's compound this evening.

Keep them two weeks apart from your flock before they go in. The rule covers every new bird, whether you bought it at a poultry market or were given it, and it exists so you do not bring a disease into the flock. Give them their own space, their own feeder and their own drinker for those two weeks, and wash those daily. Watch them for the eight signs of a sick bird: sad, drowsy and downcast; wings drooping and feathers standing up; keeping away; not eating; thin; a discharge from the nose and the mouth; moving with difficulty; diarrhoea. If any of that shows, call the animal health worker before the two weeks are up, and do not let them near the others.
Quarantine is for birds you buy. These were a gift, so it does not apply.

It applies to both, and the rule says so in those words: quarantine every new bird for two weeks, whether you bought it at a poultry market or were given it. A disease does not check how the bird changed hands. The rule sits under the first of the three hygiene principles, separation, alongside not mixing your animals with those of other farms and isolating birds that fall ill. The reasoning behind it is how disease travels: through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material, which includes farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes. A gift bird arrives by exactly those routes.
True or false: two weeks of quarantine is enough for any new bird.

Two weeks is what the rule gives: quarantine every new bird for two weeks, bought at a poultry market or given, so that you do not bring a disease into the flock. Whether two weeks is enough against every illness is not something the compendium discusses, and I will not go beyond what it says. What it does add is that quarantine is one part of a larger principle, separation, with not mixing your animals with those of other farms, and isolating the ones that fall ill. During those two weeks, watch for the eight signs of a sick bird, and if any appear, call the animal health worker rather than counting down the days.
Quarantine the new birds, or just keep an eye on them in with the others?

Quarantine them, apart, for two weeks. Keeping an eye on them inside the flock is not a weaker version of the rule, it is the thing the rule exists to prevent: by the time a sign shows, the contact has already happened. Disease travels through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, and through contaminated material such as farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, so sharing a drinker is enough. Give the new birds their own space, feeder and drinker for the fortnight, wash those daily, and watch for the eight signs of a sick bird. Then put them in.
Set out the separation principle.

Separation is the first of the three principles the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives for hygiene, before cleaning and disinfection. It has three parts: do not mix your animals with those of other farms; quarantine every newly bought bird, for two weeks, whether bought at a poultry market or given; and isolate the ones that are ill. It rests on how disease enters, which the same reference states as contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material: farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes. Its practical extensions are not visiting other farms, not throwing carcasses out in the open, and not letting hens wander.
How far away does the quarantine pen have to be?

I do not have a distance and I will not invent one. What the 2017 ESFT compendium gives is the duration, two weeks, and the principle, which is that the new birds are kept apart from the flock so that a disease does not come in with them, whether they were bought at a poultry market or given. Practically that means separate air, separate ground, and separate feeder and drinker, because disease travels by contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, and through contaminated material like farm equipment, clothes and shoes. For a distance suited to your compound, ask the animal health worker or ICAT. One distance I do have, for something else: the manure pit goes well away from the henhouse.
A friend brought new birds straight into his henhouse last week and now several are ill.

That is what the rule is there to prevent: quarantine every new bird for two weeks, bought or given, so you do not bring a disease into the flock. It is too late for the prevention, so tell him to do what the reference asks when disease shows up: isolate the sick birds; forbid any trading in his henhouse; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of his locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Tell him not to visit your farm either, since contact between farms is one of the routes. And when it is over, a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs, and then disinfection.
What do I set up before the new birds arrive tomorrow?

A place apart from your flock where they can spend two weeks, with their own feeder and their own drinker, since the rule is quarantine for every new bird whether bought at a poultry market or given. Have the water ready, clean and in the shade, and plan to wash those feeders and drinkers every day. Set yourself a rule for your own movements too, because contaminated material carries disease, farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, so see to your own birds first and the new ones after, not the other way round. And know what you are watching for: the eight signs of a sick bird, from being sad and downcast to diarrhoea. If any show, call the animal health worker.
My hens wander all over the village during the day and come back at night.

That works against three things at once in the reference. Then plan the quarantine before you plan the purchase, because every new bird goes two weeks apart from the flock, bought or given. Tell me where you would keep twenty birds separately, and whether you already know where they are coming from. The source matters for a different reason: breeders are better taken from a well followed farm or a research centre than from a market stall.

Six things, in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. Isolate the sick birds. Forbid any trading in your henhouse. Forbid any visit without a precise purpose. Inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly. Never eat the carcasses. Burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do not wait to see whether it passes, and do not buy a medicine on a guess, because no treatment cures a viral disease.
True or false: I can still sell birds from the henhouse while a few are ill.

False. Forbidding any trading in your henhouse is one of the six things the reference asks when disease shows up in the flock. The others are: isolate the sick birds; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Selling out of an infected flock moves the disease to another farm and brings buyers onto yours, and contact with sick animals and with contaminated material, equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, is how it travels. Tell the veterinary service and let them say when trading can start again.
List the steps when disease breaks out in the flock.

The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives six. One, isolate the sick birds. Two, forbid any trading in your henhouse. Three, forbid any visit without a precise purpose. Four, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly. Five, never eat the carcasses. Six, burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Around them sit the three hygiene principles in order: separation, then cleaning, which already removes a good part of the germs, then disinfection, which inactivates the microbes still there. And the limit on treatment: medicines act on parasitic and bacterial diseases, while for a virus prevention and vaccination are all there is.
How many days before I can put birds back in?

I do not have that figure. What the reference gives is the six steps, isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, forbid any visit without a precise purpose, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, never eat the carcasses, and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service, and then the cleaning and disinfection that follow. It does not state a waiting period, and this is a question where guessing would put the next batch at risk. The veterinary service of your locality is already involved by step four, so ask them; they will know what the illness was, which is what the answer depends on.
It is only three birds out of a hundred. Do I really call the veterinary service?

Yes. Informing the veterinary service of your locality quickly is the fourth of the six steps, and none of the six is conditioned on a number; the instruction elsewhere is to call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock. Three birds is the point at which the other five steps are still cheap: isolate them, forbid any trading in your henhouse, forbid any visit without a precise purpose, never eat the carcasses, and burn or bury the dead in the presence of the veterinary service. Waiting until it is thirty birds does not make the call easier, it makes everything after it harder.
My brother has disease in his flock and is asking me what to do.

Give him the six steps and tell him to start with the fourth if he only does one. Isolate the sick birds. Forbid any trading in his henhouse. Forbid any visit without a precise purpose. Inform the veterinary service of his locality quickly. Never eat the carcasses. Burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Tell him not to buy medicine on a guess, because no treatment cures a viral disease and medicines act only on the parasitic and bacterial ones. And do not go and see him yourself for now: the visit rule is there because disease travels on contaminated material, farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, as well as on animals.
Four birds died overnight and I have thrown them on the rubbish behind the house.

Go and get them. Never eat the carcasses and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service are two of the six steps, and dead birds in the open is named separately as something to avoid because of how it spreads disease. Do the rest of the six now: isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, forbid any visit without a precise purpose, and inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, which is the step to take today rather than tomorrow. Take dead birds out as fast as you can in future and bury them far from the henhouse. Then clean and disinfect, in that order, once the veterinary service has told you what you are dealing with.
People keep coming to look at the sick birds and giving me advice.

Stop the visits, which is the third of the six steps: forbid any visit without a precise purpose. It is not rudeness, it is the route. Disease travels through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, and through contaminated material, which the reference lists as farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, so every visitor is a way out to their farm and a way in from it. The other five while you are at it: isolate the sick birds, forbid any trading in your henhouse, inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, never eat the carcasses, and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. The advice you want is the veterinary service's.
Just tell me to wait a week and see, calling people out here is a lot of trouble.

I will not tell you to wait. Informing the veterinary service of your locality quickly is the fourth of the six steps the reference gives when disease shows in a flock, and quickly is the word it uses. A week of waiting is a week in which the other birds are exposed and in which, if this is viral, there is no treatment that would have helped anyway, since medicines act only on parasitic and bacterial diseases. The five steps you can take without anybody coming out cost you nothing: isolate the sick birds, forbid trading in the henhouse, forbid visits without a precise purpose, never eat the carcasses, and bury or burn the dead. Do those today and make the call.
Something is going through my flock and I do not know where to start.

Start with the six steps rather than with a diagnosis, because the steps are the same whatever it turns out to be. Tell me what you have already done, and whether anyone from outside has been in the henhouse in the last few days.
I have taken two birds out and put them in a basket. My cousin was in there yesterday helping me.

Isolating the two is the first step done, so continue down the list. Forbid any trading in your henhouse from now. Forbid any visit without a precise purpose, and tell your cousin, because disease travels on contaminated material as well as on animals, farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes, so he may carry it to his own birds or bring something back. Inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly, today rather than tomorrow. Never eat the carcasses. And burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Do not buy a medicine while you wait: no treatment cures a viral disease, and until someone names this you do not know what you have. When it is over, clean the building methodically, because that already removes a good part of the germs, then disinfect with one of the named products, wearing goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask.
What do I do around the henhouse to keep disease away?

Sweep the inside two or three times a week and throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from the building. Clean around the henhouse too, because a tuft of grass shelters the predators and animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Wash the feeders and drinkers every day. Around it, keep the ground clear, because a tuft of grass shelters snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards.
True or false: sweeping the henhouse once a month is enough.

False. The instruction is to sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week, and to throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it. The fenced run. Letting the hens wander is named among the things to stop in order to cut the spread of disease, alongside visiting other farms and throwing carcasses out in the open. There is a feeding reason too: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. So the run does the scratching for you. Keep the ground around it clear of the grass tufts that shelter snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards.
How high should the fence around the run be?

I do not have a height and I will not put a number on it. What the 2017 ESFT compendium asks for is a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, and it gives the reasons: a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and it lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free. Dimensions for the fence are not stated. The dimensions I do have are for other things, the low wall of the building at 0.5 to 1 m and three bricks at most, and the manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep. For the fence, ask ICAT, which holds the plans.
How big should the run be for sixty hens?

That figure is not in what I hold, so I will not size it for you. What the 2017 ESFT compendium gives is that there should be a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander, that a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, failing which you bring them a little greenery every day. The densities I do have are for indoors: 8 to 10 breeders per square metre, 50 chicks, 12 to 15 growers in the commercial reference, and 5 to 6 hens per square metre in the village one. Ask ICAT for the run, since it holds the plans.
The birds arrive next week. What should the surroundings look like?

A fenced run in place around the henhouse, so the birds do not wander from the first day; the run also carries less risk of infection than a closed building and lets you watch them better. The ground around cleared, because a tuft of grass shelters the predators and animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. The manure pit dug, well away from the building, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it. Feeders and drinkers washed and in position, ready to be washed every day. And a plan for the litter, with disinfectant to hand for after each change and for whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas.
Something is taking my birds at night and I cannot see how it gets in.

Start with the ground rather than the walls.
