Clean around the henhouse, because a tuft of grass shelters the predators and animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards, and anything living close by comes in the moment the building is quiet. Sweep the inside two or three times a week and take the droppings to the manure pit well away, so there is nothing drawing visitors in. Check for spilled feed under the troughs and check the feeder sizes for the age. If it is chicks going, remember that keeping predators off is one of the four things the brooder is for, and the chicks' first three weeks belong in it.
Just tell me letting them out to wander is fine, everyone here does it.

I will not, because the compendium names it directly: to cut the spread of disease, do not visit other farms, do not throw carcasses out in the open, and do not let your hens wander. Those three sit together for the same reason, which is that disease travels by contact, with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, and with contaminated material. A wandering flock meets all of that daily. What I can offer instead is the arrangement the same source prefers, which is not a closed building either: a fenced run around the henhouse, which carries less risk of infection than a closed one and lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free, and where they can still eat grass.
I lose birds to disease every year and I want to stop it happening again.

Then work on the routine rather than on medicines, because for a virus prevention and vaccination are all there is. Tell me three things: whether the birds wander, where the droppings go, and how often you wash the feeders and drinkers.
They wander during the day, the droppings go in a heap behind the henhouse, and I wash the drinkers when they look dirty.

All three are working against you and all three are free to change. Build a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander: wandering is named among the things to stop in order to cut the spread of disease, and a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one while letting you watch the birds better. Move the droppings into a manure pit well away from the building, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it; a heap against the wall keeps the germs where the birds are, and the pit both limits the spread and turns the droppings into something your fields can use. Wash the feeders and drinkers every day rather than when they look dirty, and sweep the inside two or three times a week. Clear the ground outside as well, since a tuft of grass shelters snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Then add the two things that need someone else: quarantine every new bird for two weeks, bought or given, and ask the animal health worker about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse.
My hens are laying and I do not know how much to put out each day.

Eighty grams a day for a hen in lay, which is the figure the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives and the highest of its age bands. For comparison, a bird from 1 to 60 days eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day, and from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same thing as one range, between 5 and 90 grams a bird depending on age and size. A laying hen also takes the most mineral of any band: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, against 3 kg for the younger birds.
True or false: a growing bird eats more than a laying hen.

False. A hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, while a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes 25 to 35 grams a day, and one from 1 to 60 days takes 10 to 25 grams a day. The laying hen is the biggest eater of the three, and she also takes the most mineral: 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, where the younger bands take 3 kg. Over a whole period the growers add up to about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale, and about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days.
Should I feed once a day or twice?

The reference gives the quantity rather than the number of servings, so I will not invent a schedule. What it fixes is how much: about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days, at 10 to 25 grams a day; about 5 kg a bird from 61 days to sale at six months, at 25 to 35 grams a day; and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. Where it is strict about frequency is the water, which must be freely available at all times, never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day. Whatever pattern you choose for the feed, give the chicks theirs apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and add the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots.
Why give a total in kilos and a daily rate for the same period? Justify.

Because they answer two different questions and you need both. The daily rate, 10 to 25 grams from 1 to 60 days and 25 to 35 grams from 61 days to sale, tells you what to put in the trough tomorrow morning. The total, about 1.5 kg and about 5 kg a bird for those periods, tells you what to buy or mix for the whole batch, which is how you budget: feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. A keeper with only the daily rate runs out mid-cycle; one with only the total overfeeds early and starves late. A hen in lay, by contrast, gets a single figure, 80 grams a day, because she is not passing through a stage.
Set out the rationing by period.

From the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. From 1 to 60 days: about 1.5 kg of feed a bird in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day. From 61 days to sale at six months: about 5 kg a bird in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. A hen in lay: 80 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium states the same idea as one range, between 5 and 90 grams a bird depending on age and size, and adds that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, failing which you bring them a little greenery every day. On top of the formula, whatever the age, the free extras are greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds.
How much should I feed a bird that is sick and off its food?

That is not in what I hold and I will not improvise a sick bird's ration. The figures I have are for healthy birds by age: about 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days, 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. Not eating is one of the eight signs of a sick bird, along with being sad, drowsy and downcast, drooping wings, feathers standing up, keeping away from the flock, thinness, discharge from the nose and the mouth, difficulty moving and diarrhoea. Isolate the bird or take it out, and call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary. Keep clean water in front of it whatever else you do.
Someone at the cooperative asks how much feed a bird needs to reach sale.

About 6.5 kg in all across its life, taken in two stretches: about 1.5 kg from 1 to 60 days, at 10 to 25 grams a day, and about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at six months, at 25 to 35 grams a day. Tell them the laying hens are a separate line at 80 grams a day, and that she takes the most mineral of any band, 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed. And tell them the part that saves money: the ration is built from local materials, and greenery, termites and maggots come on top of the formula at no cost. Feed is most of the first year working capital, so this arithmetic is where a unit is won or lost.
I am about to buy feed for a batch of fifty birds to raise to six months. How much?

Work it from the totals rather than the daily rate. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, so fifty birds take about 75 kg for that stretch. From 61 days to sale at six months a bird takes about 5 kg, so about 250 kg for the fifty. That is roughly 325 kg for the batch, before any losses. Buy or mix by stage, not all at once, because the formula changes with age: per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral mix from 1 to 8 weeks, then 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3 from 9 to 12 weeks, then 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3 from 12 weeks on. Add the free extras: greenery, termites and maggots.
My birds are six months old and much lighter than they should be.

Compare what they have had against the figures. From 61 days to sale at six months a bird should take about 5 kg of feed in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day, after about 1.5 kg from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day. At six months the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference expects about 1.3 kg live weight for a hen and about 1.5 kg for a cock. If the feed was short, that is your answer. If it was not, look at whether it reached them: enough feeders for the age, one for 25 adults or one for 20 chickens, and chicks fed apart from the adults so they do not have to compete. Then look at water, which must never be empty, and at the eight signs of a sick bird.
My laying hens finish their feed in the morning and stand around hungry all day.

Check the amount first: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, which is more than any other band, and the 2017 ESFT compendium gives the same idea as a range of 5 to 90 grams depending on age and size. If you are serving well under 80 grams, that is the problem. Then use what costs nothing: the free extras on top of the formula are greenery, termites and maggots, and hens should have a run where they can eat grass, failing which you bring them a little greenery every day. Check the mineral too, since a laying hen takes 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, the highest of the bands. And keep clean water in front of them at all times.
Just tell me fifty grams a day is enough for a laying hen.

I will not, because the figure I hold is 80 grams a day for a hen in lay and fifty is well under it. The 2017 ESFT compendium's range, 5 to 90 grams a bird depending on age and size, puts a laying hen at the top end rather than the middle. Underfeeding a layer costs you the thing you are keeping her for: about ten eggs per hen per laying and about six layings a year is what the projection rests on. If feed cost is the reason, work on the cost rather than the quantity: build the ration from local materials, make the mineral mix yourself, and use the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal near you.
eau poules combien de fois par jour

Freely available at all times, and the drinkers never empty. Clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. That is the rule in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and twice a day is the minimum rather than the target. For the chicks it matters most: feed them apart from the adults and never let them run short, because the 2017 ESFT compendium says chicks die easily of dehydration.
I fill the drinkers first thing in the morning and I am out in the fields until dark.

Then the birds are short for most of the day, because the rule is water freely available at all times with the drinkers never empty, renewed at least twice a day, clean and served in the shade. One filling is half the minimum. Two things to change. Put in more capacity, counted per hundred birds: four drinkers of 10 litres for adult layers, three of 10 litres for the chickens, three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days and two from 1 to 30 days. And put them in the shade if they are not, so what you leave stays drinkable. If there are chicks, this is the thing to fix before anything else, because they die easily of dehydration.
The birds drink from the puddle in the yard anyway, so the drinker does not matter much.

The rule is not only that they get water, it is what water. It has to be clean, served in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, and freely available with the drinkers never empty. A puddle is none of those. It also runs against the rest of the routine: droppings go to a manure pit well away from the building because soiled droppings and secretions are one of the ways disease travels, and standing water in the yard is where that ends up. Keep the ground around the henhouse clear and the birds in a fenced run rather than wandering to whatever they find, and keep the drinkers filled and washed.
Rainwater, tap water or from the well?

All three are named as sources in the 2017 ESFT compendium, which builds the ration on rain, tap or spring water. What matters is the state it reaches the birds in rather than where it came from: clean, served in the shade, freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, renewed at least twice a day. That is why a well appears in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference's start-up list alongside the houses, the store, the manure pit, the incubator, the brooder, the feeders, the drinkers and the nests: a source on the farm is what lets you keep to the rule. Wash the drinkers every day whichever source you use.
State the watering rule.

Water is given freely, available at all times, and the drinkers must never be empty. It has to be clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. The 2017 ESFT compendium names rain, tap or spring water as sources. Chicks are fed and watered apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and they must never run short, because they die easily of dehydration. On equipment, per hundred birds: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, and four of 10 litres for the adult layers, washed every day.
How many litres a day does a laying hen drink?

I do not have a per bird figure for water and I will not invent one. What the references give is the rule, water freely available at all times with the drinkers never empty, clean, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, and the equipment count, four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, three of 10 litres per hundred chickens, and siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres for the youngest. The per bird figures I do have are for feed: 80 grams a day for a hen in lay, 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale, 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days. For water consumption, ask ICAT or the animal health worker.
How much drinking capacity do I need for two hundred layers?

Eight drinkers of 10 litres. The count is four of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, so two hundred birds take eight. For other ages, per hundred: three of 10 litres for the chickens, three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, and two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days. Capacity is not the whole answer though: the water still has to be renewed at least twice a day, kept clean and served in the shade, and the drinkers washed every day, so eight vessels means eight to fill and wash. Spread them rather than grouping them, so the weaker birds are not pushed off.
My sister keeps hens and asks what she most often gets wrong.

Water, in my experience of the questions I am asked. Tell her the rule in full: freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. Most people do the first half and not the second, so the birds have water but it is warm and dirty by afternoon. Tell her the counts too, four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred adult layers and three of 10 litres per hundred chickens, and to wash them every day. And if she has chicks, tell her they get their own drinkers, apart from the adults, because they die easily of dehydration and a shared vessel is one they cannot always reach.
The water in the drinkers is warm and green by the afternoon.

Two parts of the rule are being missed: served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. Move the drinkers out of the sun, refill them in the afternoon as well as the morning, and wash them every day, which is asked separately. Check the capacity while you are at it, per hundred birds: four drinkers of 10 litres for adult layers, three of 10 litres for the chickens, three siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, two from 1 to 30 days. Water that sits all day in the sun is not the clean water the rule asks for, and for chicks it is the difference that kills, since they die easily of dehydration.
The chicks crowd round the drinker and some never get near it.

Give them their own, and more of them. Chicks are to be fed and watered apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and the count for them is two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres per hundred birds from 1 to 30 days, then three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days. Spread them out rather than putting them together. This is the one to fix today rather than this week, because chicks die easily of dehydration. Keep the water clean, in the shade, never empty and renewed at least twice a day, and wash the drinkers daily. For the first three weeks the chicks should be in the brooder, which also lets you watch feeding and health closely.
Just tell me once a day is fine if I use a big drinker.

I will not, because the rule has two parts and a big vessel only answers one of them. Water must be freely available at all times with the drinkers never empty, which a big drinker helps with, and it must also be clean and renewed at least twice a day, which it does not. Water standing all day gets warm and dirty, and served out of the shade it gets worse. The counts assume both: four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, washed every day. If the difficulty is being away from the farm, the honest fix is more vessels in the shade and someone to refill at midday, not a bigger one filled once. With chicks I would not bend on this at all, since they die easily of dehydration.
I think my birds are not drinking enough but I am not sure.

Tell me three things and we will know: how many drinkers you have and of what size, where they stand, and how often you refill them. The rule is water freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.
Two drinkers of about ten litres for a hundred and twenty layers, they sit by the door in the sun, and I fill them in the morning.

All three are short. On capacity, the count is four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred adult layers, so a hundred and twenty birds call for five, not two. On siting, they should be in the shade, and by the door in the sun is the worst spot you could pick, because the water heats and fouls through the day. On frequency, once a day is half the minimum: renew at least twice a day, and wash the drinkers every day. Fix the siting today, since it costs nothing, add the vessels as you can, and put in a midday round. Watch what changes: a hen in lay takes 80 grams of feed a day, and birds short of water eat less, so if the feed has also been going slowly that is part of the same picture.
How do I make the mineral mix myself?

For 10 kg, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. That mix then goes into the feed at the rate the age band calls for: 3 kg per 100 kg of feed for the young birds, and 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen in lay, which is the band that takes the most mineral of all. Making it yourself is one of the places where feed cost actually comes down, and feed is most of the first year working capital.
I have snail shells and charcoal but no bone.

Then you have two of the four and the missing one is the largest after the shell. The mix for 10 kg is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Bone powder is also named among the raw materials the ration is built from, with fish meal, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars, so it is not an exotic item; ask ICAT where to get it, since that is the office to ask about where to buy cakes and fish meal as well. Do not simply increase the shell to make up the weight: the proportions are what the mix is. The laying hens are the ones who will notice first, since they take 7.5 kg of mineral per 100 kg of feed.
Salt is salt, so I can put in as much as I like to make it go further.

The salt is the smallest part of the mix by a long way and the proportions are the recipe. For 10 kg it is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, so salt is one twentieth of it. Increasing it does not stretch the mix, it changes what the birds are getting, and the mix exists to supply the minerals the shell and the bone carry. If you want to make the feed go further, the place to do it is the free extras the reference names on top of the formula: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars for the youngest. Ask ICAT if you are short of a component.
True or false: all the age bands take the same amount of mineral.

False. Per 100 kg of feed, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives 3 kg of mineral mix from 1 to 8 weeks, 3 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 3 kg from 12 weeks on, and 7.5 kg for a hen in lay. The laying hen takes the most mineral of all the age bands, two and a half times the others. The mix itself does not change: for 10 kg, 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. What changes is how much of it goes into the 100 kg.
Give the mineral mix formula and its use rate.

The mix, for 10 kg: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal, 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Its rate in the feed, per 100 kg: 3 kg from 1 to 8 weeks, 3 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 3 kg from 12 weeks on, and 7.5 kg for a hen in lay. Those sit inside the full formulas, which for 1 to 8 weeks are 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral; for 9 to 12 weeks 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3; for 12 weeks on 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3; and for a hen in lay 57.5, 10, 10, 15 and 7.5. All from the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference.
How much mineral mix do I need to make 500 kg of layer feed?

A hen in lay takes 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, so 500 kg of layer feed needs 37.5 kg of the mix. To make that, scale the recipe: for 10 kg it is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, so for 37.5 kg you need 15 kg of shell, about 13 kg of crushed calcined bone, 7.5 kg of crushed charcoal and about 1.9 kg of salt. The rest of the 500 kg, at the layer formula, is 287.5 kg of cereals, 50 kg of cake, 50 kg of fish meal and 75 kg of bran. Ask ICAT where to buy the cakes and the fish meal.
The group wants to buy mineral supplement and it is expensive. What do I tell them?

Tell them the reference has them make it. For 10 kg: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Then the rate, per 100 kg of feed: 3 kg for the young birds and 7.5 kg for a hen in lay. Making it as a group is worth more than buying as a group, because three of the four components are things people already have or can gather. Tell them the same logic runs through the whole ration, which is built from local materials, cereals, groundnut and soya and their cakes, millet beer draff, kitchen leftovers, fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars, and that greenery, termites and maggots come free on top.
I am mixing feed for the laying hens tomorrow. What do I prepare tonight?

Make the mineral mix first, because it is the part that takes gathering. For 10 kg: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, crushed as the recipe says. Then weigh out the rest against the layer formula, per 100 kg: 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of the mineral mix. Have the free extras ready as well, greenery, termites and maggots, since they go on top of the formula whatever the age. And check the water before you start feeding: clean, in the shade, never empty, renewed at least twice a day.
My hens are laying eggs with very thin shells.

Look at the mineral first, because that is the band where the reference asks for most. A hen in lay takes 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed, two and a half times the 3 kg the younger bands take, and she is named as the one that takes the most mineral of all the age bands. Check what you are actually putting in. Then check the mix itself: for 10 kg, 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Shell and bone are most of it. Check the daily quantity too, 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. If the feeding is right and the shells stay thin, that is a question for the animal health worker.
The birds peck at the walls and at the ground all the time.

Check the mineral in the feed before anything else. The rate per 100 kg is 3 kg of mineral mix for the young bands and 7.5 kg for a hen in lay, the highest of them, and the mix itself is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt per 10 kg. Check the quantity of feed as well, 80 grams a day for a layer and 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale, and give the free extras the reference names on top, greenery, termites and maggots. Hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, bring them a little greenery every day. If it continues, ask the animal health worker.
Just tell me I can skip the mineral, the birds find what they need outside.

I will not, because the reference puts mineral into every one of its formulas and gives a recipe for making it. Per 100 kg of feed it is 3 kg of mineral mix from 1 to 8 weeks, 3 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 3 kg from 12 weeks on and 7.5 kg for a hen in lay, and it names the laying hen as taking the most mineral of all the bands. The mix is four cheap things: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, for 10 kg. What the birds find outside is counted separately, as the free extras on top of the formula, greenery, termites and maggots, not as a replacement for it. If cost is the issue, make the mix rather than buy it.
I want to start mixing my own feed instead of buying it.

Good, and start with the mineral part, because it is the one people leave out and the easiest to make. Tell me which birds you are feeding, since the rate differs: 3 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg of feed for the young bands, and 7.5 kg per 100 kg for a hen in lay.
Sixty laying hens, and I have shells and salt but I have never heard of calcined bone.

Then you have two of the four components and one question to ask. The mix, for 10 kg, is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. Bone powder is also named among the raw materials the whole ration is built from, alongside fish meal, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars, so ask ICAT where to get it locally; that is the same office to ask about cakes and fish meal. Charcoal you can crush yourself. Once you have the mix, the layer formula per 100 kg of feed is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of your mineral mix. At 80 grams a day, sixty hens eat about 4.8 kg a day, so a 100 kg batch lasts you around three weeks. Put greenery, termites and maggots on top of it, free, and keep the water clean, in the shade and renewed at least twice a day.
What goes into a hundred kilos of feed for my hens?

It depends on their age, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives four formulas per 100 kg. From 1 to 8 weeks: 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. From 9 to 12 weeks: 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3. From 12 weeks on: 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3. For a hen in lay: 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Whatever the age, the free extras go on top: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars as well for the youngest.
formule aliment poule pondeuse 100kg

For a hen in lay, per 100 kg: 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. She takes the most mineral of all the age bands. The younger formulas per 100 kg: 1 to 8 weeks, 62 cereals, 20 cake, 10 fish meal, 5 bran, 3 mineral; 9 to 12 weeks, 62, 15, 5, 15, 3; 12 weeks on, 60, 10, 10, 17, 3. Greenery, termites and maggots go on top, free.
I have birds of three different ages in the henhouse at the moment.

Then you need three mixes, because the formula changes with age. Per 100 kg: from 1 to 8 weeks, 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix; from 9 to 12 weeks, 62, 15, 5, 15 and 3; from 12 weeks on, 60, 10, 10, 17 and 3; and for a hen in lay, 57.5, 10, 10, 15 and 7.5. That is also why the housing plan asks for at least five compartments: several ages on the farm at once is the normal state, and feeding them apart is part of it. The chicks in particular must be fed apart from the adults so they do not have to compete.
One good feed for the whole flock is simpler and they all get what they need.

The four formulas differ in ways that matter at both ends. A hen in lay takes 7.5 kg of mineral mix per 100 kg, two and a half times the 3 kg the younger bands take, so a single feed either starves the layers of mineral or floods the growers with it. The cake, which carries the protein, runs the other way: 20 kg per 100 from 1 to 8 weeks down to 10 kg for a layer. And the bran runs from 5 kg up to 17 kg from 12 weeks on. Feeding one mix is choosing which group to get wrong. The quantities differ too, 80 grams a day for a layer against 10 to 25 grams from 1 to 60 days.
For birds of eleven weeks, do I use the 9 to 12 week formula or the one after?

The 9 to 12 week one, since eleven weeks falls inside it: per 100 kg, 62 kg of cereals, 15 kg of cake, 5 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. Move to the next band at 12 weeks, which is 60 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 17 of bran and 3 of mineral. The change between them is mostly fish meal going up and cake coming down, with bran rising. Plan the switch so you are not left with a half sack of the wrong mix: at 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale, you can work out how much of the current formula you still need.
Why does the bran go up as the birds get older? Justify.

I can tell you what changes but not why, because the reference gives the formulas without explaining the reasoning behind each component, and I will not construct a nutritional argument it does not make. What it shows is this: bran runs 5 kg per 100 from 1 to 8 weeks, 15 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, 17 kg from 12 weeks on and 15 kg for a hen in lay, while cake runs 20, 15, 10 and 10, and mineral runs 3, 3, 3 and 7.5. So the young bird's mix is the richest in cake and the layer's the richest in mineral. For the reasoning, ask ICAT, which holds the study. What I would not do is guess at it and have you change the proportions on my guess.
Can I swap the fish meal for something else and what proportion?

I cannot give you a substitution rate, because the reference gives formulas rather than equivalences and I will not invent a conversion. What it does give you is the list of raw materials it builds feed from, which is where a substitute would have to come from: cereals, meaning maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; then fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; then salt; then the vitamins. Fish meal appears at 10 kg per 100 in three of the four formulas and 5 kg in the 9 to 12 week one. Ask ICAT, which is also the office to ask about where to buy cakes and fish meal.
The group wants to mix feed together. What formulas do I bring them?

Bring all four, per 100 kg of feed. From 1 to 8 weeks: 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran, 3 of mineral mix. From 9 to 12 weeks: 62, 15, 5, 15, 3. From 12 weeks on: 60, 10, 10, 17, 3. For a hen in lay: 57.5, 10, 10, 15, 7.5. Bring the mineral mix recipe too, since it is the part they will otherwise buy: for 10 kg, 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. And tell them the extras that cost nothing and go on top whatever the age: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars for the youngest.
I am buying the components tomorrow for a hundred kilos of layer feed.

For 100 kg of layer feed you need 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. Make the mineral yourself rather than buying it: for 10 kg it is 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt, so you need about three quarters of that recipe. The cereals can be maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, and the cake groundnut, cotton or soya. Ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal if you do not already know. And remember what does not go on the shopping list: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula for free.
I mix the same thing for everything and my young birds grow slowly.

The young birds are the ones a single mix shortchanges most, because their formula is the richest in cake. Per 100 kg, from 1 to 8 weeks it is 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, where a layer's is 57.5, 10, 10, 15 and 7.5. If you have been feeding them the layer mix they have had half the cake and twice the mineral they should. Switch to the age formulas, check the quantity as well, about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, and feed the chicks apart from the adults so they do not have to compete. Weigh against the target: about 1.3 kg for a hen at six months.
My feed runs out faster than I planned every time.

Plan it from the totals rather than by eye. From 1 to 60 days a bird takes about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day; from 61 days to sale at six months about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day; a hen in lay 80 grams a day. Multiply by your birds and you have the batch size. Then look at waste, because that is where the rest goes: feeders sized for the age, one of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 adults, one of 125 by 10 by 12 for 20 chickens, one of 50 by 50 by 5 for 50 chicks, and enough of them so birds are not spilling feed over the side. Use the free extras too, greenery, termites and maggots.
Just tell me I can use the layer formula for everything, it is easier.

I will not, because two of the components are badly wrong for young birds. The layer formula per 100 kg is 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix. A bird from 1 to 8 weeks should be getting 20 kg of cake and 3 kg of mineral, so on the layer mix it gets half the cake and two and a half times the mineral. The layer hen is named as the band that takes the most mineral of all, which is exactly why her formula does not transfer downwards. If mixing three or four batches is the difficulty, mix less often and store it, or ask ICAT how others manage it locally.
I want to work out my feed for the year.

Then start from the birds rather than from the sacks. Tell me how many layers you keep and how many birds you expect to raise to sale, because those two use different formulas and different quantities: a hen in lay takes 80 grams a day, and a bird from 61 days to sale at six months takes about 5 kg in all.
Sixty layers, and I raise about two hundred birds to sale over the year.

Then two calculations. The layers: sixty hens at 80 grams a day is about 4.8 kg a day, which is around 1,750 kg over a year, all on the layer formula of 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 15 of bran and 7.5 of mineral mix per 100 kg. The birds for sale: about 1.5 kg a bird from 1 to 60 days and about 5 kg from 61 days to sale, so about 6.5 kg each, which is around 1,300 kg for two hundred birds, split across the three younger formulas as they grow. That is roughly three tonnes of feed in the year, and feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the same study, so this is the number to take seriously. Make your own mineral mix, use the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots, and ask ICAT where to buy cakes and fish meal in quantity.
matieres premieres aliment volaille local

Cereals: maize, sorghum, millet and fonio. Legumes: groundnut and soya, with their by-products, groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff. Kitchen leftovers. Then fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars. Then salt for the minerals. Then the vitamins. Those are the local raw materials the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names, and the point of the list is that the feed is built from what is around you rather than bought ready made.
True or false: you need bought feed to raise local hens properly.

False, and the reference is built the other way round. It names the local raw materials and expects you to mix from them: cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins. It gives you the proportions too, per 100 kg and by age, and the recipe for the mineral mix. Some components you will buy, the cakes and the fish meal in particular, and ICAT is the office to ask where. But the model is a feed made locally, and that matters because feed is most of the first year working capital.
Maize or sorghum for the cereal part?

Either, and millet or fonio as well: the reference names maize, sorghum, millet and fonio together as the cereals, without ranking them. So use what you grow or what is cheap where you are, which is the point of a list of local raw materials. The 2017 ESFT compendium says the same in its own words, putting the energy in maize, millet or sorghum grain, whole or cracked, with tchouck bran and tubers. What is fixed is the proportion rather than the grain: per 100 kg of feed, 62 kg of cereals from 1 to 8 weeks and from 9 to 12 weeks, 60 kg from 12 weeks on, and 57.5 kg for a hen in lay.
Why does the reference list insects and termites as raw materials? Justify.

Because they are protein you do not have to buy, and the whole list is organised around what is available locally. Insects, termites and caterpillars appear alongside fish meal, bone powder and oyster shells in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference, and the 2017 ESFT compendium puts protein in roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products. They also appear a second time, as free extras on top of the formula whatever the age: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds. That second mention is the important one for your pocket, because it is feed that costs nothing in a budget where feed is the largest running cost.
Set out the raw materials by what they provide.

The 2017 ESFT compendium groups them. Water: rain, tap or spring. Energy: maize, millet or sorghum grain, whole or cracked, tchouck bran, and tubers. Protein: roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products. Minerals: eggshells and fish bones. Vitamins: herbs, fruit and plant debris. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists much the same by name: cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins.
Which vitamins exactly, and how much of each?

I cannot name them or dose them. The 2017 ESFT compendium puts vitamins in the ration as herbs, fruit and plant debris, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists vitamins among the raw materials and among the first year running costs, but the names of the vitamins a hen needs are not in what I hold, and that gap is on record. A dose invented here could do real harm. Ask the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary, and ask ICAT. What I can give you is everything around it: the four formulas per 100 kg, the mineral mix recipe, and the free extras, greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars for the youngest.
Can I feed sixty hens on kitchen leftovers alone?

No, and the reference treats leftovers as one item in a list rather than as a ration. The raw materials it names are cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins. The proportions are what make a feed: for a hen in lay, per 100 kg, 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 15 of bran and 7.5 of mineral mix. And the quantity is real: sixty hens at 80 grams a day eat about 4.8 kg daily, which no household produces in leftovers. Use them as part of the mix, not as the mix.
Before the next cycle, what should I be gathering or growing myself?

Work down the list and mark what you can produce. Cereals, maize, sorghum, millet or fonio, are the biggest single share at 57.5 to 62 kg per 100 kg of feed, so anything you grow there is the largest saving. Legumes, groundnut and soya, come next. For the mineral mix you can gather three of the four components: oyster or snail shell, crushed calcined bone and crushed charcoal, with only the kitchen salt to buy, in the proportion 4, 3.5, 2 and 0.5 for 10 kg. Insects, termites and caterpillars you gather, and greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula free. What you will most likely buy is the cake and the fish meal, and ICAT is the office to ask where.
I buy everything ready mixed and the feed bill is eating the farm.

That is the largest line in the budget, so it is the right thing to attack: feed is most of the 2,150,491 FCFA of first year working capital in the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference. The same reference expects you to mix rather than buy, from local raw materials: cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, with groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins. Make the mineral mix yourself, 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt for 10 kg. And use the free extras: greenery, termites and maggots.
I cannot find soya cake anywhere this season.

The reference names three cakes, not one: groundnut, cotton and soya, listed together among the by-products of the legumes, with millet beer draff beside them. So groundnut or cotton cake is what it points you to when soya is not to be had. What I will not do is give you a substitution rate for something outside that list, because the formulas are given as proportions and not as equivalences. The cake share per 100 kg is 20 kg from 1 to 8 weeks, 15 kg from 9 to 12 weeks, and 10 kg from 12 weeks on and for a hen in lay. For where to buy cakes and fish meal near you, ICAT is the office to ask.
Just tell me maize alone will do, that is all I have.

I will not, because maize is one line of a list and the formulas make that clear. Even at its largest share, cereals are 62 kg of 100 from 1 to 8 weeks and 57.5 kg for a hen in lay, with cake, fish meal, bran and mineral mix making up the rest. Maize alone leaves out the protein, which the compendium puts in roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products, and the minerals, which it puts in eggshells and fish bones. Two of those you can gather rather than buy, and greenery, termites and maggots go on top of any formula for free. Start there rather than on maize alone, and ask ICAT where to get cake and fish meal.
I want to build my feed from what I have on the farm.

That is exactly what the reference expects. Tell me what you grow and what you can gather, and I will tell you which parts of the formula you still have to buy. The list it works from is cereals, maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya with their cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; salt; and the vitamins.
Maize and a little sorghum, some groundnut, and there are termite mounds all over the land.

Then you have the largest share covered already. Cereals are 62 kg per 100 kg of feed from 1 to 8 weeks and from 9 to 12 weeks, 60 kg from 12 weeks on and 57.5 kg for a hen in lay, and your maize and sorghum both count there. The groundnut gives you a legume, and groundnut cake is one of the three the reference names alongside cotton and soya, so if you can have your groundnut pressed locally you cover part of the cake as well, which runs 20, 15, 10 and 10 kg per 100 across the four bands. The termites count twice: as a raw material, and again as a free extra on top of the formula at any age. What you will still need is the fish meal, 10 kg per 100 in three formulas and 5 kg in the 9 to 12 week one, and the bran. The mineral mix you can make: 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt for 10 kg. Ask ICAT where to buy fish meal and have your groundnut pressed.
What can I give the birds on top of their feed?

Greenery, termites and maggots, whatever the age, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives those as free extras on top of the formula rather than as part of it, so they do not come out of your 100 kg. The 2017 ESFT compendium adds the arrangement that makes the greenery easy: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. That run is also what keeps them from wandering, which matters for disease as much as for feed.
complement gratuit alimentation poules

Greenery, termites and maggots, on top of the formula, whatever the age, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds. Those are named as extras rather than as part of the 100 kg, so they are feed that costs you nothing. Give the hens a run where they can eat grass; if they cannot have one, bring them a little greenery every day. Feed the chicks apart from the adults so they do not have to compete.
My hens are shut in all day because of the hawks and I cannot let them out.

Then bring the greenery to them, which is exactly what the 2017 ESFT compendium provides for: hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. Add the other free extras while you are at it, termites and maggots, which go on top of the formula whatever the age, with caterpillars for the youngest. On the housing itself, the arrangement asked for is a fenced run rather than a closed building, since a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one and lets you watch the birds better; a fenced and covered run may answer both your problem and that one. Keep the ground around clear, since a tuft of grass shelters the animals that bring disease.
If I give them grass and termites I can cut the mixed feed down.

Not in the way the reference sets it out. Greenery, termites and maggots are given as extras on top of the formula, whatever the age, not as a substitute for part of it. The quantities stay what they are: about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at 25 to 35 grams a day, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. What the extras buy you is better feeding at the same cost, not the same feeding at lower cost. If the feed bill is the problem, the place to work is mixing your own from local raw materials and making the mineral mix yourself.
True or false: chicks can eat with the adults as long as there is enough feed.

False. The instruction is to feed the chicks apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, and it is about access rather than quantity: a chick at a trough with grown birds eats last. Their feed differs as well, ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, and their formula per 100 kg from 1 to 8 weeks is 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral. Same for the water, which matters most of all for them because chicks die easily of dehydration.
Why does the compendium bother saying to bring greenery if the hens cannot get out? Justify.

Because it closes a gap that would otherwise be left to chance. The arrangement it prefers is a run where the hens can eat grass, and the run does several things at once: it keeps them from wandering, which is named among the ways disease spreads, and a henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one. But not every keeper can have one. Rather than leave those birds without, the compendium gives the fallback in the same breath: bring them a little greenery every day. It is the same logic as the free extras on top of the formula, greenery, termites and maggots, which are feed you do not pay for.
State the feeding practice rules beside the formulas.

Four. Whatever the age, greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds. Chicks are fed apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and if they cannot, a little greenery is brought to them every day. And water is its own rule: freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, with clean water mattering most for the chicks because they die easily of dehydration.
How much greenery a day is a little?

The compendium does not quantify it and I will not put a figure on it. What it says is that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. The quantified figures are for the formula itself: about 1.5 kg a bird in all from 1 to 60 days at 10 to 25 grams a day, about 5 kg from 61 days to sale at 25 to 35 grams a day, and 80 grams a day for a hen in lay, with greenery, termites and maggots as extras on top rather than inside those amounts. For a quantity suited to your flock, ask ICAT, which is the office for a ration scaled to your own numbers.
With sixty hens, how much am I actually putting out in a day?

About 4.8 kg of feed a day, at 80 grams a day for a hen in lay. On top of that go the extras, which are not weighed in the reference: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars for the youngest birds. If some of your sixty are not in lay, use the band they are in instead, 25 to 35 grams a day from 61 days to sale at six months, or 10 to 25 grams a day from 1 to 60 days. Check the feeders can take it without waste: for adults, one of 150 cm by 12 by 16 for 25 birds, so three for sixty hens. And keep clean water beside it, never empty, in the shade, renewed at least twice a day.
A neighbour spends a fortune on feed and asks how I manage.

Tell him about the extras first, because they are free and most people skip them: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula whatever the age, with caterpillars for the youngest. Tell him to give the hens a run where they can eat grass, and if he cannot, to bring them a little greenery every day. Then tell him the two bigger savings: mix the feed himself from local raw materials, cereals, legumes and their cakes, kitchen leftovers, fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars, and salt; and make the mineral mix rather than buy it, 4 kg of shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of salt for 10 kg. Feed is the largest running cost there is.
I feel like I am feeding the birds badly but I do not know where to start.

Start with two questions. Do the birds get anything on top of the mixed feed, and do the chicks eat with the adults? Those are the two places the references are most specific, and both are free to fix.
No extras, just the feed I mix, and yes the chicks are in with the hens.

Then you have two changes that cost nothing and one that costs a little work. First, the extras: greenery, termites and maggots go on top of the formula whatever the age, with caterpillars as well for the youngest, and they are not counted inside your 100 kg. Give the hens a run where they can eat grass, and if you cannot, bring them a little greenery every day. Second, separate the chicks: feed them apart from the adults so they do not have to compete, on ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites, in their own feeders, 50 cm by 50 by 5 deep, one for every 50 birds. Give them their own drinkers too, because chicks die easily of dehydration. Third, check your formula against the age: per 100 kg it is 62 kg of cereals, 20 of cake, 10 of fish meal, 5 of bran and 3 of mineral from 1 to 8 weeks, and 57.5, 10, 10, 15 and 7.5 for a hen in lay, which is a different mix, not the same one.
I have a corner of the compound behind the mango tree that I never use. Would that do for a heap?

It may be exactly right, and the shade is the part most people get wrong. The catalogue asks for a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, and it adds that a water point nearby is an advantage. Check those four against your corner. Shade you have under the mango. Out of the wind and rain means it is not in the open where a storm washes the heap about. Easy to reach matters because you will be carrying residues and water to it repeatedly, and turning up with a barrow. And water nearby matters because you water every layer as you lay it, not at the end. If the corner answers all four, that is your site.
A compost heap is just where you throw the farm rubbish until it rots down.

The order is the method, and that is the difference. The catalogue has you choose a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach and with a water point as an advantage, then build in layers, watering each one as you lay it: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues well trodden down, then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator. It also tells you what to leave out: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks, which rot slowly. A heap of rubbish is none of that.
True or false: the heap should be somewhere the sun can get at it to warm it up.

False. The catalogue asks for a shaded spot, and adds out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage. Sun and wind dry a heap, and the whole build is designed around keeping it wet: you water each layer as you lay it rather than watering at the end. Shade also makes the work bearable, since you will be carrying and treading. The rest of the siting is about the labour: easy to reach, because the residues, the manure and the water all have to come to it, and a water point nearby for the same reason.
Why does the catalogue care so much about where I put the heap? Justify.

Because the site decides whether the heap stays wet and whether you keep feeding it. Shade and shelter from the wind and rain keep the moisture in, and moisture is what the whole method is built around, since you water each layer as you lay it. Easy to reach decides whether the work actually gets done: a heap at the far end of the holding is one you stop carrying residues to after a fortnight. And a water point nearby is called an advantage for the same reason, because watering every layer with water fetched from a distance is what makes people skip the watering. The siting is not a preliminary, it is half of the method.
Define composting in a heap as the catalogue presents it.

It is laying plant and animal waste in a heap, on a chosen site, so that it becomes an organic fertiliser called compost, and the catalogue puts it under the aim of keeping soils fertile durably. The site: shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage. The materials: residues that rot fast, chopped, such as straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, with the slow ones left out, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks. The build: in layers, each watered as it is laid, being wood ash on the topsoil, a 10 to 20 cm base of slow rotting material, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of trodden plant residues, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator.
How big should the heap be?

The catalogue does not give a length or a width, so I will not invent one. What it does give are the thicknesses of the layers, which set the height: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues well trodden down, then a layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. It also gives the siting, shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with water nearby. For a footprint suited to your land and your residues, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that fits your holding.
I farm half a hectare. Is a compost heap worth the work at that size?

The catalogue gives no threshold and no yield figure, so I cannot tell you it pays at half a hectare or at five. What I can tell you is that nothing in the method scales with the field: the site is a shaded spot out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with water nearby, and the heap is built from what you already have as waste, chopped residues that rot fast, manure, topsoil. The catalogue also presents composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops to raise a grower's income. What it does not do is quantify any of that. For whether it suits your holding, ask ICAT.
I have decided to make compost. What do I do first, before I gather anything?

Choose the site, because everything else is carried to it. You want a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, and a water point nearby is an advantage. Walk the holding with those four in mind before you move a single load. Then sort what you have, because the catalogue divides it: the residues that rot fast go in, chopped, such as straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, while the slow ones stay out, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks. Set aside the other things the build needs: wood ash, rice husks or ronier leaves for the base, manure, topsoil. And have water at hand, because you water each layer as you lay it.
Describe the site you would choose, as if you were standing on it.

Under trees or against a wall, so there is shade on it for most of the day. Sheltered, with something breaking the wind, and not in the open where a storm would beat straight down on it and wash it about; the catalogue asks for out of the wind and rain. Close to where you work rather than at the far boundary, because you will come back to it with residues, with manure, with topsoil and with water, again and again. And within carrying distance of water, which the catalogue calls an advantage rather than a requirement, but which decides in practice whether you water every layer as you are meant to. Flat enough to stand on and tread the residues down.
My heap dries out to nothing within a week every time.

Look at where it stands before you look at what is in it. The catalogue asks for a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, and a heap in the open loses its water to the sun and the wind faster than you can carry more. Move it into shade and shelter. Then check the watering: you water each layer as you lay it, not the finished heap, so a heap built dry and sprinkled afterwards has dry material at its heart from the start. And check the site for the practical part, easy to reach with a water point nearby as an advantage, because that is what decides whether the watering keeps happening rather than happening once.
Just tell me the shade does not really matter, my only free ground is out in the open.

I will not tell you it does not matter, because a shaded spot is the first thing the catalogue names, with out of the wind and rain beside it. What I can do is take your constraint seriously. If the only ground you have is open, then make the shelter rather than move the heap: something over it and something breaking the wind, and be stricter than usual about watering each layer as you lay it, since that is what the shade was protecting. Keep the other two conditions, easy to reach and a water point nearby, which you can still choose for. And ask ICAT about the site, since it is the office for the practice that suits your land.
I want to make compost but I have never done it.

Then start with the site rather than with the materials, because the catalogue treats the site as half the work: a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage. Tell me what ground you have available and whether there is water near it, and tell me what residues you have on the farm, because some go in and some are kept out.
There is shade behind the house and the well is about thirty paces away. I have a lot of maize stalks and some groundnut leaves.

The site sounds right on all four counts, so take it. The residues are the problem: of your two, one goes in and one does not. The groundnut leaves are exactly what is wanted, named with straw and the leaves of soya and cowpea among the residues that rot fast, and you chop them before they go in. The maize stalks are on the other list, with the stalks of sorghum and millet and the husks, which rot slowly and are to be kept out of that layer. So gather more of the fast kind if you can, and ask ICAT what to do with the stalks instead, because the catalogue does not say. Then build in layers, watering each one as you lay it: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of your chopped leaves trodden down well, then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator.
What should I put in the heap and what should I keep out?

In go the residues that rot fast, chopped up first: the catalogue names straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Out stay the ones that rot slowly: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. Beside those you need the other components of the build, which are not residues: a little wood ash, manure, topsoil, and a slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves for the base of the heap. So the slow material is not banned from the heap altogether, it has its own place at the bottom, 10 to 20 cm thick; what it must not do is stand in for the 30 cm layer of fast rotting residues.
After the harvest I have a great pile of stalks and husks and almost nothing else.

Then you have plenty of what the catalogue keeps out of the residue layer and little of what it wants in. The stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks, are named as the slow rotting ones to avoid there; what goes in is the fast kind, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Two things you can do. Use a slow rotting material as the base of the heap, 10 to 20 cm thick, which is where rice husks or ronier leaves belong, so part of what you have has a place. And gather the fast kind where you can find it, from your own legumes or from neighbours. For what to do with the rest of the stalks, ask ICAT, because the catalogue does not say.
Cowpea leaves or rice husks for the main residue layer?

Cowpea leaves, and the husks belong somewhere else in the same heap. The catalogue names the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, with straw, among the residues that rot fast, and those are what the roughly 30 cm layer is made of, chopped and trodden down well. Rice husks it names as a slow rotting material for the base of the heap, 10 to 20 cm thick, with ronier leaves. So you use both, in their own places, rather than choosing. What you should not do is build the residue layer out of slow material: the husks are also on the list of things to avoid among the residues, with the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize.
Set out the materials by their place in the heap.

Wood ash: a little, spread on the topsoil at the bottom. Slow rotting material: rice husks or ronier leaves, as a base 10 to 20 cm thick. Manure: a layer 5 cm thick on that base. Fast rotting plant residues: about 30 cm, chopped and trodden down well, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Activator, as the last layer: topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. Kept out of the residue layer: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks, because they rot slowly. Every layer is watered as it is laid.
Can I put kitchen waste or ash from the fire in as well?

Wood ash yes, and it has a defined place: a little of it on the topsoil at the bottom of the heap. Kitchen waste is not something the catalogue names for composting, so I will not tell you to put it in or leave it out. What it does name is the residues that rot fast, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea; the slow ones to avoid, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks; manure; topsoil; and rice husks or ronier leaves as a base. For anything outside that list, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your holding.
For a heap on a base of two metres by two, how much residue am I gathering?

Work it from the layer thicknesses, because that is what the catalogue gives. On a two by two base, four square metres, the residue layer is about 30 cm deep, so roughly 1.2 cubic metres of chopped fast rotting material, trodden down well, which means gathering rather more than that before treading. Below it the manure layer at 5 cm is about 0.2 cubic metres, and the slow rotting base at 10 to 20 cm is 0.4 to 0.8 cubic metres of rice husks or ronier leaves. Above it goes the layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri. The catalogue gives no weights and no footprint, so these are volumes from its own thicknesses, not figures it states.
A friend is filling his heap with maize stalks because that is what he has most of.

Tell him those are on the list the catalogue keeps out. The residues that go into the heap are the ones that rot fast, chopped up first, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea; the ones to avoid are the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks, because they rot slowly. He will be waiting a long time. Tell him the slow material does have one place in the build, as the base of the heap, 10 to 20 cm thick, where rice husks and ronier leaves are named, so some of his pile can go there. And tell him to chop what he does put in, and to water each layer as he lays it.
I am going out to gather residues this morning. What am I looking for?

The fast rotting kind: straw, and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. Those are what the catalogue names for the main residue layer, and you chop them before they go in. Leave the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize where they are, and the husks too, because they rot slowly and are named as the ones to avoid there. While you are out, gather the other components as well, since the heap is not residues alone: a little wood ash, manure for the 5 cm layer, topsoil, and rice husks or ronier leaves for the 10 to 20 cm base. And make sure you can water, because each layer is watered as it is laid.
Tell me what a proper load of residues looks like before it goes in.

Chopped, first of all, because the catalogue tells you to chop up the residues that rot fast before they go in. Not whole stems lying across each other but short pieces that pack down. And it should be the right kind: straw, groundnut leaves, soya leaves, cowpea leaves, the soft material that breaks down quickly. What you should not see in it is stalks of sorghum, millet or maize, or husks, which the catalogue names among the slow rotting ones to avoid in that layer. When it goes on the heap it is trodden down well with your feet to about 30 cm, and watered as it is laid, so it should be material you can compress rather than a springy pile.
Just say the maize stalks are fine if I chop them small enough.

I cannot say that, because the catalogue puts them on the other list. It tells you to chop up the residues that rot fast, such as straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, and to avoid the slow ones, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. Chopping is what you do to residues that already belong in the heap, not a way of qualifying ones that do not. What I will not do is guess that fine chopping changes the classification, because that is not something the catalogue says. Where slow material does belong is the base, 10 to 20 cm of rice husks or ronier leaves. For another use for your stalks, ask ICAT.
couches du tas de compost ordre

From the bottom: a little wood ash on the topsoil; a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick; 5 cm of manure; about 30 cm of plant residues, chopped and trodden down well; then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator. Water each layer as you lay it, not the finished heap. Keep the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks out of the residue layer.
I have the site cleared and everything gathered. Talk me through building it.

Have water beside you before you start, because every layer is watered as it is laid. Spread a little wood ash on the topsoil first. On that, a base of slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick, and water it. Then 5 cm of manure, watered. Then your chopped plant residues, about 30 cm, trodden down well with your feet, and watered. Then the last layer, which is the activator: topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. That is the build. The order is the method, so do not tip everything on together, and do not leave the watering to the end.
The manure goes on top so it washes down through the heap.

In the catalogue's order it goes near the bottom, not on top. From below: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, then the 5 cm of manure, then about 30 cm of chopped plant residues trodden down well, then the last layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. So the manure sits between the base and the residues, and the thing on top is the activator. Each layer is watered as it is laid, which is what carries moisture through rather than relying on anything washing down.
Rice husks or ronier leaves for the bottom?

Either, and the catalogue names them together as examples of the slow rotting material that makes the base, 10 to 20 cm thick. Use whichever you have. What matters is that the base is slow rotting material rather than the soft residues, which have their own layer above it: about 30 cm of chopped straw or groundnut, soya and cowpea leaves, trodden down well. Below the base goes a little wood ash on the topsoil; between base and residues goes 5 cm of manure; on top goes the activator, topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri. Water each layer as you lay it.
Why water each layer instead of soaking the whole heap at the end? Justify.

Because water poured over a finished heap runs off the outside and down the sides, and the middle stays dry. The catalogue is explicit that you water each layer as you lay it, which is the only way the base, the manure and the bottom of the 30 cm residue layer ever get wet. It also fits the rest of the build: the residues are trodden down well, so a compacted heap is even harder for water to enter from above. That is the same reason the site is chosen shaded and out of the wind and rain, and why a water point nearby is called an advantage: the method depends on the heap being wet through, from the first layer.
Set out the build with its thicknesses.

Layer one: a little wood ash, spread on the topsoil. Layer two: a base of slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. Layer three: manure, 5 cm. Layer four: plant residues, about 30 cm, chopped beforehand and trodden down well; these are the fast rotting kind, straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and not the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize nor the husks. Layer five: the activator, being topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri. Each layer is watered as it is laid. The site is shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with a water point nearby as an advantage.
How many of these layer sets do I stack before the heap is finished?

The catalogue gives one set and does not say to repeat it, so I will not tell you to stack two or five. What it gives is the sequence and the thicknesses: wood ash on the topsoil, a 10 to 20 cm base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped plant residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, with each layer watered as it is laid. It gives no finished height, no footprint and no number of repeats. For a heap sized to your residues, ask ICAT.
My neighbour builds his heap by throwing everything on together and says it comes out the same.

It may rot eventually, but it is not what the catalogue describes, and the parts he is skipping are the ones that do the work. The build is five layers in order, each watered as it is laid: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. Thrown together, the manure is not where it should be, the activator is not on top and the middle never gets wet, since watering a finished heap runs off the outside.
The outside of my heap has rotted down but the middle is still dry material.

That is what watering the finished heap instead of each layer produces. The catalogue has you water each layer as you lay it, precisely so the inside is wet from the start: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a 10 to 20 cm base of rice husks or ronier leaves watered, 5 cm of manure watered, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down and watered, then the activator layer of topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri. Check the site as well, because a heap in the sun and wind loses moisture faster than you can add it: shaded, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with water nearby. Next heap, water as you build.
Just tell me the order does not matter as long as everything is in there.

I will not, because the order is what the catalogue gives and the positions are not interchangeable. The manure is a 5 cm layer between the base and the residues, not on top. The activator, topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri, is the last layer, which is where an activator has to be to be one. The slow rotting material, rice husks or ronier leaves, is a 10 to 20 cm base, and the same kind of material is expressly kept out of the residue layer. And the watering is per layer as you lay it, which you simply cannot do if everything goes on at once. If you want an argument about the method rather than a description of it, ICAT holds the catalogue.
I built a heap last season and it never turned into anything.
Let me narrow it. Tell me what you put in it, in what order, and when you watered it. Those three are where the catalogue is most specific, and most heaps that fail have missed one of them.
Mostly maize stalks and husks, all tipped on together, and I watered it well once it was finished.

All three, then, and each one alone would have stalled it. The residues first: the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks are named as the slow rotting ones to avoid in the residue layer, and what should go there is the fast kind, chopped, being straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea. The order second: the build is a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. Tipped together, the manure and the activator are not where they do their work. The watering third: each layer is watered as it is laid, because water poured over a finished heap runs off the outside and leaves the middle dry, which is exactly what you found. Rebuild it that way, on a shaded site out of the wind and rain, and ask ICAT what to do with the stalks instead.
mycotri c'est quoi

A powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. That is how the 2020 catalogue of good agricultural practices describes it. It is one of the three things offered for the last layer of the heap, the activator, beside topsoil and well rotted compost, and it is the only one of the three the catalogue attaches a benefit to. It does not say how much time is saved, nor where to find it. Ask ICAT for that.
Someone offered to sell me a sachet of Mycotri at the market. Should I take it?

I cannot tell you whether that sachet is what it says it is or whether the price is fair, since the catalogue gives no price and does not say where to find it. What I can tell you is what it is for. Mycotri is a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it is one of three options for the last layer of the heap, the activator, beside topsoil and well rotted compost. So you do not need it to make compost: topsoil will serve as the activator. Ask ICAT about where it is properly supplied before buying from a stall.
Mycotri is a fertiliser you spread on the field.

It is described as something for the heap, not for the field. The catalogue calls Mycotri a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and places it as one of three choices for the last layer of the heap, the activator, alongside topsoil and well rotted compost. What you spread on the field is the compost itself, once it is made. The catalogue gives no spreading rate for the compost either, so I will not give you one. For both questions, ICAT is the office to ask.
True or false: without Mycotri the compost will not work.

False. The catalogue offers three things for that last activator layer: topsoil, well rotted compost, or Mycotri. Any of the three serves, and topsoil is the one most people already have at hand.
