What it says about Mycotri in particular is that it is a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it is the only one of the three it attaches a benefit to. But it does not say how much time is saved, nor where to find the product, so it is an option rather than a requirement.
How much faster is the compost with Mycotri, and how much do I need?

Neither figure is in the catalogue and I will not invent either. It describes Mycotri as a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and that is as far as it goes: no measure of the time saved, no quantity, no price, and no indication of where to find it. It does not give a maturity time for the compost without Mycotri either, so there is nothing to compare against. What it does give is its place, the last layer of the heap as the activator, with topsoil and well rotted compost as the alternatives. Ask ICAT.
For a heap on a base of two metres by two, how much activator goes on top?

The catalogue gives a thickness for every layer except that one. It gives a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, and then simply a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator, without a depth. So I will not scale it for you: multiplying a thickness I do not have would just dress up a guess. What I can say is that it covers the heap, and that topsoil is the option you can supply in any quantity. For a rate, particularly for Mycotri, ask ICAT.
The cooperative is thinking of buying Mycotri in bulk. What should I tell them?

Tell them what it is and what is not known about it, and let them decide. It is a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, and it is one of three options for the last layer of the heap, the activator, beside topsoil and well rotted compost. It is the only one of the three the catalogue attaches a benefit to. But the catalogue gives no measure of the time saved, no quantity, no price and no supplier, so a bulk purchase would be made without any of the numbers a cooperative normally wants. Send them to ICAT before they commit money.
The heap is built up to the residue layer. What goes on last?

The activator, and you have three choices: a layer of topsoil, or of well rotted compost, or of Mycotri. Any of the three is what the catalogue offers. If you have none of the last two, topsoil is the ordinary answer and needs no buying. Water this layer as you lay it, as you did the others. Check what is under it before you close the heap: a little wood ash on the topsoil at the bottom, a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, then about 30 cm of chopped residues trodden down well. If any of those was laid dry, it is easier to fix now than later.
What does Mycotri look like and what is it doing in there?

The catalogue describes it as a powder of fungi. What it says it does is speed up the decomposition of plant and animal debris, so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. It goes on as the last layer of the heap, the activator, which is the position topsoil or well rotted compost would otherwise occupy; of the three, Mycotri is the only one the catalogue attaches a benefit to. Beyond the word powder it gives no description of the product, no quantity, no price and no source, and I am not going to fill that in from elsewhere. ICAT is the office to ask.
My compost takes forever and I want to speed it up.

Mycotri is what the catalogue offers for that: a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, laid as the last layer of the heap in place of topsoil or well rotted compost. It does not say by how much, nor where to buy it. Before you chase the product, check the two things that stall a heap for free. The residues: chopped, and of the fast rotting kind, straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, with the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks kept out. And the water: each layer watered as it is laid, not the finished heap. Those fix more heaps than any powder.
Just give me an idea, does Mycotri halve the time or not?

I have no idea to give you, and that is the honest position rather than a coy one. The catalogue says Mycotri is a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. Shorter is the whole of it. It gives no maturity time with the product and none without it, so there is no ratio to halve. If I said half you would plan a season on it. What I can tell you without guessing is that you do not need it: topsoil and well rotted compost are the other two options for the same activator layer. For a real figure, ask ICAT.
I keep hearing about Mycotri and I do not know whether to bother.

Tell me where you are with the heap: are you making compost already, and if so what are you using for the last layer? That matters because Mycotri is one of three options for that layer, the activator, beside topsoil and well rotted compost.
I am making it, and I put topsoil on top as I was told. It works but it is slow.

Then you are doing it as the catalogue describes, and Mycotri is the one change it offers for speed: a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, used in place of your topsoil in that last layer. Two honest cautions. The catalogue does not say how much time is saved, and it does not say where to find the product, so you would be buying without a figure. And before spending, check the cheaper causes of slowness. Are the residues the fast rotting kind, straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, chopped before they go in, with the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks kept out? Is every layer watered as you lay it rather than the heap watered at the end? Is the site shaded and out of the wind and rain? Fix those first, and put the Mycotri question to ICAT.
When will my compost be ready and how much should I spread?

Neither of those is in the catalogue, and I would rather say so than give you numbers you would plan a season on. It gives the site, a shaded spot out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with water nearby; the materials, the fast rotting residues chopped, with the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks kept out; and the build in layers, each watered as it is laid. It gives no maturity time, no spreading rate per hectare and no number of turnings. It also gives no cost and no yield gain for any of these practices. ICAT is the office for a figure fitted to your land.
compost pret en combien de temps

The catalogue does not say, and I will not invent a number. It describes the site, the materials and the five layers watered as they are laid, but gives no maturity time, no dose per hectare and no turning frequency. It does not even give a time saved by Mycotri, only that it shortens it. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land. Anything else you hear from me on timing would be a guess dressed up as advice.
I want to have compost ready for the sowing in about three months. Can I plan on that?

I cannot confirm three months, because the catalogue gives no maturity time at all. Planning your sowing on a date I invented would be the worst thing I could do for you. What you can do is start now rather than later, build it properly so it is not slower than it needs to be, and ask ICAT, which will know what a heap takes locally. Building it properly means the site shaded and out of the wind and rain, the residues chopped and of the fast rotting kind, every layer watered as you lay it, and the activator on top, topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri, that last being described as shortening the time without saying by how much.
You have given me all these measurements, so you must know how long it takes.

The measurements are in the catalogue and the timing is not, and knowing part of a document is not knowing all of it. It gives 10 to 20 cm for the base, 5 cm for the manure, about 30 cm for the residues, and the order of the five layers with the watering of each as it is laid. It gives no maturity time, no spreading rate, no number of turnings, no cost and no yield gain for any practice in it. The useful thing I can do is tell you exactly where that edge falls, so you know which questions to take to ICAT rather than acting on a number I made up.
True or false: composting will raise my yield by a quarter.

I cannot say true or false, because the catalogue gives no yield figure for any of its practices, composting included. It presents them as good practices in the era of climate change and gives no impact measurement, no cost and no yield gain, and it is better that I tell you that than that I confirm or deny a number on your behalf. What it does say about composting is the aim, keeping soils fertile durably, and the method: the site, the materials, and the five layers watered as they are laid. For what to expect on your own land, ask ICAT.
Compost or buy fertiliser? Which gives more for the money?

I cannot compare them on money, because the catalogue gives no cost and no yield gain for composting, and I have no price for fertiliser either. What I can set out is what composting asks of you and what it is for. It asks for a site, shaded and out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, with water nearby; for residues you already have, chopped, of the fast rotting kind; for manure, wood ash, topsoil; and for the work of building in layers and watering each one. Its stated aim is keeping soils fertile durably. The catalogue also presents composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of raising a grower's income. For the comparison you are asking for, ICAT.
Why will you not just give me an approximate figure? Justify.

Because an approximate figure from me is not approximate, it is invented, and you would treat it as though the catalogue had said it. The catalogue gives no maturity time, no spreading rate, no turning frequency, no cost and no yield gain for these practices. If I said three months, you would plan your sowing on it, and when the compost was not ready you would have lost a season on my guess rather than on a real estimate. Every figure I do give you is one the catalogue carries, and can be checked against it: 10 to 20 cm of base, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of residues. The difference between those and a guess is the whole of my usefulness.
State precisely what the catalogue does not quantify.

For composting: no maturity time, no spreading rate per hectare, no number of turnings, no heap footprint, and no thickness for the activator layer. For Mycotri: no measure of the time saved, no quantity, no price, no source. For the practices as a whole: no cost, no yield gain, and no measure of how much they offset climate change. What it does quantify for composting is the build, being a base of slow rotting material 10 to 20 cm thick, 5 cm of manure, about 30 cm of plant residues trodden down well, with a little wood ash below and the activator above, each layer watered as it is laid.
For two hectares, how much compost do I need to make?

I cannot scale that, because the catalogue gives no spreading rate per hectare to scale from. It is not a case of my not knowing your soil: the catalogue simply does not carry that figure, any more than it carries the maturity time or the number of turnings. What the catalogue does give in per hectare terms belongs to its other practices, such as 25 to 30 adult trees and 60 to 80 young shoots per hectare for assisted natural regeneration in the dry savanna zone, and 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for laying out a lowland. For compost on two hectares, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land.
A man from a project told the village that compost doubles the harvest.

That may be his figure, but it is not in the catalogue and I cannot confirm it. The catalogue presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and gives no impact measurement, no cost and no yield gain for any of them, composting included. Ask him where his number comes from, because a figure with a source behind it is worth something to the village and one passed along is not. What the catalogue does say about composting is its aim, keeping soils fertile durably, and its method, the site, the materials and the five layers watered as they are laid. For what to expect locally, ICAT.
Before I commit to doing this, what should I know that you cannot tell me?

Four things, and they are worth getting from ICAT before you start rather than after. How long a heap takes to mature where you are, because the catalogue gives no maturity time. How much compost to spread per hectare, because it gives no rate. How often, if at all, to turn the heap, because it gives no number. And whether it pays, because the catalogue gives no cost and no yield gain for any of its practices. What I can give you completely is the method: the site, shaded and out of the wind and rain; the residues, chopped and of the fast rotting kind; and the five layers, each watered as it is laid.
How will I know the compost is finished when I look at it?

The catalogue does not describe a finished heap, so I have no test to give you and I will not invent one. It uses the phrase mature compost when describing what Mycotri is for, speeding up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time, but it does not say what mature looks like, nor how long it takes. It also offers well rotted compost as one of the three activators, which tells you the distinction exists without defining it. This is a good question for ICAT, and a good one to ask a neighbour who has made compost, because it is a thing more easily shown than written.
It has been sitting there for months and I do not know whether to use it or wait.

I cannot tell you, because the catalogue gives no maturity time and no description of a finished heap, and guessing would either waste your work or put unready compost on your field. Take that one to ICAT, or to someone nearby who has made it, since it is the kind of judgement made by looking. What I can help with is whether the heap was built to give it a chance: the residues chopped and of the fast rotting kind, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks kept out, each layer watered as it was laid rather than the heap watered at the end, and the site shaded and out of the wind and rain. If any of those was missed, that is likely why it is slow.
What is the difference between putting manure on my field and making compost?

Manure is one ingredient of a compost heap; compost is what comes out of it. In the catalogue's build, manure is a layer 5 cm thick, laid on the base of slow rotting material and under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues, with a little wood ash below and topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri above as the activator, each layer watered as it is laid. So the two are not alternatives at the same stage. The catalogue also names composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops that raises a grower's income.
fumier ou compost difference

Manure goes into the heap; compost comes out of it. In the catalogue's layering, manure is the 5 cm layer between the slow rotting base and the roughly 30 cm of chopped plant residues. Compost is the organic fertiliser the whole heap becomes. The catalogue also lists composting animal droppings and plant debris among the ways of combining trees, animals and crops to raise a grower's income. It gives no spreading rate and no maturity time for either.
True or false: I can use manure instead of compost and skip the heap.

I cannot judge that for you, because the catalogue does not compare the two as field treatments and gives no yield figure for either. What I can tell you is that inside the method they are not interchangeable: manure is a 5 cm layer in the heap, between the slow rotting base and the roughly 30 cm of chopped residues, and compost is the product of the whole build. Skipping the heap means you have manure and not compost, which is a different thing, not a shortcut to the same thing. The catalogue presents composting animal droppings and plant debris as a way of raising income. For the comparison, ask ICAT.
I have poultry droppings. Straight on the field or into the heap?

The catalogue gives them a place in the heap: manure is the 5 cm layer laid on the slow rotting base, under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues. It also names composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops that raises a grower's income. Separately, poultry droppings have their own handling before they get anywhere: swept from the henhouse two or three times a week into a manure pit well away from it, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, which limits the spread of disease as well as turning them into something the fields can use. Whether straight spreading beats composting is not something the catalogue settles; ask ICAT.
Why go to the trouble of layering when the manure is the useful part anyway? Justify.

Because the manure is 5 cm of a heap whose residue layer is about 30 cm, so on volume alone most of what you end up with is not manure. The layering is what turns the rest into fertiliser rather than leaving it as a pile of leaves: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a base of slow rotting material 10 to 20 cm thick, the manure, the chopped residues trodden down well, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, with each layer watered as it is laid. The catalogue presents this as the way to keep soils fertile durably, and as composting animal droppings and plant debris together rather than either alone.
How much manure do I need for one heap, and how much compost will it give me?

The first I can turn into a volume, the second I cannot give at all. The manure layer is 5 cm thick, so on a base of two metres by two that is about 0.2 cubic metres; scale that to whatever footprint you choose. What the catalogue does not give is any yield of compost from a heap, nor a maturity time, nor a spreading rate per hectare, so I cannot tell you what comes out or how far it goes. It gives no cost and no yield gain for its practices either. Take those to ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land.
My henhouse gives me a lot of droppings. Can I make several heaps?

Nothing in the catalogue limits you to one, and the manure layer is only 5 cm of each heap, so droppings go further than people expect: on a base of two metres by two that layer is about 0.2 cubic metres. What will limit you is the other component, the roughly 30 cm of chopped plant residues of the fast rotting kind, straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, since that is six times the manure by depth. Gather that before multiplying heaps. Meanwhile the droppings you are not using belong in the manure pit, at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam, well away from the henhouse.
I am clearing out the henhouse tomorrow. How do I keep the droppings for the heap?

Put them in the manure pit, which is where they belong between the henhouse and any use: at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, roofed with an apatam, and sited well away from the building. That serves two purposes, turning the droppings into something your fields can use and limiting the spread of disease. Sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week rather than in one annual clear-out. Then when you build the heap, the manure is the 5 cm layer, laid on the base of slow rotting material and under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues, watered as you lay it like every other layer.
Describe where the manure sits in the heap.

Third from the bottom and thin. Underneath it, first a little wood ash spread on the topsoil, then a base of slow rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. The manure goes on that base as a layer 5 cm thick. Above it comes the bulk of the heap, about 30 cm of chopped plant residues of the fast rotting kind, trodden down well with your feet. On top of everything goes the activator, a layer of topsoil, or of well rotted compost, or of Mycotri. Every one of those layers is watered as it is laid, including the manure.
The droppings I spread last year burned the young plants.

The catalogue does not discuss spreading raw droppings on a crop, so I will not diagnose that and I will not give you a rate. What it does with animal droppings is put them into the heap: manure as a 5 cm layer on the slow rotting base, under about 30 cm of chopped plant residues, with the whole built in watered layers and finished with topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator. It names composting animal droppings and plant debris as one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops. Take the question about raw droppings on young plants to ICAT, since that is a real question and I have nothing on it.
Just tell me compost is better than manure, that is all I want to hear.

I will not, because the catalogue does not rank them and I would be making the comparison up. In its method they are not rivals: manure is a 5 cm layer inside the heap, between the slow rotting base and about 30 cm of chopped plant residues, and compost is what the whole heap becomes. It gives no yield figure, no cost and no impact measurement for any of its practices, so there is no basis in it for saying one beats the other on a field. What it does say is that composting animal droppings and plant debris is one of the ways of combining trees, animals and crops that raises a grower's income. For a comparison, ICAT.
I have droppings from the henhouse and a pile of leaves, and I am not sure what to do with either.

You have two of the components of a compost heap, which is convenient. Tell me what kind of leaves they are, because that decides whether they go in: the catalogue wants the fast rotting kind, straw and the leaves of groundnut, soya and cowpea, and keeps out the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize and the husks.
Cowpea leaves mostly, and the droppings have been sitting behind the henhouse for weeks.

Then both can be used, and one of them needs moving first. Cowpea leaves are named among the residues that rot fast, so chop them and they make the main layer, about 30 cm, trodden down well. The droppings are your manure layer, 5 cm thick, laid on the base and under the leaves. But a heap behind the henhouse is the thing to change today whatever you do with it: droppings belong in a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep with an apatam over it, sited well away from the building, because that limits the spread of disease as well as turning them into something the fields can use. Then build the heap on a shaded site, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach and near water: a little wood ash on the topsoil, a 10 to 20 cm base of rice husks or ronier leaves, the 5 cm of droppings, about 30 cm of your chopped cowpea leaves, then topsoil or well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, watering each layer as you lay it.
ecartement arbres cultures en couloirs

Two to four metres between the plants inside a row, and 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next, with the crop grown in the alley between. Lay the rows across the slope, never up and down it. The fertiliser trees named are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. The crops named for the alleys are maize and cowpea. First pruning between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, with a high cut at 2 m above the ground advised.
My field slopes down towards the stream and I lose soil every rainy season.

Then the direction of the rows is the part to get right, and the catalogue is explicit about it: lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. Rows running downhill channel the water; rows across it hold. Set your tree rows with 2 to 4 m between the plants inside a row and 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next, and grow your maize or cowpea in the alleys between them. The fertiliser trees named are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida. Plant them during the rainy season. Ask ICAT which of the three is available as plants near you.
How much will alley cropping add to my maize yield?

The catalogue gives no yield figure, no cost and no measure of how much these practices offset climate change, and I am not going to supply one. What it gives is the method: alleys laid across the slope, trees 2 to 4 m apart inside the row, 10, 20 or 30 m between rows, maize or cowpea grown between; Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida as the fertiliser trees; and pruning first between 15 and 20 months at 1.50 m tall or more, with a high cut at 2 m advised. For what it does on your own land, ask ICAT.
My field is 100 m across. How many trees in a row?

At 2 to 4 m between plants inside the row, a row of 100 m carries between 25 and 50 trees. How many rows depends on the spacing you choose between them, since the catalogue offers 10, 20 or 30 m between one row and the next: on a field 100 m deep that is roughly ten rows at 10 m, five at 20 m, or three at 30 m. Lay them across the slope, never up and down it, and grow maize or cowpea in the alleys. What the catalogue does not give is which spacing suits which land, so take that choice to ICAT along with the question of which species is available near you.
A neighbour wants to try trees in his field and asks what alley cropping involves.

Tell him it is growing his seasonal crops in the alleys between rows of fertiliser trees, and give him the four numbers. Two to four metres between plants inside a row. Ten, twenty or thirty metres between one row and the next. Rows laid across the slope, never up and down it. And the first pruning between 15 and 20 months, once the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, with a high cut at 2 m above the ground advised, then regular pruning after that. The trees named are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida, and the crops for the alleys are maize and cowpea. Send him to ICAT for what is available locally.
Describe what the field looks like once it is set up.

Lines of trees running across the slope, not down it, each line with its plants 2 to 4 m apart, so a run of trees rather than a hedge. Between one line and the next, a wide strip of ordinary field, 10, 20 or 30 m across depending on the spacing chosen, and that strip is what you crop, with maize or cowpea. The trees are kept low rather than allowed to shade the alley: the first cut comes between 15 and 20 months, when they are at least 1.50 m tall, and a high cut at 2 m above the ground is advised, with regular pruning after that. What you cut becomes firewood or organic fertiliser.
The trees I planted are shading my maize and it is doing badly underneath.

Two things to check, the spacing and the pruning. The catalogue leaves 10, 20 or 30 m between one tree row and the next precisely so the alley is a field and not a wood, with 2 to 4 m between plants inside a row. If your rows are closer than that, the alley is too narrow. Then the pruning: the first cut comes between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, with a high cut at 2 m above the ground advised, and after that you prune regularly, according to the trees and to whether you want firewood or organic fertiliser. Trees left unpruned will shade the crop. What you cut is not wasted.
Just tell me I can put the rows straight up and down the field, it is easier to plough.

I will not, because the catalogue says the opposite in plain words: lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. That is the one instruction in the whole practice given as a prohibition rather than a measurement, which tells you how much weight it carries. Rows running up and down a slope give the water a path; rows across it hold the soil, which is much of the point of putting trees in the field at all. If ploughing along the contour is the difficulty, that is a real problem and worth taking to ICAT, but the answer is not to turn the rows. The rest of the layout is flexible: 2 to 4 m between plants, and 10, 20 or 30 m between rows.
I want to put fertiliser trees into my maize field.

Then alley cropping is the practice, and I need two things to give you a layout: which way the land slopes, and how wide you want the cropped strips. The catalogue is firm on the first, the alleys go across the slope and not down it, and offers a choice on the second, 10, 20 or 30 m between one tree row and the next.
It slopes gently to the west, and I want the strips wide enough to work with the oxen.

Then run your rows north and south, across that westward slope, and take the widest spacing, 30 m between one row and the next, which leaves you strips you can work without turning constantly. Inside each row, space the plants 2 to 4 m apart. Grow your maize in the alleys, or cowpea, which are the two the catalogue names. Plant the trees during the rainy season. The three fertiliser trees it names are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, which it describes as a fertilising plant resistant to drought, and Faidherbia albida; ask ICAT which is available as plants near you. Then hold one date in mind from the start: the first pruning comes between 15 and 20 months, when the plants are at least 1.50 m tall, and a high cut at 2 m above the ground is advised. After that you prune regularly, and what you cut is firewood or organic fertiliser for the field.
What is the Taungya method?

It is for where land is scarce. Replanting the trees is the first aim, and crops are grown under them for only two or three years so that the trees can grow. You plant the trees about 2 m by 2 m, then grow cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, and sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. After that the crop stops and the trees have the ground. The trees the catalogue names for it are teak, gmelina which it also calls Indian teak, Anacardium which it also calls atchan and which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna which it also calls zanguerati, and neem.
taungya combien d'annees de culture

Two or three years, and then the crop stops. In Taungya the replanting of the trees is the first aim and the crops are grown under them only for those years, so the trees can grow. The sequence is cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. Trees planted about 2 m by 2 m. The species named are teak, gmelina or Indian teak, Anacardium or atchan, which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna or zanguerati, and neem.
So Taungya is just alley cropping with closer trees.

The spacing differs, but the aim is what separates them. In alley cropping the crop continues season after season in wide alleys, with trees 2 to 4 m apart inside the row and 10, 20 or 30 m between rows, laid across the slope. In Taungya the replanting of the trees is the first aim, the trees go in at about 2 m by 2 m all over, and the crops are grown under them for only two or three years so the trees can grow. So one is a cropping system with trees in it and the other is a planting scheme that lets you crop while the trees establish. The species lists differ too, and Taungya is offered for where land is scarce.
Cowpea or maize in the first Taungya year?

Cowpea, and the order is part of the method. The catalogue has you grow cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. So maize belongs to years two and three, not to year one. Beyond that choice, remember what the practice is for: the trees are the first aim, planted about 2 m by 2 m, and the cropping lasts only two or three years so they can grow. The trees named are teak, gmelina, also called Indian teak, Anacardium, also called atchan, the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna, also called zanguerati, and neem.
Why stop cropping after three years? The land is still mine. Justify.

Because in Taungya the trees are the point and the crop is what makes the waiting bearable. The catalogue is explicit: replanting the trees is the first aim and crops are grown under them for only two or three years so that the trees can grow. At about 2 m by 2 m the trees close in, and a crop under them after that would be competing with what you planted them for. If you want to keep cropping year after year, the practice you want is not Taungya but alley cropping, where the trees stand in rows 10, 20 or 30 m apart and the alleys are cropped season after season. That is a different layout and a different species list, so choose which you are doing before you plant.
Set out the Taungya method.

Purpose: where land is scarce. Replanting the trees is the first aim; crops are grown under them for only two or three years so the trees can grow. Tree spacing: about 2 m by 2 m. Cropping sequence: cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year; sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. Species named, in the catalogue's own words: teak, gmelina which it also calls Indian teak, Anacardium which it also calls atchan and which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna which it also calls zanguerati, and neem. Planting season: the trees go in during the rainy season. No cost, no yield figure and no impact measurement are given.
Which of those trees grows fastest and which pays best?

The catalogue ranks them in neither way, so I will not. It names them as a list for Taungya: teak, gmelina which it also calls Indian teak, Anacardium which it also calls atchan and which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna which it also calls zanguerati, and neem. It gives no growth rate, no yield and no price for any of them, and no cost for the practice. The one species it does characterise anywhere is Senna siamea, called zanguerati, which it describes as a fertilising plant resistant to drought, and that is in the alley cropping section. For what grows and sells well near you, ask ICAT, which is also who to ask about which species is available as plants.
A friend has been given land on condition he plants trees on it. What should I tell him?

That is exactly the case Taungya is written for. Tell him the replanting of the trees is the first aim and that he can crop under them for two or three years while they grow. Trees planted about 2 m by 2 m. Cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize in the two following years. The species named are teak, gmelina or Indian teak, Anacardium or atchan, which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna or zanguerati, and neem. Tell him to plant during the rainy season, and to ask ICAT which of those is available as plants near him. And tell him plainly that the cropping stops after the third year.
I am planting the Taungya trees next week. What do I have settled before I start?

The spacing, the species and the first crop. Spacing is about 2 m by 2 m across the plot. Species: choose from teak, gmelina which is also called Indian teak, Anacardium which is also called atchan and is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna which is also called zanguerati, or neem, and settle it with ICAT according to what is available as plants near you. First crop: cowpea, groundnut or pea, with sorghum, millet or maize kept for the two following years. Settle also that you are stopping after two or three years, because that is what the practice is, and plant during the rainy season rather than outside it.
Describe the plot in the second year.

Young trees standing right across it on a grid of about 2 m by 2 m, not in rows with wide gaps but spread over the whole plot, since the replanting is the first aim. Between and under them, your second year crop, which in the catalogue's sequence is sorghum, millet or maize, the legume year having been the first. The trees are still short enough to crop under, which is why the cropping is limited to two or three years in total. By the third year the same picture, a little tighter. After that the crop stops and the plot is a young stand of teak, gmelina, Anacardium, leucaena, acacia, senna or neem.
My Taungya maize did poorly this year and the trees are getting big.

That may be the practice working rather than failing. In Taungya the trees are the first aim and the crops are grown under them for only two or three years, precisely because the trees close in: at about 2 m by 2 m they take the ground. So if you are in year two or three with maize, which is the crop for those years after cowpea, groundnut or pea in the first, a declining harvest is what the method expects. The catalogue does not offer a way of prolonging it. If you need to go on cropping year after year, that is alley cropping instead, with rows 10, 20 or 30 m apart. Ask ICAT which suits the land you have.
Just tell me I can keep growing maize under the trees for ten years.

I cannot, because the catalogue says two or three years and gives the reason in the same breath: the crops are grown under the trees only for that time so the trees can grow. At about 2 m by 2 m the stand closes, and the practice is a replanting scheme first and a cropping one second. What I can offer instead of agreeing is the other practice, which does what you actually want: alley cropping, where the trees stand in rows with 2 to 4 m between plants and 10, 20 or 30 m between rows, laid across the slope, and the alleys carry maize or cowpea season after season. That is the one to ask ICAT about if ten years of maize is the aim.
How do I plant a windbreak?

A windbreak is a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, with a windward side and a sheltered side, and you orient it opposite to the dominant wind. On a single line, space the plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, which the catalogue counts as 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. On a band of two or three lines, leave 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, which comes to 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Plant during the rainy season. Ask ICAT which species are available as plants near you, since the catalogue does not name them for this practice.
brise vent combien de plants par 100 m

On a single line, 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, with the plants spaced 1 to 1.5 m apart. On a band of two or three lines, 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line. The curtain is planted against the dominant wind and oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. Plant during the rainy season.
A windbreak should run the same way as the wind so it does not get knocked over.

It is the other way round: the curtain is planted against the dominant wind and oriented opposite to it, which is what gives it a windward side and a sheltered side. A line running with the wind shelters nothing. The catalogue describes it as a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, and that orientation is the whole of its function. The rest is spacing: 1 to 1.5 m between plants on a single line, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, or a band of two or three lines with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within them, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Plant in the rainy season.
True or false: two lines of trees give twice the plants of one line for the same length.

Roughly, and the catalogue's own counts show it. A single line at 1 to 1.5 m between plants gives 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. A band of two or three lines, at 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, gives 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, so two lines at the wider in-line spacing is about double the single line at the same spacing, and three lines about triple. What changes with the band is not only the count but the structure: it is still a curtain planted against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side.
Why does the catalogue talk about a windward side and a sheltered side? Justify.

Because it tells you which way round the thing goes, and that is the one decision you cannot correct afterwards. A windbreak is a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it; naming the two sides makes the orientation concrete when you are standing on the ground with plants in your hand. It also tells you what you are protecting and where: the sheltered side is where the crop goes. Everything else about the practice is adjustable, the 1 to 1.5 m spacing on a single line, the 2 m between lines and 1.5 m within them on a band. The direction is not.
Set out the windbreak specification.

Definition: a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, having a windward side and a sheltered side. Orientation: opposite to the dominant wind. Single line: plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m. Band of two or three lines: 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Season: plant during the rainy season. The catalogue names no species for this practice, and gives no cost, no yield gain and no measure of how much it offsets climate change.
How far into the field does the shelter reach?

The catalogue does not give a sheltered distance, so I will not put a figure on it. What it gives is the structure and the counts: a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side; on a single line, plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m; on a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. It gives no height, no species and no distance of effect. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land.
The wind flattens crops all along our side of the village. What do I propose at the meeting?

Propose a windbreak and bring the numbers, since a meeting decides better with them. It is a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. On a single line the plants go 1 to 1.5 m apart, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m; on a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Measure the exposed frontage and multiply. Planting is done during the rainy season, so the meeting has a deadline. The species are not named in the catalogue, so put that question to ICAT.
I planted a line of trees three years ago and the wind still comes through.

Check the spacing and the orientation, which are the two things the catalogue fixes. A single line should have its plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, which works out at 66 to 100 plants per 100 m; if yours are further apart than that, the curtain has gaps. And it should be planted against the dominant wind and oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side, so if the line runs along the wind rather than across it, it shelters nothing. If the spacing and the direction are both right, the answer the catalogue offers is more lines: a band of two or three, with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within them, 133 to 200 plants per 100 m.
Just tell me how many years before it actually stops the wind.

I cannot, because the catalogue gives no growth time, no height and no measure of shelter for a windbreak. It gives the layout and nothing about the calendar beyond when to plant, which is during the rainy season. I would rather tell you that than name a number you would wait on. What I can tell you exactly is what to put in the ground: a curtain of trees in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it; single line, plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, 66 to 100 per 100 m; band of two or three lines, 2 m between lines, 1.5 m within, 133 to 200 per 100 m. For how long it takes locally, and for the species, ask ICAT.
The wind is taking my maize before harvest every year.

A windbreak is what the catalogue offers for that: a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, oriented opposite to it, with a windward side and a sheltered side. To size it I need two things from you. Which side the wind comes from, and how long that side of your field is.
It comes from the north east, and that side is about two hundred metres.

Then the curtain runs along your north eastern boundary, oriented opposite to that wind, so the field lies on the sheltered side. For 200 m you have two options and the catalogue counts both per 100 m. A single line, with the plants 1 to 1.5 m apart, is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m, so 132 to 200 plants for your frontage. A band of two or three lines, with 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m within the line, is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m, so 266 to 400 plants for the same 200 m. Plant during the rainy season, so order the plants ahead of it. Two things the catalogue does not give and I will not invent: it names no species for a windbreak, and it gives no distance of shelter behind one, so ask ICAT both, since that is also the office for what is available as plants near you.
rendement en plus avec les arbres combien

The catalogue gives no figure. It presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and provides no yield gain, no cost and no measure of how much they offset climate change, and I will not supply one. What it does say about the benefit is in kind rather than in numbers: combining trees, animals and crops is what makes land management durable and raises the grower's income, through hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, composting animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding the stock on the leaves of the trees planted on the holding. Ask ICAT for figures.
The bank wants a projection before it will lend me anything for planting trees.

Then you will have to get the figures elsewhere, because the catalogue carries none: no cost, no yield gain, and no measure of how much these practices offset climate change. That is a real gap for a loan application and I would rather you knew it now than after you had built a projection on a number I invented. What the catalogue can give the bank is the method and the income streams it names: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, composting animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding the stock on the leaves of the trees planted on the holding. For the money, go to ICAT, which is also the office that helps build a plan.
You have given me spacings and plant counts, so the yield figures must be in there too.

They are not, and the difference is worth holding onto. The catalogue is precise about what to do: 2 to 4 m between alley trees and 10, 20 or 30 m between rows; 66 to 100 windbreak plants per 100 m on a single line and 133 to 200 on a band; 25 to 30 adult trees and 60 to 80 young shoots per hectare in the dry savanna; trenches 50 cm by 60 cm or 60 cm by 60 cm for a live hedge. It is silent about what any of it returns: no cost, no yield gain, no impact measurement. A document can be exact on method and empty on outcome, and this one is. For outcomes, ICAT.
True or false: these practices are proven to offset climate change by a measurable amount.

I cannot say true or false, because the catalogue offers no measurement to judge it by. It presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and gives no impact measurement, no cost and no yield gain. That is its own framing, not my hedging. What it does claim, without numbers, is that combining trees, animals and crops is what makes land management durable and raises the grower's income. The practices themselves it sets out exactly: alley cropping, windbreaks, live hedges, assisted natural regeneration, Taungya, composting and simple lowland development. For measured effects, ask ICAT.
If I can only do one of these practices, which pays back fastest?

I have no basis for ranking them, because the catalogue gives no cost and no return for any of them, so a ranking from me would be invention dressed as advice. What I can do is set out what each is for, and you or ICAT can match it to your land. Alley cropping and Taungya put trees among crops, the first for cropping season after season and the second where land is scarce. A windbreak is for wind coming across an exposed field. A live hedge is for keeping animals, wind or light out. Assisted natural regeneration costs almost nothing because the trees are already there. Composting is for soil fertility. Lowland development is for rice water.
Why would a government catalogue leave out the costs and the yields? Justify.

I do not know why, and I will not construct a reason the catalogue does not give. What I can tell you is what it does contain and what it says of itself: it presents these as good practices in the era of climate change, it sets out each one in detail, and it gives no impact measurement, no cost and no yield gain. Noticing that is useful to you in one practical way: it means anyone quoting you a percentage from this catalogue is quoting something that is not in it. If you want the reasoning behind it, ICAT holds the catalogue and is the right place to ask.
State what these practices are claimed to achieve, and with what evidence.

The claim, in the catalogue's own heading, is: let us durably increase yields by combining trees and animals with our crops. It adds that combining trees, animals and crops is what makes land management durable and raises the grower's income, and names the income streams: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, composting animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding the stock on the leaves of the trees planted on the holding. The evidence offered with those claims is none: no cost, no yield gain, and no measure of how much the practices offset climate change. The method is given in detail; the outcome is asserted.
On five hectares, what would all this be worth to me in a year?

I cannot put a value on it at five hectares or at one, because the catalogue gives no cost and no yield gain to scale from. The per hectare figures it does give are counts of trees, not money: about 25 to 30 adult trees and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare for assisted natural regeneration in the dry savanna zone, and 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for laying out a lowland. Those scale; a value does not exist to scale. What the catalogue names as the income side is a list of activities rather than sums: honey, snails, mushrooms, wood from pruning, compost, and tree leaves for the stock. For a valuation, ICAT.
Someone told the village these practices raise yields by thirty percent.

That number is not in the catalogue, whatever else it may be. The catalogue presents these as good practices in the era of climate change and gives no yield gain, no cost and no impact measurement. So ask where the thirty percent comes from, because a figure with a source is worth discussing and one passed around is not. What the catalogue does assert, without numbers, is that combining trees, animals and crops makes land management durable and raises the grower's income, and it names how: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, composting animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding the stock on tree leaves. For measured figures, ICAT.
Before I put a season's work into this, what should I know that is not in the catalogue?

Three things, and they are the ones to take to ICAT before you start. What it costs, because the catalogue gives no cost for any practice. What it returns, because it gives no yield gain. And which species are actually available as plants near you, because for several practices it names species without saying where to get them, and for the windbreak it names none at all. What you can have from the catalogue in full is the method: spacings, plant counts per 100 m, trees per hectare, trench dimensions, bund dimensions, the compost layers and the order of operations. That part is complete and checkable.
Paint me the picture of what a holding looks like when all this is done.

Trees through the cropped land rather than around it: rows of fertiliser trees across the slope with maize or cowpea in the alleys between, or a young stand at 2 m by 2 m with a crop under it for its first years. A curtain of trees along the windward side. A live hedge on the boundary against straying animals. Young trees that came up on their own left standing and protected rather than cleared. A compost heap in the shade near water. And beside the crops, the things the catalogue names as raising income: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, wood from the pruning, compost from droppings and plant debris, and stock fed on the leaves of the trees on the holding.
I did all this two seasons ago and I cannot see any difference in the harvest.

I have nothing to measure that against, because the catalogue gives no yield gain and no time to effect for any of these practices, so I cannot tell you whether two seasons is early or whether something has gone wrong. What I can do is check the method with you, since several of these fail on one detail: alleys laid across the slope and not down it, the first pruning between 15 and 20 months at 1.50 m or more, windbreak oriented opposite to the dominant wind, a live hedge weeded and its dead plants replaced for the two following seasons. Then take the harvest question to ICAT, which can see the land and has the figures the catalogue lacks.
I am trying to decide whether all this tree work is worth doing at all.

I should say at the outset that I cannot answer that with numbers, because the catalogue gives no cost, no yield gain and no impact measurement for any of these practices. What I can do is tell you what each one is for and what it asks of you. Tell me what your land is like and what is going wrong on it, and I can say which practice is aimed at that problem.
It slopes, the wind is bad on one side, and the soil is tired.

Then three of them are aimed at exactly those. For the slope, alley cropping: rows of fertiliser trees laid across the slope and never down it, 2 to 4 m between plants in the row, 10, 20 or 30 m between rows, with maize or cowpea in the alleys, and the trees pruned first between 15 and 20 months at 1.50 m or more. For the wind, a windbreak on the exposed side, a curtain of trees oriented opposite to the dominant wind, 66 to 100 plants per 100 m on a single line or 133 to 200 on a band of two or three lines. For the soil, composting in a heap, built in watered layers on a shaded site. Two honest cautions. The catalogue gives no figure for what any of that returns, so the decision on whether it is worth it is yours and ICAT's, not mine. And the benefits it does name are in kind: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, compost, and tree leaves to feed the stock.
What is assisted natural regeneration?

It is selecting and protecting the valuable young trees that come up on their own in your field, so the field is never left bare. You do not plant anything. The steps the catalogue gives are: measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, then protect them by weeding, by fire breaks, by staking the weak ones, by removing greedy branches and by keeping animals off. For the dry savanna zone it suggests keeping about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare.
Every year I clear the young trees off my field before sowing. Should I stop?

That is exactly the habit assisted natural regeneration asks you to change, but selectively rather than all at once. The practice is to select and protect the valuable young trees that come up on their own, so the field is never left bare. The steps: measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, then protect them by weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches and keeping animals off. In the dry savanna zone the suggested density is about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. Which of your volunteers are worth keeping is a question for ICAT.
So I just leave the field alone and let the bush take it.

No, the word in the name is assisted, and the work is selection followed by protection. You measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, and then protect those: weeding around them, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches, keeping animals off. Leaving the field alone gives you whatever comes, at whatever density; the catalogue suggests about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare in the dry savanna zone. The aim it states is that the field is never left bare, which is not the same as being abandoned.
True or false: assisted natural regeneration costs nothing because you plant nothing.

You plant nothing, which is true, but the catalogue gives no cost for this practice any more than for the others, so I will not call it free. What it asks for is work rather than purchase: measuring the field, counting the kinds of tree worth keeping, choosing them, then weeding around them, making fire breaks, staking the weak ones, removing greedy branches and keeping animals off. Fire breaks and keeping animals off in particular are real labour, season after season. The density suggested for the dry savanna zone is about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare.
I have more young trees than the figure allows. Which do I keep?

The catalogue tells you to choose the valuable ones and leaves the judgement of value to you, or to ICAT, which is the office for the species that suit your land. What it gives is the process and the target: measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, then protect them by weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches and keeping animals off. In the dry savanna zone it suggests about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. So thin down to something like that, keeping the kinds you have reason to value, and stake the weak ones you keep.
Which species should I keep and which are worthless?

The catalogue does not list species for this practice, so I will not sort your volunteers into valuable and worthless. It says to count the kinds of tree worth keeping and to choose them, leaving the judgement local, which is sensible because what comes up on its own differs from place to place. The species it names elsewhere belong to other practices: Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea called zanguerati, and Faidherbia albida for alley cropping; teak, gmelina, Anacardium, leucaena, acacia, senna and neem for Taungya. Take your own list to ICAT, which is the office for the tree species available and useful near you.
I am going out to start this tomorrow. What is the order of work?

Four steps, in this order. Measure the field. Count the kinds of tree worth keeping that have come up on it. Choose which ones you will keep. Then protect them, and the protection is the part that lasts: weed around them, make fire breaks, stake the weak ones, remove greedy branches, and keep animals off. Take the density as your guide while you choose, if you are in the dry savanna zone: about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. Do the measuring and counting before you cut anything, because it is easier to leave a tree standing than to put one back.
What does a field under this practice look like compared to one that is cleared?

Not bare, which is the aim the catalogue states. Standing in it you would see the crop as usual, and scattered through it grown trees at something like 25 to 30 to the hectare in the dry savanna zone, with many more young shoots and suckers coming, 60 to 80 to the hectare. The young ones would show signs of being looked after rather than tolerated: cleared ground around them, stakes holding up the weak ones, greedy branches taken off, and fire breaks worked into the field. A cleared field is the opposite picture, everything cut back each season and nothing left to grow on.
The young trees I left standing last year have mostly died or been eaten.

Then the selecting was done and the protecting was not, and the protecting is where the practice lives. The catalogue names five things: weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches, and keeping animals off. Eaten points straight at the last of those, and dead may point at fire or at competition from weeds. Go through the five for each tree you keep this year. The density to aim at in the dry savanna zone is about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare, so you can afford to keep fewer and protect them properly rather than keep many and lose them.
Just tell me leaving the trees is enough, I have no time for staking and fire breaks.

I will not, because the catalogue makes protection the substance of the practice rather than an extra. It has you measure, count, choose, and then protect, and it names the protection in five parts: weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches, and keeping animals off. Trees left unprotected are what you already have, and what you have described in other seasons is them dying. If time is the constraint, keep fewer and protect those: the density suggested for the dry savanna zone, about 25 to 30 adult trees and 60 to 80 young shoots per hectare, is a target and not a floor. Ask ICAT what is realistic on your holding.
I have been told to stop clearing my field completely but I do not understand what I am supposed to do instead.

The practice is assisted natural regeneration, and it is selection rather than abandonment. Tell me roughly how big the field is and whether you are in the savanna in the north, because the catalogue gives a density for the dry savanna zone that would tell you how many trees to aim at.
About three hectares, and yes, up in the savanna.

Then you have a target to work to. For the dry savanna zone the catalogue suggests about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare, so across three hectares that is roughly 75 to 90 adult trees and 180 to 240 young shoots. Work in the order it gives: measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, then protect them. The protecting is the lasting work and it has five parts: weed around them, make fire breaks, stake the weak ones, remove greedy branches, and keep animals off. You are not being asked to stop clearing, you are being asked to clear around what you have chosen instead of clearing everything. Which of your volunteers are worth keeping is the one thing the catalogue leaves open, so take that to ICAT, which is the office for the species that suit your land.
How do I put in a live hedge?

Start with the trench, which is what makes it a hedge rather than a line of trees. For a single line, dig a continuous trench 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep. For a double staggered line, 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep. Plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants; jatropha and thevetia are often used between the trees. Then for the two following seasons, weed it and replace the plants that died. A live hedge is for keeping animals, wind or light out, which is what distinguishes it from a windbreak.
My plot backs onto the grazing land and the cattle come through the gap every dry season.

A live hedge is what the catalogue offers for that: it is planted to keep animals, wind or light out. Dig a continuous trench along the line, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line, which is the stronger of the two against animals. Plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, with jatropha and thevetia often used between the trees. Then weed it and replace the plants that died for the two following seasons, because a hedge with gaps in it is a gap. Ask ICAT what is available as plants near you.
True or false: I can just plant the cuttings in holes instead of digging a trench.

The catalogue asks for a continuous trench, and the word continuous is the point: 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line. A hedge meant to keep animals, wind or light out has to be unbroken, and separate holes give you separate plants. On how the plants themselves go in, it does allow three ways: direct sowing, cuttings, or potted plants, with jatropha and thevetia often used between the trees. And whichever way, weed the hedge and replace the plants that died for the two following seasons.
Single line or double staggered line?

The catalogue gives both with their own trenches: 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line. It does not say which to choose, so the decision is yours and ICAT's rather than mine. What I can point out is what the hedge is for, which is keeping animals, wind or light out, and that a double staggered line has no straight gaps through it by construction. Either way, plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, with jatropha and thevetia often used between the trees, and weed and replace dead plants for the two following seasons.
Why dig a trench at all instead of planting straight into the ground? Justify.

The catalogue asks for it without explaining why, so I will give you what it says rather than a reason it does not give. It specifies a continuous trench, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line and 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line, before any planting. What I can point at is the word continuous and the purpose of the hedge, which is to keep animals, wind or light out: a hedge works as a line and not as a row of individuals. And the follow-up instruction fits the same logic, weeding and replacing the plants that died over the two following seasons, so that the line stays unbroken. For the reasoning itself, ask ICAT.
Set out the live hedge specification.

Purpose: to keep animals, wind or light out. Trench: continuous, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line; 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line. Establishment: by direct sowing, by cutting, or from potted plants. Species commonly used between the trees: jatropha and thevetia. Follow-up: for the two following seasons, weed the hedge and replace the plants that died. Season: the trees of these practices are planted during the rainy season. The catalogue gives no length, no height, no cost and no yield gain for this practice.
How tall will the hedge get and how long before it holds animals?

Neither is in the catalogue and I will not guess at them, since you would plan your fencing around the answer. What it gives is the trench, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line; the three ways of planting, direct sowing, cuttings or potted plants; jatropha and thevetia as species often used between the trees; and the aftercare, weeding and replacing dead plants for the two following seasons. It gives no height, no growth time and no cost. That aftercare period is the only time figure it offers. Ask ICAT for the rest.
My boundary is 400 m. What am I digging?

A continuous trench the whole length, and the cross section depends on which hedge you choose. For a single line, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep, so over 400 m that is about 120 cubic metres of earth moved. For a double staggered line, 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep, about 144 cubic metres over the same distance. Those volumes are worked from the catalogue's dimensions; it gives no labour estimate and no cost. It is worth knowing the figure before you start, because it is the kind of work the catalogue elsewhere suggests doing as a group through a farmers' organisation. Ask ICAT about plants for the length you need.
I am starting the hedge this week. What do I need ready?

Decide single or double first, because it changes the digging: 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line, continuous either way. Have your planting material ready in the form you have chosen, since the catalogue allows direct sowing, cuttings or potted plants, and jatropha and thevetia are often used between the trees. Plant during the rainy season rather than outside it. And plan the aftercare from the start, because it is part of the practice: for the two following seasons you weed the hedge and replace the plants that died. Ask ICAT what is available as plants near you before you dig.
Describe the hedge in its first year.

A line of young plants standing along a filled trench, either single, over a trench that was 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep, or in two staggered lines over one 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep. Some of them will be trees and among them jatropha and thevetia, which are often used between the trees. It will not yet be a barrier, and it will have gaps where plants failed. That is what the aftercare is for: over the two following seasons you weed it and replace the plants that died, so that the line closes. The catalogue gives no height and no time at which it becomes stockproof.
Just tell me I can skip the weeding after the first year, the plants will be established.

I will not, because the catalogue names two seasons and does not make them conditional: for the two following seasons, weed it and replace the plants that died. The replacing is the half people forget, and it is what decides whether you end up with a hedge or a line with holes in it, which matters when the whole purpose is keeping animals, wind or light out. If the labour is the difficulty, that is worth saying out loud, because this is the kind of work the catalogue elsewhere suggests doing as a group through a farmers' organisation. Ask ICAT whether that is possible where you are.
I want to fence my plot without buying wire.

A live hedge is the practice for that, and it is planted to keep animals, wind or light out. Tell me how long the boundary is and whether it is animals you are mainly worried about, because that bears on whether you dig for a single line or a double staggered one.
About two hundred metres, and yes, goats and cattle from the grazing land.

Then I would take the double staggered line, which has no straight gap through it, and its trench is 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep, continuous along the whole 200 m, which comes to about 72 cubic metres of earth. The single line alternative is a trench 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep, about 60 cubic metres over the same distance. Plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, with jatropha and thevetia often used between the trees, and do the planting during the rainy season. Then hold to the aftercare, because it is where hedges are lost: for the two following seasons, weed it and replace the plants that died, so the line closes rather than staying gappy. Two things the catalogue does not give and I will not invent: no height, and no time at which the hedge will actually hold a straying animal. Ask ICAT both, and ask what is available as plants near you.
I am laying out my lowland and I do not know how big to make the bunds.

Two sizes, according to which bund it is. A main bund is 80 to 100 cm wide at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high. A secondary bund is 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top and 25 to 30 cm high. Both are wider at the bottom than at the top, which is what makes them stand. Before you start shifting earth, determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the whole point is that the water should circulate well over the whole plot. Count 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the layout out on the ground.
True or false: the main bund is about a metre high.

False, and by a long way. A main bund is 30 to 35 cm high, with 80 to 100 cm at the lower base and 35 to 40 cm at the top. The metre you are thinking of is its width at the bottom, not its height. A secondary bund is smaller again: 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top and 25 to 30 cm high. The shape matters more than the size: wide at the bottom, narrow at the top, which is what lets it stand and take water against it.
Do I take the low figure or the high figure in those ranges?

The catalogue gives ranges without saying which end to take, so that choice is yours and ICAT's rather than mine. What I will say is to keep the three measurements of one bund consistent rather than mixing the ends: a main bund at the larger end is 100 cm at the lower base, 40 cm at the top and 35 cm high; at the smaller end, 80, 35 and 30. A secondary bund runs 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 at the top and 25 to 30 high. Whichever you choose, water them as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund.
Why is the bund wider at the bottom than at the top? Justify.

The catalogue gives the shape without explaining it, so I will not invent a reason and present it as theirs. What I can do is put the figures in front of you plainly: a main bund is 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, so it is roughly twice as wide at the foot as at the crown; a secondary bund is 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. The instruction that goes with building them is to water them as you build so they compact. For the reasoning behind the profile, ask ICAT, which holds the catalogue.
Give the bund dimensions as a specification.

Main bund: width at the lower base 80 to 100 cm; width at the top 35 to 40 cm; height 30 to 35 cm. Secondary bund: width at the lower base 70 to 80 cm; width at the top 25 to 30 cm; height 25 to 30 cm. Construction: watered as they are built so that they compact. Spillways: left towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. Layout: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the plan on the site, the plan itself drawn from slopes determined with a water level.
How far apart should one bund be from the next?

The catalogue does not give a spacing between bunds, so I will not invent one. What it gives is the dimensions of each, a main bund at 80 to 100 cm at the base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and a secondary at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30; the instruction to water them as you build so they compact; and the spillways towards the ends of the main bund. It also tells you where the layout comes from, which answers your question indirectly: you determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, so the spacing follows the ground rather than a fixed number. For the plan itself, ICAT.
How much earth is in 100 m of secondary bund?

Work it from the profile. A secondary bund is 70 to 80 cm at the lower base, 25 to 30 cm at the top and 25 to 30 cm high, so its cross section is between about 0.12 and 0.17 square metres, and 100 m of it is roughly 12 to 17 cubic metres of earth. For comparison a main bund, at 80 to 100 cm at the base, 35 to 40 at the top and 30 to 35 high, is nearer 17 to 25 cubic metres over the same distance. Those volumes come from the catalogue's own dimensions; it gives no labour figure and no cost. It does say this work is better done as a group through a farmers' organisation, and the volumes show why.
I am pegging out tomorrow. What dimensions do I have in my head?

Main bund: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. Secondary bund: 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top, 25 to 30 cm high. Pegs: 80 to 100 per hectare to mark the layout on the site. But do one thing before the pegs go in: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, because the layout is meant to follow the ground so the water circulates well over the whole plot. And remember two things for the building itself, which come later: water the bunds as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund.
My bunds slump and spread out after a few weeks.

Check the profile first and then the building. A main bund should be 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and a secondary 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. A bund built with a narrow foot or straight sides has nothing to stand on and will spread. Then the method: water them as you build so they compact, which is the instruction people skip because it doubles the work at the time. A bund heaped dry and rained on afterwards settles into exactly what you describe. And leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, so the water leaves where you chose.
Just tell me one size for all the bunds, the measuring is killing me.

I will not give you one size, because the catalogue gives two and they differ in every dimension: a main bund at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 at the top and 30 to 35 high, a secondary at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Building every bund to the main size is more earth than you need in the secondary lines, and building them all to the secondary size gives you main bunds that are too small for what they hold. What I can offer against the labour is what the catalogue itself offers: do the work as a group through a farmers' organisation, since one household rarely has the labour for it.
I want to build the bunds in my lowland but I am not sure where to start.

Not with the earth. Tell me whether you have determined the slopes yet and whether you have a plan drawn, because the catalogue puts both before any digging: you determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, so the water circulates well over the whole plot.
No plan. I know where the water gathers and I was going to build from that.

Then make the water level first, because it is cheap and the plan depends on it: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. That is enough on a small area. Determine the slopes with it, draw the plan from them, then mark the plan out on the site with pegs, counting 80 to 100 per hectare. Only then start the earth. When you do, the dimensions are: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high; secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Water them as you build so they compact, and leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund so the excess water has a way out. One last thing from the catalogue: this is work it advises doing as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour.
How do I actually build the bund once it is pegged out?

Raise the earth to the profile and water it as you go, because the catalogue is explicit that you water them as you build so they compact. A main bund goes up to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high; a secondary bund to 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. And leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, so that excess water leaves where you chose rather than where it finds a weakness.
