Do not skip the watering to save time; a dry heap of earth is not a bund.
construire diguette comment

Raise the earth to the profile and water it as you build, so it compacts. Main bund: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. Secondary: 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30. Leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Before any of it, determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them and mark it out with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare.
We are six of us working on the lowland this week. How do we organise the building?

Six is closer to what this work asks for, and the catalogue advises doing it as a group through a farmers' organisation precisely because one household rarely has the labour. Work to the plan you drew from the slopes, marked out with pegs at 80 to 100 per hectare. Build the main bunds to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and the secondary ones to 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. Keep someone on water, because the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact, and that is what gets dropped when a team is in a hurry. Leave the spillways towards the ends of the main bund.
Watering while building is a waste of time, the rain will pack it down.

The catalogue puts the watering into the building itself: water them as you build so they compact. Rain falling on a loose heap does not do the same thing, it runs off the outside and washes the sides, which is how bunds end up slumped and spread. The compaction has to happen layer by layer while the earth is being raised. It is the single instruction in this practice that costs time at the moment and saves the whole structure, which is why it is worth the argument. The rest of the profile is the other half: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base for a main bund, 35 to 40 at the top, 30 to 35 high.
Build all the main bunds first, or finish one basin completely?

The catalogue does not set an order of work, so I will not pretend it does. What it does fix is that the plan comes first: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, mark it out with pegs at 80 to 100 per hectare, and only then build. Within the building, what must not be split is the watering from the raising, since the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. And the spillways belong to the main bund, towards its ends. For the sequence on your particular site, ask ICAT, and remember the catalogue advises doing the work as a group through a farmers' organisation.
Set out the construction procedure.

Before construction: determine the slopes with a water level; draw the plan from them; mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Construction: raise the bunds to profile, main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30; water them as they are built so that they compact. Openings: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site.
How wide should the spillways be and how many per bund?

The catalogue does not give a width or a number, so I will not invent either; a spillway sized wrong is a breach you built yourself. What it says is where they go and what they are for: leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. The dimensions it does give are the bund profiles, a main bund at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and a secondary at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. For the spillways, ask ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land.
The men in the village build bunds by eye and they have always done it that way.

Then two things from the catalogue are worth putting to them, because they are the ones most often lost when a thing is done by eye. The first is that the plan comes from measurement: you determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them, so the water circulates well over the whole plot, and the level itself is cheap to make, two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. The second is the watering: bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. And the profiles are worth having: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the base, 35 to 40 at the top, 30 to 35 high.
Describe a bund being built properly, as if I were watching.

Pegs already in the ground along a line that was drawn from measured slopes, not chosen by eye, at 80 to 100 pegs to the hectare. Earth being brought to the line and raised in layers rather than tipped, and someone watering each layer as it goes on, because the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. The shape growing wider at the foot than at the crown: for a main bund, 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high. And towards the ends of that main bund, gaps deliberately left rather than filled in, which are the spillways for the excess water.
Just tell me I can build them dry and come back to water them.

I will not, because the instruction is to water them as you build so they compact, and coming back later is exactly what it rules out. Water poured over a finished bund runs off the sides; what compacts the earth is the water going in with it as it is raised. A bund built dry is the one that slumps and spreads after a few weeks, which is the commonest complaint I am asked about. If the difficulty is carrying the water while you build, that is a labour problem, and the catalogue has an answer for labour: carry out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has enough.
The bunds we built last year did not survive the season.

Let me narrow it. Tell me two things: how you built them, in particular whether you watered as you went, and whether you left any openings in the main bund. Those are the two instructions in the catalogue that decide whether a bund survives, and each one is easy to skip.
We heaped the earth and let the rain settle it, and we made the main bund solid all along so nothing could get through.

Both, then, and they failed in two different ways. The earth first: the catalogue says to water the bunds as you build so they compact. Rain on a finished heap runs off the sides and washes them; the water has to go in with the earth as it is raised, layer by layer. That is why yours spread. The openings second: you are meant to leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund, to let excess water out. A bund made solid all along does not stop the water, it makes the water choose its own way out, which is usually through the middle and at the worst moment. This year, peg the plan out again from slopes you have measured with a water level, build the main bunds to 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, water as you go, and leave the spillways where the catalogue puts them.
niveau d'eau paysan fabrication

Two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. That is the farmer-made water level the catalogue describes, and it says it is enough on a small area. You use it to determine the slopes, and you draw the plan of the basins and drains from those slopes, so that the water moves properly over the whole plot. Then mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare, before any earth is moved.
I have about a hectare of lowland and no instruments of any kind.

You can make what you need. The catalogue describes a farmer-made water level as two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and says it is enough on a small area, which a hectare is. Use it to determine the slopes across the plot, then draw the plan of the basins and drains from those slopes, so the water moves properly over the whole of it. Mark the plan out with pegs, counting 80 to 100 per hectare, so for your hectare that is 80 to 100 pegs. Only then start on the bunds. And the catalogue advises doing the work as a group, because one household rarely has the labour.
A water level tells you where the water will go.

It tells you the slopes, and you work out where the water will go from them. The catalogue has you determine the slopes with the level and then draw the plan from them, so the instrument gives you the ground and the plan is your reading of it. The level itself is simple: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, which it says is enough on a small area. What the plan is for is stated too: basins and drains built so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which is what lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel.
True or false: the water level needs to be bought from a shop.

False. The catalogue describes one you make yourself: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and it says that is enough on a small area. That is the whole specification. You use it to determine the slopes, then draw the plan of basins and drains from them so the water circulates well over the whole plot, then mark the plan out with pegs at 80 to 100 per hectare. The instrument is the cheapest part of the whole development; the earth is where the work is.
Measure the slopes myself with the level, or go by where the water already stands?

Measure. The catalogue puts it as the first step: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from them. Where the water already stands tells you about this year's rain on this year's ground, and the plan you are drawing has to work over the whole plot, not just around the wet corner. The level is not a barrier either, since you make it yourself from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and the catalogue says that is enough on a small area. Then peg the plan out, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and build.
Why measure slopes at all? The lowland is flat. Justify.

Because a lowland that looks flat is what the level is for: differences too small to see are exactly the ones that decide where water sits, and the aim stated in the catalogue is that the water should move properly over the whole plot so you can regulate how much sits on each parcel. Eye judgement gives you the obvious low corner and nothing else. The catalogue therefore has you determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan from those slopes, before pegging and before any earth is moved. The level costs you two sticks graduated every 5 cm and a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top.
Is the home-made level good enough for a plot of five hectares?

The catalogue says a farmer-made water level is enough on a small area, and five hectares is stretching what that phrase plainly covers, so I will not tell you it is fine. The level it describes is two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top; a 5 m hose across five hectares is a great many readings. Put that question to ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land. What does scale from the catalogue is the pegging, 80 to 100 per hectare, so five hectares is 400 to 500 pegs, and the advice to do the work as a group through a farmers' organisation.
The group wants to develop the lowland together and asked me to explain the first steps.

Tell them nothing is dug until the ground has been measured. Step one, make a water level: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, which the catalogue says is enough on a small area. Step two, determine the slopes with it. Step three, draw the plan of the basins and drains from those slopes, so the water moves properly over the whole plot. Step four, mark the plan out on the site with pegs, 80 to 100 per hectare. Then the earth. Tell them also that the catalogue advises exactly what they are proposing, carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, and that trees cleared from the site are to be replanted elsewhere.
Describe the level so I can make one.

Two sticks, each graduated every 5 cm along its length. Between them a garden hose 5 m long, joining one to the other, with a clear tube at the top of each stick so you can see the water inside. That is the whole of what the catalogue describes, and it calls it enough on a small area. What it does not give is how to hold it, how to read it or how many readings to take, so I will not add those from memory; ask ICAT or someone who has used one. What you do with the readings is stated: determine the slopes, and draw the plan of basins and drains from them.
Water stands in one part of my plot and the other end never gets enough.

That is the problem the whole practice is aimed at. The catalogue's stated aim is to build basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Start where it starts: determine the slopes with a water level, which you can make from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and draw the plan from those slopes rather than from where the water happens to stand now. Then peg it out, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and build the bunds, watered as you build, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund.
Just tell me I can lay it out by eye, I have farmed this lowland for twenty years.

I will not, and the twenty years are the reason to bother rather than the reason to skip it. You know where the water stands; the plan has to make it move properly over the whole plot, which is a different question and one that turns on differences too small to see. The catalogue puts the measurement first: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then build. The level costs two sticks graduated every 5 cm and a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. Set against the earth you are about to move, 17 to 25 cubic metres per 100 m of main bund, it is nothing.
I want to develop my lowland properly this year.

Then the first question is not about earth. Have you measured the slopes? The catalogue begins there: determine the slopes with a water level and draw the plan of the basins and drains from them, so the water moves properly over the whole plot. Tell me the size of the lowland and whether you have any way of measuring.
Two hectares, and no, I have nothing to measure with.

Then make the level, because it is the cheapest part of the whole job: two sticks graduated every 5 cm, joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, which the catalogue says is enough on a small area. Determine the slopes with it, then draw your plan of basins and drains from what you find. Mark that plan out on the site with pegs, counting 80 to 100 per hectare, so for two hectares between 160 and 200 pegs. Then the earth: main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30, watered as you build so they compact, with spillways left towards the ends of the main bund. Two more things the catalogue asks. Do the work as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. And replant elsewhere any trees you clear from the site.
Who should be doing this lowland work?

A group, if you can manage it. The catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, and it gives the reason plainly: one household rarely has the labour for it. The volumes show why, since 100 m of main bund is something like 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth. There is a second instruction about the site itself that is easy to overlook: replant elsewhere the trees you clear from it. So the work is a group undertaking and the clearing carries an obligation with it.
amenagement bas-fond seul ou en groupe

As a group, through a farmers' organisation. That is what the catalogue advises, because one household rarely has the labour for the work. And whatever is cleared from the site is to be replanted elsewhere: the trees you take off the lowland go back somewhere. The rest of the work follows the plan you drew from slopes measured with a water level, pegged out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare.
It is my plot, so it is my work and nobody else's business.

The catalogue is advising rather than ruling, but it advises the opposite and says why: carry out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. That is an observation about the size of the job rather than about ownership. A hundred metres of main bund is roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth, raised and watered as it is built so it compacts, and that is before the secondary bunds and the drains. The other site instruction does reach beyond your plot, though: the trees you clear from the lowland are to be replanted elsewhere.
True or false: I can clear the trees off the lowland and that is the end of it.

False. The catalogue asks for a compensatory replanting: the trees cleared from the site are to be replanted elsewhere. That instruction sits directly beside its advice to carry out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. So clearing is allowed and it carries an obligation. Plan where the replanting goes before you start clearing, not after, and remember the catalogue's other practices give you places to put trees: an alley cropping layout, a windbreak on an exposed side, a live hedge on a boundary.
Why does the catalogue tell me to work in a group? Justify.

It gives the reason itself: one household rarely has the labour. The figures behind that are in the same practice. A hundred metres of main bund is roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres of earth at the profile given, 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, and the secondary bunds add more. All of it is watered as it is built so it compacts, which means carrying water alongside the earth. And it has to be finished within a season to be of use. That is a quantity of work a family does not get through, which is why the advice is to do it as a group through a farmers' organisation.
State the organisational and site requirements.

Organisation: the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group, through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. Site: replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site. Those sit alongside the technical sequence, which is to determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of basins and drains from them, mark that plan out on the site with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then build the bunds to profile, watering them as they are built so they compact, with spillways left towards the ends of the main bund.
How many people do I need and how many days will it take?

Neither figure is in the catalogue and I will not invent them, because you would plan a season around them. What it says is that one household rarely has the labour and that the development is better carried out as a group through a farmers' organisation. The quantities I can give you are of earth rather than of labour: at the profile given, 100 m of main bund is roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres, and 100 m of secondary bund roughly 12 to 17. Take those to ICAT, or to a group that has done it, and they will turn them into people and days better than I can.
On half a hectare, could one family manage it alone?

The catalogue does not set a threshold, so I cannot tell you half a hectare is under it. What it says is general: one household rarely has the labour, and the development is better carried out as a group through a farmers' organisation. What does scale is the pegging, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, so 40 to 50 for your half, and the earth, at roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres per 100 m of main bund. Work out the length of bund your plan actually calls for and you will have a real idea of the job. For whether a family can do it, ask someone locally who has, or ICAT.
Before we start clearing the site, what do we settle?

Two things the catalogue puts at this stage. Where the cleared trees will be replanted, because it asks you to replant elsewhere the trees cleared from the site, and that is much easier to arrange before the clearing than after. And who is doing the work, since it advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, one household rarely having the labour. Settle both before the first tree comes down. Then the technical order: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and only then move earth.
Describe how this work is meant to be organised on the ground.

Not as one family working a corner at a time, but as a group working to one plan. The catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. On the ground that means the slopes measured once for the whole lowland, one plan of basins and drains drawn from them, the whole thing pegged out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and then earth raised along those lines with water carried alongside, since the bunds are watered as they are built so they compact. And somewhere off the site, the trees cleared from it going back into the ground.
We started this two seasons ago and it is still half finished.

That is the failure the catalogue's advice is meant to prevent: it says to carry out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour. Half a development is often worse than none, because water diverted by an incomplete set of bunds goes somewhere you did not plan. Two things to do. Get more hands, through the farmers' organisation if there is one, and finish to the plan rather than adding pieces. And check what is already built, because bunds raised in a hurry are often the ones built dry, where the instruction is to water them as you build so they compact.
Just tell me I can do it alone over a few seasons.

I will not encourage it, because the catalogue's own words are that one household rarely has the labour, and because an unfinished development redirects water without controlling it. If you have no group available, that is a real constraint and worth taking to ICAT, which is the office for the practice that suits your land; there may be a farmers' organisation you have not been offered. What I would not do is start the earth before the plan is complete: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan, peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. And whatever the pace, replant elsewhere the trees you clear from the site.
There is a lowland below the village that nobody has developed.

Then the first questions are about people rather than about earth. Is there a farmers' organisation in the village, and who holds the land? The catalogue advises carrying out this kind of development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour for it.
There is a growers' group, and the land is shared between several families.

That is the arrangement the catalogue has in mind, so take it to the group rather than doing a corner yourself. Put three things in front of them. The sequence: determine the slopes across the whole lowland with a water level, which you can make from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top; draw one plan of basins and drains from those slopes so the water moves properly over the whole plot; peg that plan out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. The work: main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30, watered as they are built so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund. And the obligation: any trees cleared from the site are to be replanted elsewhere, so the group should decide where before the clearing starts.
How do I mark the layout out on the ground?

With pegs, and the catalogue gives the count: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the plan out on the site. But the pegs come third rather than first. You determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of the basins and drains from those slopes, and then set the pegs along what you have drawn. Only after that do you move earth, building the bunds to profile and watering them as you build so they compact. Pegging before the slopes are known is marking out a guess.
The plan is drawn and I am ready to mark it out on the lowland tomorrow.

Then count your pegs against the area: 80 to 100 per hectare is what the catalogue gives for marking the plan out on the site. Cut them before you go, because running short halfway leaves you guessing the rest of the line. Mark the main bunds and the secondary ones distinctly if you can, since they are built to different profiles: main at 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, secondary at 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. And mark where the spillways go, towards the ends of the main bund, so they are not filled in by mistake when the earth goes up.
The pegs are just to show where to dig, so a few will do.

A few will not hold a line. The catalogue counts 80 to 100 pegs per hectare for marking the plan out on the site, which is a peg every few metres rather than one at each corner, and the reason is that the lines are not straight runs but a plan drawn from measured slopes. The whole point of that plan is that the water should move properly over the whole plot, so a line that wanders between two distant pegs is a line that does not follow the ground you measured. Cut the full number before you start, and keep the spillway positions marked, towards the ends of the main bund.
True or false: eighty pegs is enough for any lowland.

False as stated, because the figure is per hectare and not per lowland: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the layout out on the site. On one hectare, 80 to 100; on three, 240 to 300. Count your own area first. And the pegs are only the third step: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of basins and drains from them, and then peg that plan out. If the lowland is large, that is also a signal about labour, since the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation.
Eighty pegs or a hundred? Which end of the range?

The catalogue gives 80 to 100 per hectare without saying which end to take, so I will not pretend it does. What should push you towards the upper end is a plan with many turns in it, since the pegs are there to hold lines drawn from measured slopes rather than straight runs; a simple layout on gentle ground needs fewer. Cut extra rather than fewer, because running short in the middle of pegging is what makes people straighten a line that should have curved. And mark the spillway positions among them, towards the ends of the main bund.
Why does the catalogue count pegs per hectare at all? Justify.

Because it is the one figure that lets you prepare before the day. Pegs have to be cut and carried, and a team that arrives with too few either stops or straightens lines it should not straighten. Giving it per hectare, 80 to 100, makes it something you can work out from your own plot before you start. It also tells you indirectly how fine the marking is meant to be: at that density the pegs follow the plan closely rather than marking corners, which matters because the plan came from slopes you measured with a water level and its whole purpose is that the water moves properly over the whole plot.
Specify the layout stage.

Inputs: the slopes, determined with a water level; the plan of basins and drains, drawn from those slopes. Operation: mark the plan out on the site. Material: 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. Outputs to mark: the lines of the main bunds, which will be built 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high; the lines of the secondary bunds, 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30; and the spillway positions, towards the ends of the main bund. The catalogue gives no peg length, no spacing in metres and no cost.
The group asked me how many pegs to prepare for Saturday.

Eighty to a hundred per hectare, which is what the catalogue counts for marking the plan out on the site. Multiply by the area of the lowland and cut a few over rather than under. Tell them also that the pegging is not the first job: the slopes have to be determined with a water level and the plan of basins and drains drawn from them before anything is marked, so if that has not been done, the day is for measuring rather than for pegs. And remind them that the catalogue advises exactly this way of working, carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour.
What do I do the evening before the pegging?

Cut the pegs, counting 80 to 100 per hectare, and count the area rather than guessing it. Have the plan with you in a form you can read on the ground, since it is what the pegs are marking: the plan of the basins and drains drawn from slopes you determined with a water level. Decide how you will distinguish the main bund lines from the secondary ones, because they are built to different profiles. And mark on the plan where the spillways go, towards the ends of the main bund, so they are pegged as openings rather than forgotten once the earth starts going up.
Describe the lowland once it is pegged and before any earth is moved.

Lines of pegs following curves rather than straight runs, because the plan came from slopes measured with a water level and not from the eye. Enough of them to read the line without guessing, which at 80 to 100 to the hectare is a peg every few paces. Two kinds of line, the main bunds and the secondary ones, which will become different profiles: 80 to 100 cm at the lower base for a main bund against 70 to 80 for a secondary. And towards the ends of the main bund lines, gaps marked deliberately, which will be left open as spillways when the earth goes up.
We pegged it out last month and now half the pegs are gone.

Then peg it again from the plan rather than joining what is left, because a line reconstructed by eye between surviving pegs is no longer the line you measured. Count what you need afresh, 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and work from the drawn plan of basins and drains. If the plan itself has gone, the slopes have to be determined again with a water level, which you can make from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. And once pegged, move sooner: the catalogue advises doing this work as a group through a farmers' organisation, which is also how it gets finished before the marks disappear.
Just tell me twenty pegs will do, I know the shape of my land.

I will not, because the figure is 80 to 100 per hectare and twenty is a small fraction of it. The pegs are not there to remind you of a shape you know, they are there to hold a line drawn from slopes you measured, and at twenty you will be joining distant marks by eye, which is the thing the measuring was for. If cutting pegs is the burden, that is a labour question, and the catalogue's answer to labour on this practice is to carry out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation. Ask ICAT if you want the count argued rather than asserted.
amenagement simple bas-fond c'est quoi

Building basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. The sequence: determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan from them, mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, then raise the bunds to profile, watering them as you build so they compact, leaving spillways towards the ends of the main bund. The catalogue advises doing the work as a group through a farmers' organisation.
True or false: the aim is to keep as much water as possible on the plot.

False as stated. The aim the catalogue gives is that the water should move properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Regulate, not maximise: that is why there are drains as well as basins, and why you leave spillways towards the ends of the main bund to let excess water out. A plot that simply holds everything is the problem, not the solution, which is usually why one corner stands in water while the other end dries. The control comes from the plan, drawn from slopes measured with a water level.
Basins or drains, which do I build first?

The catalogue does not set an order between them, so I will not invent one. What it does fix is that both come after the plan: you determine the slopes with a water level, draw the plan of the basins and drains from them, and mark it out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare before moving earth. The two work together, since the stated aim is that the water moves properly over the whole plot so you can regulate how much sits on each parcel, which needs somewhere for it to go as well as somewhere for it to stay. For the order of work on your site, ask ICAT.
Why go to all this trouble instead of just growing rice where the water already is? Justify.

Because where the water already is, is one corner, and the rest of the plot is either dry or drowned. The aim the catalogue states is that the water should move properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel, and that regulation is what makes the whole lowland usable rather than the part that happens to be right this year. It also turns the water from something that happens to you into something you decide about, through the basins, the drains and the spillways towards the ends of the main bund. The catalogue gives no yield figure for this, and I will not supply one.
Is this worth doing on a small lowland, say half a hectare?

The catalogue sets no minimum area and gives no cost or yield figure, so I cannot tell you it pays at half a hectare. What it does say fits a small plot: the farmer-made water level, two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, is described as enough on a small area. The pegs would be 40 to 50 for your half hectare at 80 to 100 per hectare. The earth is what it is, roughly 17 to 25 cubic metres per 100 m of main bund. For whether it is worth it on your ground, ask ICAT.
Someone asked me to explain in one go what developing a lowland involves.

Say it in five steps. Make a water level, two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. Determine the slopes with it. Draw the plan of basins and drains from those slopes, so the water moves properly over the whole plot and you can regulate how much sits on each parcel. Mark the plan out with 80 to 100 pegs per hectare. Then build: main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 at the top, 30 to 35 high, secondary 70 to 80, 25 to 30, 25 to 30, watered as you build so they compact, spillways towards the ends of the main bund. And do it as a group.
We have agreed to do it. What is the very first thing?

Make the water level and measure. The catalogue starts there: determine the slopes with a water level, and draw the plan of the basins and drains from them. The level is two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and it says that is enough on a small area. Everything after depends on it: the plan, the pegging at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, and the earth. Two other things to settle at the same time, before clearing: who does the work, since it advises doing it as a group through a farmers' organisation, and where the trees cleared from the site will be replanted.
Describe a developed lowland so I know what I am aiming at.

A plot divided into basins by bunds that follow the ground rather than straight lines, because the layout came from slopes measured with a water level. Main bunds broad at the foot and narrow at the crown, 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, with smaller secondary bunds between them. Drains running with them, so the water has a way through as well as a place to stay. Towards the ends of the main bunds, spillways left open for the excess. The whole thing arranged so the water moves properly over the plot and you can regulate what sits on each parcel.
My rice drowns at one end and burns at the other in the same season.

That is exactly the condition this practice is aimed at. The aim the catalogue states is to build basins and drains so that the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. Begin where it begins, with measurement rather than with earth: determine the slopes with a water level, made from two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, and draw the plan from them. Then peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare and build, watering the bunds as you go so they compact, with spillways towards the ends of the main bund.
The lowland floods and then dries and I get almost nothing from it.

That is the problem simple lowland development is written for: basins and drains built so the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much sits on each parcel. Tell me how big the plot is and whether anyone else farms the same lowland, because both bear on how to go about it.
A bit over a hectare, and three other families have plots beside mine.

Then go to them before you start, because the catalogue advises carrying out the development as a group through a farmers' organisation, one household rarely having the labour, and because water does not stop at a plot boundary: a plan drawn for your hectare alone will move water onto theirs. Measure the whole lowland together. Make the water level first, two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top, which the catalogue says is enough on a small area. Determine the slopes, draw one plan of basins and drains from them, and peg it out at 80 to 100 pegs per hectare, so a little over 80 to 100 for your own share. Then build: main bunds 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bunds 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30, watered as you build so they compact, and spillways left towards the ends of the main bund. Any trees you clear go back in elsewhere.
I want to fill a compost heap but I am not sure what I am allowed to put in it.

Tell me what you have on the farm after the harvest and I will sort it for you. The catalogue divides residues in two: the ones that rot fast go in, chopped first, and the ones that rot slowly are kept out of that layer.
Groundnut haulms, a lot of maize stalks, some rice husks, and straw.

Three of those four have a place and one does not. The groundnut leaves are exactly what is wanted, named with straw and the leaves of soya and cowpea among the residues that rot fast, so chop them and they make the main layer, about 30 cm, trodden down well. Your straw goes in with them. The rice husks are named as a slow rotting material, and that is not a rejection: they are one of the two the catalogue gives for the base of the heap, with ronier leaves, 10 to 20 cm thick. The maize stalks are the ones with no place here, named with the stalks of sorghum and millet among the slow rotting ones to avoid, so keep them out and ask ICAT what to do with them instead, because the catalogue does not say. Build on a shaded site out of the wind and rain: a little wood ash on the topsoil, the husks as the base, 5 cm of manure, then your chopped groundnut and straw, then topsoil, well rotted compost or Mycotri as the activator, watering each layer as you lay it.
acheter semence mais ou

Only from approved sellers. The ITRA and ICAT maize brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, and against sowing grain taken from your own granary, because it germinates badly. For the list of approved sellers near you, ask ICAT or ITRA; they are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season. The list of released varieties in the brochure dates from 2008 and may have grown since, so the current one is with ICAT.
I have a good crop in the granary this year and I was going to keep some back for seed.

The brochure advises against it: sowing grain taken from your own granary germinates badly, and that is the reason it gives. Good grain to eat and good seed to sow are not the same thing. Buy improved seed from an approved seller instead, and the same brochure warns against buying it anywhere else. What you get for the trouble is what the released varieties carry: cycles from 75 to 115 days, potential yields from 3 to 7 tonnes a hectare, tolerance to striga in TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, tolerance to drought in Amen. ICAT or ITRA holds the list of approved sellers near you.
True or false: seed from a neighbour who grew improved maize last year is as good as buying it.

I have no line on a neighbour's seed specifically, so I will not rule on that case. What the brochure does say is twofold: buy improved seed only from approved sellers, and do not sow grain taken from your own granary because it germinates badly. Both point the same way, which is that seed is bought as seed rather than picked out of a harvest. If the cost is what pushes you towards the neighbour, weigh it against what you are buying: the released varieties run from 75 to 115 days of cycle and 3 to 7 tonnes a hectare of potential yield. Ask ICAT or ITRA for the approved sellers near you.
Cheap seed from the market or the approved seller further away?

The approved seller. The brochure is explicit: buy the seed only from approved sellers, and it warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. Seed sold cheap at a market may be anything, including grain out of somebody's granary, which the same brochure says germinates badly. The cost of being wrong is a season, not the price difference. Ask ICAT or ITRA for the list of approved sellers near you, and ask them at the same time which variety suits your region this season, since that is the other thing they hold.
Why insist on approved sellers? Seed is seed. Justify.

Because what you are buying is not visible in the bag. A variety is a set of properties, the cycle, the potential yield, the tolerance to striga or to streak or to drought, and none of those can be seen in a grain; you are relying on the seed being what it is said to be. That is what approval is for. The brochure puts it as an instruction, buy the seed only from approved sellers, and warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. It adds the related warning, that grain from your own granary germinates badly, which is the other way people end up sowing something other than what they intended.
State the brochure's seed sourcing rules.

Two rules. Buy the seed only from approved sellers; the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. And do not sow grain taken from your own granary, because it germinates badly. Alongside them the brochure gives the basis for choosing what to buy: weigh the variety on its cycle and on its yield, those being the two things it tells you to consider. For the list of approved sellers near you, and for which variety suits your region this season, it refers you to ICAT or ITRA. The released list it carries is that of 2008 and may have grown since.
Who are the approved sellers in my prefecture?

I cannot name them. The brochure tells you to buy the seed only from approved sellers and warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, but it does not list them, and the list would change from year to year in any case. ICAT or ITRA holds it, and that is the same place to ask which variety suits your region this season. What I can give you without guessing is what to ask for once you are there: cycle and yield are the two things the brochure says to weigh, and the released varieties run from 75 to 115 days and from 3 to 7 tonnes a hectare of potential yield.
I am sowing three hectares. Does buying approved seed still make sense at that size?

The brochure gives no threshold and its rule is not conditioned on area: buy the seed only from approved sellers, and do not sow grain from your own granary because it germinates badly. If anything the argument is stronger on three hectares than on one, because a poor germination is multiplied by the area. What I cannot give you is the seed rate per hectare or the price, neither of which is in what I hold, so the total cost is a question for the approved seller and for ICAT. Ask them at the same time which variety suits your region this season.
Half the village sows seed from their own granaries. What do I say to them?

Say what the brochure says and why. It advises against sowing grain taken from your own granary, and the reason it gives is that it germinates badly, which is the thin patchy stand people then blame on the rain. And it says to buy improved seed only from approved sellers, warning against buying it anywhere else. Then give them the reason it is worth the money: the released varieties carry properties you cannot get from granary grain, tolerance to striga in TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, tolerance to drought in Amen, tolerance to streak in most of them. ICAT or ITRA has the approved sellers.
My maize germinated badly this year, whole stretches with nothing.

Where the seed came from is the first thing to ask. The brochure advises against sowing grain taken from your own granary precisely because it germinates badly, and against buying improved seed anywhere but from approved sellers. If your seed came from either of those places, that is the likeliest answer and it is one you can change next season. If it came from an approved seller, the cause lies elsewhere and is not something I can diagnose from here; take it to ICAT or ITRA, who are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season. Keep the bag and the seller's details if you still have them.
Just tell me granary grain will do this once, I have no money for seed.

I will not tell you it will do, because the brochure says the opposite and gives the reason: grain taken from your own granary germinates badly. Saying yes would cost you the stand rather than the seed money. What I can do is take the constraint seriously. Go to ICAT or ITRA and ask two things: who the approved sellers are, and whether there is any arrangement for seed where you are, because that is a question they can answer and I cannot. And if you must sow a reduced area with bought seed rather than a full one with granary grain, that is a real option and worth putting to them.
I am getting my seed together for the season.

Then two questions before you buy. Where are you getting it from, and do you know which variety you want? The brochure is firm on the first, buy the seed only from approved sellers and not from anywhere else, and it says to choose the variety on its cycle and on its yield.
There is a man in the market who sells it cheaper, and I was going to take whatever he has.

Then change both halves. On the seller: the ITRA and ICAT brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere but from approved sellers, and a bag bought in a market may be granary grain, which the same brochure says germinates badly. Ask ICAT or ITRA for the list of approved sellers near you. On the variety: taking whatever he has means taking a cycle and a yield you did not choose, and those are the two things the brochure tells you to weigh. The released list runs from TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM at 75 to 85 days and 3 tonnes a hectare potential, through Amen and AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR in the middle, to Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days and 6 tonnes, and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka at 105 to 115 days and 7 tonnes. If striga grows in your field, the two marked for it are TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W; if your season is short of rain, Amen is the one marked drought tolerant. That list is from 2008 and may have grown, so ask ICAT for the current one.
The variety with the biggest yield is the right choice for everybody.

The brochure tells you to weigh two things, not one: the cycle and the yield. The biggest yields belong to ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, both at 7 tonnes a hectare potential, and both take 105 to 115 days. If your rains do not run that long, that yield is on paper. It also tells you to match the variety to your constraint: if striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two marked striga tolerant; if your season is short of rain, take Amen, the one marked drought tolerant. Which suits your region this season is a question for ICAT or ITRA.
True or false: there is one variety that answers both striga and short rains.

False, on the brochure's own markings. The two it marks as striga tolerant are TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days. The one it marks as drought tolerant is Amen, 90 to 95 days. No variety carries both marks. If you have both problems, that is a real choice to make and the brochure does not make it for you; take it to ICAT or ITRA, who are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season. Note in passing that the short striga tolerant one, TZEE W Pop STR QPM at 75 to 85 days, is the shortest cycle on the list.
Striga in the field and a short season. Which of the two striga varieties?

TZEE W Pop STR QPM, on cycle. The two marked striga tolerant are TZEE W Pop STR QPM at 75 to 85 days and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W at 105 to 115 days, and with a short season the second is thirty to forty days longer than you can carry. What you give up is yield: TZEE W Pop STR QPM is 3 tonnes a hectare potential and 1.5 to 2 on average, against 7 and 3 to 4 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. That is the trade the brochure puts in front of you when it says to weigh the cycle and the yield. Ask ICAT or ITRA whether it suits your region this season.
Why should the problem in my field decide the variety? Justify.

Because for two of the problems the variety is the control, and no other action replaces it. Most of the improved varieties are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the control against streak. For striga, the brochure names two that tolerate it, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. For a season short of rain it names Amen. Choosing on yield alone leaves those problems to be dealt with some other way, and the brochure does not offer another way in this section. That is why it says to weigh the cycle and the yield, and then points you at the constraint.
Set out the decision rule for choosing a variety.

First, the two criteria the brochure names: the cycle and the yield. Second, the constraints, which override: if striga grows in the field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, the two marked striga tolerant; if the season is short of rain, take Amen, 90 to 95 days, the one marked drought tolerant; for streak, most of the improved varieties are tolerant, so choosing an improved variety is itself the control, and AB11 is the one marked for it. Third, the seed rule: buy only from approved sellers. Fourth, refer: ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.
Which variety is best for Kara specifically?

I cannot answer by region, because the brochure's table does not carry one: it gives cycle, potential and average yield, grain colour and the tolerances, and nothing about where each variety suits. Which variety suits your region this season is exactly what it refers you to ICAT or ITRA for. What I can do is narrow it by your own constraints: striga in the field points to TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, a season short of rain points to Amen, and the cycle has to fit the rains you actually get, which run from 75 to 85 days at the short end of the list to 105 to 115 at the long end.
I have two fields, one with striga and one clean. Two different varieties?

Nothing in the brochure stops you, and the constraint rule points that way: if striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two it marks as striga tolerant. On the clean field you are free to choose on the cycle and the yield alone, which are the two criteria it names, so you could take a higher yielder such as Obatanpa at 6 tonnes potential and 3.5 to 4 on average, or Sotubaka at 7 and 3 to 4, if your rains carry 100 to 115 days. Buy both from approved sellers, and ask ICAT or ITRA whether both suit your region this season.
A neighbour's field is full of striga and he is about to sow whatever he has.

Tell him the variety is the lever here. The brochure names two tolerant to striga: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 tonnes a hectare potential and 1.5 to 2 on average, and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, 7 tonnes potential and 3 to 4 on average. Which of the two depends on how long his rains run. Tell him also to buy from an approved seller, since the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else and against sowing granary grain, which germinates badly. And send him to ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits the region this season.
I am going to buy seed tomorrow. What do I settle tonight?

Settle three things. Your constraint: is there striga in the field, and are your rains short? If striga, the two marked for it are TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W; if short rains, Amen. Your cycle: what length of season you can actually carry, since the list runs from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115. And your seller: an approved one, because the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else and against granary grain, which germinates badly. Then ask at the counter which variety suits your region this season, or put that to ICAT or ITRA, since the brochure sends it there.
Describe how the choice actually goes, step by step.

You start from the field rather than from the table. If striga grows in it, you are choosing between TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. If your season is short of rain, you are looking at Amen. If neither, you are free. Then you take the cycle: what your rains carry, somewhere between 75 to 85 days at the short end and 105 to 115 at the long. That usually leaves two or three names. Then you take the yield among those that are left, potential and average side by side. Then you go to an approved seller, and you ask ICAT or ITRA whether what you have chosen suits your region this season.
Every year my maize is caught by the dry spell at the end.

Then look at the cycle before anything else, because a variety that needs longer than your rains give will be caught every year whatever else you do. The list runs from TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM at 75 to 85 days, through Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95, AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR at 90 to 100, Obatanpa at 100 to 110, to ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka at 105 to 115. And the brochure names one specifically for your case: if your season is short of rain, take Amen, the one marked drought tolerant, 90 to 95 days. Ask ICAT or ITRA whether it suits your region.
Just give me one name and I will sow it, I do not want a list.

I will give you one name if you give me one fact: is there striga in the field, and do your rains run short? Without that I would be choosing for a field I cannot see, and the brochure's whole instruction is to match the variety to the constraint and then weigh the cycle and the yield. If you tell me striga, the answer is TZEE W Pop STR QPM for a short season or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W for a long one. If you tell me short rains, the answer is Amen. If you tell me neither, and your rains carry 100 days, the answer is Obatanpa. Then buy it from an approved seller.
What do the two numbers mean, potential yield and average yield?

The potential yield is the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, and the brochure names what it means by good: rain, fertilisation, pest attack, upkeep of the field. The average column stands beside it in the same table and is what the variety gives ordinarily. So Obatanpa shows 6 tonnes a hectare potential and 3.5 to 4 on average; Sotubaka shows 7 and 3 to 4; TZEE W Pop STR QPM shows 3 and 1.5 to 2. Plan on the average column and treat the potential as what good conditions could give, not as what you are owed.
cycle court ou long mais

Both are on the list and the brochure tells you to weigh the cycle against the yield. Short: TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 tonnes a hectare potential, 1.5 to 2 on average. Long: ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, 105 to 115 days, 7 tonnes potential, 3 to 4 on average. The longer varieties carry more yield and need the rains to last. Choose the cycle your season actually gives you first. ICAT or ITRA for which suits your region this season.
My rains usually run about ninety days and I want the most I can get.

Then the varieties that fit your season are the ones at 90 to 95 and 90 to 100 days, and among those the best yielder on the list is Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100 days, 5 tonnes a hectare potential and 2 to 3.5 on average, which the brochure also marks as very steady in yield. Beside it sit Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95 days and AB11 at 90 to 100, all at 4 tonnes potential and 2 to 3 on average. Going longer would mean Obatanpa at 100 to 110 days, which is more than ninety. Check with ICAT or ITRA that it suits your region this season, and buy from an approved seller.
A seven tonne variety gives more than a five tonne one, so it is the better buy.

Only if your season carries it, and the averages narrow the gap. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka show 7 tonnes a hectare potential but 3 to 4 on average, and both take 105 to 115 days. Ikenne 9449 SR shows 5 potential and 2 to 3.5 on average over 90 to 100 days, and the brochure marks it as very steady in yield. Between 3 to 4 and 2 to 3.5 there is less than the seven against five suggests, and the long varieties need twenty more days of rain. That is why the brochure tells you to weigh the cycle and the yield together rather than reading the yield column alone.
True or false: the potential yield is what a good farmer gets.

Not as the brochure defines it. The potential yield is the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, and it lists what it means: rain, fertilisation, pest attack, upkeep of the field. Only one of those four is entirely in your hands. So it is the yield when everything goes well, including the weather, rather than a reward for good farming. The average column beside it is what to plan on: 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare for Obatanpa against 6 potential, 3 to 4 for Sotubaka against 7, 1.5 to 2 for TZEE W Pop STR QPM against 3.
Set out the relation between cycle and yield across the list.

The two rise together on this list. At 75 to 85 days, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 3 tonnes a hectare potential, 1.5 to 2 average. At 90 to 95 days, Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 4 potential, 2 to 3 average. At 90 to 100 days, AB11, 4 potential, 2 to 3 average, and Ikenne 9449 SR, 5 potential, 2 to 3.5 average. At 100 to 110 days, Obatanpa, 6 potential, 3.5 to 4 average. At 105 to 115 days, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, 7 potential, 3 to 4 average. Note that Obatanpa's average is the highest on the list although its potential is not.
How many days of rain will I actually get this season?

I have no way to know that, and it is the number the whole choice turns on. I work offline and cannot see a forecast, and the brochure carries no rainfall data; it gives the cycles, from 75 to 85 days at the short end of the list to 105 to 115 at the long, and leaves the matching to you and to whoever knows the season. For a forecast, ANAMET is the service. For which variety suits your region this season, ICAT or ITRA. What I can tell you is what each cycle costs and buys: the short varieties are 3 tonnes a hectare potential, the long ones 7.
Before I settle on the cycle, what should I be looking at?

How long your rains actually run, in your own experience, rather than the best year you remember. Then set that against the list: 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, 105 to 115 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. Choose a cycle that finishes inside your season rather than one that just reaches the end of it. Then look at the yield among what is left, taking the average column rather than the potential. And ask ANAMET about the season's start if you can.
Describe the trade I am making when I take a longer variety.

You are buying yield with time. Going from the short end of the list to the long, the potential yield rises from 3 tonnes a hectare to 7, and the average from 1.5 to 2 up to 3 to 4, while the cycle stretches from 75 to 85 days out to 105 to 115. What you are spending is rain you may not have: the extra thirty days have to be there at the end of the season, and if they are not, the crop is caught. The brochure puts it as weighing the cycle and the yield, which is exactly this trade. Obatanpa is worth noticing in the middle of it, 100 to 110 days with the highest average on the list, 3.5 to 4.
I sowed a high yielding variety and got less than my neighbour with a small one.

Look at the cycle against your season before concluding anything about the variety. The high yielders on the list, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, need 105 to 115 days, and if your rains stopped short, the 7 tonnes a hectare potential never had a chance to become the 3 to 4 average. Your neighbour's smaller variety may simply have finished in time. Note too what the potential column means: the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, meaning rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field. Next season choose the cycle first. ICAT or ITRA can say which variety suits your region.
I want to get more out of my maize this year.

Then start with the cycle rather than the yield column, because the two have to be chosen together. Tell me roughly how many days your rains run, and whether there is striga in the field, since that would narrow the list before anything else.
About a hundred days, no striga that I have seen.

A hundred days gives you most of the list and puts the best average within reach. The varieties that finish inside it are TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM at 75 to 85 days, Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen at 90 to 95, and AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR at 90 to 100. Of those, Ikenne 9449 SR is the strongest, 5 tonnes a hectare potential and 2 to 3.5 on average, and the brochure marks it as very steady in yield. Obatanpa, at 100 to 110 days, carries the highest average on the whole list, 3.5 to 4, but it is at the edge of your season rather than inside it, so it is a gamble on the rains rather than a plan. Remember what the potential column means: the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, that is rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field, so plan on the average. Buy from an approved seller, not from a market and not from your own granary, which germinates badly, and ask ICAT or ITRA whether Ikenne 9449 SR suits your region this season.
How many improved maize varieties are there in Togo and what are they?

Nine on the list ITRA and ICAT published in 2008: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, Pool 18 QPM SR, Amen, AB11, Ikenne 9449 SR, Obatanpa, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. Their cycles run from 75 to 85 days at the short end to 105 to 115 at the long, and their potential yields from 3 to 7 tonnes a hectare. Seven have white grain and two, Pool 18 QPM SR and Sotubaka, are yellow. That list is the 2008 release list and may have grown since, so ICAT holds the current one.
The seller showed me a bag marked Ikenne and I do not know what it is.

Ikenne 9449 SR is on the released list: 90 to 100 days, 5 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3.5 tonnes on average, white grain, and the brochure notes it as very steady in yield. That steadiness is worth something if your seasons vary. Check two things at the counter. That the seller is an approved one, since the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else. And that the variety suits your region this season, which is a question for ICAT or ITRA rather than for the seller. If your rains run much under ninety days, look instead at the shorter ones, TZEE W Pop STR QPM or EV99 QPM at 75 to 85 days.
The yellow varieties must be the local ones and the white the improved.

Grain colour does not divide them that way. Of the nine improved varieties on the ITRA and ICAT list, seven have white grain and two have yellow: Pool 18 QPM SR, 90 to 95 days, 4 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 on average, and Sotubaka, 105 to 115 days, 7 potential, 3 to 4 on average. Both are improved. The colour is simply recorded in the table alongside the cycle, the yields and the tolerances, and the brochure does not rank the varieties by it. What it tells you to weigh is the cycle and the yield.
Why does the table bother recording the grain colour? Justify.

The brochure records it without saying why, so I will not construct a reason for it. What I can tell you is what it does say to choose on, which is the cycle and the yield, and that colour is not among the criteria it names. The colours as recorded: white for TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, Amen, AB11, Ikenne 9449 SR, Obatanpa and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W; yellow for Pool 18 QPM SR and Sotubaka. If colour matters to your buyers, that is a market question rather than an agronomic one, and a cooperative or ICAT would know more about it than I do.
Which of the nine is grown most in Togo?

I do not know, and the brochure does not say. Its table gives for each variety the cycle, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, and nothing about how widely each is grown or where. What it records is what was released, not what was adopted, and the list is that of 2008 in any case, so the picture may have moved. ICAT holds the current list and is the office to ask which variety suits your region this season. What I can give you in full is the table itself, variety by variety.
Rank the nine by average yield for me.

From the top of the average column down. Obatanpa, 3.5 to 4 tonnes a hectare. Then ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, both 3 to 4. Then Ikenne 9449 SR, 2 to 3.5. Then Pool 18 QPM SR, Amen and AB11, all 2 to 3. Then TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, both 1.5 to 2. Note that this is not the same order as the potential column, where ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka lead at 7 tonnes and Obatanpa follows at 6. And the ranking ignores the cycle, which the brochure tells you to weigh alongside the yield: the top four all need 90 days or more.
The cooperative wants the whole list written up for its members.

Give them the nine with their four figures each. TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 t/ha potential, 1.5 to 2 average, white, striga tolerant and high in quality protein. EV99 QPM, 75 to 85, 3, 1.5 to 2, white, high in quality protein. Pool 18 QPM SR, 90 to 95, 4, 2 to 3, yellow, high in quality protein. Amen, 90 to 95, 4, 2 to 3, white, drought tolerant. AB11, 90 to 100, 4, 2 to 3, white, streak tolerant. Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100, 5, 2 to 3.5, white, very steady yield. Obatanpa, 100 to 110, 6, 3.5 to 4, white, high in quality protein. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115, 7, 3 to 4, white, striga tolerant. Sotubaka, 105 to 115, 7, 3 to 4, yellow, high yield. Add that this is the 2008 list and ICAT holds the current one.
What should I take with me to the seed seller?

Take two or three names rather than one, with their cycles, so you are not stuck if the first is out of stock. Know which constraint applies to your field: striga points to TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, short rains to Amen. Know the cycle your season carries, from the range on the list, 75 to 85 days at the short end up to 105 to 115. And know the averages rather than the potentials, since the potential is the yield when growing conditions are good. Go to an approved seller, since the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, and ask ICAT or ITRA which suits your region this season.
Describe how the table is laid out.

One row per variety and five things recorded across it: the cycle in days, the potential yield in tonnes a hectare, the average yield in tonnes a hectare, the grain colour, and a note of what the variety is good for. So Obatanpa reads 100 to 110 days, 6 tonnes potential, 3.5 to 4 average, white grain, high in quality protein; and Amen reads 90 to 95 days, 4 potential, 2 to 3 average, white grain, tolerant to drought. The two yield columns stand side by side deliberately, since the potential is defined as the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, that is rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field.
I planted one of these and got nothing like the tonnage on the bag.

Check which column the bag was quoting. The potential yield is defined in the brochure as the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, and it names them: rain, fertilisation, pest attack, upkeep of the field. The average column beside it is what the variety gives ordinarily, and the gap is large: 6 tonnes a hectare potential against 3.5 to 4 average for Obatanpa, 7 against 3 to 4 for Sotubaka, 3 against 1.5 to 2 for TZEE W Pop STR QPM. Then check the cycle against your rains, because a long variety caught by a dry end will fall short of even the average. ICAT or ITRA for which suits your region.
Just tell me the names, I do not need all the numbers.

The names are TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, Pool 18 QPM SR, Amen, AB11, Ikenne 9449 SR, Obatanpa, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. But a name without its cycle is not much use at the counter, so take at least that much with you: 75 to 85 days for the first two, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, 105 to 115 for the last two. The brochure tells you to weigh the cycle and the yield, and the cycle is the one that decides whether the crop finishes. This is the 2008 list; ICAT holds the current one.
Somebody gave me a list of maize names and I do not know what any of them mean.
Read me the names and I will tell you what the ITRA and ICAT table records for each: the cycle, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and what the variety is good for.
Amen, Obatanpa and Sotubaka.

All three are on the released list and they are quite different from each other. Amen: 90 to 95 days, 4 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 on average, white grain, and it is the one the brochure marks as tolerant to drought, so it is the answer when the season is short of rain. Obatanpa: 100 to 110 days, 6 potential, 3.5 to 4 on average, white grain, high in quality protein, and its average is the highest on the whole list. Sotubaka: 105 to 115 days, 7 potential, 3 to 4 on average, yellow grain, marked simply for high yield. So the choice between them is mostly a choice of cycle: ninety days, a hundred and ten, or a hundred and fifteen. Take the one your rains actually carry, plan on the average column rather than the potential, buy from an approved seller, and ask ICAT or ITRA which suits your region this season.
What do I do about maize streak?

Choose an improved variety, and that is the control. Most of the improved varieties released in Togo are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the protection; AB11 is the one the table marks specifically as tolerant to streak, 90 to 100 days, 4 tonnes a hectare potential, 2 to 3 on average, white grain. That is also an argument against sowing grain from your own granary, which the brochure warns against because it germinates badly, and against buying improved seed from anywhere but an approved seller. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.
striga mais quelle variete

TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. Those are the two the ITRA and ICAT table marks as tolerant to striga. TZEE W Pop STR QPM is 75 to 85 days, 3 tonnes a hectare potential, 1.5 to 2 on average, white grain, also high in quality protein. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W is 105 to 115 days, 7 potential, 3 to 4 on average, white grain. Choose between them on the length of your season. Buy from an approved seller.
Striga and streak are two names for the same problem.

They are different things and the brochure answers them differently. Streak is maize streak virus, and most of the improved varieties are tolerant to it, so choosing an improved variety is itself the control; AB11 is the one marked specifically for streak. Striga is the weed with the purple and pink flowers that comes up between the plants, and only two varieties on the list are marked tolerant to it: TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W. So an improved variety covers you for streak almost by default, while striga requires you to pick one of those two by name.
True or false: a striga tolerant variety will clear the striga out of my field.

The brochure says tolerant, not resistant, and it does not claim the weed is removed. What it says is that if striga grows in your field you should take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two marked striga tolerant. Tolerance is about the crop standing up to the problem rather than about the problem going away, and I will not go further than the word the table uses. If what you want is to clear the striga rather than crop alongside it, that is a different question and not one this brochure answers; put it to ICAT or ITRA.
Between the two striga tolerant varieties, what decides it?

The length of your season, and the yield follows from it. TZEE W Pop STR QPM is 75 to 85 days, 3 tonnes a hectare potential, 1.5 to 2 on average, white grain, and high in quality protein. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W is 105 to 115 days, 7 potential, 3 to 4 on average, white grain. So the long one carries more than twice the average yield, and needs about thirty more days of rain to do it. That is the trade the brochure sets up when it tells you to weigh the cycle and the yield. Ask ICAT or ITRA which of the two suits your region this season.
Set out what the brochure says on these two problems.

Streak: most of the improved varieties released in Togo are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the control against streak. AB11, 90 to 100 days, 4 t/ha potential, 2 to 3 average, white grain, is the variety the table marks as tolerant to streak. Striga: if striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 t/ha potential, 1.5 to 2 average, or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, 7 potential, 3 to 4 average, the two the table marks as striga tolerant. Both answers are varietal; the brochure offers no other control in this section.
What does streak look like on the plant so I can recognise it?

The brochure does not describe the symptoms in what I hold, so I will not describe them from memory: a wrong description would have you treating the wrong thing. What it gives is the control, which is varietal: most of the improved varieties are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the protection, and AB11 is the one the table marks specifically for streak. For recognising it in the field, ask ICAT or ITRA, or the extension agent who can look at the plants. Striga, by contrast, is recognisable, and it is the weed with purple and pink flowers between the plants.
Only a corner of the field has striga. Do I change the variety for the whole field?

The brochure does not deal with part of a field, so I will not invent a rule for it. What it says is that if striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two marked striga tolerant. Sowing two varieties in one field is possible in principle, but it means two cycles running side by side, 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM against whatever you put elsewhere, and that complicates the harvest. Put the practical question to ICAT or ITRA, who can see the field and who are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season.
I am about to sow. What do I check about striga and streak first?

Walk the field and look for the weed with the purple and pink flowers, because striga is the one that forces your hand: if it is there, your variety is TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, and which of the two depends on whether your season carries 75 to 85 days or 105 to 115. Streak needs no separate check at this stage, since most of the improved varieties are tolerant to maize streak virus and choosing an improved variety is itself the control. Then make sure the seed is from an approved seller, because the brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else and against granary grain, which germinates badly.
Describe how the variety protects the crop here.

It is a property of the plant rather than something you apply. For streak, the improved varieties released in Togo are for the most part tolerant to maize streak virus, so the protection is already in the seed you buy: choosing an improved variety is itself the control, and AB11 is the one the table marks for it. For striga, only two of the nine carry the mark, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, so the protection exists but you have to choose it by name. In both cases nothing is sprayed and nothing is added; the decision is made once, at the seed counter.
Just tell me what to spray for striga, everybody sprays something.

I have nothing to give you, and I will not name a product I have no source for. What the ITRA and ICAT brochure offers against striga in this section is varietal and nothing else: if striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two it marks as striga tolerant. No spray, no dose, no product name. If something is sprayed for striga in your area, ICAT or ITRA is the place to ask, and they can also tell you which variety suits your region this season. I would rather send you there than guess at a chemical.
Something is wrong with my maize and I am told it is a disease.

Tell me what you are actually seeing on the ground, because two different things get called disease here and they have different answers. Is there a weed with purple and pink flowers coming up between the plants, or is it the plants themselves that look wrong?
There are purple flowers all through it, and the plants between them are stunted.

Then that is striga, which is a weed rather than a disease of the plant, and the brochure's answer to it is the variety you sow. If striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two the table marks as tolerant to it. TZEE W Pop STR QPM is 75 to 85 days, 3 tonnes a hectare potential and 1.5 to 2 on average; ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W is 105 to 115 days, 7 potential and 3 to 4 on average, so choose between them on the length of your season. Two things I should be plain about. The word in the table is tolerant, so it is about the crop standing up to the weed rather than the weed going away, and the brochure offers no other control here.
