And for anything beyond the variety, including whether the striga can be cleared from the field, ask ICAT or ITRA, who are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season. Buy the seed from an approved seller.
How far apart do I sow these varieties?

The spacing is not in what I hold. The ITRA and ICAT variety table gives, for each of the nine, the cycle, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, and it tells you to buy the seed only from approved sellers and to weigh the cycle and the yield when choosing. It does not give sowing distances, and those differ enough between varieties that guessing would cost you. Ask ICAT or ITRA, who are also the ones to tell you which variety suits your region this season and where the approved sellers are near you.
prix semence mais amelioree

I do not have it. The ITRA and ICAT brochure carries no prices: it gives the nine released varieties with their cycles, potential and average yields, grain colours and tolerances, and tells you to buy only from approved sellers. It does not name the sellers or what they charge, and I work offline in any case, so any figure from me would be invention. Ask ICAT or ITRA for the approved sellers near you and ask them the price. They are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season.
I want to plant something released in the last few years, not an old variety.

I cannot tell you which are recent, because the list I hold is the 2008 release list from ITRA and ICAT and it may well have grown since. What it contains is those nine: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, EV99 QPM, Pool 18 QPM SR, Amen, AB11, Ikenne 9449 SR, Obatanpa, ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, with their cycles, yields, grain colours and tolerances. Which of those is still recommended, and what has been released since, is exactly what ICAT holds. Go to them with your two constraints, the length of your season and whether there is striga in the field, and they can answer both questions at once.
Should I take a variety from your list or whatever ICAT recommends this year?

Whatever ICAT recommends, and use the list to ask better questions. The nine I hold are the 2008 release list and the brochure itself says which variety suits your region this season is a question for ICAT or ITRA. What the list is good for is knowing what to ask about: the cycle, since yours has to fit your rains, somewhere between 75 to 85 days and 105 to 115; the two yield figures, potential and average, since the potential is the yield when growing conditions are good; the tolerances, striga, streak, drought; and the grain colour. Go with those five questions and the answer you get will be a real recommendation.
Why keep telling me the list is from 2008? Justify.

Because a variety list is the kind of thing that changes, and you would act on mine as though it were current. The nine names I hold are the released list published by ITRA and ICAT in 2008, and what has been released since is not in what I have. If you walk into a seed shop asking for a name that has been superseded, you will either be told it is unavailable or sold something else under it. Saying the date lets you check rather than assume. ICAT holds the current list, and the brochure itself refers you there for which variety suits your region this season.
State precisely what this brochure does not cover on varieties.

It does not give sowing distances or plant densities. It does not give seed rates per hectare. It does not give prices, nor name the approved sellers it tells you to buy from. It does not say where in Togo each variety suits, only what each one is and what it tolerates. It does not describe the symptoms of maize streak. And its list is the 2008 release list, so it does not cover anything released since. What it does give in full is, for each of nine varieties, the cycle in days, the potential yield, the average yield, the grain colour and the tolerances, plus the rule to buy only from approved sellers and not to sow granary grain.
Someone told the group that a new variety gives ten tonnes a hectare.

That is not on the list I hold, where the highest potential yields are 7 tonnes a hectare, for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka, with averages of 3 to 4. But my list is the 2008 release list from ITRA and ICAT and may well have grown since, so I cannot say the claim is wrong, only that it is not in what I have. Ask where the figure comes from, and ask whether it is a potential or an average, because the difference is large: the potential is defined as the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, meaning rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field. ICAT holds the current list.
What should I ask ICAT before I buy, given what you cannot tell me?

Five things. Which varieties are on the current list, since mine is that of 2008. Which of them suits your region this season, which the brochure itself sends you there for. Who the approved sellers are near you, since it tells you to buy only from them without naming them. What the seed costs and how much you need for your area, neither of which it gives. And the sowing distance for whichever variety you take, which is not in what I hold either. Take with you what I can give: the cycle, the potential and average yields, the grain colour and the tolerances for each of the nine.
Describe the edge of what you actually know here.

I have one table well and everything around it badly. The table is the nine varieties released in Togo as listed by ITRA and ICAT in 2008, each with its cycle, its potential yield, its average yield, its grain colour and what it tolerates, and I can give any row of it exactly. Around that I have two rules, buy only from approved sellers and do not sow granary grain because it germinates badly, and one definition, that the potential yield is the yield obtained when growing conditions are good. Outside that: no prices, no sellers named, no sowing distances, no seed rates, no regional fit, and nothing released after 2008.
I asked for Obatanpa and the seller said he had something better.

He may have, and I cannot judge it, because the list I hold is the 2008 release list from ITRA and ICAT and things may have been released since. What you can do is make him answer in the terms the brochure uses. What is its cycle in days? What is its potential yield and what is its average yield? What is it tolerant to? Obatanpa reads 100 to 110 days, 6 tonnes a hectare potential, 3.5 to 4 on average, white grain, high in quality protein, and that average is the highest on my list. If his variety cannot be described that way, be careful. And check he is an approved seller.
Just give me the spacing, everyone knows it is about eighty by forty.

I will not confirm a spacing I do not hold, even one you have already heard. The variety table gives cycles, potential and average yields, grain colours and tolerances, and it says to buy the seed only from approved sellers and to weigh the cycle and the yield. It does not give sowing distances. If I agreed with your figure and it were wrong for the variety you are sowing, you would have sown a whole field on my agreement. Ask ICAT or ITRA, who are also who to ask which variety suits your region this season, and ask specifically for the spacing of the variety you have bought.
I have bought my seed and now I want to know how to put it in.

Tell me which variety you bought and I will give you everything the variety table holds on it. I should say at the outset that the sowing distances are not in what I have, so that part will have to come from elsewhere.
Obatanpa, two bags, for about a hectare.

On the variety I can be exact. Obatanpa is 100 to 110 days, 6 tonnes a hectare potential, 3.5 to 4 tonnes on average, white grain, high in quality protein, and its average is the highest of the nine on the ITRA and ICAT list. So check your rains carry a hundred days or more, because that is the one thing that would undo the choice. Plan on the average column: the potential is defined as the yield obtained when growing conditions are good, meaning rain, fertilisation, pest attack and upkeep of the field. On what you actually asked, I have to be straight with you: the spacing between pockets and rows is not in the table I hold, and neither is the seed rate per hectare, so I cannot tell you whether two bags is right for your hectare. Ask ICAT or ITRA both questions, and ask at the same time whether Obatanpa is still what they recommend for your region, since my list dates from 2008.
I am thinking of putting a hectare into maize and I want to know what I am in for.

The costed hectare in the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure gives charges of 391,000 FCFA against a sale of 480,000 FCFA, leaving a profit of 89,000 FCFA on a yield of 3,500 kg. Those are 2005 evaluations for one hectare of Obatanpa, not today's prices, and they have to be read that way. Two things in them shape the answer. The profit depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, so it is not a harvest-time figure. And the charges are more than four fifths of the sale, so the margin is thin. Take the rows to ICAT and put today's prices beside them.
True or false: a hectare of maize makes about ninety thousand francs.

That is the study's figure, and it is a 2005 evaluation rather than a fact about this year. The costed hectare of Obatanpa in the ITRA and ICAT brochure shows 391,000 FCFA of charges, 480,000 FCFA of sales and 89,000 FCFA of profit, on a yield of 3,500 kg. Two conditions come with it. The sale is after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, not at harvest. And every price in it is from 2005. So the right way to use it is as a template: write your own quantities in the same rows, put today's prices beside them, and see whether your own hectare still leaves a profit.
Maize or something else on that hectare?

I can only cost one side of that question, so I cannot choose for you. What I have is the maize side: charges 391,000 FCFA, sales 480,000 FCFA, profit 89,000 FCFA on 3,500 kg a hectare, in 2005 prices, with the sale made after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. I have no costed hectare for any other crop, and I will not build one by analogy. What I would do is use the same rows for the other crop, which is what the brochure suggests anyway: write your own quantities in, put today's prices beside them, and compare. ICAT is the office that builds budgets with current prices.
Why does the study bother showing the total sale as well as the profit? Justify.

Because the two tell you different things about the risk you are taking. The sale, 480,000 FCFA, is what has to come in; the charges, 391,000 FCFA, are what goes out whether or not it does; and the profit, 89,000 FCFA, is what is left. Seeing all three together shows how thin the margin is: the charges are more than four fifths of the sale, so a fall of a fifth in the price or in the yield wipes the profit out. A profit figure alone would hide that. It also lets you see what the profit depends on, which is selling after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags.
State the totals of the costed hectare.

From the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure, for one hectare of Obatanpa, in 2005 prices, from a 2005 internal communication: charges 391,000 FCFA; sales 480,000 FCFA; profit 89,000 FCFA; yield 3,500 kg a hectare. The sale is made after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. Within the charges, the inputs and machine work are 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for renting the plot and 10,000 for 25 kg of commercial seed; labour is counted in man-days at 700 FCFA each.
What would that hectare give me today?

I cannot tell you, and I would rather say so than update the figures by guesswork. Every number in that costed hectare is a 2005 evaluation: 391,000 FCFA of charges, 480,000 of sales, 89,000 of profit, 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, on 3,500 kg a hectare of Obatanpa. Fertiliser, tractor hire and grain prices have all moved since, in directions I cannot see. What the brochure itself tells you to do is use it as a template rather than a price list: write your own quantities in the same rows and put today's prices beside them. ICAT builds budgets with current prices, and SIM broadcasts the cereal prices on the radio.
A young man in the village says maize is a losing crop and not worth planting.

The study does not say that, but it does show why people believe it. The costed hectare gives 391,000 FCFA of charges against 480,000 FCFA of sales, so a profit of 89,000 FCFA on 3,500 kg, in 2005 prices. The margin is less than a fifth of the turnover, which is thin enough that a bad price or a poor yield turns it negative. And the profit as the study builds it depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags: sold at harvest into the glut, the same hectare looks quite different. Tell him to build his own version of the rows with ICAT rather than arguing from a feeling.
Before I commit the land, what figures do I need in front of me?

The three totals and the condition attached to them. Charges 391,000 FCFA, sales 480,000 FCFA, profit 89,000 FCFA, on a yield of 3,500 kg a hectare of Obatanpa, all in 2005 prices. The condition is that the sale is made after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, so you need somewhere to store and the means to wait. Then put your own prices beside each row, because 2005 is the whole caveat: the six bags of NPK and urea at 72,000, the tractor ploughing at 40,000, the pulverising pass at 25,000, the plot rent at 20,000, the 25 kg of seed at 10,000, and the labour at 700 FCFA a man-day. ICAT will help you do it.
Describe the shape of that budget, roughly.

Four fifths cost, one fifth profit. On one hectare of Obatanpa the charges come to 391,000 FCFA and the sale to 480,000, leaving 89,000. Inside the charges, three roughly equal blocks: the inputs and machine work, being 72,000 for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for the plot rent and 10,000 for 25 kg of seed; the labour, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA each; and the small things people forget, 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle and 20,000 of sundries. All 2005 prices.
I grew a hectare and came out with nothing at the end.

Compare it against the study's shape rather than its prices, since the prices are 2005. There, charges of 391,000 FCFA against sales of 480,000 leave 89,000, which is a margin of less than a fifth, so coming out at nothing is not far off the model. Two places to look. When you sold: the study's profit depends on selling after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, and selling into the harvest glut is a different result. And the small costs, which are easy to leave out of your own reckoning but not out of the study: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries.
Just tell me maize is worth it or it is not.

I cannot answer that for your hectare, and the honest reason is that the only costed hectare I have is from 2005. What it shows is 391,000 FCFA of charges, 480,000 of sales and 89,000 of profit on 3,500 kg, with the sale made after six months of storage at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. Whether that shape still holds depends on today's fertiliser, tractor hire and grain prices, none of which I can see. What I will not do is turn a 2005 study into a verdict for this season. Take the rows to ICAT, put current prices in, and the answer will be yours rather than mine.
I want to know whether to put my land into maize this year.

I can give you the shape of a costed hectare and not the answer, because the only one I hold is from 2005. Tell me how much land you are thinking of and whether you have anywhere to store grain, because the second matters more than people expect.
One hectare, and no, I would sell straight after the harvest.

Then the study's own profit does not apply to you as it stands, and that is worth knowing before you decide. Its costed hectare of Obatanpa shows charges of 391,000 FCFA, sales of 480,000 and a profit of 89,000, on 3,500 kg. But the brochure is explicit that the sale is made after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, and that keeping the maize six months is what lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Selling at harvest means selling into the glut, and the 89,000 was never a large cushion: the charges are more than four fifths of the sale. Two things to do rather than decide now. Price a store, because the brochure says maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack, and the pallets are already in the budget at 20,000 FCFA. And take the rows to ICAT with today's prices, since every figure I have just given you is a 2005 evaluation. SIM broadcasts the cereal prices on the radio, which will tell you what the difference between harvest and lean season looks like now.
What are the big costs in a hectare of maize?

In that costed hectare, the inputs and the machine work lead: 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for renting the plot and 10,000 for 25 kg of commercial seed. Labour is the other half, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA each, the largest being 55 days for harvest and transport. The whole charge comes to 391,000 FCFA against a sale of 480,000. Those are 2005 evaluations for one hectare of Obatanpa, so treat the rows as a template and put your own prices in them.
Fertiliser is the whole of the cost, the rest is small change.

It is the biggest single line and nowhere near the whole. The six bags of NPK and urea are 72,000 FCFA of a total charge of 391,000, so under a fifth. Beside them stand 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for the plot rent and 10,000 for 25 kg of seed. Then the labour, in man-days at 700 FCFA each, with 55 days for harvest and transport alone. Then the small things the study still counts: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries. All 2005 prices.
Why does the study count renting the plot when the land is mine? Justify.

Because it is costing a hectare as an enterprise rather than describing one farmer's pocket, and the land has a value whether or not money changes hands for it. In the study the plot rent is 20,000 FCFA of a 391,000 FCFA charge. If you own your land, that row is where you see what the land is worth to you, and you can strike it out or leave it in when you build your own version. The brochure invites exactly that: use it as a template rather than a price list, write your own quantities in the same rows and put today's prices beside them. The same argument applies to family labour, counted at 700 FCFA a man-day.
What does a bag of NPK cost now?

I have no current price and will not invent one. What the study carries is 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea together, in 2005, which is a 2005 evaluation inside a costed hectare and not a price list. It does not even split the six bags between NPK and urea, so I could not give you a per bag figure from it honestly. For today's price, ask at an approved input outlet, or ask ICAT, which is also the office to build a budget with current prices. CAGIA or its approved distributors are where subsidised inputs are handled, and ICAT can tell you this season's outlet.
What do the charges come to on two hectares?

Doubling the study's rows gives 782,000 FCFA against 391,000 for one hectare, with sales of 960,000 and a profit of 178,000, on 7,000 kg. But that is arithmetic rather than a second study, and two of its assumptions do not scale cleanly: the tractor ploughing at 40,000 and the pulverising pass at 25,000 may be priced differently for a larger job, and the labour, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA, has to be found. All of it is 2005 in any case. Build the two hectare version with ICAT rather than multiplying mine, and remember the profit depends on selling after six months of storage.
The cooperative wants to see where the money goes on a hectare.

Give them the three blocks. Inputs and machine work: 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for renting the plot, 10,000 for 25 kg of commercial seed. Labour, in man-days at 700 FCFA each: 55 for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing, 25 for the second weeding, 20 for spreading NPK, 20 for treatment and bagging, 10 for sowing, 10 for the urea, 10 for drying. Small costs: 14,000 grain protectant, 21,000 jute bags, 20,000 pallets, 2,000 twine and needle, 20,000 sundries. Total 391,000 FCFA, all 2005 prices.
Before the season starts, which of these costs do I need money for first?

The ones that fall before the crop exists. Renting the plot, 20,000 FCFA in the study. The tractor ploughing, 40,000, and the pulverising pass, 25,000. The seed, 10,000 for 25 kg. Then the fertiliser, 72,000 for six bags of NPK and urea, though the urea goes on later than the NPK, which is why the labour rows separate 20 man-days for spreading NPK from 10 for the urea. What comes later is the harvest side, the 55 man-days for harvest and transport, the 21,000 of jute bags, the 20,000 of pallets and the 14,000 of grain protectant. All 2005 prices; price your own with ICAT.
Describe what the charge rows look like.

Three kinds of row. Things you buy or hire, priced outright: six bags of NPK and urea at 72,000 FCFA, tractor ploughing at 40,000, the pulverising pass at 25,000, the plot rent at 20,000, 25 kg of commercial seed at 10,000. Work, priced in man-days at 700 FCFA each, from 55 days for harvest and transport down to 10 days for sowing, for the urea and for drying. And the small items, which are the ones people leave out of their own reckoning: 14,000 of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle, 20,000 of sundries. They add to 391,000 FCFA in 2005 prices.
My costs always come out higher than I planned.

Look at which rows you are leaving out of your plan, because the study counts several that people do not. The small ones especially: 14,000 FCFA of grain protectant, 21,000 of jute bags, 20,000 of pallets, 2,000 of twine and needle and 20,000 of sundries, which is 77,000 of a 391,000 FCFA charge. And the labour, which is easy to treat as free when the family does it but which the study prices at 700 FCFA a man-day across 55 days for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing and more. Write your own quantities into the same rows and the surprises stop.
Just give me one figure for the inputs and forget the rest.

The inputs and machine work in the study come to 167,000 FCFA: 72,000 for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for the plot rent and 10,000 for 25 kg of seed. But taking that alone is how people arrive at a profit that is not there, because the total charge is 391,000, with the labour and the small items making up the rest. The small items alone are 77,000. If you want one number, take 391,000 rather than 167,000, and remember it is a 2005 evaluation for one hectare of Obatanpa.
I need to work out what a hectare of maize will cost me.

I can give you the study's rows and you can put your own prices in them, which is what the brochure itself asks. Tell me two things first: do you have your own land, and will you hire a tractor or work with a hoe? Both change which rows apply.
The land is mine and I have no tractor, I use a hoe.

Then two of the study's largest rows come out and one grows. Out go the plot rent, 20,000 FCFA, and the tractor ploughing, 40,000, with the pulverising pass at 25,000 likely to follow if you are not using machinery at all. That is up to 85,000 FCFA of a 391,000 charge. Two hectares. How many days and can my family do it?

Every year I am short of hands exactly at harvest.

Your own, and keep the study's beside them as a check. The brochure asks for exactly that: write your own quantities in the same rows and put today's prices beside them. Two columns beside the study's. In the first, your quantities: your hectares, your bags of fertiliser, your kilos of seed, your days of work operation by operation, your bags and pallets. I would rather send you to them than put a name in your hand that I cannot stand behind.
Something is taking over my maize field and I do not know what to do.

Describe what you are seeing. If it is a plant coming up between the maize with purple or pink flowers, that is striga and the brochure has a specific answer for it. If it is the maize plants themselves that look wrong, that is a different question.
Purple flowers, all through it, and it has been getting worse for three or four years.

Then it is striga, and the worsening over three or four years is the part to act on rather than the flowers. The brochure gives three actions together. Use a striga tolerant maize variety, which you have to buy as such, from ITRA or a registered seed seller. Grow it with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut. And pull the striga plants out before they flower, which means going into the field earlier than you would otherwise. Behind those sits the general point that a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops, so if that field has carried maize year after year, breaking the run is part of the answer: the rule is maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. Two honest limits. The word is tolerant, not resistant, so the weed is not promised to disappear. And neither source says how many seasons this takes. Ask ICAT, which can see the field.
I have one plot and I want to start a rotation next season.

One plot is all a rotation needs, since the catalogue defines it as a succession of crops in time on the same plot. Its worked four year example: year one, the improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen, being beans, groundnut or cowpea; year two, maize, a hungry plant that takes a lot, sown now that the soil is rich in nitrogen; year three, a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam; year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to year one. Before you fix it, take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season.
True or false: the okra year is a wasted year.

The catalogue does not treat it as wasted; it has a place in the sequence. Year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra, coming after year three's root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam, and before the return to year one's legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen. So it is the light year between the deep feeder and the restorer, and it is still a crop you harvest. The brochure's own rule ends its cycle differently, with a fallow after the root crop, so both a light crop and a fallow appear in the sources for that position.
Set out the four year rotation and the role of each year.

Year one: improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen, named as beans, groundnut and cowpea. Year two: maize, described as a hungry plant that takes a lot, placed here because the soil is now rich in nitrogen. Year three: a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, the example given being yam. Year four: an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then the cycle returns to year one. The stated purposes of a rotation, in the catalogue's words, are that it improves soil fertility and that it helps fight the enemies of the crops, a rotation being a succession of crops in time on the same plot.
Can I swap okra for something else in year four?

The catalogue describes the position rather than fixing the crop: year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, and okra is its example. So the requirement is undemanding, and okra is one answer to it rather than the only one. What I will not do is name a substitute of my own and have you plan a year on it, because the catalogue names no others for that slot. Ask ICAT, which is the office for the rotation that suits your plot and your region. The same caution applies to year three, where yam is the example of a root or tuber crop.
The group wants a simple rotation they can all follow.

Give them the four year example, since it explains itself. Year one, legumes, the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut or cowpea. Year two, maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, going in when the soil is rich in nitrogen. Year three, a root or tuber that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as okra. Then round again. Tell them the two reasons given for it, that a rotation improves soil fertility and helps fight the enemies of the crops, and the one instruction before fixing it: take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season.
What do I need to know before I fix the sequence?

Two things, and the catalogue names them both: the fertility of the soil, and what grew there last season. The second decides where in the cycle you start. If the plot has just carried maize, the next year is the legume, since the brochure's rule is maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. If it has just carried a legume, maize follows, which is where the catalogue's four year example puts it, the soil now being rich in nitrogen. If there is striga in the plot, plan the legume alongside a striga tolerant variety. ICAT for what suits your plot.
Describe what each year takes and gives.

Year one gives: the legumes are improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, and the catalogue names beans, groundnut and cowpea. Year two takes: maize is described as a hungry plant that takes a lot, and it is put here precisely because the soil is now rich in nitrogen. Year three takes from lower down: a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four takes little: an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then year one gives again. That alternation of giving and taking is what the catalogue means when it says a rotation improves soil fertility.
My yam does badly when I plant it after a fallow.

The catalogue's four year example does not put yam after a fallow; it puts it in year three, after the legumes of year one and the maize of year two, as a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper. The brochure has one succession that does start that way, fallow then yam then maize then fallow, so both orders appear in the sources. I have nothing that explains why yours does badly in that position, and I will not construct a reason. What the catalogue does tell you to do before fixing a rotation is to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. Ask ICAT.
Just tell me I can do maize two years in a row inside the rotation.

I will not endorse that, because neither source puts two maize years together. The catalogue's four year example has maize once, in year two, after the legumes and before the root crop. The brochure's rule is maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, and its successions space the maize out in the same way: maize then cowpea or groundnut then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow. Maize is described as a hungry plant that takes a lot, which is the reason it is not repeated. If you have a constraint that pushes you towards it, take it to ICAT.
I have been told to rotate but nobody has told me what order.

There are two orders in the sources and they agree with each other. Tell me what the plot carried last season, because the catalogue says to take account of that and of the fertility of the soil before fixing anything.
Groundnut last season, and before that maize.

Then you are already partway through the cycle and the next year is settled. Groundnut is a legume, one of the improving plants that feed the soil with nitrogen, which the catalogue puts in year one alongside beans and cowpea. So the year that follows it is maize, the hungry plant that takes a lot, sown now that the soil is rich in nitrogen. After that, year three is a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper, such as yam. Year four is an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable, okra. Then back to the legumes. The brochure's version of the same idea reads maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow, so if you prefer a fallow to the okra year, that is in the sources too. One plot is enough for all of it, since a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot. Take it to ICAT for what suits your region.
How do I decide between associating and rotating?

Start from where you are, because the brochure splits the country. In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops, and it lists maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut and the combinations of those. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize is more often grown pure and it recommends running a succession instead of an association. Then take account of the two things the catalogue names before fixing a rotation: the fertility of the soil, and what grew there last season. For what suits your plot and your region, ICAT.
association ou rotation nord togo

A succession, in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The brochure says maize is more often grown pure there and recommends running a succession instead of an association. Association is the southern practice, in Maritime and Plateaux. Before fixing a succession, take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. The rule for the order is maize at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. ICAT for what suits your plot and your region.
Association and rotation are just two names for growing different crops.

They differ in time. An association is two or more crops sharing the same ground at the same time, such as maize with cowpea or maize with cassava. A rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, which is the catalogue's own definition, so the crops follow one another rather than sharing. That is why the brochure can recommend one in one region and the other elsewhere: association is usual in Maritime and Plateaux, while in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it recommends a succession instead. The two can also be combined, as when a striga tolerant variety is grown with or in rotation with a grain legume.
True or false: I can run the same plan anywhere in Togo.

False on the brochure's own terms. It divides the country: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is more often grown pure and it recommends running a succession instead of an association. So the same plan is not what it proposes. Beyond the region, it also asks you to take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season before fixing a rotation, which is a plot by plot matter. For what suits your plot and your region, ICAT.
Why does the brochure divide the country like that? Justify.

It records the difference rather than explaining it, and I will not supply a reason it does not give. What it states is the practice: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops, with a list of the associations; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize is more often grown pure, and there it recommends running a succession instead of an association. Notice the wording: it is describing what is usually done as much as prescribing. For why, and for what suits your own plot, ask ICAT, which is the office the brochure refers you to for the association or rotation that fits your region.
Set out the regional rule and its exceptions.

Region. South, Maritime and Plateaux: maize usually grown with other crops; associations listed are maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. Centre and north, Centrale, Kara and Savanes: maize more often grown pure, and a succession recommended instead of an association. Plot. Before fixing a rotation, take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. Special case. Where maize is followed by cotton in the same year, sow an extra early variety of 75 to 85 days and sow the cotton into the maize two to three weeks before the maize harvest.
Does the size of my holding change any of this?

Nothing in the sources conditions the choice on area. What they condition it on is the region, association being usual in Maritime and Plateaux and a succession recommended in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, and on the plot, since before fixing a rotation you take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. One practical point about size: a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, so a single small plot can run one; it simply means one crop a year rather than several at once. More plots let you run several stages of the cycle at the same time. ICAT for what suits yours.
Somebody from a project told our village to associate everything.

That is the southern practice, and whether it applies depends on where the village is. The brochure says maize is usually grown with other crops in Maritime and Plateaux, and lists the associations; but in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it says maize is more often grown pure and recommends running a succession instead. So one instruction for the whole country is not what it proposes. Ask where the advice comes from, and ask ICAT, which is the office the brochure refers you to for the association or rotation that suits your plot and your region. And whatever is chosen, the fertility of the soil and what grew last season come into it.
Describe how the cotton and maize year works.

The two crops overlap at the end rather than sharing the whole season. The brochure's instruction is that when maize is followed by cotton in the same year, you sow an extra early variety of maize, 75 to 85 days, so that the two crops do not sit together for long, and you sow the cotton into the maize two to three weeks before the maize harvest. So the cotton is already up and growing when the maize comes off. The extra early cycle is what makes the calendar fit: on the variety list, 75 to 85 days is the shortest band, TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM. Cotton then maize then cotton is one of its listed successions.
My cotton always goes in too late after the maize.

Then two things in the brochure are aimed exactly at that. Sow an extra early maize variety, 75 to 85 days, so the two crops do not sit together for long; on the variety list that band is TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM. And do not wait for the maize to come off: sow the cotton into the maize two to three weeks before the maize harvest. Those are given together as the way to fit both crops into one year. If your maize variety is a long one, 100 to 115 days, that alone would explain the lateness. ICAT for what suits your plot and your region.
saisons des pluies togo

Two calendars, not one. The south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons; the north, Kara and Savanes, has one; Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way. FAO GIEWS describes the pattern as two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October, and one in the north, around May to October. Those are shapes rather than dates, because the useful rains do not start on the same day every year. ANAMET for this season's onset, ICAT for the calendar of your own prefecture.
I farm in Sokode and I am never sure which calendar applies to me.

Centrale is the region the sources themselves treat as uncertain: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons, the north, Kara and Savanes, has one, and Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way. So your doubt is in the sources themselves rather than in your head. For the main season operations the maize brochure puts Centrale with the north: clear the plot in April and May, plough at the first rains in June and July, and sow when the rains are properly settled in June and July. For which pattern your prefecture follows this year, ICAT, and ANAMET for the rains.
Should I plan for one season or two?

It depends where you are, and the answer is in the division. In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, there are two rainy seasons, so two are possible. In the north, Kara and Savanes, there is one. Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way, so there the answer is local. FAO GIEWS puts the southern seasons around March to June and again around October, and the northern one around May to October. If you do plan a second season in the south, note the warning: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings there, so that crop needs an improved tolerant variety.
Why does the country have two different calendars? Justify.

The sources record the difference rather than explaining it, and I will not supply a meteorological reason they do not give. What they state is the pattern: two rainy seasons in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, one in the north, Kara and Savanes, and Centrale between the two, able to behave either way. FAO GIEWS puts the southern ones around March to June and again around October, and the northern one around May to October. What follows from it is practical and that is what matters to you: every operation in the maize brochure is dated twice, once for Maritime and Plateaux and once for Centrale, Kara and Savanes.
Which exact week does the rainy season start in Kara?

I cannot give you a week, and no source I hold does. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is the reason the calendar is written as months and as an instruction to watch rather than as a date: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and do not sow on one isolated shower. For Kara the brochure's band is June to July for sowing, with ploughing at the first rains in June and July and the plot cleared in April and May. For this year's onset, ANAMET is the service; for your prefecture's calendar, ICAT.
How far apart are the northern and southern calendars?

About two months on every operation. Clearing the plot: February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Ploughing at the first rains: April and May in the south, June and July in the centre and north. Sowing when the rains are properly settled: April to May in the south, June to July in the centre and north. The choice of plot for the main season is January in the south against April in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. So a southern farmer is sowing about when a northern one is clearing.
I am planning the year. What do I need to settle first?

Which calendar you are on, because every date follows from it. If you are in Maritime or Plateaux, you have two rainy seasons and the main season runs clearing in February and March, ploughing at the first rains in April and May, sowing when the rains are settled in April to May. If you are in Kara or Savanes, one season, with clearing in April and May and ploughing and sowing in June and July. If you are in Centrale, it can behave either way and you should ask ICAT for your prefecture. Then watch the rains rather than the calendar: sow when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower.
Describe the farming year in the south compared with the north.

In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, two rainy seasons, around March to June and again around October in the FAO GIEWS description. The main season begins early: the plot is chosen in January, cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, and sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. Then a second, shorter season, with the plot chosen in July. In the north, Kara and Savanes, one season, around May to October, with the plot chosen in April, cleared in April and May, and ploughed and sown in June and July. Centrale sits between and can behave either way.
I moved north and everything I do seems to be at the wrong time.

You are probably still on the southern calendar, and the gap is about two months on every operation. In Maritime and Plateaux the plot is cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, and sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is cleared in April and May and ploughed and sown in June and July. That is because the south has two rainy seasons and the north one, around May to October. Ask ICAT for the calendar of your new prefecture, and follow ANAMET for this season's onset.
Just give me one sowing date for the whole country.

There is not one, and giving you a single date would be the most harmful thing I could do here. The country has two calendars: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, sows when the rains are properly settled in April to May, and Centrale, Kara and Savanes in June to July. Centrale can behave either way. And within those bands the instruction is not a date at all but a condition: sow when it rains regularly, and do not sow on one isolated shower, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. For your prefecture, ICAT; for this year's rains, ANAMET.
I am new to farming here and I do not know the year at all.

Then start with which part of the country you are in, because Togo has two calendars rather than one. The south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons; the north, Kara and Savanes, has one; Centrale sits between and can behave either way.
I am in the Plateaux, near Atakpame.

Then you are on the southern calendar and you have two seasons to work with. For the main one, the maize brochure dates each operation: the plot is chosen in January, cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, and sown when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, in April to May. Do not sow on one isolated shower, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Then there is the second, shorter season in the south, for which the plot is chosen in July; FAO GIEWS puts the southern rains around March to June and again around October. One warning attaches to that second season: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so a second season crop needs an improved tolerant variety. Two things I cannot give you: which crop to sow in a given month, since no source I hold says that, and this year's onset. ICAT for the calendar of your prefecture, ANAMET for the rains.
How do I know when the rains are settled enough to sow?

The test the brochure gives is regularity rather than quantity: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and do not sow on one isolated shower. The months put around that are April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, but they are a band rather than a date, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. So watch the pattern across days rather than the calendar, and follow ANAMET for this season's onset and its forecasts. ICAT holds the calendar of your own prefecture.
semer apres premiere pluie ou attendre

Wait. The instruction is to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not to sow on one isolated shower. The months are April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, but the condition matters more than the month, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. ANAMET for this season's onset; ICAT for your prefecture's calendar.
It has rained twice this week in the Plateaux and I am tempted to put the seed in.

Two rains in a week is closer to settled than one shower, but the test is regularity rather than a count, and the brochure puts it as sowing when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, with a warning not to sow on one isolated shower. You are in the right band for Maritime and Plateaux, where sowing goes in April to May, so the calendar is not against you. What I cannot tell you is whether these rains will hold, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year and I work offline. ANAMET is the service for this season's onset and forecasts.
The calendar says April, so I sow in April whatever the weather.

The calendar gives the band and the rain gives the moment. The brochure's instruction is to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not to sow on one isolated shower; the months, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, sit around that condition rather than replacing it. The reason is stated: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Sowing to the date in a year when the rains come late is how a crop is lost before it is up. ANAMET for the onset, ICAT for your prefecture.
True or false: one good heavy rain means the season has started.

False, on the brochure's own wording: do not sow on one isolated shower. What it asks for is that the rains be properly settled, that is that it rains regularly. Heaviness is not the test; repetition is. The months around it are April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, and the reason the instruction is a condition rather than a date is that the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. For this season's onset, ANAMET; for the calendar of your own prefecture, ICAT.
State the sowing rule precisely.

Condition: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. Prohibition: do not sow on one isolated shower. Bands: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux; June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Preceding operations: the plot cleared in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes; ploughing at the first rains, April and May in the south, June and July in the centre and north. Reason the rule is a condition and not a date: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Referrals: ANAMET for this season's onset and forecasts, ICAT for the prefecture's calendar.
How many days of rain in a row counts as settled?

No source I hold puts a number on it, and I will not invent one, because you would sow on it. What the brochure gives is the description: the rains are properly settled when it rains regularly, and you do not sow on one isolated shower. That is deliberately a judgement rather than a count, and the reason is given: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Two places to get better than a guess. ANAMET, for this season's onset and its forecasts. And ICAT, for the calendar of your own prefecture, where the local reading of settled will be known.
I have three plots. Do I sow them all at once when the rains settle?

Nothing in the sources addresses staggering across plots, so I will not make a rule for it. The condition applies to each sowing: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. What the sources do give you, if the plots are in different regions, is that the bands differ: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And if any of the plots is a second season crop in the south, that one needs an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings there.
The whole village sows the day after the first big rain. What do I say?

Say what the brochure says, which is short: do not sow on one isolated shower; sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. And give the reason it gives, that the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, so a date or a single rain is not a signal. The month bands are there as a frame, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, not as the decision. If they want something better than an argument, ANAMET gives this season's onset and its forecasts, and ICAT holds the calendar of the prefecture.
I sowed and then it did not rain again for three weeks.

That is what the instruction is written against: do not sow on one isolated shower, and sow only when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly. It is easy to say afterwards and hard in the moment, which is why the brochure states it as a rule rather than leaving it to judgement. For next season, two things. Watch for regularity rather than for a first rain, within the band for your region, April to May in Maritime and Plateaux or June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. And follow ANAMET for this season's onset and forecasts, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year.
Everyone is telling me a different thing about when to sow.
Then take the rule rather than the opinions, but tell me where you are first, because the month band differs: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes.
Savanes, and it rained heavily two days ago for the first time.

Then hold off, on two counts. The rule first: the brochure says to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not to sow on one isolated shower. One heavy rain two days ago is exactly the case it names. The calendar second: in Centrale, Kara and Savanes sowing goes in June to July, with ploughing at the first rains in the same months and the plot cleared in April and May, so unless you are already in that band, a first rain is early rather than late. What to do instead of sowing: get the ploughing done at these first rains, which is what those months are for, and watch whether the rain repeats. Follow ANAMET for this season's onset and its forecasts, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, and ask ICAT for the calendar of your own prefecture. One more thing for your region: late sowing is to be avoided in the north, because that is where maize streak virus does its damage there, so once the rains are settled do not delay either.
quoi semer en octobre

I cannot tell you, because no source I hold says which crop to sow in a given month such as October. What I have is the maize calendar of the main season, dated by region, and the shape of the seasons: two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October, and one in the north, around May to October.
