My maize is harvested and the field is empty in August. What do I put in?

I cannot name a crop for August, and I would rather say so than invent one: none of my sources says which crop to sow in a given month. What I do have that bears on your case: in the south, Maritime and Plateaux, there is a second, shorter season, and for it the plot is chosen in July, so the timing you describe is not empty in the sources, only the crop is. If you are in the south and the second crop is maize, it needs an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings there. ICAT for your prefecture, ANAMET for the rains.
You have given me months for everything, so you must know what to plant in each.

The months I have are for operations on one crop, not a choice of crops. What the maize brochure dates is clearing, ploughing and sowing, region by region: clear in February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes; plough at the first rains in April and May, or June and July; sow when the rains are settled in the same bands. That is the maize calendar of the main season. Which crop suits a given month in a given prefecture is a different question and no source I hold answers it. ICAT for that, and ANAMET for this year's rains.
True or false: there is a national calendar saying what to sow each month.

Not in what I hold, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I have is the maize calendar of the main season, dated by region, plus the shape of the seasons: two rainy seasons in the south, around March to June and again around October, one in the north, around May to October, with Centrale able to behave either way. None of my sources gives a month by month choice of crop for a region. If such a calendar exists, ICAT will know, since it is the office for the calendar of your own prefecture. ANAMET is the service for this season's rains.
Cowpea or groundnut for the short season? Which fits the months better?

I cannot choose between them on the calendar, because no source I hold gives the cycle of cowpea or of groundnut, nor says which crop suits which month. The calendar I have is the maize one, dated by region for the main season, plus the second season in the south for which the plot is chosen in July. For maize I could answer a question like yours, because the variety list gives cycles from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115. For cowpea and groundnut I have no such figures. Ask ICAT for your prefecture, which is exactly the office for this.
Why will you not just estimate a sowing month for my crop? Justify.

Because a sowing month is the kind of estimate you cannot recover from. You would clear, plough, buy seed and sow on it, and if it were wrong the season would be gone before the mistake showed. My sources give the maize calendar of the main season and the shape of the seasons, and they say plainly that none of them gives a month by month choice of crop; they add that the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why even the dates they do give are bands around a condition. ICAT holds the calendar of your prefecture and ANAMET this year's rains. Both can answer; I cannot.
State exactly what calendar information exists and what does not.

Exists: the shape of the seasons, two rainy seasons in the south around March to June and again around October, one in the north around May to October, Centrale able to behave either way. The maize calendar of the main season, dated by region: plot chosen in January in the south and April in Centrale, Kara and Savanes; cleared February and March in the south, April and May elsewhere; ploughed at the first rains April and May, or June and July; sown when the rains are settled, same bands. The second season plot chosen in July in the south. Does not exist in my sources: any month by month choice of crop for a region, and any date for this year's onset.
Could you at least give me a rough calendar for three crops?

I can give it for one, and that honestly. For maize, the main season by region: plot chosen in January in Maritime and Plateaux and April in Centrale, Kara and Savanes; cleared in February and March, or April and May; ploughed at the first rains in April and May, or June and July; sown when the rains are properly settled in the same bands. For a second maize crop in the south, the plot is chosen in July. For any other crop I have no dates at all, and three rough calendars from me would be one real one and two invented. ICAT for your prefecture.
The group wants a planting calendar they can pin on the wall.

What can honestly go on that wall is the maize main season, dated by region, and the shape of the year. Maritime and Plateaux: plot chosen January, cleared February and March, ploughed at the first rains April and May, sown when the rains are settled April to May; second season plot chosen July. Centrale, Kara and Savanes: plot chosen April, cleared April and May, ploughed and sown June to July. Across the top, the rule: sow when it rains regularly, never on one isolated shower. What cannot go on it is a crop for each month, because no source I hold gives that. Put ICAT and ANAMET at the bottom for the rest.
Before I plan the year, what should I go and find out?

Two things I cannot give you. The calendar of your own prefecture, from ICAT, which is where a month by month choice of crop would come from, since none of my sources carries one. And this season's onset and forecasts, from ANAMET, because the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. Take with you what I can give: the maize main season dated by region, the shape of the seasons, two in the south and one in the north with Centrale either way, and the sowing rule, which is to sow when it rains regularly and never on one isolated shower.
I keep missing the right moment and sowing too late.

Then fix the two ends of the problem, because one is a calendar matter and one is not. The calendar end: in Maritime and Plateaux the plot is cleared in February and March and ploughed at the first rains in April and May, so that when the rains settle in April to May you are ready to sow; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is cleared in April and May and ploughed in June and July. Being late at sowing usually means being late at clearing. The other end is watching: sow when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. And in the north, avoid late sowing, since that is where maize streak virus does its damage there.
Just tell me something I can sow in October, anything.

I will not name a crop, and this is one of the clearest cases where an invented answer would cost you real money. None of my sources says which crop to sow in a given month such as October, and I have no cycle figures for anything but maize. What I can tell you about October is only the shape: FAO GIEWS puts a second rainy season in the south around that time, and the northern season running around May to October. If you are in the south and thinking of a second maize crop, the plot for it is chosen in July and it needs an improved tolerant variety. For an actual crop, ICAT, and ANAMET for the rains.
I want to plan what goes in each month of the year.

I have to be straight with you before we start: none of my sources gives a month by month choice of crop for a region, so I can help with part of this and not all of it. Tell me where you are and which crops you actually grow, and I will tell you which parts I can date and which I cannot.
Plateaux, and I grow maize, cassava and some cowpea.

Then maize I can date and the other two I cannot, which is the honest split. For maize in Maritime and Plateaux, the main season runs: plot chosen in January, cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, sown when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, in April to May. Never on one isolated shower. For a second maize crop, which the south allows because it has two rainy seasons, the plot is chosen in July, and that crop needs an improved tolerant variety because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south. For cassava and cowpea I have no sowing months at all, and I will not estimate them. What I can say is that both appear in the associations recorded for your region, maize with cassava, maize with cowpea and maize with cassava and cowpea, so the question of when they go in relative to the maize is a real one for ICAT, which holds the calendar of your prefecture. ANAMET for this year's rains.
I have just taken land in Dapaong and I want to get the timing right.

Dapaong is in Savanes, so you are on the northern calendar and there is one rainy season rather than two. The maize brochure dates the operations for Centrale, Kara and Savanes like this: the plot is chosen in April, cleared in April and May, ploughed at the first rains in June and July, and sown when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, in June to July. Do not sow on one isolated shower. One warning for your region: avoid late sowing, because maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings in the north. ICAT for your prefecture's calendar, ANAMET for this season's onset.
True or false: ploughing and sowing happen in the same months.

In the brochure's bands they overlap, which is true but worth reading carefully. Ploughing is at the first rains: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Sowing is when the rains are properly settled: April to May in the south, June to July in the centre and north. So the months are the same, but the triggers are different, the first rains for one and settled rains for the other, and the order is fixed. What comes earlier is the clearing: February and March in the south, April and May in the centre and north.
Should I clear now or wait until nearer the rains?

Clear in the months given for your region, which are well before the rains: February and March in Maritime and Plateaux, April and May in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. The ploughing is what waits for the rain, being done at the first rains in April and May in the south or June and July in the centre and north, and the sowing waits longer still, for the rains to be properly settled. The order is the point: clearing early is what makes it possible to plough as soon as the first rains come and to sow as soon as they settle, rather than being a month behind the season.
Why plough at the first rains rather than before or after? Justify.

The brochure fixes the trigger without explaining it, so I will give you what it says rather than a reason it does not give. Ploughing is at the first rains, which is April and May in Maritime and Plateaux and June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. What I can point out is the sequence it sits in: the plot is cleared earlier, in February and March or April and May, so that the ploughing can follow the first rains immediately, and the sowing then waits for a different signal, the rains being properly settled, that is raining regularly. Three stages, three triggers. For the agronomy behind it, ask ICAT.
What date in April exactly should I plough in the Plateaux?

There is no date, and the reason is stated in the sources: the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. The brochure gives April and May for ploughing in Maritime and Plateaux and attaches it to an event rather than a day, which is the first rains. The same logic runs through the calendar: sowing is when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. So what you are watching for is the rain, inside the month band. ANAMET is the service for this season's onset and its forecasts; ICAT holds the calendar of your prefecture.
The cooperative wants the operations calendar written out for both halves of the country.

Two columns. Maritime and Plateaux: plot chosen in January; cleared in February and March; ploughed at the first rains in April and May; sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May; second season plot chosen in July. Centrale, Kara and Savanes: plot chosen in April; cleared in April and May; ploughed at the first rains in June and July; sown when the rains are properly settled in June to July. Across both, one rule: sow when it rains regularly, never on one isolated shower. And two notes: avoid late sowing in the north, and a second season crop in the south needs a tolerant variety.
The clearing is done. What comes next and when?

Ploughing, and it waits for the first rains rather than for a date: April and May in Maritime and Plateaux, June and July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. After that, sowing, on a different signal again, when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, in the same month bands. Do not sow on one isolated shower. Between now and then is the time to settle the variety, since the cycle has to fit your season, and to get the seed from an approved seller. Follow ANAMET for this season's onset so the first rains do not catch you unready.
Walk me through the main season from start to finish.

In Maritime and Plateaux: the plot is chosen in January, cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, and sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes everything shifts about two months: the plot is chosen in April, cleared in April and May, ploughed at the first rains in June and July, and sown when the rains are settled in June to July. The last step is the one with a condition rather than a date attached: it rains regularly, and not one isolated shower. After sowing, the calendar in my sources stops; the rest of the crop year is not dated there.
By the time I finish clearing, the rains have already come.

Then the clearing is starting too late for your region. In Maritime and Plateaux it is dated February and March, which is a month or two before the first rains of April and May; in Centrale, Kara and Savanes it is April and May, before first rains in June and July. The whole point of that gap is that the ploughing can follow the first rains at once and the sowing follow the settled rains. If clearing runs into the rains, you are ploughing late and sowing later, and in the north late sowing is what maize streak virus punishes. Bring the clearing forward to the band for your region.
Just give me the months and skip the conditions.

The months are these. Maritime and Plateaux: plot January, clearing February and March, ploughing April and May, sowing April to May. Centrale, Kara and Savanes: plot April, clearing April and May, ploughing June and July, sowing June to July. But I will not skip the condition on the last line, because it is the one that loses crops: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and never on one isolated shower. The months are a band and the rain is the signal, since the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. ANAMET for this season's onset.
I want to know exactly what to do and when this season.
Tell me your region and I will give you the dated operations, because the brochure gives each one twice, once for Maritime and Plateaux and once for Centrale, Kara and Savanes.
Kara, and I am starting from an uncleared plot.

Then you are on the northern calendar and the sequence is this. Choose the plot in April, which for you is effectively now if the season is ahead of you. Clear it in April and May. Plough at the first rains, June and July. Then sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, in June to July, and not on one isolated shower. Two things specific to your region. There is one rainy season rather than two, around May to October, so there is no second crop to fall back on if this one is missed. And avoid late sowing, because maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings in the north, which means the clearing has to be finished on time for the rest to follow. Use the weeks before the rains to settle your variety and buy seed from an approved seller, since the cycle has to fit your season. Follow ANAMET for this season's onset, and ask ICAT for the calendar of your own prefecture.
How does the second season work in the south?

It exists because the south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons rather than one; FAO GIEWS puts them around March to June and again around October. For it the plot is chosen in July, against January for the main season, and it is the shorter of the two. One warning comes with it: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so a second season crop needs an improved tolerant variety. That points you at the variety list, where most improved varieties are tolerant to streak. ICAT for the calendar of your prefecture.
The second season is just the main season done again.

It is shorter and it carries a risk the main one does not. The plot for it is chosen in July, against January for the main season, so the preparation is compressed. And the maize brochure warns that maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, which is why a second season crop needs an improved tolerant variety rather than whatever you sowed in the main season. The shortness also bears on the variety: the list runs from 75 to 85 days at one end to 105 to 115 at the other, and a short season calls for the short end.
True or false: I can run a second season anywhere in Togo.

False. The second season belongs to the south, Maritime and Plateaux, which has two rainy seasons; the north, Kara and Savanes, has one. Centrale sits between the two and can behave either way, so there it is a local question for ICAT. FAO GIEWS puts the southern pattern at around March to June and again around October, and the northern one at around May to October. Where a second season does exist, the plot for it is chosen in July, and the crop needs an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south.
Set out the second season.

Where: the south, Maritime and Plateaux, which has two rainy seasons; FAO GIEWS puts the second around October. Not in Kara or Savanes, which have one; Centrale can behave either way. Plot chosen: July, against January for the main season. Character: the shorter of the two seasons. Risk: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so the crop needs an improved tolerant variety. Corresponding note for the north: late sowings are where the same virus does its damage there, so late sowing should be avoided. Referrals: ICAT for the prefecture's calendar, ANAMET for this year's rains.
When exactly do I sow the second season crop?

I do not have a sowing month for it, and I will not construct one. What the sources give for the second season in the south is that the plot is chosen in July, and that the season is the shorter of the two; FAO GIEWS puts the southern second rains around October. The sowing months I have, April to May in the south and June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes, are the main season bands. The rule that does carry over is the condition: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, not on one isolated shower. ICAT for your prefecture, ANAMET for the rains.
Is a second crop worth it on a small plot?

The sources give no yield or cost figure for a second season, so I cannot answer on value and will not pretend to. What they do give is what it demands: the plot chosen in July, a shorter season than the main one, and an improved tolerant variety, because maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south. The variety requirement is the part that costs money regardless of plot size, since it means buying seed rather than using what you have. Whether that pays on your plot is a question for ICAT, which holds the calendar of your prefecture.
People in my village sow a second crop with leftover seed from the first.

That is the practice the warning is aimed at. The brochure says maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, and that a second season crop therefore needs an improved tolerant variety. Leftover seed is whatever the first season was, chosen for a different purpose, and if it was not a tolerant variety the second crop is exposed. There is a second problem with leftover grain in general: the brochure warns against sowing grain taken from your own granary, because it germinates badly. Tell them the plot is chosen in July for that season, and to buy tolerant seed from an approved seller.
The main harvest is nearly in and I want a second crop. What do I do now?

Choose the plot, which the sources date to July for the second season in the south, and settle the variety at the same time, because that is where the risk sits: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so the crop needs an improved tolerant variety. Buy it from an approved seller rather than using leftover seed. Take the cycle into account too, since this is the shorter season and the variety list runs from 75 to 85 days at the short end. Then apply the same sowing rule as ever: when the rains are properly settled, not on one isolated shower.
Describe the difference between the two southern seasons.

The main season is long and prepared early: the plot is chosen in January, cleared in February and March, ploughed at the first rains in April and May, sown when the rains are properly settled in April to May. The second is shorter and prepared in July, when the plot for it is chosen; FAO GIEWS puts those rains around October, against around March to June for the first. The other difference is the risk: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so that crop needs an improved tolerant variety where the main season crop may not.
My second crop is always poorer than the first.

Two things in the sources speak to that. It is the shorter of the two seasons, so a variety chosen for the main season may not finish in it: the list runs from 75 to 85 days at the short end to 105 to 115 at the long. And the risk is concentrated there: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, which is why the brochure says that crop needs an improved tolerant variety. So check the cycle and check the variety before looking further. The plot for that season is chosen in July. ICAT for your prefecture's calendar.
Just tell me I can use the same variety for both seasons.

I will not, because the brochure singles out the second season for a reason: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so a second season crop needs an improved tolerant variety. If what you sowed in the main season was already an improved tolerant variety, then you are covered, and most of the improved varieties are tolerant to streak. If it was not, the second season is the wrong place to find out. The other thing that may differ is the cycle, since this is the shorter season. Ask ICAT or ITRA which variety suits, and buy from an approved seller.
I want to get two crops off the same field this year.

Whether you can depends on where you are, so tell me that first. The south, Maritime and Plateaux, has two rainy seasons; the north, Kara and Savanes, has one; Centrale sits between and can behave either way.
Maritime, and I have already sown the main season maize.

Then a second crop is possible where you are, and the timing is already close. The plot for the second season is chosen in July, against January for the main one, so that is the decision in front of you. Three things to settle with it. The variety, which is the one the brochure is firm about: maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south, so a second season crop needs an improved tolerant variety, and most of the improved varieties are tolerant to streak. Buy it from an approved seller rather than keeping back seed from the first crop. The cycle, because this is the shorter of the two seasons and the released varieties run from 75 to 85 days up to 105 to 115. And the sowing signal, unchanged: when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, never on one isolated shower. I do not have a sowing month for the second season itself, only that the plot is chosen in July and that FAO GIEWS puts those southern rains around October, so ask ICAT for your prefecture and follow ANAMET for the rains.
The rains are late this year. What do I do?

Wait for them rather than sowing to the calendar: the rule is to sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower, and the reason given is that the useful rains do not start on the same date every year. While you wait, get the earlier operations done, since ploughing is at the first rains and the clearing should already be behind you. And think about the variety, because a shortened season may call for a shorter cycle: the released list runs from 75 to 85 days at one end to 105 to 115 at the other. ANAMET for this season's onset.
pluies en retard semer quand meme

No. Sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and never on one isolated shower. The useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why the calendar gives month bands rather than dates: April to May in Maritime and Plateaux, June to July in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. If the season is shortened, look at a shorter cycle variety, from 75 to 85 days at the short end of the list. ANAMET for this season's onset, ICAT for your prefecture.
If the rains are late I should sow a longer variety to catch up.

That is the wrong way round. A longer variety needs more days of rain, not fewer, so a late start makes it more likely to be caught at the end. The released list runs 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, 105 to 115 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. A shortened season points to the short end. And whatever you sow, sow it when the rains are properly settled, not on one isolated shower. ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season.
True or false: a late sowing is as good as an early one if the variety is right.

Not in the north, where the sources are explicit: maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings in the north, so late sowing should be avoided there. In the south the corresponding warning falls on second season sowings rather than on late ones. So the answer depends on where you are, and in Kara or Savanes lateness carries a named risk beyond the shortened season. The variety does matter as well, since the cycle has to finish inside the rains, and most improved varieties are tolerant to streak, which is itself the control against it.
Sow late with what I have, or wait a year?

I cannot make that call for you, and the sources do not either, but they give you the two things that should weigh. If you are in Kara or Savanes, late sowing carries a named risk: maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings in the north, and late sowing should be avoided. And whatever the region, the cycle has to fit what is left of the season, which points to the short end of the list, 75 to 85 days. What they do not give is any comparison between sowing late and not sowing. ICAT for your prefecture's calendar, and ANAMET for what is left of this season.
Why is late sowing worse in the north than in the south? Justify.

The brochure records where the damage falls rather than explaining why, so I will not construct a mechanism. What it states is that maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and on late sowings in the north. What sits behind that in the calendar is that the north has one rainy season, around May to October, while the south has two, around March to June and again around October, so a late sowing in the north has no second season behind it and the exposure falls there instead. The practical conclusions it draws are the ones to act on: avoid late sowing in the north, and use a tolerant variety for a second season crop in the south.
State what the sources say about late and shifted seasons.

One, the useful rains do not start on the same date every year, which is why the calendar gives month bands and ties the operations to events: ploughing at the first rains, sowing when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and never on one isolated shower. Two, maize streak virus does its damage mainly on second season sowings in the south and on late sowings in the north, so late sowing should be avoided in the north and a second season crop in the south needs an improved tolerant variety. Three, for this year's onset and forecasts, ANAMET; for the prefecture's calendar, ICAT. No source gives a cut-off date after which sowing should stop.
After what date is it definitely too late to sow?

No source I hold gives a cut-off date, and I will not invent one, because you would either sow on it or abandon a season on it. What they give is a direction rather than a line: avoid late sowing in the north, where maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings. And the arithmetic you can do yourself, which is the cycle of the variety against the rain you have left: the released list runs from 75 to 85 days at the short end up to 105 to 115. For how much season is left this year, ANAMET; for a judgement on your own plot, ICAT.
I have three weeks less rain than usual. What does that change?

It changes which varieties can finish, and that is something you can work out. The released list gives cycles of 75 to 85 days for TZEE W Pop STR QPM and EV99 QPM, 90 to 95 for Pool 18 QPM SR and Amen, 90 to 100 for AB11 and Ikenne 9449 SR, 100 to 110 for Obatanpa, and 105 to 115 for ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W and Sotubaka. Three weeks is about twenty days, so a variety that was just fitting at 105 to 115 no longer does. What it does not change is the sowing rule: when the rains are properly settled, not on one isolated shower. ANAMET for what is left of the season.
Describe how a late season plays out if I do nothing differently.

The clearing and the ploughing sit waiting, since the ploughing is tied to the first rains rather than to a date. Then the sowing goes in late, because the rains settled late. Then the crop runs into the end of the season: a variety of 105 to 115 days sown three weeks late finishes three weeks late, into whatever rain is left. In the north there is an added exposure, because maize streak virus does its damage on late sowings there. What changes the picture is the variety, taking a shorter cycle from the list, and watching ANAMET rather than the calendar for the onset.
Just tell me to sow now and get it over with.

I will not, on the one test the sources give: sow when the rains are properly settled, that is when it rains regularly, and not on one isolated shower. If that condition is met where you are, then sow, and nothing I have says otherwise. If it is not, sowing now is sowing into ground that may not get rain again for weeks, and the seed is spent. What I can help with instead of agreeing is the variety, since a shortened season points to the short end of the list, 75 to 85 days. And ANAMET is the service that can tell you what this season is actually doing, which I cannot.
I am in Kara. When do I clear the plot and when do I sow?

For Kara the brochure gives April and May for clearing the plot, and June and July for sowing. Ploughing sits between them, also in June and July, at the first rains. Kara is grouped with Centrale and Savanes throughout, so those are your months. The dates are bands, not fixed days: sow when the rains have properly settled rather than after one isolated shower, and have the plot cleared and ready in advance so that you can sow the week they arrive. ANAMET can tell you how this season's rains are starting in your area.
Savanes region. Give me my clearing month and my sowing month, nothing else.

Clearing in April and May. Sowing in June and July. Savanes is grouped with Centrale and Kara in the ITRA and ICAT brochure, and those are the bands it gives for that group. Ploughing falls in June and July as well, at the first rains, if you need the third one. Treat the months as bands and let the rains decide the exact week: settled rain, not the first shower.
I farm near Lome. When do I clear and when do I sow?

For Maritime the brochure gives February and March for clearing the plot, and April and May for sowing. Ploughing comes in April and May too, at the first rains. Maritime is grouped with Plateaux, so those are the bands for both. The south also carries a second season later in the year, which the north does not. As everywhere, the months are bands: sow once the rains are properly established, not on an isolated shower, and have the plot ready beforehand.
Someone told me everyone in Togo clears in February. Is that right for me in Kara?

Not for you. That month belongs to the southern group, Maritime and Plateaux. Kara is grouped with Centrale and Savanes, and for that group the brochure puts clearing in April and May, ploughing at the first rains in June and July, and sowing in June and July once the rains are settled. The country has two calendars and they do not overlap, so a date heard from someone farming near the coast will be about two months early for your plot. Work from the northern band and let ANAMET tell you how the rains are starting this year.
What does it cost to grow one hectare of maize and what do I get back?

In the costed hectare the charges add up to 391,000 FCFA and the crop sells for 480,000 FCFA, which leaves a profit of 89,000 FCFA on a yield of 3,500 kg per hectare. Those come from the budget for one hectare of Obatanpa maize that ITRA and ICAT published in their 2008 maize brochure, drawn from a 2005 evaluation. They are 2005 figures for one hectare, not today's prices, and they only hold if the crop is sold after storage rather than at harvest. Use the structure as a template and put your own current prices into it.
Just the two totals for a hectare of maize. Charges and revenue.

Charges 391,000 FCFA. Revenue 480,000 FCFA. The difference is a profit of 89,000 FCFA, on a yield of 3,500 kg per hectare. That is the 2005 evaluation for one hectare of Obatanpa maize, published by ITRA and ICAT in their 2008 brochure. They are 2005 amounts, so treat them as the shape of the budget rather than as current prices, and rebuild it with what inputs cost you this season.
I read somewhere that a hectare of maize costs about 72,000 FCFA. Is that the whole cost?

No, that is one line inside the budget and not the bottom of it. In the 2005 evaluation published by ITRA and ICAT the charges for one hectare of Obatanpa maize add up to 391,000 FCFA in total, and the crop sells for 480,000 FCFA, leaving 89,000 FCFA of profit on 3,500 kg per hectare. A single item is easy to mistake for the total because it is the one people quote, and a budget built on it would leave you short by a wide margin. Work from the total and check which items your own plot actually needs.
Is the 480,000 the money I keep?

No, that is what the crop sells for, not what stays with you. In the 2005 evaluation for one hectare of Obatanpa maize the crop brings 480,000 FCFA, the charges take 391,000 FCFA, and what remains is a profit of 89,000 FCFA. The yield behind it is 3,500 kg per hectare, and the sale price assumes the maize is held in store rather than sold straight off the field. No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

Your heifer is dealing with a tick-borne disease, either gall sickness or redwater, caused by parasites carried by Amblyomma variegatum or Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus ticks. You need to call the veterinary service this same day so they can determine which disease it is and prescribe the right drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour because a red to black colour indicates redwater, while a yellow-brown colour indicates gall sickness. Keep the sick heifer in shade, provide clean water nearby and do not make her walk as she is short of red blood cells. Hand-pick all ticks you see on the whole herd, not just on the heifer, because ticks on other animals can infect them later. Never reuse a needle on two animals because gall sickness can be transmitted that way. See the veterinary service the same day.

If I increase the urea to twice the normal rate on my corn, will I get double the output?

No. More urea than recommended does not give more maize: over-dosing wastes your money and can even cut the yield. For maize, the ITRA and ICAT fiche gives about 100 kg of urea per hectare, put at panicle initiation, 30 to 45 days after sowing, in a pocket away from the stem so it does not burn the plant. What raises the harvest is putting the right amount at the right time, after the base NPK, and keeping the weeding on schedule. If you think your soil needs more, ask ICAT for an adjustment to your soil.

If I put double the urea on my corn, will I get double the harvest?

There are dark round spots on my peanuts leaves and they turn yellow then fall off. What is the disease and what can I do?

The disease is groundnut leaf spot caused by Cercospora fungi. Begin by rotating groundnut with cereals so you avoid planting it on the same land each year. Then use a tolerant groundnut variety and remove or bury the previous groundnut residues. After that, harvest at the right time because a weakened groundnut will drop its pods early. For resistant varieties or to know if a fungicide is needed, see ICAT.
The leaves of my peanut are turning yellow and dropping early with dark spots, how can I fix it?

It is groundnut leaf spot, a disease caused by Cercospora leaf-spot fungi. Begin by not growing groundnut on the same plot year after year; rotate the plot with cereals instead. Next, plant a tolerant groundnut variety and clear or bury all old groundnut residues in the field. Then, make sure to harvest the crop on time because a weakened crop will lose its pods. If you need information on resistant varieties or fungicide use, see ICAT.
The young groundnut leaves are shrot, mottled yelow and green, and look bunched, plus I keep finding tiny insects on them.

The symptoms point to groundnut rosette, transmitted by aphids. Begin by roguing out and destroying the severely damaged plants to cut the virus spread. Afterwards, sow the next groundnut crop early and use the close spacing that is recommended, as dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field completely weed-free to limit aphid hosts. For the following season, plant a tolerant groundnut variety. You can get resistant varieties from ICAT.
My goat kids are not eating and they keep drooling, and their cotas look thin. What could be wrong?

Your goats are suffering from leucaena poisoning because leucaena makes up too much of their feed. Reduce the amount of leucaena to only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Combine the remaining leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen receives enough roughage. Introduce this new mix gradually over several days. Always give the animals clean water and a source of mineral or salt. If the loss of appetite does not improve, or you notice continued drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat, you should consult the veterinary service.
In my field the corn whorl leaves have holes that look like glass panes and the middle shoot has died, but the outer leaves are still alive. Inside the stem I find tunnels and frass.

The symptoms indicate a maize stalk borer problem caused by the pink Busseola fusca or the spotted Chilo partellus. For young maize, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram covers roughly 1,500-2,000 plants and you must repeat the treatment every 8-10 days. Never use neem powder alone because the oil will scorch the maize, always combine it with the inert carrier. After you have harvested the maize, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop the area with a legume like cowpea or soybean. Should a large block be heavily attacked, contact ICAT promptly for approved control.
My maize is looking very short and I see white lines along the veins, plus a lot of leafhoppers hopping around.

You are dealing with maize streak virus, which makes maize plants stunted and shows chlorotic spots that turn into pale streaks along the veins. First, rogue out and destroy the most badly affected maize plants to remove the virus source. Then, for the following season, plant an improved MSV-tolerant maize variety and ask ICAT which seed is recommended. Also be sure to sow your maize early because planting late increases infection risk. For confirmation and the tolerant variety recommendation, see ICAT.
The maize in my garden has broken pale lines along the veins and stays short, and I keep seeing leafhoppers.

Also plant your maize early, because late sowing raises the likelihood of infection. For disease confirmation and the tolerant variety advice, go to ICAT.
The pepper seedlings I raised are tipping over at the soil line, any ideas?

Those chili seedlings are showing signs of damping-off, caused by fungi that love wet, airless beds. Water the beds so they stay uniformly moist but not soggy, and do not water them late at night. Plant seed that has been coated with a fungicide-insecticide and thin the sowing to avoid dense planting. Take out the seedlings that have collapsed, and improve both drainage and airflow in the nursery beds. If the disease continues to spread, you need to see ICAT for an approved nursery drench and the correct dosage.
My chilli seedlings are falling over as soon as they reach the soil line, any clue?

The seedlings are being affected by damping-off, a fungal issue that appears in wet, crowded beds. Water the beds so they stay evenly moist but never soggy, and do not water them late in the evening. Sow seed that has a fungicide-insecticide coating and sow it at a lower density. Take out the collapsed seedlings, and improve drainage and airflow in the nursery. If the problem persists, you should visit ICAT to obtain an approved nursery drench and the proper rate.
why do my pepper seedlings fall flat at the ground level and what can i do about it

Those pepper seedlings are being hit by damping-off, a fungus that thrives in overly wet, crowded nursery beds. Maintain the bed with even moisture, never letting it become soggy, and stop watering in the evening. Use seed that carries a fungicide-insecticide coating and sow it more sparsely to avoid thick planting. Eliminate the fallen seedlings, then enhance drainage and increase airflow in the bed. Should the disease keep spreading, go to ICAT to obtain an approved nursery drench and the proper dosage.
The litte chickens have blood in their droppings and they look sick, what should I do?

The condition you see is coccidiosis in chicks. Quickly make the bedding dry and change it, and keep the house tidy. Give the anticoccidial medication in the feed or water according to the dose supplied by the vet or auxiliary. Separate the ill chicks, provide fresh water and do not let them be overcrowded. why are my hatchlings dumping brown droppings and staying together not eating

Then separate the sick birds, give them clean water and ensure they are not overcrowded. If the chicks still die after you have a dry litter and have treated them, see a veterinary auxiliary. The problem is coccidiosis in chicks and the disease is coccidiosis.
My hens have hard bumps on their combs and some are coughing because of yellow spos in their throats.

The bumps and yellow throat spots are signs of fowl pox in your chickens. First you must isolate the sick chickens so they cannot pass the disease to the healthy ones. While they are isolated give them extra feed and clean water as the dry form passes. Then eliminate mosquito breeding by draining any standing water and keeping the area around the coop tidy. After mosquito control, vaccinate the whole flock against fowl pox. If the wet form with throat lesions appears, you should consult the veterinary service.
i see my chickens with wart-like lesions on their faces and some can t swallow because of yellow lesions in their mouths

Wart-like lesions on the face and yellow mouth lesions are typical of fowl pox in chickens. First isolate the infected chickens so they do not infect the rest of the flock. While they are isolated, give them extra feed and fresh water as the mild dry form passes. Next, cut down mosquito breeding by removing standing water and keeping the surroundings clean. After mosquito control, vaccinate all chickens against fowl pox. If you encounter the wet form with mouth or throat lesions, you should consult the veterinary service.
I found many of my flock dead at once and the others have nasal discharge, what should I do?

The problem is Newcastle disease in your chickens. Isolate each surviving chicken from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Burn or bury the carcasses and any contaminated litter, then disinfect the poultry house. After that, vaccinate the flock with the La Sota or B1 strain either in the drinking water or as eye-drops, and repeat the vaccination as advised. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary without delay.
My chick lost several birds suddenly and the rest have eye discharge, is this disease serious?

It is Newcastle disease striking your chickens. First, keep every healthy bird away from the sick ones and do not move, sell or gift any bird. Then destroy the dead birds by burning or burying them, remove soiled litter and disinfect the coop. Afterwards, vaccinate the remaining chickens with the La Sota or B1 strain through water or eye-drops, following the recommended repeat schedule. You need to see the veterinary service or the village livestock auxiliary right now.

In my market garden the tomato levaes are gettting dark, soggy patches and a white mold appears on the lower side when it's humid, and the fruit is blackening and falling off.

The problem is tomato late blight caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Begin by removing any affected plants or leaves and destroying them right away to stop spores from moving. Then space the remaining tomatoes and stake them so air can flow through the canopy. Avoid overhead watering late in the day to keep the leaves dry. Afterwards, use a resistant tomato variety and, if needed, apply an approved fungicide at the rate indicated on the label. To obtain the proper fungicide and its application rate, go to ICAT.
The leaves on my tomato crop are curling uppward, looking yelllow, and the vines are stunted and crowded with few tomatoes. Can you tell me what to do?

Your crop is suffering from tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Begin by controlling the whitefly, keeping the garden tidy and acting as soon as you notice insects.
