Climate smart practices togo. These practices come from the catalogue of five technical sheets of good agricultural practices in the era of climate change. Steps: These practices come from the catalogue of five technical sheets of good agricultural practices in the era of climate change, published in 2020 by the Togolese Ministry of Agriculture with the PASA project and the World Bank. Its own heading is: let us durably increase yields by combining trees and animals with our crops. Alley cropping: grow your seasonal crops in the alleys between rows of fertiliser trees. Lay the alleys across the slope, not down it. Space the trees 2 to 4 m apart in the row and leave 10, 20 or 30 m between alleys, then grow maize or cowpea in between. The fertiliser trees the catalogue names are Leucaena leucocephala, Senna siamea, called zanguerati, which it describes as a fertilising plant resistant to drought, and Faidherbia albida. Prune the alley trees the first time between 15 and 20 months, when they are at least 1.50 m tall; a high cut at 2 m above the ground is advised. After that prune regularly, according to the trees and to whether you want firewood or organic fertiliser. Windbreak: a curtain of trees planted in lines against the dominant wind, with a windward side and a sheltered side. Orient it opposite to the dominant wind. On one line, space the plants 1 to 1.5 m, which is 66 to 100 plants per 100 m; on a band of two or three lines, 2 m between the lines and 1.5 m in the line, which is 133 to 200 plants per 100 m. Plant during the rainy season. Live hedge, to keep animals, wind or light out: dig a continuous trench 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line. Plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants; jatropha and thevetia are often used between the trees. For the two following seasons, weed it and replace the plants that died. Assisted natural regeneration: simply select and protect the valuable young trees that come up on their own in your field, so the field is never left bare. Measure the field, count the kinds of tree worth keeping, choose them, then protect them by weeding, fire breaks, stakes for the weak ones, removing greedy branches and keeping animals off. In the dry savanna zone the catalogue suggests keeping about 25 to 30 adult trees per hectare and 60 to 80 young shoots or suckers per hectare. Taungya, where land is scarce: replanting trees is the first aim and crops are grown under them for only two or three years so the trees can grow. Plant the trees about 2 m by 2 m; grow cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two following years. The trees used, in the catalogue's own words, are teak, gmelina which it also calls Indian teak, Anacardium which it also calls atchan and which is the cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna which it also calls zanguerati, and neem. The catalogue adds that combining trees, animals and crops is what makes land management durable and raises the grower's income: hives for honey, snail rearing, mushrooms, selling the wood from pruning, composting animal droppings and plant debris, and feeding the stock on the leaves of the trees planted on the holding. Composting in a heap, to keep soil fertile: choose a shaded spot, out of the wind and rain, easy to reach, and a water point is an advantage. Chop up the residues that rot fast, such as straw and groundnut, soya or cowpea leaves, and avoid the slow ones, the stalks of sorghum, millet and maize, and the husks. Build the heap in layers, watering each one as you lay it: a little wood ash on the topsoil, then a base of slow-rotting material such as rice husks or ronier leaves 10 to 20 cm thick, then 5 cm of manure, then about 30 cm of plant residues well trodden down, then a layer of topsoil, or well rotted compost, or Mycotri, as the activator. The catalogue describes Mycotri as a powder of fungi that speeds up the decomposition of plant and animal debris so as to have a mature compost in a shorter time. It is one of the three things offered for that last activator layer, beside topsoil and well rotted compost, and it is the only one the catalogue attaches a benefit to. It does not say how much time is saved nor where to find it. For rice growers, simple lowland development: build basins and drains so the water moves properly over the whole plot, which lets you regulate how much water sits on each parcel. A farmer-made water level is enough on a small area: two sticks graduated every 5 cm joined by a 5 m garden hose with a clear tube on top. For the bunds: a main bund is 80 to 100 cm wide at the base, 35 to 40 cm at the top and 30 to 35 cm high; a secondary bund is 70 to 80 cm at the base, 25 to 30 cm at the top and 25 to 30 cm high. Water them as you build so they compact, leave spillways at the ends of the main bund to let excess water out, and count 80 to 100 pegs per hectare to mark the layout. The catalogue advises doing this lowland work as a group through a farmers' organisation, because one household rarely has the labour, and replanting elsewhere the trees cleared from the site. Where: all; the assisted natural regeneration figures are given for the dry savanna zone. When: plant the trees during the rainy season. Who to see: ICAT for the practice that suits your land and for the tree species available near you. the catalogue gives no cost, no yield gain and no measure of how much these practices offset climate change, so do not promise a figure.

Making compost. Heap alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure and a little soil. Steps: Heap alternating layers of crop residues, animal manure and a little soil; keep it damp like a wrung-out cloth. Turn it every few weeks; it is ready when dark, crumbly and no longer smells raw. Work it in before sowing (aim ~5 t/ha, about 50 wheelbarrows); leave/bury field residues rather than burning. When: any. Where: all. Who to see: ICAT for a composting method suited to your residues.

Sowing cowpea. Use a resistant improved 55-75 day variety. Host: cowpea. Steps: Use a resistant improved 55-75 day variety. Extra-early varieties (60-65 days): 60-65 cm between rows, 40 cm between pockets. Intermediate: 80 cm x 40 cm. Three grains per pocket. First weeding ~2 weeks after sowing; then the three flowering-stage sprays for pod protection. Where: all. When: sow mid-June to early July when rains are strong. Who to see: ICAT for a variety matched to your grain or fodder aim.

Storing cowpea grain. Sort and fully dry the grain first (damp grain moulds and undoes everything). Host: cowpea. Steps: Sort and fully dry the grain first (damp grain moulds and undoes everything). Ash/sand method: mix an equal volume of sifted ash or fine sand through the grain in a canari/tin, topped with a 3 cm ash layer, then seal. Oil method: 15-30 ml of groundnut, palm or neem oil per 2.5 kg bowl, mixed well, stored sealed. Or an approved storage insecticide (e.g. an Actellic type) at the labelled dose. Who to see: ICAT for the currently approved storage product. Where: all. When: post-harvest.

Cropping systems togo. In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops. Host: maize. Steps: In the south, Maritime and Plateaux, maize is usually grown with other crops; the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure lists maize with cassava, maize with cowpea, maize with groundnut, maize with cassava and cowpea, and maize with cassava, cowpea and groundnut. In Centrale, Kara and Savanes maize is more often grown pure, and the brochure recommends running a succession instead of an association. The successions the brochure gives are: maize then cotton then sorghum then groundnut or cowpea then maize; maize then cowpea or groundnut then maize then cowpea or groundnut then fallow; maize then cassava then cowpea then maize; fallow then yam then maize then fallow; and cotton then maize then cotton. The rule behind all of them: maize comes at the head of the rotation, followed by a legume, then a root crop, then a fallow. If you put cowpea, groundnut or cassava in with your maize, widen the spacing between the pockets; the brochure says to do it and does not give a reason. Against striga, use a striga-tolerant maize variety together with or in rotation with a grain legume such as soya, cowpea or groundnut, and pull the striga plants out before they flower. When maize is followed by cotton in the same year, sow an extra-early variety of 75 to 85 days so the two crops do not sit together for long, and sow the cotton into the maize two to three weeks before the maize harvest. Why a rotation works, in the words of the Ministry and PASA catalogue of good practices: a rotation is a succession of crops in time on the same plot, it improves soil fertility and it helps fight the enemies of the crops. Their worked four-year example says what each crop does for the soil. Year one, improving plants, the legumes that feed the soil with nitrogen: beans, groundnut, cowpea. Year two, the soil now being rich in nitrogen, a hungry plant that takes a lot: maize. Year three, a root or tuber crop that goes down for the nutrients left deeper: yam. Year four, an undemanding plant such as a leafy vegetable: okra. Then back to year one with legumes. Before fixing a rotation, take account of the fertility of the soil and of what grew there last season. When you associate crops, the same catalogue says to respect the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs and the period over which the two crops share the plot. Cereals with legumes is the association it recommends: maize, millet or sorghum grown with beans, cowpea or soya on the same plot. It also shows maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. You can also alternate a line of maize and a line of soya, keeping in mind that grown pure, maize is spaced 80 cm by 40 cm and soya 40 cm by 20 cm. Who to see: ITRA or a registered seed seller for a striga-tolerant variety. ICAT for the association or rotation that suits your plot and your region. Where: associations mostly in the south (Maritime and Plateaux). successions mostly in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. When: the whole cropping year.

When you associate crops, the same catalogue says to respect the rooting system of each plant, the sowing density, the nutrient needs, the leaf development, the light needs and the period over which the two crops share the plot. Cereals with legumes is the association it recommends: maize, millet or sorghum grown with beans, cowpea or soya on the same plot. It also shows maize with pigeon pea, yam with okra and maize, moringa with maize and cucumber, and soya with maize. You can also alternate a line of maize and a line of soya, keeping in mind that grown pure, maize is spaced 80 cm by 40 cm and soya 40 cm by 20 cm. When: the whole cropping year. Where: associations mostly in the south (Maritime and Plateaux). successions mostly in Centrale, Kara and Savanes. Who to see: ICAT for the association or rotation that suits your plot and your region. ITRA or a registered seed seller for a striga-tolerant variety.

Dry-season feeding of goats and sheep. At harvest, gather cereal straw, legume haulm (cowpea, groundnut) and dried tuber peelings. Steps: At harvest, gather cereal straw, legume haulm (cowpea, groundnut) and dried tuber peelings; store on raised racks in a dry place. Treat dry cereal straw with urea so animals eat more: ~2.5 kg urea in 25 L water per 100 kg straw, layered and packed in a lined pit, covered, opened after curing (wear gloves/boots). Sprinkle salt water on cobs/stover; give clean water and a mineral source. When: dry season. Who to see: ICAT to demonstrate the urea-treatment pit safely. Where: all, especially the north.

Growing groundnut. Grow on light, well-drained soil. Host: groundnut. Steps: Grow on light, well-drained soil; sow early and at the recommended close spacing (reduces rosette). Do not grow groundnut on the same land two years running; rotate with cereals. At harvest, dry the pods HARD before shelling (damp nuts grow aflatoxin); sort out mouldy nuts. Plant a cereal after the groundnut to use the fixed nitrogen; cut stems at ground level to leave the nodules. When: sow early when rains are set. Where: all. Who to see: ICAT for a tolerant variety if rosette or leaf spot is a yearly problem.

Raising guinea fowl keets. Brood keets (under 3 months) with a mother-hen in a clean, dry brooder, sheltered from wind/rain, separate from adults. Host: guinea fowl. Steps: Brood keets (under 3 months) with a mother-hen in a clean, dry brooder, sheltered from wind/rain, separate from adults. Feed and water little and often, several times a day, in their own low feeders, with a fine protein-rich starter; keep water always clean. Keep litter dry and disinfected; check morning and evening and shut in any that look weak. Where: all. Who to see: livestock auxiliary if keets keep dying or show discharge/diarrhoea. When: any.

Maize farm budget: give me the complete overview, signs, cause, what to do, who to see.

Maize farm budget. The figures below come from one study: the costed hectare of Obatanpa maize published by ITRA and ICAT in their 2008 maize brochure, from a 2005 internal communication. Host: maize. Steps: The figures below come from one study: the costed hectare of Obatanpa maize published by ITRA and ICAT in their 2008 maize brochure, from a 2005 internal communication. They are 2005 evaluations for one hectare, not today's prices, and they must be given that way. In that costed hectare the charges add up to 391,000 FCFA and the crop sells for 480,000 FCFA, leaving a profit of 89,000 FCFA on a yield of 3,500 kg per hectare. The big items are the inputs and the machine work: 72,000 FCFA for six bags of NPK and urea, 40,000 for tractor ploughing, 25,000 for the pulverising pass, 20,000 for renting the plot and 10,000 for 25 kg of commercial seed. Labour is the other half, counted in man-days at 700 FCFA: 55 for harvest and transport, 30 for the first weeding and thinning, 30 for shelling and winnowing, 25 for the second weeding, 20 for spreading NPK, 20 for treatment and bagging, 10 for sowing, 10 for the urea and 10 for drying. Do not forget the small things that the study still counts: 14,000 FCFA of grain protectant, 21,000 for jute bags, 20,000 for pallets, 2,000 for twine and needle and 20,000 of sundries. The profit in that study depends on selling after six months of storage, at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags. The brochure's own words are that keeping the maize six months lets you sell it dearer when the time comes. Storing well is therefore part of the budget, not separate from it: the brochure says a maize kept on treated pallets in an airy store holds six months without weevil attack, which is what lets you sell dearer when the time comes. Use this as a template, not as a price list: write your own quantities in the same rows, put today's prices beside them, and see whether your own hectare still leaves a profit. Where: all. Who to see: SIM for the cereal prices broadcast on the radio before you decide when to sell. ICAT to build your own budget with current prices. Limits: Never give a current price from this catalogue entry: its figures are from 2005. When: the whole cycle, from land rent to sale.

Fertilising maize. Base: NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg/ha (4 bags), placed in a pocket 5-10 cm from the plant 10-15 days after sowing, NOT touching it. Host: maize. Steps: Base: NPK 15-15-15 at 200 kg/ha (4 bags), placed in a pocket 5-10 cm from the plant 10-15 days after sowing, NOT touching it. Regional complement: Maritime +30 kg potassic; Kara and Savanes +30 kg phosphate; Plateaux and Centrale NPK only. Top-dress urea 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation (30-45 days after sowing). Who to see: ICAT for a soil-specific adjustment (over-dosing wastes money and can cut yield). When: at/after sowing. Where: all (dose varies by region).

Sowing maize. Use 20-25 kg/ha of treated improved seed. Host: maize. Steps: Use 20-25 kg/ha of treated improved seed. Sow in rows 80 cm apart; in-row pockets 35 cm for varieties under 90 days, 40 cm for 90-100 days, 50 cm for over 100 days; 2-3 seeds per pocket at 3-5 cm deep. First weeding 10-15 days after sowing; thin to 2 plants where 3 emerged. Do not sow on a first isolated shower (false start); wait for reliable rains. Who to see: ICAT for an improved variety suited to your region and season. When: sow when rains are established: Apr-May in Maritime/Plateaux, Jun-Jul in Centrale/Kara/Savanes. Where: all; timing differs by region.

Storing maize grain. Dry the grain hard (about 13-14% moisture, snaps rather than dents) before storing. Host: maize. Steps: Dry the grain hard (about 13-14% moisture, snaps rather than dents) before storing. Clean the store and remove all last-season residues (where the larger grain borer carries over). Store in sound, sealed bags/bins; protect with an approved grain protectant or dried neem-leaf powder mixed through the grain. Where: all. Who to see: ICAT for the currently approved storage insecticide if infestation persists. When: post-harvest.

Maize varieties togo. Buy seed only from approved sellers. Host: maize. Steps: Buy seed only from approved sellers; the ITRA and ICAT maize brochure warns against buying improved seed anywhere else, and against sowing grain taken from your own granary because it germinates badly. Choose the variety on its cycle and on its yield: those are the two things the brochure tells you to weigh. The nine improved varieties released in Togo, as listed by ITRA and ICAT in 2008, with cycle, potential yield and average yield: TZEE W Pop STR QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 t/ha potential, 1.5 to 2 t/ha on average, white grain, tolerant to striga and high in quality protein. EV99 QPM, 75 to 85 days, 3 t/ha potential, 1.5 to 2 t/ha on average, white grain, high in quality protein. Pool 18 QPM SR, 90 to 95 days, 4 t/ha potential, 2 to 3 t/ha on average, yellow grain, high in quality protein. Amen, 90 to 95 days, 4 t/ha potential, 2 to 3 t/ha on average, white grain, tolerant to drought. AB11, 90 to 100 days, 4 t/ha potential, 2 to 3 t/ha on average, white grain, tolerant to streak. Ikenne 9449 SR, 90 to 100 days, 5 t/ha potential, 2 to 3.5 t/ha on average, white grain, very steady yield. Obatanpa, 100 to 110 days, 6 t/ha potential, 3.5 to 4 t/ha on average, white grain, high in quality protein. ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, 105 to 115 days, 7 t/ha potential, 3 to 4 t/ha on average, white grain, tolerant to striga. Sotubaka, 105 to 115 days, 7 t/ha potential, 3 to 4 t/ha on average, yellow grain, high yield. The potential yield, says the brochure, is the yield obtained when growing conditions are good: rain, fertilisation, pest attack, upkeep of the field. The average column stands beside it in the same table. Most of these improved varieties are tolerant to maize streak virus, so choosing one of them is itself the control against streak. If striga grows in your field, take TZEE W Pop STR QPM or ACR97 TZL Comp 1 W, the two the brochure marks as striga tolerant. If your season is short of rain, take Amen, the one marked drought tolerant. When: choose before sowing. Where: all. Who to see: ICAT or ITRA for which variety suits your region this season, and for the list of approved seed sellers near you.

market-selling. Steps: Store well-dried grain and, if you can, hold part of it past the harvest glut to sell in the lean season when prices rise. Learn your area's weekly market days (e.g. Broukou in Kara is Friday) and follow the SIM cereal prices on the radio before selling. Sell as a group/cooperative to reach bigger buyers and cut per-bag transport cost. For cereals, compare local price plus transport against a Lome/urban market before carrying grain. Where: all. Who to see: a cooperative or ICAT to reach larger buyers; ANSAT for grain. When: sell in the lean season (about June-August). Limits: never quote a live price.

Growing chili pepper. Do NOT grow after tomato, eggplant or gboma (shared Solanaceae pests/diseases). Host: chili pepper. Poultry commercial housing. The housing described here is the commercial model of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for local hens. Host: chickens. Steps: The housing described here is the commercial model of the 2020 ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference for local hens. It is not the improved traditional henhouse of the family compound, which is smaller and built in banco: check which one you are building before you take any of these dimensions. That reference asks for a henhouse of at least five compartments, well aired and roomy: one compartment with a shared yard for the breeders; one for brooding, where the eggs collected and given back to the hens are hatched; a chick room; and two fattening compartments for the growers, with a yard. The chick room, the poussiniere, is the compartment meant for keeping the chicks warm, and it has fewer openings than the breeder and grower compartments so the warmth stays in. Plan two more things beside the henhouse: a grassy run for the birds, and a store. Size each compartment on its density: 8 to 10 birds per square metre for the breeders, 50 per square metre for the chicks, and 12 to 15 per square metre for the growers. The worked layout in that reference is a breeder compartment of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 140 birds at 10 per square metre; and two grower compartments for the 3 to 6 month birds, one of 7 m by 4 m, so 28 square metres for 420 birds, and one of 4 m by 3.5 m, so 14 square metres for 210 birds, both at 15 per square metre. Build the low wall 0.5 to 1 m high, three bricks at most. For the chick room, raise the whole wall but leave openings for air. And keep tarpaulins to close against rain and wind. Dig a manure pit at least 1.5 m wide, 2 m long and 1 m deep, and roof it with an apatam. It is there for two reasons the reference gives: to turn the droppings into something your fields can use, and to limit the spread of disease. Drinkers go by age, counted per hundred birds: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, and four of 10 litres for the adult layers. Feeders go by age too. For chicks, 50 cm long by 50 wide and 5 deep, one for 50 birds. For chickens, 125 cm by 10 by 12, one for 20 birds. For adults, 150 cm by 12 by 16, one for 25 birds. You can buy feeders and drinkers in the shops, but a local craftsman can make the feeders for you, which is often cheaper. Fit out the rest as well: nest boxes, egg trays for keeping the eggs to be hatched, and for the keeper a cool box, work clothes, a wheelbarrow, spades, rakes and boots. The brooder is for the chicks' first three weeks. A brooder of 0.6 cubic metres, that is 2 m long by 1 m wide by 30 cm high, holds 60 chicks. After that the chicks move into the chick room to finish growing. What the brooder buys you, in the reference's own list: it saves the fuel of heating the chicks, it handles small hatchings in series, it keeps predators off, and it lets you watch feeding and health closely. A gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens. The reference notes that at that size you should hatch for other keepers as well, otherwise the machine does not pay for itself. When: build before the birds arrive. Who to see: The reference does not say which way the building should face, nor whether red wood shavings can be used as litter: do not answer those from memory. a local craftsman for the feeders. ICAT for the plans and for the technico-economic reference itself. Where: all.

Poultry local hens business. The figures below all come from one study: the technico-economic reference for commercial local hen farming published in 2020 by ICAT and the PASA project. Host: chickens. Steps: The figures below all come from one study: the technico-economic reference for commercial local hen farming published in 2020 by ICAT and the PASA project. They are 2020 evaluations and annual projections for one unit, not today's prices, and they must be presented that way. Start with a breeding nucleus of 60 hens and 6 cocks; the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference calls that the minimum for a commercial unit to hold, and it sets the sex ratio at one cock for ten hens. Choose breeders from a well-followed farm or a research centre, vigorous and agile, the cocks with a well developed bright red comb; at six months a hen weighs about 1.3 kg and a cock about 1.5 kg, and both hens and cocks are culled at 24 months. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference plans on six production cycles a year, about ten eggs laid per hen per laying, about six layings a year, a natural hatching rate near 70 percent and a mortality rate near 10 percent. Collect the eggs every day and keep them somewhere cool, airy and dry; discard eggs that are too small, too dirty, deformed, too big, cracked or with no pointed end; keep them seven to ten days at most and set them pointed end down. A brooding hen sits on twelve to fourteen eggs; with an electric, gas or solar incubator the incubation lasts twenty-one days, after which the chicks come out of the shells. One gas incubator of 300 eggs suits a flock of 60 breeding hens, and the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference notes that the owner should hatch for other farmers as well to make that equipment pay. For start-up, the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference evaluates the investment at 3,850,124 FCFA in 2020 prices: the houses, a store, a manure pit, the gas incubator, a brooder, a well, feeders, drinkers, nests, and the 60 hens and 6 cocks themselves. For the first year of running, the same 2020 reference evaluates the working capital at 2,150,491 FCFA in 2020 prices; feed is most of it, with breeder, chick and grower rations, plus Newcastle and fowl pox vaccines, vitamins, dewormer, disinfectant and litter. Count three products, not one: birds, eggs and droppings. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference projects a first year selling 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA, 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA and 50 kg of droppings at 1,000 FCFA, so 3,487,181 FCFA in all, again in 2020 prices. Expect a small first year and a real second one: the annual projection of the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference gives a net result of 131,785 FCFA in year one and 2,790,400 FCFA in year two, and it explains the jump by the larger number of birds sold and by the fall in financial charges. Look for your buyers before the batch starts, not after; keep a client register, sign contracts with them where you can, and honour what the contract says. Set your price from your own figures: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head, compare that price with the market price, and readjust if the market asks for it. Make the farm known through radio announcements, fairs, leaflets on the quality of your birds, word of mouth and a signboard. Keep the registers: visits, movements (sales, hatchings, deaths), a prophylactic calendar for vaccinations and treatments, health follow-up, and money in and out. Where: all. Limits: Never give a current price: the figures above are 2020 evaluations, and a buyer's price today must be checked on the market. When: any. Who to see: the veterinary service for the vaccination programme. ICAT for the 2020 technico-economic reference itself and for help building a business plan.

Poultry local hens husbandry. Two Togolese references describe local hen keeping and they do not describe the same farm. Host: chickens. Steps: Two Togolese references describe local hen keeping and they do not describe the same farm. The ESFT and Elevages Sans Frontieres compendium of 2017 describes the improved traditional henhouse of a village family; the ICAT and PASA technico-economic reference of 2020 describes a commercial unit. Their figures differ for that reason, and both are right for what they describe. For the village henhouse, the 2017 compendium works on an average density of 5 to 6 hens per square metre; the 2020 commercial reference works on 8 to 10 breeding birds per square metre and 12 to 15 for the growers. Say which one you are talking about before giving a density. Keep a fenced run around the henhouse so the birds do not wander. A henhouse opening onto a run carries less risk of infection than a closed one, and lets you watch the birds better than if they roam free. Sweep the inside of the henhouse two or three times a week and throw the droppings into a manure pit well away from it. Those droppings then fertilise your fields. Clean around the henhouse too: a tuft of grass shelters the predators and animals that bring disease, snakes, rats, shrews, ants and lizards. Wash the feeders and drinkers every day. After changing the litter, and whenever there are lice, ticks or fleas, spray disinfectant inside the shelter. Quarantine every new bird for two weeks, whether you bought it at a poultry market or were given it, so you do not bring a disease into the flock. To cut the spread of disease: do not visit other farms, do not throw carcasses out in the open, and do not let your hens wander. When a bird falls ill, isolate it or take it out to treat it, and take dead birds out as fast as you can and bury them far from the henhouse. Call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary every time you see disease in the flock, and ask about the prophylaxis suited to a henhouse. A rule worth knowing before you buy anything: no treatment cures a viral disease. Medicines treat parasitic and bacterial diseases. For a virus, prevention and vaccination are all you have. After a bird has been treated, its meat and its eggs can hold drug residues, so do not eat them for a few days. Feed between 5 and 90 grams a bird, depending on age and size. Hens should have a run where they can eat grass; if they cannot, bring them a little greenery every day. Build the ration from what is around you: rain, tap or spring water; energy from maize, millet or sorghum grain, whole or cracked, tchouck bran and tubers; protein from roasted soya, cowpea, fish, insects and animal products; minerals from eggshells and fish bones; and vitamins from herbs, fruit and plant debris. Feed the chicks apart from the adults so they do not have to compete: ground sorghum, ground millet or maize grain, tchouck bran, bone meal or a mix of salt and fish meal, maggots and termites. Clean water matters most of all for them, because chicks die easily of dehydration. Keep the mother hen with the chicks for the first weeks; she protects them and she knows how to adjust the warmth from the sound of their cries. A healthy newly hatched chick has a well developed body, bright dry thick coloured down, a soft belly with a clean dry navel, and strong legs with straight separated claws. Keep one cock for about ten hens, and choose that cock carefully, because he decides whether the chicks are well grown and healthy. Managing the flock also means selling the cockerels born on the farm and culling the poor layers. On when to cull the breeding cocks the two references differ: the 2017 village compendium says after three years of keeping, the 2020 commercial reference says at 24 months for hens and cocks alike. Give the figure with the reference it comes from. Know the signs of a sick bird, because they are what you will notice first. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference lists eight: the bird is sad, drowsy and downcast; its wings droop and its feathers stand up; it keeps away from the flock; it does not eat; it is thin; it has a discharge from the nose and the mouth; it moves with difficulty; and it has diarrhoea. Hygiene comes down to one idea in that reference: keep the animals away from the germs, or keep the germs away from the animals. Disease comes in through contact with sick animals, with soiled droppings and secretions, or through contaminated material: farm equipment, a vehicle, clothes and shoes. The first principle is separation: do not mix your animals with those of other farms, quarantine every newly bought bird, and isolate the ones that are ill. The second is cleaning, and the reference says a good cleaning of the building already removes a good part of the germs. The third is disinfection, which after a methodical cleaning inactivates the microbes still there. For disinfecting, the reference names caustic soda at 1 percent, a formol solution at 10 percent, bleach at 2 to 3 percent, cresyl in emulsion at 5 percent, and quicklime at 10 percent. It adds one instruction you must not skip: goggles, protective gloves and a gas mask are compulsory. When disease shows up in the flock, the reference gives six things to do: isolate the sick birds; forbid any trading in your henhouse; forbid any visit without a precise purpose; inform the veterinary service of your locality quickly; never eat the carcasses; and burn or bury the dead animals in the presence of the veterinary service. Who to see: The animal health worker or village livestock auxiliary for any illness and for the vaccination programme. Neither reference gives the orientation of the building, whether red wood shavings may be used as litter, the names of the vitamins a hen needs, nor whether a hen lays without a cock: do not answer those from memory. ICAT for the improved henhouse and for the technico-economic reference. Where: all. When: any.

Poultry local hens ration. Build the feed from what is around you. Host: chickens. Steps: Build the feed from what is around you. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference names the local raw materials: cereals, that is maize, sorghum, millet and fonio; legumes, groundnut and soya, and their by-products, groundnut, cotton and soya cakes and millet beer draff; kitchen leftovers; then fish meal, bone powder, oyster shells, insects, termites and caterpillars; then salt for the minerals; then the vitamins. Feed changes with age, and the reference gives a simplified formula for 100 kg of feed for local hens. From 1 to 8 weeks: 62 kg of cereals, 20 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 5 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix. From 9 to 12 weeks: 62 kg of cereals, 15 kg of cake, 5 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, for 100 kg of feed. From 12 weeks on: 60 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 17 kg of bran and 3 kg of mineral mix, for 100 kg of feed. For a hen in lay: 57.5 kg of cereals, 10 kg of cake, 10 kg of fish meal, 15 kg of bran and 7.5 kg of mineral mix, for 100 kg of feed. The laying hen is the one that takes the most mineral of all the age bands. Whatever the age, the reference adds the same free extras on top of the formula: greenery, termites and maggots, with caterpillars as well for the youngest birds. Make the mineral mix yourself. For 10 kg the reference gives 4 kg of oyster or snail shell, 3.5 kg of crushed calcined bone, 2 kg of crushed charcoal and 0.5 kg of kitchen salt. How much to serve, by period: from 1 to 60 days a bird eats about 1.5 kg in all, at 10 to 25 grams a day. From 61 days to sale at six months, about 5 kg in all, at 25 to 35 grams a day. A hen in lay takes 80 grams a day. The 2017 ESFT village compendium gives the same idea in one range: serve between 5 and 90 grams a bird depending on age and size. It adds that hens should have a run where they can eat grass, and that if they cannot, you must bring them a little greenery every day. Water is a rule of its own. Give it freely, available at all times; the drinkers must never be empty. It has to be clean, served in the shade, and renewed at least twice a day. Feed the chicks apart, so they do not compete with the adults, and never let them run short of clean water: the 2017 compendium says chicks die easily of dehydration. When: any. Where: all. Who to see: the animal health worker if birds go off feed, which is one of the signs of a sick bird. ICAT for the ration scaled to your own flock and for where to buy cakes and fish meal.

Sowing sorghum. Sow on ridges after a heavy rain, 3-5 grains per pocket at 3-5 cm. Host: sorghum. Steps: Sow on ridges after a heavy rain, 3-5 grains per pocket at 3-5 cm; 6-8 kg/ha of treated seed. Thin to 2-3 plants/pocket at 2-3 weeks; first weeding without breaking the ridges. NPK 150-200 kg/ha after weeding, then urea 50-100 kg/ha; earth up against lodging. Guard ripening panicles from birds; manage Striga (pull before flowering). When: early-mid June in Savanes, mid-June to early July in Kara/Centrale. Where: mainly the north. Who to see: ICAT to match a variety's cycle to your prefecture's rains.

Growing soybean. Sow certified seed treated against damping-off. Host: soybean. Steps: Sow certified seed treated against damping-off; weed at 2 weeks and again 3 weeks later. Do not grow soy on the same plot more than two years running. At harvest cut stems at ground level (leave the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil). Yam mounds. Choose deep, rested, stone-free soil (fallow >=5 years, or a Mucuna fallow if land is short). Host: yam. Steps: Choose deep, rested, stone-free soil (fallow >=5 years, or a Mucuna fallow if land is short). Build mounds 40-80 cm high: ~5,000/ha at 1.4x1.4 m on rich soil, 6,500/ha at 1x1.5 m; fewer on poor soil. Use healthy seed setts; let cut faces heal in shade and dust with wood ash before planting. Stake the vines and do the first weeding on time. Who to see: ICAT/ITRA for a foufou or good-storage variety (e.g. TDr 747, Florido). When: plant early varieties Nov-March. Where: all; grow where >=5 months of rain.

Cassava bacterial blight. The bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Host: cassava. Signs: Angular, water-soaked spots on the leaves, wilting of young leaves then shoot die-back, sometimes gum exuding on stems. Who to see: ICAT to confirm the diagnosis. ITRA/registered producer for clean resistant cuttings. Spread: Moving diseased stems/cuttings, contaminated tools, and rain splash. Prevention: Clean cuttings. Tool hygiene. Resistant varieties. Rotation. Look-alike: Cassava mosaic disease: "Cassava mosaic (yellow mottling + leaf deformation, no wilting). Cassava brown streak disease: "Cassava mosaic (leaf deformation) and bacterial blight (angular wilting spots). Where and when: all cassava zones. rainy season (rain-splash spread). What to do: Use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy affected plants; disinfect tools between plants. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. Cause: The bacterium Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. Losses: Yield loss 8-60% plus lost planting material.

cassava-mosaic. Host: cassava. Signs: plants stunted in severe cases. Yellow or pale mottling of the leaves together with leaf distortion (twisted, puckered, shrunken leaves). The leaf DEFORMATION is the key tell. Cause: The commonest, most damaging cassava disease in Togo. African cassava mosaic virus (a begomovirus). Losses: losses 15-95%. Where and when: any (worse at whitefly peaks). all cassava zones, especially Maritime and Plateaux. Look-alike: Cassava bacterial blight: "Cassava bacterial blight (angular water-soaked spots + wilting and shoot die-back, NOT deformation). Cassava brown streak disease: "Cassava mosaic (leaf deformation) and bacterial blight (angular wilting spots). Prevention: Clean planting material from healthy plants only. Resistant/tolerant varieties (disease incidence in a susceptible variety is lower when it is mixed with resistant varieties than when grown alone). Uniform dense stand (a uniform dense stand rather than irregular widely spaced plants helps reduce disease incidence). Who to see: If it is angular spots with wilting instead of deformation, ICAT to confirm; ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings. Spread: whiteflies carrying it plant to plant (so it appears in patches). Two ways: planting cuttings taken from already-infected stems (main way, field to field). What to do: No spray cures an infected plant. Uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. Next planting, take cuttings ONLY from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer; keep a uniform, well-fed stand.

Cattle tick borne. Parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks: Anaplasma marginale for gall sickness, Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis for redwater. Host: cattle. Signs: Look at the urine: red to almost black is redwater (babesiosis). yellow-brown but never red is gall sickness (anaplasmosis). Fever, pale or white gums and eyelids, a dull animal that lags behind the herd, eats less and drops its milk, with many ticks in the ears, under the tail and between the legs. What to do: Call the veterinary service the same day - only they can say which of the two it is and give the right drug and its dose (guessing a drug or a low dose loses the animal and breeds resistant parasites). Tell the vet the colour of the urine (red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red to gall sickness, and the two are not treated the same). Keep the sick animal in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make it walk (it is short of red blood cells, so any effort can bring it down). Hand-pick the ticks you can see, on the whole herd and not only on the sick animal (the ticks left on the others carry the parasite to them next). Never use the same needle on two animals (gall sickness travels on a needle carrying infected blood). Look-alike: Cattle trypanosomiasis: "Trypanosomiasis (nagana): also pale gums and a thin animal, but in tsetse bush, wasting slowly, with few ticks and no red urine. A worm burden or a mineral shortage also makes a thin animal, but without the fever. Prevention: Hand-pick ticks weekly. A clean needle for each animal. Watch newly bought or moved animals closely. Ask the vet before starting any acaricide programme. Who to see: Every drug and every dose comes from them. Veterinary service, the same day. Spread: It is not caught by contact. Only through the bite of an infected tick - Amblyomma variegatum and the blue tick Rhipicephalus (Boophilus) microplus are the common ones here. Gall sickness also passes on a dirty needle used from one animal to the next. Where and when: worst in and just after the rains, when ticks are most numerous. all cattle-keeping areas. ticks collected from cattle across districts of Togo and Benin. Cause: Parasites of the red blood cells carried by ticks: Anaplasma marginale for gall sickness, Babesia bigemina or Babesia bovis for redwater. Both destroy red cells, which is why the gums go pale.

Cattle trypanosomiasis. A trypanosome parasite transmitted by the tsetse fly (the disease herders call nagana). Host: cattle. Signs: Progressive weight loss, weakness, a rough coat, and pale (anaemic) gums/mucous membranes, in animals grazing where biting tsetse flies live. Spread: Tsetse fly bites. Look-alike: Worm burden / mineral deficiency (also cause thinness - vet diagnosis distinguishes). Cattle tick borne: "Trypanosomiasis (nagana): also pale gums and a thin animal, but in tsetse bush, wasting slowly, with few ticks and no red urine. A worm burden or a mineral shortage also makes a thin animal, but without the fever. Cause: A trypanosome parasite transmitted by the tsetse fly (the disease herders call nagana). Where and when: any. tsetse-fly areas (riverine bush). What to do: Report it to the veterinary service for diagnosis and the right trypanocide - do NOT guess a drug or dose. Reduce fly exposure: avoid grazing tsetse-infested riverine bush in the biting hours; consider fly control. Keep animals well fed and watered so they can withstand and recover. Who to see: Veterinary service (diagnosis and treatment must be professional). Prevention: Reduce tsetse exposure. Fly control. Good nutrition.

Cowpea field pests. Flower thrips, pod borers (e.g. Maruca) and aphids - waves of insects through flowering. Host: cowpea. Signs: Damaged, dropped flowers and bored pods. poor pod set. aphids clustering on shoots. Prevention: Resistant variety. Three well-timed sprays. Early weeding. Who to see: ICAT for the CURRENT approved product and exact dose before spraying. Cause: Flower thrips, pod borers (e.g. Maruca) and aphids - waves of insects through flowering. What to do: Sow a resistant improved 55-75 day variety when rains are strong (mid-June to early July). Spray THREE times around flowering: first at 30-35 days when flower buds appear, second 10 days later, third 10 days after that, with an approved product at the labelled rate. Weed early (first weeding ~2 weeks after sowing). Look-alike: Storage weevils (that is post-harvest, use ash/oil/approved insecticide). Where and when: flowering to podding. all cowpea zones. Spread: Insects re-invade in waves, so a single spray leaves gaps.

Groundnut leaf spot. Cercospora leaf-spot fungi. Host: groundnut. Signs: Dark, roundish spots on the leaves (early/late leaf spot), leaves yellow and drop EARLY. Prevention: Rotation. Tolerant variety. Sanitation. Who to see: ICAT about resistant varieties and whether a fungicide is justified. Look-alike: Groundnut rosette: "Rosette (mottling + stunting, viral). Spread: Carries over in crop residues. spreads in humid conditions. Where and when: groundnut zones. mid-late season. Cause: Cercospora leaf-spot fungi. Early defoliation is what cuts yield (fewer leaves to fill pods). What to do: Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year - rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear/bury old groundnut trash. Harvest on time (a weakened crop drops its pods).

What to do: Do not grow groundnut on the same land year after year - rotate with cereals. Use a tolerant variety and clear/bury old groundnut trash. Harvest on time (a weakened crop drops its pods). Who to see: ICAT about resistant varieties and whether a fungicide is justified. Cause: Cercospora leaf-spot fungi. Early defoliation is what cuts yield (fewer leaves to fill pods). Prevention: Rotation. Tolerant variety. Sanitation. Look-alike: Groundnut rosette: "Rosette (mottling + stunting, viral). Spread: spreads in humid conditions. Carries over in crop residues. Where and when: groundnut zones. mid-late season.

Groundnut rosette. Groundnut rosette virus complex, transmitted by aphids. Host: groundnut. Signs: Stunting with yellow or green mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves. Leucaena and mimosine. Mimosine, the natural toxin in leucaena, building up when it is fed as too large a share of the ration. Signs: Loss of appetite (the early sign), drooling, and over time hair/wool loss and thyroid trouble, in animals fed too much leucaena. Where and when: any. all. Spread: Not infectious (a feeding/toxicity problem). Cause: Mimosine, the natural toxin in leucaena, building up when it is fed as too large a share of the ration. Prevention: Limit leucaena share. Gradual introduction. Mixed ration + minerals. Look-alike: Bloat in ruminants: "Frothy bloat from a sudden lush-legume switch (swollen left flank - emergency). Who to see: Veterinary service if appetite does not recover, or you see drooling, a swollen throat, or bloat. What to do: Cut leucaena back to a supplement - roughly a quarter to a third of the ration at most, never the main feed. Mix it with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days; ensure constant clean water and a mineral/salt source.

Nitrogen leaching in maize. Nitrogen washed down below the young roots by heavy rain. Host: maize. Signs: Even yellowing/paling of the LOWER leaves soon after heavy rain, from the bottom up, with NO spots or streaks. Worse where water sits (waterlogging). Prevention: Good drainage. Split nitrogen application (nitrogen uptake is slow in the first month after planting and reaches its maximum at ear formation and tasselling). Do not over-apply then lose it to rain. Look-alike: Maize streak virus, Maize stalk borer: "Maize streak virus (pale streaks along veins); stalk borer (dead-heart). Soil depletion north: "Nitrogen washed out by heavy rain: the same yellowing, but it appears suddenly after a downpour on a crop that was green, instead of coming back worse every year. A disease makes spots with edges, not a uniform pale colour. Spread: Not infectious. Cause: waterlogged soil also starves roots of air. Nitrogen washed down below the young roots by heavy rain. Not a disease. What to do: Open a shallow drainage channel so water runs off the plot instead of standing. Once the soil drains, side-dress urea in a pocket 5-10 cm from each stem, about 100 kg/ha at panicle initiation, kept off the plant so it does not burn. Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. Who to see: ICAT if streaks or dead-hearts appear (that is disease/pest, not nitrogen). Where and when: all; tell region for exact fertiliser complement. after heavy rain.

Maize stalk borer. Stem borers: Busseola fusca (pink) or Chilo partellus (spotted). Host: maize. Signs: caterpillars tunnel into the stem, with frass. Window-pane holes on the whorl leaves and a 'dead-heart' (dead central shoot) while outer leaves look alive. Look-alike: Nitrogen leaching in maize: "Maize streak virus (pale streaks along veins); stalk borer (dead-heart). Maize streak virus: "Maize streak (leaf streaks); nutrient problems (no tunnels/dead-heart). Spread: Caterpillars feed in the funnel then bore into the stem. carry over in old stalks. Who to see: ICAT quickly if a large block is attacked at once (for approved control). Cause: Stem borers: Busseola fusca (pink) or Chilo partellus (spotted). Where and when: all maize zones. young crop, before flowering. What to do: While plants are young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; 1 kg treats ~1,500-2,000 plants; repeat every 8-10 days. Never apply neem powder alone (the oil scorches the plant) - always mix with an inert carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks; rotate/intercrop with a legume (cowpea, soybean). Prevention: Destroy crop-residue overwintering sites. Legume rotation/intercrop. Habitat management.

Maize streak virus. Maize streak virus (MSV). Host: maize. Signs: Chlorotic spots that run into broken pale/white streaks ALONG THE VEINS; plants stunted. Where and when: worst on second-season sowings in the south and late sowings in the north. all maize zones. growing season. Prevention: MSV-tolerant varieties. Avoid late sowing. Next season plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety (ask ICAT). Avoid late sowing, which raises infection. Cause: Maize streak virus (MSV). Damping-off of pepper seedlings. Nursery soil fungi (damping-off), thriving in too-wet beds, especially moisture held overnight. Host: chili pepper. Signs: Seedlings topple over and collapse right at the soil line in the nursery. Where and when: nursery stage. all. Cause: Nursery soil fungi (damping-off), thriving in too-wet beds, especially moisture held overnight. What to do: Keep the bed evenly moist but never soggy, and do NOT water late in the evening. Sow treated seed (fungicide-insecticide coat) and do not sow too thickly. Remove collapsed seedlings; improve drainage and airflow. Prevention: Watering discipline (never late evening). Thin sowing. Treated seed. Drainage. Look-alike: Transplant shock (older plants, not nursery collapse). Who to see: ICAT for an approved nursery drench and rate if it keeps spreading. Spread: Wet, airless, crowded beds.

African swine fever. African swine fever (ASF) virus. Host: pigs. Signs: High fever, red/purple blotches on the ears, belly and thighs, bloody diarrhoea, and rapid death (often 7-9 of every 10 sick pigs). Look-alike: Classical swine fever, erysipelas (differential - lab needed). What to do: NO treatment and NO vaccine. NOTIFIABLE. Confine your pigs and STOP all pig movement on/off the place; let no outside visitor near the pen. Disinfect the pen, install a footbath at the entrance, and boil any food scraps before feeding. Dispose of dead pigs safely (bury/burn); never sell or eat a sick animal. Losses: rapid death (often 7-9 of every 10 sick pigs). Who to see: Notify the veterinary service immediately (notifiable; they guide containment). Where and when: all. any. Cause: African swine fever (ASF) virus. Spread: and swill (food scraps). Contact; on boots, clothes, vehicles. Prevention: Biosecurity (confinement, footbath, visitor control). Boil swill. No movement of sick pigs.

poultry-newcastle. Host: chickens. Signs: noisy laboured breathing with the neck stretched or twisted. greenish watery droppings. eye/nostril discharge. a sharp fall in laying. Several birds dying SUDDENLY at once (often mistaken for poisoning). What to do: No medicine cures an infected bird. Bloat in ruminants. Bloat - gas/froth trapped in the rumen, usually after a sudden change to lush wet pasture or too many legumes, or a blockage. EMERGENCY. Signs: The LEFT flank swells up tight like a drum, the animal goes off feed, breathes hard, may collapse and die within an hour or two. Prevention: Introduce lush green feed and legumes gradually. Always keep roughage in the diet. Never turn hungry animals onto rich wet pasture. Look-alike: Choke (foreign body) - also sudden, vet distinguishes. Leucaena and mimosine: "Frothy bloat from a sudden lush-legume switch (swollen left flank - emergency). Cause: Bloat - gas/froth trapped in the rumen, usually after a sudden change to lush wet pasture or too many legumes, or a blockage. EMERGENCY. Where and when: start of rains / lush pasture. all. Who to see: Veterinary service immediately (emergency). Spread: Not infectious. What to do: Get the animal up and MOVING, keeping its head raised (helps it belch the gas). Drench a little vegetable or mineral oil by mouth to break the froth so gas can escape. Call the veterinary service immediately - a severe case needs their intervention without delay.

Tell me everything you know about Soil depletion north, the complete sheet.

Soil depletion north. A nitrogen shortage on a soil whose organic matter has been run down by cropping without giving anything back - residues carried off or burnt, no fallow, no manure. Host: maize. Signs: A uniform pale yellowing of the OLDER, lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener, plants short and thin, and a yield that falls a little more every year on the same plot. Limits: Do not take the merchant's word. Losses: 2016, 'Understanding variability in crop response to fertilizer and amendments in sub-Saharan Africa', Agriculture, Ecosystems & Environment, PMC4913530, read 12/09/2026: 'In upto 25% of fields, maize is non-responsive to fertilizer and amendments.' The figure is for sub-Saharan Africa across sentinel sites, NOT a Togolese measurement, and must be given as such. Prevention: Return the residues instead of burning them. Manure or compost every year. A legume in the rotation. A soil check before a big purchase. Where and when: Kara and Savanes (northern Togo), on old land cropped year after year. shows at the start of the wet season. Cause: A nitrogen shortage on a soil whose organic matter has been run down by cropping without giving anything back - residues carried off or burnt, no fallow, no manure. The old leaves go first because the plant moves its nitrogen up to the young ones. What to do: Read the leaves before buying anything: yellowing that starts on the OLD lower leaves and climbs is hunger for nitrogen, not a disease (no fungicide can green a hungry plant). Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound and a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word - on a run-down soil the mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back (in trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments). Bring the organic matter back first - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt (mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it). Put a legume in the rotation - cowpea, groundnut or soybean - and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing root nodules stay in the soil. Ask ICAT for a soil check before any large purchase; the dose that fits your plot comes from them, not from the seller. Spread: Not a disease and not catching: it is the state of the plot, and it worsens each season the residues leave the field. Look-alike: Nitrogen leaching in maize: "Nitrogen washed out by heavy rain: the same yellowing, but it appears suddenly after a downpour on a crop that was green, instead of coming back worse every year. A disease makes spots with edges, not a uniform pale colour. Who to see: ICAT for a soil analysis and the dose for your plot.

Tomato late blight. The oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Host: tomato. Signs: Dark, water-soaked lesions on leaves and stems, a whitish mould on the underside in humidity, rapid collapse of foliage, and dark rot on fruit. Spread: Spores in wet, humid, crowded canopies; splashing water. Where and when: cool, humid, wet weather. market-garden areas. Cause: The oomycete Phytophthora infestans. Spreads fast in cool wet weather. Look-alike: Early blight (target-like concentric rings on older leaves). Who to see: ICAT for the approved fungicide and rate. What to do: Remove and destroy affected plants/leaves quickly. Space and stake plants for airflow; avoid overhead watering late in the day. Use a resistant variety and, if needed, an approved fungicide at the labelled rate. Prevention: Resistant variety. Spacing/airflow. Rotation away from Solanaceae.

What does the extension fiche say about Tomato sucking pests? Everything, please.

Tomato sucking pests. Two different sap-sucking insects: whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) and aphids (Aphis gossypii, Myzus persicae). Host: tomato. Signs: Shake the plant and watch: a cloud of tiny white insects flying up and settling straight back down means whiteflies. insects that stay put in packed colonies on the shoot tips and leaf undersides, often with ants walking on the plant, means aphids. Tiny insects on the underside of the leaves, leaves turning yellow, a sticky film and black sooty mould on the leaves underneath. Prevention: Look under the leaves every week. Keep the plot and its edges weed-free. Yellow sticky traps for whitefly. Protect the natural enemies. Look-alike: Tomato yellow leaf curl: "Tomato yellow leaf curl virus, which the whitefly carries: there the young leaves stay curled with yellow edges even after the insects are gone. Spider mites make a fine webbing and are not insects you can see fly up. What to do: Shake the plant and look before you treat: the two pests are not held back by the same thing, and a wrong name wastes the spray and the money. Turn the leaves over: both sit underneath, and that is where you count them on a few plants before deciding to treat at all. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves, and keep the plot and its edges free of the weeds that host them between crops. Against whiteflies, yellow sticky traps catch the adults; against aphids, a strong jet of water and the natural enemies - ladybirds, lacewings - often hold them on their own. If the attack is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate - do not guess a product or a dose. Cause: Two different sap-sucking insects: whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) and aphids (Aphis gossypii, Myzus persicae). Both take sap and both leave honeydew, but they are not the same insect and they do not carry the same viruses. Where and when: hottest and driest spells are the worst. all market-garden areas. Who to see: ICAT for the approved product and its rate. Spread: the aphid carries other viruses, and most of its damage is the sap it takes and the sooty mould that grows on its honeydew. Both fly in from neighbouring plots and from weeds. The whitefly is the one that carries tomato yellow leaf curl virus.
